generated_text: Rather annoying when a kid’s got a cough, isn’t it? I was just trying to put Josh to bed, and he’s been hacking away all evening. Poor little sod. I've been over this with Clara, and she swore up and down the cough came as soon as he started at that new crèche. I'm beginning to wonder if it was the right move to put him in full-time care with a work deadline coming up.      Aw, poor thing. If you're concerned, maybe you should call one of the pediatricians. You know the one in Sutton? That bloke came recommended by my cousin. He sorted Mary’s chest infection last year with no hassle. I’d rather do something about it early than wait and see if it gets worse. Speaking of, you haven’t told me if you’re coming on Friday for Mum’s birthday. She’s been raving about it for weeks and would love for you and the boys to come along.      Oh, yes, thanks for reminding me. I’m planning to take the day off. Clara offered to stay with Josh for the evening, and I know Mary can handle Lucy for a bit if necessary. What did you and the rest of the family have planned?      Well, we’re thinking of doing a nice little dinner at the old man’s bistro—up in Small Heath. You remember the one with that balcony view of the canal? We can have a few glasses of wine and catch up while the kids run around in the playground at the back. After that, we’ll head over to your brother’s place for the actual present-giving and some family snaps with the grandparents being their usual dramatic selves!      That all sounds about right. I’m not sure about the man talking the kids around the canal, though — what if they get too rowdy and kick up a stink? Mary’s not handled to the idea of ‘letting go’ very easily. Though I suppose it's better than watching them suffer the whole time.      True, but it’s their night too, don'tcha think? They’ll be fine as long as we keep an eye on them. And speaking of letting go, do you ever think you’ll let Josh start school with the other kids his age? He's getting really clever for his age, and I think he'd thrive.

Rather annoying really, having to sort through all that red tape for a simple trip. Me and ‘im wanted to pop to Amsterdam over Christmas, but now it's all about visas and cover letters and where we're staying for how long. Chuffed to bits I wasn’t!      Aye, I know what ye mean. Same with me and me sister. We were tryin’ to sort a holiday to Barcelona before New Year’s, but this lot changed every week. One week she was in, next it was a whole different form. Bit of a faff when yer gettin’ older and don’t like to run about much!      That's the worst, innit? You want to relax, not chase after forms! So what’d ye end up doin’?      Oh, I just gave up and went to an agency, far as I’m concerned. I paid extra for 'em to handle all the paperwork and in the end it was worth it. We went to Lisbon in the end. Beautiful city.      Oh I do like Lisbon—personally I think it's one of the most chilled cities in the EU. I did a trip there as part of me research—very useful it was, met a few academics. Excellent food too – especiallly at the Miradouro areas.      Yeah, the food was brilliant. We did Silves Tuna—didn’t know fish could taste like that! Our foodie sister found an awesome little place near the castle. Best time, really.      That is a proper treat, I’d say. Made sure I took notes for the next project! Though I did get a bit homesick for a bangers and chips!      Haha—that fails to surprise me not at all. Still, it does give one incentive to do something a bit different every now and again.      Aye, me too. I'm just not too sure I fancy anywhere with a long flight from here. I did a crack to Sicily once—lovely place, but always trying to find the right bus or train to the next location. Wasn't for the fainthearted.      Mm, Sicily was wild. If ye like history and sun, it ticked all the boxes. But the box might have been a bit heavy to carry round. I have to say, me and this travel’s grown on me. It’s strange how different places view the world, innit?      Oh, very much so. You start to see how one's upbringing and environment shape people.

Rather annoyingly, I've run out of shortbread. Again. I was just about to put some on... What's the matter, love?      Not shortbread, we want chocolate! Only chocolate!      Oh, come now! You wouldn't say that if you tasted it! I've just made a fresh batch, and it's got raisins in as well.      What’s raisins? Sounds weird.      Raisins, Liam, are dried grapes. They’re sweet. You might like them when they're in shortbread.      No! We  only  like chocolate! Plain and simple, no surprises!      Okay, fine. I suppose I could melt some chocolate and pour over some biscuits if I had any. But I used the last of the chocolate for brownies last night.      I still have some of that brownie leftover! You made too many!      Yes, Liam, we do have some brownie. Good job, too, or we would be out of treats for the day.      Well, if that’s the best we’ve got, then I might go on a walk and pop to the shop in Comberton. It's only a short one: ten minutes along, and then it's back again. I could pick up some dark chocolate and maybe even something for tea if I’m passing the bakery.      Can I come with you? I’ll behave!      No, we are definitely staying with the monopoly board. We were in the money and being rich and stuff.      But we’ve played about five times this week! And you always win! That’s not fair!      Because I am very good at it! I’m very, very good!      You’re very good at arguing about it after you lose, yes. But I do leave the property cards where any of you can adjust them.      I always get all the best bits as well. You always say, 'Take two to go to jail' or 'pay rent!', and then you win, you do!      Because the dice are gods, love. I don’t know why they always land so well for me, but it’s not that I’m playing better.      Maybe we should make up some new rules. Maybe we can live in one street together and start a chocolate monopoly?      Yes! And the chocolate can be our money!      Now that I can get behind. Chocolate currency sounds like a far kinder and healthier game than real money anyway.      We could play again tomorrow?      Of course. But while we play monopoly, I’ll start those biscuits on their second batch of chocolate.

Rather annoying this, innit? Traffic’s mental again, stuck outside the roundabout. They’ve been piling up for an hour or so. I’m runnin’ late for that corpus meeting, gotta meet this bloke from Liverpool to discuss some phonetic markers—  Lancashire drawl, innit?   Always makes me chuckle a bit.      Aye, well, stuck in traffic’s only gonna make you more stressed. Why don’t you send ‘im a message and tell ‘im to be a bit lenient? Bit of leeway for the Tyne and Wear accent.      Maybe. Though honestly, I don’t really care what people think of my accent. It’s well what it is. You’ve met enough interns to know we spend most of the time correcting the pronunciation of words they ain’t even used before.   Bleedin’ spell-checks try to make me breakfast British into ‘breakfast bricked’!        I know the feeling. I got some project documents once that turned ‘plastic tubing’ into ‘plastic twibing’—personally I think that’s one of the most ridiculous errors I’ve seen. I tell ‘em it still works as long as it ain't got any leaks in it. Logic tends to take a back seat in these meetings.      That’s exactly what I said when som’un was correcting my “innit” use. Like it’s not a proper tag question, innit? They just don’t get it—language is alive, man. It changes, it breathes. Some folks just want to weigh it down and call it proper English.      Yeah, there’s a bit about how people try to dress the language up to sound more professional, but it just ends up sounding awkward and forced. “Whereabouts are you?” instead of “Where are you?”—why do people do that?      Dunno, but personally, I reckon if you know what you’re talkin’ about, you don’t need to sound all posh. We’re not in a bloody Shakespeare play. Although, if it comes with lunches and a new Lamborghini, do tell.       laughs  Then I’d say you best get to that go-kart on time, if you don’t wanna end up stuck in meetings all day, mate. Or maybe we go box this traffic and head to your place instead?      That might be the best idea we’ve had all week, innit? It’s a right laugh talkin’ ‘bout this stuff anyway—ain’t like we’re alone in it.

Rather annoying this wet weather, eh, George? Thought we’d get a bit of a break by now. I’ve been trying to sort out the dining room floor and I can’t get it to dry properly! Got it up only last week after those termites got into the corner.      Aye, mind you, I don’t think they ever   do   dry properly in this place come this time of year. What with the damp and the wind off the eastern side, it’s a wonder any of us don’t catch pneumonia. My Edith once called me a “walking bilateral,” I swear.      Oh George! Not again! You promised you'd stop talking about Edith like she's still here.      Well, she’s in this house more than I am, what with all these silly trinkets she bought and her green cloths for polishing the mantel! Still breakfasts in her usual spot!      Aye, well, you know as well as I do that’s just the memories talking. Good ones, mind, but memories none the less. Speaking of, I dug out the old fishing photos yesterday. You both in ’em, of course, by the river near Costessey. I reckon we must’ve gone fishing every Sunday from 1969 to ’72, least. Any of you remember catching that big one?      Oh yes! That was the one we lost, mind. Pulled and pulsed and someone said, "Blimey! That's a proper carp!" and we let it go outta the boat and it   smacked   the back of my head like a wall!      Aye, I laughed until I cried! That man had the wind knocked out of ’im and Edith was shrieking “George! Leave him be!” while poor George was sprawled on the deck, ‘cos he was the one that pulled the rod too tight. Bled all over the nets it did.      Honestly, I thought you boys were mad! Didn't know whether to laugh or faint. But of course, always trying to catch fish with the big rod! "Ooh, let’s try for a pike!” You were like kids sometimes.      I suppose life was more of a laugh then. Still, I do miss the old days. Never could go back to that pace now what with all this technology. I have a phone, but I swear it’s smarter than me. Try to send a photo, and it wants me to log into five different accounts.

Rather annoying when a measurement isn't clear on a product, isn't it? I mean, if you're selling beauty products online, you have to be precise with your dimensions! I saw you posted a new product listing for your Honest Skincare range last night and didn't you forget the size again?      Oh no, I meant to put it in but I got distracted by my cat pawing at a paper towel roll! I swear he's got this obsession with anything squishy. Anyway, it’s 50 millilitres, like the others. Didn’t even want to label it at first because I thought people would assume it's the same as our best-selling 100ml bottle. But I figured that could be a bit confusing, especially for new customers.      Yes, clarity is key. I know how you love the creative side of your business, but customers often rely on details when they can't actually see the product in person. You know in my language classes, even small misunderstandings can throw off the whole lesson. Also, I've noticed you're starting to get repeat buyers, which is brilliant!      I know, honestly , it still feels like only yesterday I was selling my lavender body butter out of my parents' garage in Birmingham. I mean, okay, my nan still calls it a “bit of a side hustle”, but she’s the one who taught me about natural ingredients and the whole idea of what “honest” skincare even means, really.      That’s so lovely! That personal angle is really what sets Honest Skincare apart—everyone’s looking for something authentic these days. Speaking of, I was wondering if you’ve thought about how you want to do your summer launch? I’ve had a couple of colleagues express interest in stocking your products in their local yoga studios or wellness centers.      That does sound promising. I was thinking, maybe for the summer we could do a limited-edition mix with some lighter ingredients, like aloe vera and something fresh, maybe cucumber or mint. I could pack little sample sizes for events. As for marketing, I’m toying with short-form video clips on TikTok and Reels—my cousins do that with their fashion brand and it seems to be growing like wildfire.      That sounds brilliant! I could even volunteer to film one of those videos from my language students, you know, explaining how your blends could be perfect for people with sensitive skin or post-surgery care.

Rather annoying this wet weather isn't it? I was supposed to visit the gardens in Eastbourne today but couldn't be bothered to get out with it this poor.      Oh, that's a shame. You do love your gardens, I remember as a child you'd race me to the flower patch to pick the sweet peas before the sun went down. Still, better to stay in on days like these. I only just dusted off the old box and got to send some of those records to Charles; you'll be wanting to hear what I found for sure.      Oh really? Get on to it, will you! Last time you promised me something and I found out you'd left the good bit at the bottom. You know I still keep the photo album you gave me, the one with the Darcy and the dog I think he turned out alright for an old tomcat. Cats do better than humans, no doubt about that.      Oh don't remind me about Darcy, he ate the wedding ring once—and I still haven’t forgiven him for that. I do tell you—personally I think it takes one to know one. Now as to this weather and the other news... Have you heard on the telly what's going on in Brussels? That government is playing at being cheeky with new trade laws, and now it's all on the back of us poor folk.      You know what I blame? When education comes in, they never tell you someone at the top is also blundering. Children are brought up to believe that the world’s made for the law-abiding, and then life comes through and tells them all lies. I spoke to my old class about this last week—well not "old," I still write to Jane, and she said what you said! Going into that new school barely a week and she’s up against the council. My, they've made it treacherous for young teachers these days.      I'm told it was different when you were teaching. I remember your little ones always making me smile, such as when that sprite of yours, Monica, topped the lunches on a new boy from Africa. Not unfriendly, no, just trying to help. Said it was customary where he came from.      Oh Monica, wherever she is now—still active in the community, I expect.

Rather annoying the temperature in here, isn't it? Cold enough to make you think it's December in Antarctica... What's the heating been doing?      Honestly, I've been over that system three times this week. The thermostat seems fine, but sometimes it's one of those things — if it's not broken, don't fix it, they say. But if it  is  broken...      Spare a thought for the mulberry bush outside, then. If this weather continues, there's no way the berries will ripen. I swear that tree is mocking me.      Right, because mulberries aren’t already tricky enough without British weather complicating things. Still, at least you're working on a PhD, right? So it's research material — just more outdoor "lab work."      I think the world needs a PhD in assembling heating systems. Speaker_2 would get it in a year.      Very funny. But hey, at least I keep the team running in manufacturing. Tools never lie, people do.      Tools tell you a story, though. Like the one I read yesterday about a man in Cumbria who started his own tool design business in retirement. He's making custom multipurpose tools from scrap. Absolute legend.      I'm not surprised. I met a few like him at a maker's fair in Cardiff last year. Silly place, actually — we were outside shivering, and the man next to me was soldering a toaster to a vacuum cleaner. It just goes to show, isn't it? You don’t need a mansion to live a rich life — you need  time  and  tools .      That's gold. But talking of tools, I had to borrow a torque wrench last weekend to fit that new plug. Took me three hours. No wonder my stepdad retired.      Retiring early can be tempting, can't it? Though I don't think I was ever quite  that  disappointed fixing a boiler or waiting for a heating system to come good.      It's always the little things, right? Like the mulberry bush, the heating, or how festive everything smells around this time. I baked a Christmas cake go-to recipe my nan taught me. It’s got so much brandy in it it’s practically a fortified tree.      A what?      A Christmas cake! You know, the one we had every December with all the dry fruits, soaked to within an inch of their lives over weeks.      It's a marathon, not a sprint.

Rather annoying that half the cutlery’s missing again. I swear we had more forks last week when we had grandparents and Claire over.      I can’t be sure, but I think Clara borrowed a few when she cooked lasagne for her flatmate last weekend. She said it was an emergency—something about  not having a knife bigger than a butter knife .      Aye, I’ve seen this before. We were all at my mam’s last week, and it’s like a warzone when people just grab the first thing that looks pointy or sharp. You’d think with everything we’ve got cluttering the drawers, someone would manage it better.      I still can’t get used to the number of knives you boys hoard. I once had a drawer with a fork I bought in the 70s in it. Never used it. Just looked at it fondly and said, “Ah, I remember when this was brand new.”      Aye, when I was a lad, we shared one knife and fork between the table. Wooden ones, mind you. I still keep a few as keepsakes. Polished real well with use.      You lot are both making it sound way worse than it is. I borrowed one fork off the table, it wasn’t a huge heist.      Right, and that’s the same logic as telling the in-laws you found one sock and insisting they won’t miss a pair.      Let’s not get started on the sock situation. I’m still under the impression  someone  hid mine because they wanted me to live off the floor all week.      Honestly, you’re not alone. I lent you one once and it hasn’t shown up in my sock bin for  years . Maybe it’s forming part of the sofa now.      I think we should make a system. Or maybe someone should just take charge of the cutlery from now on. I’ll propose we vote tonight. Winner gets to plan a new drawer regime.      Then I’m definitely voting for the drawer regime go back to the 70s. If it was good enough for Grumpy Old Greg, it’s good enough for us blokes.      I’ll help. We can take it out every night and play a round of  take what you need and return it where you found it . Old school, natural order.      I like that. At least then I can keep track of which knives are missing and which ones are just being arrogant about their spot at the top of the drawer.

Rather than chuck a sock in the bin if it misses a few days of washing, it would be better if you got the rather cold one out of the drawer and actually boiled it properly, like we discussed last week. I don’t think we can afford the sort of things you picked out yet again.      But  this  one’s very nice. I reckon it might be all the nice ones. I’ve only had it once or twice so far and I promise I’ll be more careful now, Mummy. Please can we go to the shops and get me another when it breaks? I really like the... the sparkly bits around the bottom.      I know you do. It's like that My Little Pony one with the melamine and the reflector bits. Probably, if you’re lucky, we can pick one up in the sale after Half-Term if it’s still going at the weekend. But no promises.      I suppose that’s fair, thanks ever so! By the way, Grandpa told me that he might actually be going away with us over Christmas, if he gets some of his work done properly in time. Like a week to go and we only started on it today. He was on the phone with Granny and it sounded very exciting indeed.      Oh, right! That’s actually fantastic news. I didn’t imagine he’d manage it after that whole thing with the council projects and the village fete at Milton Keynes, but if it’s all sorted now then that’ll be lovely. He was a bit worried he'd miss the school’s Christmas concert, wasn’t he?      That’s the one he was talking about! He reckons he's going to take the train instead of the car this time because it’s much cheaper and nicer and not corroded by frost like last year. He also said we should all go up and get some real snow gear like he used to have. Said Mummy would look smashing in a red ski jacket.      I dunno about smashing, but I could stick out my thumb and he’ll have to take me anyway. What with lunches to keep and snowball fights waiting to be had. I’d be mad to miss it. Plus, I told my boss I go every other year now and if I don’t get booked in for some remote work in the lead-up, I could go with a clear conscience.

Okay, I just can't get my head around this maths homework. I've done it three times and it still got the wrong answer. Have you tried it yet?      Yeah, I did it yesterday. Wait, which question are you stuck on?      The one about percentages and fractions. Like, I don't even know where to start. First they give you the sale price and you’ve got to find the original one. Why can't they just tell you how to do it properly like in the examples?      Oh that one. It's annoying because you have to use like three steps. First you figure out what percentage is left after the discount, then you convert it into a fraction of the total, and multiply by the new price. It makes more sense if you write it down in steps, I used a table to help me.      Honestly, sometimes I think I'm just not cut out for maths. I'm fine in English and food tech, and I actually quite like Spanish even though I say so myself. But maths is just... brutal.      I used to feel the same. I sort of turned a corner when I started doing past paper questions with my mum. It helps to see how it's asked in the exam. You want me to go through it with you right now?      Yeah, please. I promise not to roll my eyes if you have to explain the basics again.      Har har. Last week I had to explain how gravity works because my little bro thought it was magic. Look, so if something is on sale for 75 and it’s 20% off, then the 75 is 80% of the original price. So 80% is 75.      Oh... So then I need to divide 75 by 80 and then times by 100 to get the original 100%? Like...      ...75 divided by 80 is 0.9375, times 100 is 93.75?      Yes! That’s spot on. You just remember that the discounted price is a percentage of the total, go from there. It helps if you think of it like fractions of money, like in food tech when you're halving a recipe or something.      So all that time I spent baking cakes and making lunch in food tech wasn’t wasted?      Nope, it was basically training for this exact moment.      Okay, I owe you one. Can you help me with my Spanish next?

Rather do a bit o’ cleanin’ up, ‘ow’s about that? Felt like it was ages since I've done a proper sort-out o’ the DVDs! Mind, some o’ this lot are still in full box sets with the instruction manuals and whatnot — wouldn't you know it, they’re all in Italian, of all languages! ‘Ad me sister-in-law sent ‘em over from Rome a while ago. Dubbed rubbish or summat! I never got round to watching ‘em.      Oh, no way! They’re foreign films? I can be into that. You know I like to mix it up!  laughs  I mean, we’ve seen all the usual blockbusters by now anyway. Got a couple of Marco Bellocchio left from uni — they’re Italian, if I remember correctly. He delves into politics, the history of Italy, religious stuff — a bit heavy if you’re not in the mood.      Well, if they're any good, I’d say give ‘em a try. I mean, why not, eh? I was just thinking, you and me used to watch loads of films together in the old days. We still should do more o’ that. You’ve got good taste, love. Never seen a film from the 80s – 90s I’ve not still got somewhere!      Yeah, it’s been a while! Remember that time we spent the whole weekend watching every Godfather movie and then fell asleep before the Spaghetti Westerns?  laughs  That was ages ago. I’d definitely make popcorn hotter than the fury of a red-coated brigadier this time! Although I  would  prefer watching something a bit about Italian politics... or not — you decide the mood.      Well, what d'you think of that one you told me about, the one with the priest? The one where ‘e finds ‘is faith challenged. Sounds like it could be quite sombre, but the reviews said it was ‘important’ or something.      You’re talking about  The Son of God Likes You  — written by Fabrizio Caporello. It’s fairly psychological, but also quite poetic in parts. You know, it’s not the usual church stuff goin’ on — it’s more about internal conflict and guilt, and the line between redemption and punishment. It could go either way!      Sounds like the sort o’ thing that might leave ya with a bit o’ a headache, but I’m up for it. Just don’t start ‘aving a go at me at the end like I’m the problem!

Rather annoying the wet weather isn't it?      That it is, love. We had proper sunshine in Birmingham last week. I’m more than a bit fed up with the rain putting a stop to everything. Not to mention the roads - driving conditions at their worst.      Right? I spilled my coffee the other day because the potholes were so bad. Honestly, I’ve considered buying a four-wheel-drive just so I can survive the journey to work. It's costing me fortunes in repairs and fuel.      Oh dear, don't say that. You can't afford that right now, can you? I know you’re saving up for that summer trip to visit your sister in turkey, weren’t you?      Yes! I’m really looking forward to it, but these extra expenses are cutting into my savings faster than I’d like. I better start breakfast clubs again at school; I used to get a bit on the side from that.      Oh, I remember when you used to do that directly after school. I do miss you bringing me some of those homemade flapjacks you used to make as treats. Did you tell your brother about the trip yet?      I did, and he said he’ll chip in with something for you two - he still owes us for the last birthday present. You know how he is, always making promises at the last minute.      That’s the old joke again, but he’s a good boy. He works a lot, but I can tell he’s trying hard to be a better father and son these days. I still wish he had your grandmother’s love for books, about half his time is spent on the bingos or watching old football matches.      Yeah, that is sad. I mean, it’s up to him to do something, but for now, I’ll be taking you to the book shop on the weekend. I know it's a hobby you really love.      You're a star, love. Bookshop and then a nice walk by the canal? Do you think I can manage that with the legs?      I think so. We’ll go slow, and if you start feeling it, we’ll sit down or cut it short. You’re not in the court anymore, Mummy; you can afford to relax.      That I can! And I suppose you won't mind lending me your pen to write down new hearing case details?

Rather annoyingly, I've got to do a six-hour train journey back to Beijing tomorrow, since the university is relocating my contract to another campus now.      Oh, really? That's inconvenient at all. When do they expect you to be there for the new semester?      Officially, I don't start the new semester on the new campus until next month, so I've been given a week to settle in and meet my new colleagues. But since I'm going to be transferred to a new city altogether, I'll need to pack up the flat and hire a removals company... everything seems to be falling into place rather suddenly.      Yeah, that does sound stressful. But at least you’ve got your new apartment arranged? I remember you mentioned you found one via the university housing office, didn't you?      Yes, it’s a nice place – modern, with all the essentials and even a balcony with a garden view. The only issue is the location. It's on the outskirts near the motorway. Good for getting away from the city noise, but not ideal for public transport.      Right, as if trains and early mornings weren’t stressful enough already.      Exactly! And then of course, I’m worried about all the boxes and the relocation, and who's going to help me. You and I are quite busy with our own things at the moment.      Absolutely. But maybe I could give someone a call and ask if they'd be able to lend a hand one day. I know James and Emily are at a loose end over the next couple of weekends – they might be up for it.      That would be a tremendous help. Thank you for offering. I'll let James know what's going on and ask if they'd be up for it.      My pleasure. And while you're shifting, I can at least come over on the weekend for a weekend getaway before you're stuck all the way up North. Maybe you can pop back down for a while to clear your head.      That would be perfect. It’ll do me the world of good. I’ve just been delivering a run of lectures every day, and I can go for weeks on that grind if necessary.      You’re a trooper. Hopefully, this new chapter with the university works out for your career. It's all part of the gig, really, isn't it?

Rather annoyingly, I've got to do a six-hour train journey to Exeter today, so I won't be home until well after six. I’m so sorry I can't cover the babysitting this evening like we planned. Do either of you have plans for what you were going to do?      I was going to stay overnight with one of my friends if it wasn’t all sorted. But I reckon I can swap if Phoebe wants me to stay.      I don’t mind if you do go to your friend’s, Louis. We’ve been doing the coursework all week—we can just crash out on the sofa if we need. I don’t care, honestly.      Thanks Phoebe, I really appreciate you saying that. It’s just that I had this reading group I committed to, and I couldn’t back out at the last minute, you know? They’re waiting for my feedback on that new Ruth Ozeki book.      It’s no problem! I told you to ask earlier. I was going to do my pyjamas party with Niamh and book some photos too—mom I can still do that.      Actually, Louis, while we’ve got a free evening, maybe we could bake something from the recipe box. We haven’t really been in the kitchen, and I’ve seen Haylie’s Instagram stories and her photos of those cookies would be something to replicate. I could probably mail you the photos if you want.      That sounds lovely. Just don’t burn the house down, okay? I remember what you did the last time with the marshmallows and the stove. I still had to get a new hob cleaned.      That was you standing behind talking the whole time saying “trust me I’ve done this before” and that was you barely reading the recipe. So don’t side step the blame, Lucy.      Okay okay, fair enough. But just make sure to wash the mixing bowls before you start, and maybe don’t attempt them on your own unless you stick to my Instagram story.      Honestly, you two are like a couple of drama queens. Now, about the haircuts—Louis, you’re due another one soon, right? Are you still seeing my friend Tom from Comberton again or one of those chain salons? I remember you rated Tom’s boxers last time.      So embarrassing. I made him help me pull the plug after I spilled tea on the floor and then gave me a lollipop for calming me down over the scissors.

Honestly, I am just fed up with this food. Like, I know it's university canteen prices, but I could literally go to Nando's and get a better chicken casserole than this.      Hah, I agree — although I think it was slightly better on Tuesday. But  Tuesday , not today. Which   do   you reckon's the worst of it? The gelatinous stuff they call pie, or the pasta that somehow ends up seeing into the future and dries up before you even take the lid off?      Oh my god, the pasta is like baked in. Last time I tried to scrape the last of it off with a spoon like that Mycroft Holmes, I had meltable pasta left on the plastic. Probably still on the plate now, haunting it.      Oooh, classic uni trauma — better than breakfast, though. You remember this happened last month when I accidentally ate a whole bagel and milk in one go, thinking it was cereal? I thought I was full for days.      Hah, yeah — I mean, don’t get me wrong, credit where it’s due for the bagel. It was good, it just wasn’t supposed to be eaten with milk at 8 a.m. I feel like I’ve barely seen you since the start of term, though. What with all your late-night library sessions and all my barista shifts. What's up with you this week? Spotted you in the library again.      I  should  be resting up for my anatomy test next week, but I’ve been watching  Bridgerton  most nights about half past 10. I just can’t help myself. I'm trying to be academic, and fails.      Oh, unashamedly? I respect that. I’ve just been waiting for the right weather to actually venture into London for the day. Thought about going to the National Museum again. You in? I miss your mad commentary tour of the dinosaurs.      Oh, yeah, I’m  definitely  in. I took the 5-year-old cousins a couple of months ago and ended up with a museum goody bag on me for about a week. They still haven’t stopped calling me “Dino Queen.”      So what your actual plan is to be the Queen of the 21st century is to start with fossils, huh? You might be on to something. But for now, let's just not be tourists here. I’m not paying £15 to watch canteen jollof rice fight me for attention.

Rather annoying I had to cancel me trip to Bath last week. My sister was supposed to take me up first thing in the mornin’ and she skived off at the last minute.      Aww, proper bummer, I ken what you mean. I had a night planned in een Brighton and my mate Nick stood me up an’   didn't even tell me   until two hours before.      That’s a bit cheeky. Oh but I watched   this interesting show   the other night,  The Chi , on Netflix. It’s set in Chicago and it reminds me a bit o’ some o’ the social issues me nan used to talk abou’ in her youth.      I   haven’t got time   for Netflixr, to be honest. D’you know how I   ate the other night  ? Left-over pizza, and   inש breakfast, no less  , I just happened to still be hungry in the mornin’.      Ha bloody ha. I mean, why not, right? I’ve been doin’ a similar routine this week—napkin notes on the floor, as if I live in the wild. Honestly, I’ve been   chucked   by workin’ too much. So I’m takin’ it easy this weekend.      Good for you. I’ve been trying to get out more. Earlier this week I joined one o’ them fancy weekend cookin’ classes at someone’s house in Cambridge.   It was a real laugh  , half the people had no clue what a ‘sous-vide’ was.      That’s your posh side showin’ again, Gary. I wouldn’t know a sous-vide from a soup du jour. I just stick things in the oven an’   hope they taste like something   by the time I take ‘em out.      Aww, come on, Claire, you used to say you could roast a chicken like it was a national sport.      I can! I just…   do it out o’ habit   now, innit? More importantly, have any of you booked any road trips for the holidays? I was thinkin’ of cruising up to Scotland on me own if nobody’s goin’ no’ else.      Honestly, I’ve been working on a project due in early January. I’m planning to stay in the UK and maybe do some walking in the Cotswolds or somethin’. Just need some peace ‘n’ quiet.      That’s a solid plan. I’ve got a client trip in Aberdeen next month, so I’ll see if I can make the most o’ that and maybe explore a bit.

Rather annoying this wet weather, eh? You’d think for once we’d have a bit o’ sun. I got the telly on earlier—BBC weather, eh? Not a hint they’d say we’d see anything but sun and blue skies. Look outside, mind you—proper drizzle it was. Got eeny plans for the weekend, then?      Well, I wanted to go on a trip to London, if the weather ever clears up. I’ve heard tell there’s a nice new exhibition at the National Gallery. Not sure me car’d cope with the journey, but the Youth Hostel in Cornwall’s still open, if you fancied a week away.      That sounds nice and like a good break, definitely. I’ve been thinking about selling one o’ the houses I’ve got—just a spare, and I could do with the cash. It’d be enough to put something better on eBay, maybe even pick up a new car. Horses in the fields next door, ever looked at that, Ken?      Aye, I’ve noticed—vast fields, big ley lines, and them horses crop about in there. Like a walk to see em early in the morn. Reminds me o’ when I was a lad in Costessey. Not much else for doing back then, just fields, and now it’s all houses and building sites.      It’s all changing too fast these days, Mark. Everything’s been knocked down for supermarkets and someone’s always knocking up a new school. Ever seen a teacher struggle more than I do now with all the cuts and policies these days?      Margot, I heard on the telly most people about our age vote—Turnout’s always the problem, especially with this election coming. I’ve already registered! Going to be voting with purpose, not like the last lot who thought voting was just a formality. I’ve got my mail out ready.      Aye, it is a time for all us to have a say, I suppose. I always did stick to my paper as soon as it’s out. Next to me tea and toast, that paper is my must-do in the morning. Even if I don’t understand half it.      I still think it’s funny you lot talk about buying or building, when I just started looking into that purchase of a house further out—nice place near your place, actually. It’s priced right, and I think it’s in good condition.

Honestly, I don't know how you do it, Em. Every time I go to help with the baby, I end up feeling more confused than anything. One day I think I've got the hang of it and suddenly it's all wrong again. Was I even supposed to burp her after that night feed?      Ugh, I swear,   burp   is not in the dictionary most days. I just hold her up and press her gently and hope for the best. Sometimes she spits up like it’s a whole meal was coming out and sometimes she’s just,  ‘meh.’  I barely have time to even notice half the time. I’m sleep-deprived and still trying to coordinate my older kids, don’t get me started.      Oh no, someone’s had an explosion again — look at this! Wait, is this even Winnie this time or has she taken someone else’s nappy tray again?      That’s Casper again. Good job, Sami—did you do a full body change?      I did, honestly, as quick as I could. Poor kid looks like someone tried to paint her with mess. But it’s all good. You want to know the weirdest thing? Casper, like, giggled during it. Like the mess was fun. I did not giggle.      Honestly, I’m just amazed they don’t all have hair full of mucky nappies from me. I just handed Winnie a lemon out of the fruit bowl the other day and she thought it was some premium snack.  Squeaky jawy noises,  about five minutes of pure chaos. I’m the baby-food expert, I swear.      Don’t worry, I know I’m not the only uncool one in this bunch. The first thing Lewi ever tasted was lube. I was changing his nappy, and the tube was still in my hand from earlier. I tried to stuff it in my pocket quick and the cap didn’t close. He’s doing a jazz hands imitation with his mouth right now.      Was it the coconut one or the normal one? Because if it's the coconut one, that’s practically healthy.      No, it was the mint one, sorry, guys. He’s a total bad breath from now on.      Honestly, it's all madness and I wouldn’t change it for the world. But, hey, while we talk about bad practices, does anyone actually know how to  sleep train  the baby?

Rather annoying the wet weather isn't it? I was supposed to get the garden tidied up before the first frost, and now it's just muck under your feet. Not a hint of sun in sight!      Honestly, the weather this year is a bit wild. I was trying to photograph the cat in the sunshine last week, and the cloud just timed it perfectly to spoil every shot! I’ve been indoors all week working on press releases too. I’m feeling quite cabin-bound.      Well, nothing for it. Might as well chase the chores today while it's not too wet. I’ve already sorted the bins and started mending the fence at the back. That rot on the wood is driving me mad. You’ve still got the left-hand side to do by the way, Jane—don’t think I’ve forgotten.      I was about to tackle it! Wait breakfast, no doubt about that.      Oh don’t remind me of food! I’ve been ordering in for the past two days. Training is exhausting, and I swear the coffee at the station is less than warm and about as appealing as glue. Leftover lasagne and lukewarm shepherd's pie aren’t cutting it for me.      You really must try my Instant Pot recipes, Sam. I mean, it's a game-changer. You can set it and forget it and still have something vaguely edible. Last night’s stir-fry was up in 30 minutes with no effort—just hit a button!      I’m with you, Ange. I crave a bit of normalcy through cooking. I’ve had a colleague at work who developed a stomach infection from contaminated food at the hospital canteen last week. Very scary. Made me keen to control what goes into my mouth.      Right, well if the garden isn’t for today, I’ll put in an order for a pizza. I’m not sure the lasagne is any longer fit for human consumption. Slide it under my door with a note reading ‘food for you and that sprite of yours’ and I shall be eternally grateful.      Okay, pizza sounds good, but I’m branching out! I met someone at the Writers' Network meeting who had a recipe for pesto pizza that made my eyes water in delight. I might give it a go—should be easy and all plant-based. It’s about time I gave the others a break from my meat-centric menus, don’t you agree?

: "Liz, don't you love it when we get days off before Christmas? I've been  dreading  the science test we had this week."     : "I know! It was so hard. Rather annoying this new rat puppet they've got at the village fete, ain't it, Beryl? It's got rather too much of a cheeky sort of grin, if you ask me. Keeps leaping about like it's moonlighting from a music hall!      Oh, I saw it too, Harold. The children simply adore it. They think it's dashing. Though I must say, I never thought I'd see a puppet dressed in a pinstripe waistcoat, pulling pranks. Makes me chuckle, mind you. Didn’t it look rather like it was trying to fetch its tea tray with its paws?      You two still going to the fete? My loo breaks down every time I try to go, you know! I’m far too busy, really, but I’ve been meaning to pop down to get my eyes tested sooner or later. That breakfast-time squint of mine is getting worse! Hattie mentioned she saw the optician by the bus stop, didn’t she say he was taking people over the age of sixty-five for free screenings, maybe?      I think that’s a government thing, dear. It started two years ago, didn’t it, Harold? You'd think it was a humble way to look after the old folk of Norfolk. I wouldn’t mind it myself—my sight’s not what it was before the cataracts. Silly things! I blame the dust at the childminding centre in the ‘70s. Constantly had splinters in the cornea.      C’d you have a red and white bus being crowded out by a lorry last week, Beryl? I about lost me footing while I was trying to board! Only got on because the busdriver said I looked “inclined to be bumped off by the wind”. Rather unkind, but to the point, I suppose. I’ve always preferred the route passed the bell-ringing tower at All Saints. They do a fine afternoon ringing there.      You mustn’t stick about to listen, Harold. You'll miss out on the regular service. I keep meaning to go to the church myself, but I’ve too many headaches with the property accounts. I told the caretaker goon he needn’t worry about the gutters—that I personally made my dent in the estate, between you and me, I’m not getting out of bed for that.      You and your estate, Henry! Always so superior. But I expect hearing a bell on a Friday or two does help one’s mind, don’t you think?

Rather annoying to be honest. Loads of tourists swarming around. I’d much rather get a real feel for it, you know, not just the normal stuff like the gondola rides or whatever.      Aye, I understand what ye mean. When I was a lass, it een’t like that at all. It een’t as   touristy   as it is now. More   peaceful   and proper.      So what did ya used to   get up to   round here when ye was me age?      Oh well, not too much like you young ones. I used to come down with me mam and dad, drink a   spill of tea   and look around the   markets  . The food is different back then, ain’t like now, with all the chains and   overpriced coffee shops   like this one.      Aye, I noticed that. They serve   espresso and panini   and it's quite fiddly looking for a proper   rest stop  .      Aye, well, there’s place up near the   San Polo district   where they sell proper   Venetian sausages   and   risi e bisi  , which is like rice and peas stew – very traditional. Worth a try, and way cheaper than this café.      Mate, you know   I’m all for it  ! When d’ya suggest we go?      Maybe   after this coffee  ? It’ll give ye a proper taster o’ the real Venice. Not just the   postcard stuff   – the  real    old stuff  , y’know.      Sounds good to me. I’d rather get a feel for the city than another   cheese and ham wrap  .      That’s the   spirit  ! And tell ye what, once we’ve had that, maybe we could go   along the Grand Canal   and   see the bridges  . You can see the   architecture   from up close.      Aye, I’ve heard it’s incredible. I took an art class at uni once, where they showed slides of the place. I reckon goin’ on the actual spot is a   game changer   for how I see it.      That bloke in your class must’ve known his stuff. Venice is full of   history and charm  . Different from anywhere else, I’ll say that.      So, what time’s the food place open? I’m ready for something   real  , not   crammed in a sandwich  !      Aye lass. We’ll be the   first in the queue   and before ye know it, we’ll have some of the   best food on the canals  , and   Moke a memory   of a grand day out.      I bet this is going to be   one to remember  !

So did you go to the gym this weekend? I remember you saying something about it last week.      Yeah, I went on Sunday. Honestly, it was a bit of a struggle because I got thrown off the treadmill after 10 minutes—some guy wouldn't move out of my way and I couldn't speed up fast enough.      Oh no! Sounds like a Nandos nightmare before breakfast.      Haha, exactly. It was quite a session. But I managed to do the full circuit. Didn’t even want to touch the squats though... still not ready for that!      That's harsh, only 10 minutes of cardio?      Hey, I’m a beginner. I told you I haven’t touched a gym in ages. But I'm determined. I want to be healthier, and working in health doesn’t exactly help if I’m slacking!      I hear you. I started going back to the group classes a few weeks ago.      Oh, you're into the instructor with the crop top?      Yep, and the one with the impossible voice—every move is always "barbel rhythm," then all of a sudden "let’s power it up with a moonwalk and a crunch."      That's him! I tried one of his Zumba sessions. Ended up with sweat drips on my eyebrows for a week.      That sounds like a bonding experience. I should definitely buy you a drink—maybe a mojito to wash it down.      You better make it a Virgin one. I’m not trying to undo the good work of this morning. Speaking of which, thanks for not rolling your eyes when I told you I haven't managed to run more than two miles in two weeks.      No judgment here. I just have too many deadlines. Last week was bloody stressful at the office. My project is due in two days, and the client is as mysterious as a Nando’s starter.      At least your job doesn’t involve going back and telling clients that something is ‘vivo’ when it's really goenvironmental. But it was hilarious when I got so confused at the meeting and started smiling when I was meant to be ‘unhappy’ with the reports.      I seriously think I live in a world of Microsoft Word and broken project timelines now.      How ‘bout this—on the note of healthy living, have you got any plans for the summer yet? I was thinking of going to Cornwall, maybe a beach house with some mates.

Rather exciting isn't it, eh Harry? That grandchild of mine – born in France, no less. I got the news from Judith just after tea today. Absolute whirlwind of an announcement. She said the little one was born in Lyon – seems the nursing home there is very well set up, much better than I would've thought, given the usual nonsense one hears about the French.      Oh a grandchild, now, that’s the best kind of news, Miss Eleanor. I’ve had quite a few years under my belt to appreciate the little milestones. Didn’t your son always toy with the idea of settling in Europe? He even mentioned France once, I recall, when the idea of property ownership was on his mind.      Oh he did! He’s a qualified architect – or at least he was, back when he used to make plans for little local projects. He was fascinated by old European architecture. I still remember him going on about Chichester Cathedral and the spire collapse, thanks to that dreadful architect, what was his name? Porden? Yes, Porden, I think it was.      Oh yes, I remember that. Horrible business. But back to the continent, Eleanor. I’ve been thinking a lot about it – quite a curious mix of anarchists and bureaucrats, if you ask me. I’ve spent a fair bit of time in the British Library, poring over old tomes and letters about Philip of Spain and Mary Tudor. The archives in Spain are quite something. Dusty and full of secrets.      That sounds oddly romantic. You always had a soft spot for adventure, didn’t you? Still, I must say I’m somewhat wary of the bureaucratic tangle. I’m told buying property there can be such a different experience – especially for an older woman like myself! Though it does make you think about enterprise and how things are run in France. My sister had Burgundy wine trellised out toward the road, with people just popping in to buy it by the glass.      Yes, I’ve had my fair share of visitors from such ventures over the years. Rather fond of the English with lunches and a little shopping trip to the various markets – oysters, baguettes, the lot.      Of course, of course! But I do miss open days – one of those small exhibitions in the garden, art competitions with the local blokes, arguing about where to plant the latest bollard.

Yo, this dumpling is amazing. I’ve never had anything like this in my house before. Mum’s got this weird thing against takeaway—only cooked chicken and boiled veg. Literally      Lol, that’s the same in our house. My bro can’t make a sandwich without asking if there’s permission from the “chilli monitor” at home. Mum’s like, “No spice today, love, your heart can’t handle it.” She’s so overprotective.      But anyway, how’s school going for you, Jerry? Still being stuck in that sixth form limbo with mostly people who can’t decide between doctor and fireman yet?      Oh, I’ve already narrowed it down. It’s either a doctor or a psychiatrist—because if they pick fireman, I’m just gonna spend my days putting out the drama at their place.      Lmao, that’s harsh. I’m still figuring out what I’m even into besides comic books and taking notes over them. Last week I presented a slide show on Marvel character psychology. My teacher looked like she was about to faint.      You should’ve been at my school last week. We had that substitute who looked like he was just trying to get out of his last job. He tried to quiz us on the periodic table and failed halfway through. We all started chanting his name. Rhymed with “Cluck,” for some reason.      Sounds like my chem teacher, Mr. P. He’s hotter than the lab Bunsen burner and still thinks “combustion” is a ballet move.      You know the real bummer though? Me and Charlie had plans to hang out last weekend, but her family got stuck in a food coma after a Sunday roast. Three generations passed out like overcooked sausages. Dad said they had to cut potatoes and gravy into portions so it’d last.      My sister tried to start a “diet” last week—eat 10 grapes a day, ignore the lunches, keep the chocolate in the top drawer. It lasted until Friday when she opened the fridge with tears and a bag of chocolate in her hand. I think it was more of a Roald Dahl action plan than a real diet.      Same here. My little cousin’s into smoothies now, big believer in the green monster one. We forced him to try one and now he draws superheroes who exclusively drink kale and sound like hippies.      I’m so over trying to make sense of this.

Rather annoying this new supermarket’s branding, isn't it, Sarah? I was in there yesterday and it felt like every product had some ridiculous jingle now.      Oh Joan, I know what you mean. Not only that, the shelves are so low — you can barely see what’s at the end of them without straining your back. It’s just ridiculous! But at least their prices are a bit better, though I still miss the old place.      Grandmo, are you gonna help me clear out the garage? It's so messy when we get stuff out for the moving truck. It's like a whole  other  house in there.      Yeah Joan, Sarah, you know we have to clear this place within the week. Ten boxes already gone and I still haven’t sorted through the attic. A writer might need to pack in a far more orderly way than I do, but even then... this is madness!      I remember the day we moved into this place, Joan. You and I were over, helping Sarah bring in the furniture, and we had to climb over boxes for three days! Felt a bit like a proper archaeological site in here by the time we got settled.      Oh, yes, that was a right adventure. I got a ladder, and ended up stuck halfway trying to get the photo frames down. Sarah did try and pull me down with the ladder and nearly collapsed!      Haha — sounds like fun. But seriously, why do we have so many oddly-shaped items? Some of them don’t even fit in the boxes and it’s driving me mad packing!      I did suggest getting storage boxes from the DIY shop the other week — they have some really neat options now. Not very techy, but you barely need an app to unstack them.      True, though if you’re anything like me, you’ll just end up stacking the wrong box on top and all your unpacking gets reversed! I tried to label them, but the numbers got mixed up.      Well, whatever we do, it better be ready by next week. I’ve already been invited to come with you to the new house to set up the kitchen on your birthday weekend, Jonathan. Any plans for the event?      Well, I was thinking maybe something small. Maybe some virtual cake with all the family over Zoom to help us celebrate?

Okay, so I've been thinking about our GCSE options. I still can't decide whether to do geography or art and design. I mean, geography seems more useful if I ever want to get a proper job, but art is just honestly more fun, y'know?      I get that. My mums  constantly  badgers me about doing things like business studies or economics. But I'm just more into stuff like music and drama. I mean, I'm doing the clarinet, which is kinda useful if you want to do music GCSE or further in life or whatever. But I don’t even know what I want to  do  when I leave school.      Exactly! And that’s the thing, isn’t it? You think you have to be super sure right now, but honestly, I feel like I’ll be choosing between being an astronaut and a pizza chef by the time we’re, like, actually working!      Ha! No, I know what you mean though, though. My older brother was a proper workaholic at that age—he did like ten GCSEs, and now he doesn’t even use most of it. He works in a call centre, for crying out loud. It’s kind of ridiculous. Still, when he got into that job, he said they looked at your GCSEs, so maybe it  does  matter.      Ugh, yeah. I've been watching some YouTubers, and some of them just talk about how they didn’t do well at school and they just started their own thing online—like make-up, vlogs, and all that. I wish I could skip school and be a blogger or something.      I know! Like the ones who review Makeup or clothes or whatever. But you  do  have to learn to make a living while doing stuff online, right? I mean, they probably do courses or stuff after GCSEs.      Well, the one thing I do know is I don’t want to do PE for GCSE. My PE teacher is such a  git , and the bogs here are  so  basic. They're literally just buckets with a plastic lid, you remember?      Oh man, I still go there sometimes on bike rides if I'm going through Linton! You’re not in the same school as me anymore, but I can tell you what your PE teacher’s like—it’s that big bloke with the moustache, right? He shouts at people for not doing star jumps right!

Rather annoying this new tablet of mine. You know, me being a retired civil engineer, I designed bridges and all sorts, and yet I can’t for the life of me figure out how to install this bloody app. Seems like the more we build, the harder it is to use.      Aye, I know exactly what you mean, Ted. I tried to set up this email thing they told me about. A chap at the library said it was easy, but I swear it’s got more gears than one of those old Ford engines we used to work on back in the day. Let’s see… you fetch the key from the page, type it in like a crossword clue and— whoosh —you’re in the turkey shop. I’ve sent an email to myself no fewer than three times.      Roight, I think it’s just a case of being too old for all this gadget nonsense. When I was a childminder, I didn’t need a tablet to tell me the time! Just looked out the window and said to the kids, “If it’s dark, it’s time for a biscuit.” These days, I can barely keep up with the news without flicking through ten apps. Tell me there was something on the radio, and I’m all ears.      Mateys, with all due respect, none of this is rocket science. Let me show you. All these devices are loaded with intuitive tools meant to simplify life. You don’t even have to type out someone’s full name to send them an email. Just a tap here, a bit of swiping there, and hey presto. Ted, want me to help you install that app?      I’d be grateful, Anna. Although I’m starting to think my old tools—like a wrench or a level—might still be easier to use. Still, if a youngster like you can do it, I suppose I can give it another go.      And while we’re on the subject of tools, have either of you seen the wildlife about the place? I was out the other morning and spotted a sprite of a bird—looked like a sparrow with spots and a mustache! Was perched on a rail near the pond.      Oh, go on then! Don’t be getting all wistful at your age, Albert. That must’ve been a sandpiper, or something equally rare.

Rather annoying when the new lads bring deliveries to the door. A few weeks ago, one ‘ow poked me wi’ ‘is bike basket while he run down the path. I've nearly ‘adc a ‘ead knockin' off! No manners, no respect!      ‘Course eeny harm done, I'm still ‘ere, but I reckon it's about time we sorted out a clean-up ‘ere. An’ I mean  proper  clean. Not just ‘mop wiv a stick’!      Oh Rod, when are we gonna learn to not hold a grudge against bikes and broomsticks? I reckon it's the government supplyin’ ‘em wiv that 'youth stimulation grants'!      Tenr, I hear you, but at least the lads in our area aren't all that bad now. My pupils giggle when I tell ‘em about the ‘80s when I used to live in Birmingham. Mega oversized tops hides, you know, for the 'I'm not gonna fit in that doorframe' look!      Yer I remember that, quite a few lasses were into the real  belt  action back in those days. Overdone.      Rod, remember – no swearin’ in my house – not that you do much these days. More somethin’ to do wi’ the tea and the Tabby cat than the old BBC shows!      That reminds me. Did you read about the teacher who thought they had a  live  pigeon in their classroom and spent the whole lesson being ‘fee fie fum’?      I did! My news feed was full of the thing. Although, I had to delete a few things after my sister posted that she'd gone out and started ‘dance pooling’ in her local bin!      Geo., you shouldn’t mix with that lot at the pub. They start a laugh ‘n can’t stop it!      Honestly, the amount of time people spend on Twitter. I mentioned to a few buddies that I walked five miles to the shop last week, no less than  that , and one bloke said the NHS should set up a walking map for life improvements!      You’re just in a good mood coz you’ve done your walks an’ your stretchin’ thing you learned at the doctor’s!      Well, those jokes are never intended to be taken to heart, Jos. But ‘ee, I do like to keep active. I tell the kids all the time to stretch and get outside.      And always take a tea ‘n biscuit. ‘E’s the only one who remembers how to make ‘alfways, Geo!

Rather annoying this lot o’ snow, innit? Me an’ the cat got trapped out ‘ere first thing this mornin’—we was lucky enough to make it back by the time the sun came out.      No, I know what you mean. I tried to make my way een to the uni, but the buses ain’t running proper. Ay, I’m actually workin’ from ‘ome today. I think I’m in too much of a state anyway after last night.      What you mean, “last night”? Didn’t you get the stag party under control?      Oh,  yes , I did, but the groom, he turns out to be like a MySpace-era laddie with a taste for bursts and neon bottle tops. We had five bottles of prosecco, and I think he turned up dressed as an Ed Sheeran impersonator. I breakfasted with him at 7 a.m. after I’d cleaned up his bathroom. Bless ‘im, he didn’t even remember a word of it!      Ah, classic stag party—personality changes overnight, innit? Anyway, your turn. We still on for the hen on Friday?      Course we are. I been planning it like a military op. My nan’s been helping me—she’s organisin’ the chicken thing. She’s somethin’ of a legend when it’s come to outfits and vibes. We might even do a fake 'Come Dine With Me' round. Just not my flat, though. That’s a disaster waiting to happen.      You mean the ivy in the hallway?  laughs  Oh, come on, I thought that bit was a nice touch. But okay, we’ll keep it out th’ house. What else you got planned?      Well, we got the main do on Friday, then the big breakfast cruise up the Cam on Saturday. I’m thinkin’ we might try to sneak in a nice pottery class or somethin’ for the girls. After all the shenanigans.      Sounds grand! And what about holiday plans after that? I’m thinking of going back to Sunderland once the snow clears. Mawn’s started gettin’ goin’ on the garden again—apparently, she wants me to dig a veg patch out the back. I tried to suggest bunnies might eat all of it. She said I was too much of a gert weedy nancy to know proper gardenin'.      Oh, classic over-competitive gardening Mums. You know I’m goin’ up to the Peak District for a ski trip with some uni folk, but I think I need to make sure I’ve got proper boots, not just the ones I wear to theatres.

Rather lovely to have you all under one roof, what with it being the first Sunday in ages that we've all got together. Never mind the weather, I say. I’ve been on the stove all afternoon, and I must say, we’re having the bird with some stuffing and a nice gravy to go with it. That and a bit of Yorkshire pudding, if I do say so myself.      Oh, that sounds divine, dear! I always swoon for a good roast. I’ve brought some fresh treacle scones to go with the tea later. Do you want me to put ’em in the oven to warm through?      That’d be the ticket, Nancy. You know me like that—never a doorstep for home baking. And you brought a thermos of horseradish as well, didn’t you?      I did, for you, and for the boys when they come in. I know they’d fancy a bit on their meat. I’ve also brought a salad, you know, for the ladies—just to give it a touch of something green.      That’s so thoughtful, Nancy! Sometimes your mother’s meals are a bit rich for me. I might pass on the Yorkshire pudding, if you don’t mind. I’ve been dieting for about three weeks now. I know I say it every other Sunday, but this time I’m serious!      You know what they say about diets, don’t you, Eve? They work until the relatives come over. And God help me, I’ve already been eyeing up the stuffing like it’s some kind of secret delicious mission.       laughs  Oh, come off it, Luke! You’re a grown lecturer living the high life in London. Surely you can resist a bit of good stuffing?      Doesn’t sound like we should be educating the lot of you on restraint. Let’s get eating before the bird goes cold. Nancy, d’you mind passing the gravy?      With pleasure, George. I always cook a bit extra, you know. You can’t never have enough.      speaking of cooking, I took the liberty of bringing a veggie lasagne with me. I know it might not go with the rest of it, but I thought some of you might fancy a change of pace for dessert.      Well, I might fancy some of that. I have been craving something a little less traditional, to be honest. It’s strange—living in London, you start craving some hearty Norf food, but then you get here and crave something Italian!

Rather annoyingly, I haven't brought anything to cook with. I blame the internet—the grocery website kept timing out, and I ran out of luck. I'm down to just a few ingredients      Well, don't worry—I have some mince at home, and the butcher was kind enough to give me a few extra mushrooms. We could make bolognaise!      I’ve been craving some good lasagne, so this sounds promising. Is anyone else up for helping in the kitchen?      I.Fatalfanstay outside of the mess, but I won’t complain about the food! Still, if I can stir a pot or fold napkins, I’ll lend a hand. My hands still know what they're doing!      I’m good at seasoning, if anyone needs a hand. A good administrator knows how to measure, organize, and balance!      I'll measure out the tomatoes and spices while someone else handles the noodles. I'm not the best at multitasking when I cook.      I do tell you lads, I’ve had my fair share of cooking in a large family. We didn’t have fancy gadgets, but we knew how to stretch a meal. I remember when ingredients cost more than they fetch now!      That actually sounds really interesting, Dad. Did you have to grow your own vegetables or something?      Oh aye, we had a big garden. We planted cabbages, onions, even some potatoes. Rations were tricky at times—everyone had to pitch in.      I still love a good veggie lasagne, but I do miss the old fashioned meat type you could get in the shops. Do you think they make lasagne sheets any thinner now than they used to?      Thickness? I think that’s for show. The thinner ones often break more easily, personally. I always prefer to go for the sturdier ones—they last longer in the sauce.      This is such a wholesome way to spend the evening—cooking with the family. It’s better than the usual stream of doomscrolling on my phone after work. Plus, it's good to get goin' on stuff early if you've got a big day tomorrow.      I genuinely could go on forever about the merits of proper conversation and family time. I sometimes miss it all. We should do it more often.      True to life, it is, lass. Family’s the one thing that stays when everything else changes. The lasagne comes and goes, but love and company stick around!

So do you remember that time we worked on that social story-telling project back in New Zealand? The first one got heaps of shares on Facebook—ended up going viral in a couple of days. It was a mad experience.      Oh, I do! You wouldn't believe it was my writing on that one. I remember we were both twitching at the computer, watching the numbers grow like it was a rocket launch. I think that's one of the reasons I’m interested in how education can leverage social media to engage students.      Exactly! That story was about a startup guy who'd just frozen his money in some dodgy venture. I reckon that's the real-world connection students need to make now. My company, TouchPoint, is branching into ed-tech, you know. I’m thinking about creating simulations for university students—like problem-solving mini-games based on real-life entrepreneurial pitfalls and successes.      That’s clever. I’m actually teaching in a university next term, and I plan to introduce some project-based learning. If I could incorporate one of your simulations—something with a narrative, maybe akin to your viral story—into the curriculum, it might really help the students apply the theory we’ve been covering in class.      Absolutely. Have you got a broad topic in mind?      Yeah, I’m thinking about a unit on social entrepreneurship. We want the students to understand the real-world impact of their decisions—ethics, sustainability, profit models. A simulation where they're running a social enterprise trying to break even while making a difference. It could include community feedback, peer reviews, and even real-world scenarios through video storytelling.      Ooh, I love that. We could even add a feedback loop where the students get input from real entrepreneurs or social workers. That would make it feel like actual problem-solving. And if we tie in some of the viral video techniques we used back in the day, like real human stories that hit emotional triggers, the students might just remember the lessons for years.      You're getting me all inspired now! How soon could we get something drafted? I’ve got a conference in two weeks where I was planning to present some ideas, and this would be perfect.      No worries. I’ve got some initial storyboards and character concepts already. Let me sketch out a few options, and we can go from there.
