Rather lovely day today, isn't it love? Thought it was going to pour for hours, but it's holding off and rather bright out there. I’m just watering the herbs in the pot by the window there. You pop in with a cuppa, I bet?      Yeah, actually that'd be nice. I've been tied up for the last hour sorting out some deliver deadlines for work—they keep adding last-minute things, but I'll be right there. So much easier being home, yeah?      Oh, it's a treat when you're not out and about. You know what I like to do on days like this—settle down with the wireless on, maybe knit a bit and contemplate the state of the garden. Still too early to think about anything much more dramatic, mind you.      Ha! That’s the perk of being an office job at home. Though honestly, I envy you sometimes. I've been thinking about how much I miss having a garden. Rent is enough as it is to not spare a thought for anything more than pots on the window sill.      Well, listen—there are plenty of young landladies in Cambridge, and I'd be surprised if one of them didn't have room for a little flat with a garden. You might try the estate agents in Newnham, I've seen quite a few come through the paper.      Maybe you're right. I could probably save enough for a deposit, and the rent feels more stable in an area like that. Although my flat's alright, it's so far out—takes half the morning just to get into town and be late for lunch.      Oy, I do miss those old walkabouts. You remember the little butter shop near the Crown and thistle? There was always someone baking fresh scones or laying out the crumpets in that window. Makes you stop and admire the quiet little things in life.      Oh yeah, I used to pass that all the time when I was at Cambridge uni. I always envied the townspeople—there's a real community feel here. Sometimes with my work I feel like I'm just moving from schedule to schedule, you know?      That's the tricky thing goin' on in life, love. If you're not mindful, you just tick off each item without thinking. But with bloomin’ gardens and your own space you might at least take time for a few deep breaths in between.

Rather annoying this, innit? I mean, I knew it was snowin’ in France ‘ere first... got us stuck in this tiny b_and’t_ in Grenoble. No signal, no wi-fi, just a chippy floor and a bit o’ continental bread for dinner.      Right? I  told  you we should’ve checked the forecast before bookin’ that budget romcom holiday. I mean, I love you too much to mention it, but yeah...      Aww, come on. It's not all bad, is it? We came specially for the football match, even if it’s dead snowin’. That French referee, though, blimey. Thought the turkey on the telly was biased!      I’m not obsessed with football, but I’d say the translation of the ref’s instructions in the commentary was dodgy. Like when he said ‘arrêtez’ everyone here thought it meant ‘start’ not ‘stop.’ Classic!      Yeah, the guy shouting,  ‘Wait! Wait!’  and then the French team ran off the pitch! Bahahaha! What did he teach you in uni for, then, Cambridge brat? Scientific methods? You could’ve been a proper translator by now.      I’m not a  translator , Haylie. I study Chem. We don’t deal with mortal French referees. If I could translate atoms, I might be on to summat useful. But speaking of—what’re you even plannin’ to do after sixthform? Cos you’d better have a plan if you want to ‘ave a decent career after your ballet career’s over.      I’m not a ballet dancer, Cam, I just dance for a lark and take photos of that lot. I’m thinkin’ uni, probably in Manchester. My sister ‘ad a mate who got a grant for bio-media or sundry. Signals, sort o’.      Ooh, that sounds fancy. You’d sort out all the technical bits for some cool art thing or a film. I’d be happy with that. More fun than being in the lab all day analysin’ something that’s not going to make the world better.      Nah, I think work at uni could be fun. Imagine making that art alive with signals, bloomin’ biosensors and all. It could be proper work  and  proper kinaesthetic expression.      You do say that like it’s some kind o’ hippy-futurism! But I’m not entirely against it. Least it's better than the corporate kind o’ work, y’know? Right, unless we freeze to death here and our conversation goes digital.      Aye, speaking of, I reckon them Euros work on their methods for science, ‘Methinks we better head back to the car.

Rather annoying when a spider turns up in the kitchen when you're cooking dinner, isn't it? The first thing I do is panic and fling the pan off the side! Honestly, I think they have a sixth sense for when I'm making lasagne.      Oh, I’ve had far worse than that, I can tell you. One time I was on my hands and knees cleaning the kitchen floor and I found a mouse just sitting in the corner, staring at me like,  “What’s she gonna do now?”       Blimey! That's a bit too close for comfort. I once had a mouse scuttle across the hallway and I accidentally kicked my son's toy across the room trying to get away from it. Fun childhood memories, really.      Ha! Kicking toys around in a panic? That’s an adventure for the kids. I suppose it doesn’t help that I’m constantly in the house – I see these little rascals setting up shop everywhere, you know? I once caught a mouse in the loo, like it was doing its own round of cleaning!      At least it did the job better than me sometimes. Honestly, I’ve never understood how mice can get in through such little spaces. You’d think they were magic carpet ones with the way they appear. At least the spiders don’t come with tea set.      You know what I find far more disconcerting, though? Our birds. I have one who keeps coming to the window like a prat, chirping away at me with its beady little eyes. It wants to come in, I swear – like  it’s  the employer and I’m just the cleaner.      Ha! We have a blue tit that absolutely refuses to take no for an answer. I’ve tried to shoo it away, fed it, even opened the window just to show it out – and it still comes back. I think it’s plotting something.      I tried feeding them once when I was doing a crack in the side wall. Next thing I know, there’s a squirrel in the back yard with a mismatched pair of socks. You think you get something for trying to be kind, don’t you go there?      If it was just the critters, it would be bearable. But the worst thing is when they all come at once. I once had a bird, a spider and a mouse in the kitchen at the same time.

Rather lovely to finally meet in person, Delyth. I've heard so much about you through the family... Our dear cousin James often talks about the side of the family you're on.      A pleasure, Georgia! I have to admit, it's been years since I was in Stevenage—felt like meeting you was long overdue. Iừng just got onto family trees myself, trying to reconstruct my late mother's ancestry.      Oh, I'm very sorry to hear about your mother. What was wrong with her?      Lung cancer, late diagnoses—we lost her three years back. It was terribly sudden. That prompted me to look into the family history; I like to think of it as preserving what I can. Would you believe I found a relative on her side who was a blacksmith and lived in the same little village she did in the 1800s?      That’s fascinating... I suppose it’s the teacher in me, but I always found genealogy incredibly compelling—and a great way to understand culture and family identity over time. I’ve had some of my students work on it in the past.      It must be such a rewarding experience, teaching others. I used to teach in a primary school in South Wales too—until I retired, fairly recently, and, well, these long afternoons gave me time to dig into my roots.      You were a teacher? That’s great! I've been in education for over two decades. I teach at a secondary school here in Hertfordshire. Also, I've spent the last few years putting together a bit of research on educational trends in the south of England.      That's such an important area of work. I always thought you teachers had your hands full these days! I remember it being a lot calmer in the 1980s.      There's certainly been more change in the system in recent years than ever before. Budgets are tighter, expectations higher. I honestly can't imagine doing anything else. Though being academically trained probably helps—I hold a postgraduate degree in history from the University of Manchester.      Pardon my surprise—did you go straight from school to university?      Yes, I left school in Dorchester at 18, went up to study what fascinated me most. You were lucky enough to live in Bristol, though—such a bustling place with a great history of its own to explore.      Oh, I was lucky!

Rather lovely to be out here today, isn't it? The sky looks just right for a hot air balloon... Well, if they were flying. I’m so envious of people who've gone up in them. I keep meaning to book one of those flights, but somehow the days keep slipping by.      Yeah, I used to think they were just a bit tacky when I was younger, but you’ve got a point. The views from up there must be incredible. And seeing the countryside from above like that—it just can't be matched. Still, I’d probably get too cold up there.      Oh, you'd have a coat and everything. What I'm really thinking about is the wildlife that must be watching them go by too. I saw a buzzard just over there the other day, perched on a fence post staring straight up like it had an opinion on the whole thing.      Bucksy? He probably thinks they're some sort of ornithological disruption. I remember one flight, the wind picked up so much the balloon actually brushed against a power line—fortunately, the guy had nerves of steel and he got it sorted. A bit unnerving for the passenger, though, let me tell you.      Wait, Bucksy? Is that the new dog? Mate, you got a dog?      Oh, he's not new. It's just... he's always trying to run off toward the hills every time we take a walk. I've got to keep a firm grip on his leash or he'll be halfway up Wymondham Chase before I blink.      That hill is a bit much for a little terrier, isn't it? I mean, he's got the desire—but the stamina? I had a spaniel once who could outrun me on the flat and up and down. I miss him.      Burgundy? That old guest speaker in dog form?      Ha, something like that. Anyway, I was talking to someone about camping the other day. They said the best places to go are just off the power lines because you've got higher birds and more foxes come out at night. I’d be terrified, honestly. You're out there, basically waiting for goings-on on your own.      Not for me, love. I’m a city man. But, blooming honest, what your lot do with the countryside is sometimes beyond me. You live in one of the most beautiful places, yet people still worry about making more money and selling the land over to developers.

Rather chilly for a midweek afternoon, isn't it? I was half expecting it to be warmer when I cycled over.      Aye, I know what ye mean. It’s a proper British spring if you ask me—two days of sun and seven days of drizzle. Still, I wouldn’t miss a session like this one for the world. Got me groove on in that tennis class earlier.      Fair enough! I always find it inspiring to see people of all ages pulling up to the courts. It was me turn to warm up the beginners, but honestly, some of them picked it up faster than I did at their age. I swear teaching the language of tennis is almost as tough as teaching the English language itself.      Ha, you and your languages. I reckon you're a pro at explaining things in simple enough terms for even us in the North to understand. Although, I still can’t say I've mastering all those odd spellings you Brits cook up!      Oh, spare me the compliments. I'm just glad that I can give it a go—personally, I’ve always found it fascinating how different a dialect from Leeds to Hitchin can be. Have you ever been out to Hertfordshire?      Once or twice for work. Little quieter than Leeds, and not half as steep! But I imagine Hitchin's quite the gem. You ever think about taking a break from language teaching? I mean, from what you’ve told me, it’s a bit more bookish than a rush of adrenalin.      Fair point. I do sometimes consider being an outdoor instructor—I mean, your colleague, Laura, manages a circuit class that’s absolutely packed. I’m the kind of person who’d get vibes from a good sprint and not just another chapter of Jane Austen.      You’re not getting too ‘YOLO’ on me, are you? Although, personally, I reckon coaching’s a whole different beast. It's all about motivation, patience, and scheming sessions that don't crack people's backs.      Sounds like you've got coaching down to a fine art. I took an interest in that for a bit after my teaching certificate course—every good teacher should go back to basics once in a while.      You’re not wrong, luv. Never hurts to remind yourself that sometimes it’s your job to make people feel capable, not overwhelmed.

Rather chilly this morning, ain't it? I’ve just boiled the kettle and made us a pot o’ tea. You lot fancy one?      I’d murder for a cup, thanks! Got to keep me brain running for Chemistry this afternoon. It’s a bit like staring at a coordinates grid and wondering if there  is  a formula for brain freeze.      Oh come on, lad. A bit o’ revision never killed anyone. I used to love watching Brian bless me nan’s brains with her books when she was me size. Funny old things, books. Gave ’er more use out o’ life than knitting.      That’s because Brian only read ’em in bits and bits of light. When the electricity went out, so did the learning! I had to count sheep in them, bless ’im.      Oh dear, aren’t you two a pair. Right, then, I’ve been thinking – since you’re both at home, maybe we could plan that shopping day to do up the spare room. Emily over at the mercy shop said she’s got some lovely bookshelf sturdy enough for maps and riddles, quite a few to choose from.      A bookshelf? Sounds good! I could put my Geography project on it. Though I – er… borrowed a couple o’ Grandad Brian’s old books for “research.” Doesn’t quite know that they’re all about sailing and whatnot.      Aye, lad, someone’s gotta read to the sea dogs. I once tried to write a letter to a ship out in the Med, told ’em I worked the docks here in Hull – all I got in reply was a biscuit about the size o’ a fly’s knee and a postcard of a lighthouse. To be fair, though, it were signed by some officer with handlebar moustaches.      Oh, Brian treasured that biscuit like it was cut by the Queen. He said it was a biscuit with  class .      Right, enough biscuit talk! We’ve got a room to sort and grandkids with lunches to keep on track. Would you like to grab a coat and set off, love? We’ve got a couple o’ hours goin’ on before it gets too nippy.      Yeah sure, I’m in. Although – just one question: when we get to the mercy shop, is it allowed if I take one o’ Brian’s nautical tales to read under the new shelf to “get into the vibe”?

Rather annoying this new satnav eh?      Aye, it's guiding through the pews of the church, not the road! It's laughin' at me sure enough. Best chuck it out the windae!      Don’t be daft Andrew, it’s only een! I remembah weel when they didn’t even hev maps in cars. Nae a guide but Auld Nick himself would knaw this road back to Timbuktoo.      Well, you might ken the way from here to Muirhouse but the satnav isn’t fetchin’ jokes! Still, it’ll be a nice drive once the roads are clear. You know I like a good curve in the road, especially when it’s not a plot from one of my own books.      I’ll be the judge of that if you crash us into a gig! Wait, it says turn right at this cow field here... I’m sure this was a planting field not a cow feth in 1998!      You mean when we both got a bit tipsy after ceilidh in Lockerbie and ye tried to drive back and ended up on the wrong side o’ the country? Nae bother, it was a good laugh. Though I remember that collar bone injury fairly well, still rattles when it rains up north.      Aye, and Silvia was meant to be our plus one that weekend, she never did make that gig in Dumfries. Just a stone in a field and a hangover later. Some weddings eh?      Some indeed. Still, at least we had your colleague, Neil, to bairn me back to us. Bloke can knit better than he can drive.      Neil? Nae that school rhoast and handlebar moustache galoot. My, time for a cuppa and a sit down at the gig. They’re playin’ a ceilidh tonight, nice and lively. I hear there’s a ceilidh band who are from Glasgow, and that they’ve een written a bit of their own tunes.      Now, that is no far cry from a writer's dream then. I’ll get the pen goin’ on that ceilidh stage once again.      Just don’t forget to mention the mud, the bad sig’n, your crooked tie and how you tried to dance to a kilt’s tune wi’ those loafers on!      And you in that ‘dancing queen’ skirt and them glasses like binoculars! You were near to collision course wi’ the fiddle player.      Well, we've had many a journey to and from such places over the years, and now it seems, we're still dancing in our own little world.

Rather skip the new barista today – I think they grinded the coffee beans for the smoothie section by mistake. You want to order first before I’m tempted to make a scene again?      Honestly, with the amount of coffee I've consumed since our dawn site visit, I think they might have grated my  bones  into this one. Give me the same as always – black with a dollop of nutmeg, if they still have stock.      Imagine what Dan’s like right now. You remember the guy from the depot team? Apparently, the site manager has been riding him like he's juggling wonky rebar. I heard he's been taken off plumbing inspections for "clarity of purpose".      Yeah, he tried to redesign the electrical setup for safety, and they called it "overreaching". Half the team is too scared to voice concerns. Wait, does he even know how to read a socket circuit?      Don’t! That’s what the site manager told him in the staff review. He was like “Mr. Jacobs, I had inappropriate educational ambition.”      What did he reply? I love that bloke.      He asked if it was against the staff manual to request a – and I’m quoting – “semi-serious act of self-punishment” like being set on fire to “decrease cognitive inflation.”      God, he’s a saint. Who signs people up for this sort of insanity?      Tell me about it. We’d better not be in the mood for being “empowered through crude feedback loops” when we start our new university project. I hear the architecture brief is the most litigious, chaotic thing I’ve seen in 10 years.      Yeah, communal spaces for students? That just means they want every room to be guest speaker proof and tragedy resistant. The health and safety board will probably want a fire exit per desk.      You’re getting your stick out already? I was thinking about suggesting we split the space like a modern co-living setup – flexible zones with acoustic separators.      Co-living like in the '70s, but with better loo paper. If we can manage that, I think we’ll out design the brief before the box gets delivered.      So, have you made it to the conference seminar yet where they discussed those “girls” in the new muralists' collective? I heard they were doing something architectural on silence and sound.      I did. Very Channel 4 drama kind of thing.

Rather annoying the new kid in the playpark isn’t she? Always sticks her nose in and takes sides. I got to go home mid-session after she sniggered at me for talking to the wrong kid!      Yes, the one who looks frightened half the time and then suddenly yells at you if you passive-aggressively look the wrong way?      Yeah, her! I don’t know if she's got a clipboard or a pulse under that green coat.      You might be doing the right thing avoiding her though, don't want to feed her ego like the others. Still, it made me chuckle when someone said out loud "I think she's like that MySpace look, but outdoor education."      Probably, but I would never say something like that. I think it's just jealousy because most of the other ladies here are better at breakfasts and baking then playing this mastering everyone with a clipboard in a park routine.      They are definitely more maternal and less management. I would expect that from Waterstones or a yoga studio - inappropriate clipboarding is the speciality of the land!      Haha! Tell me about it… watching her try to trot rhythmically when all the other mums are just doing their laps with their respective partners and/or kids is a comedy act. One time her dance failed and she tripped and dropped her clip board.      Oh no! Like a someone at Spilsby race course with a clipboard missing?      Exactly! Only instead of race horses, it was preschoolers being their usual curious and untamed selves. They all started encircling her like she was a type of roundabout! She looked like she had wings and a clipboard missing and thought she was suddenly the newest ride in the park.      My, my! Then someone like Enid or Janet passed by, probably with a baby in a sling and a thermos full of tea and thought it was a perfect time to rescue her.      Oh they did. And then they all went off to a new area of the park like it was a heist set and delivering something around with trolleys and baby carriers as go-betweens. I think it was a real organisational disaster!      It could go further, imagine someone from the Financial Times writing about it all as a big management metaphor. Like "she represented poise and purpose, while the children were her organisational elements."      Only except at the end the clip board was irretrievable and she had to hold her clipboard in her child's toy bag, which was clearly too delicate for the job.

So did you read the job description throughly? I remember they mentioned they wanted someone with experience in both print and broadcast journalism.      I did actually. I highlighted the key requirements. The problem is, I only have proper experience in the radio side—some print stuff is on my portfolio, but it’s mostly self-published blogs. Do you think that’ll be an issue?      Maybe not. A lot of employers nowadays value a show of initiative. You can frame those blogs as supplemental or as a way you’ve maintained your understanding of written journalism outside of your radio work. You could even compare the content styles of both formats. That might show a depth of understanding they’re looking for.      That’s a good point. I suppose the interview is going to be the real test then.      I think the structure is a mix of general questions about your media background and technical questions about editing and production values. Should I read through some of your old scripts from Leeds Radio?      If you have the time, yeah. I’d love a fresh pair of ears, especially one used to listening for nuance in language. You’ve marked students’ essays and theses, after all—you’ve probably got a good eye for spotting rhythm in speech and structure.      I’m flattered, but I think it’s more about listening for the clarity of expression. In interviews, especially for media roles, what you say and how you say it are just as important as someone’s technical knowledge. Let me read through a few of those old scripts.      Thanks, this means a lot. I want to make sure I come across as confident, but not arrogant. I don’t want to sound like someone who’s just talking the talk without walking the walk.      You know that line you used in the series on community radio? The one where you said ‘broadcast is the heartbeat of a city’? That was beautiful. It shows you have a strong voice and something to say—exactly what someone in media should be looking for. We just need to sharpen your pitch a little.      I think I’m starting to feel more confident already. Once I get through this, I can start thinking about applying for the wider network roles. But one day at a time.      One day at a time. And between us, you’ve got the background, the drive—and now you’ll have the technique.

So, I’ve been doing a fair bit of thinking, Sarah. I know it's been a while since I got out of university, but I really think it’s time I take the plunge into setting up a business doing what I’m passionate about. That workshop thing—  Lifestyle Ecology  —I’ve been running for the holidays, yeah? It’s been going really well.      Yeah, I remember that. You were talking about permaculture and helping people create gardens that are both productive and sustainable. That’s a great idea, especially nowadays. So you're considering turning that into a proper business?      Exactly! I’ve started researching a bit more and talking to people in the industry. Being in Australia’s been a bit of a cultural shock for starting a business, but I’m picking it up fast. I think there’s a real niche for what I want to do here, and it better suits our values—like sustainability and community.      And what about me, love? You know, you didn’t have to mention me. I’m just going to keep teaching and forget my dreams of being a full-time artist?      No, no, of course not! I know you’ve been watching for the perfect opportunity to mix teaching with your art. How’s the mural project with that school in Melbourne going, by the way?      It’s amazing, honestly. The kids are so engaged. And the school director loves the idea of turning art into part of the curriculum. Maybe I can work my own art practice into that.      That’d be brilliant. So, let’s be honest—what if we  both  do what we love and support each other’s ambitions? I can handle the business stuff, and you can focus on designing projects and your own portfolio. Teamwork makes the dream work, right?      That does sound like the dream. But tell me honestly—how much are we talking? Like a weekend business or a full-time commitment?      I’ve been speaking with a business coach from the local co-op here. She’s mentioned space co-sharing and coaching programs. So maybe we do part-time together, building it up slowly, learning as we go. That way, we can go at a pace that works for both our worlds.      That makes sense. I’d be behind you, 100%. But also behind  myself —so if I ever want to take it full-time, I can.

Rather annoying this new school situation, isn't it? Every time we try to enrol our little Jamie in a nursery or primary school, they’re full up like buses. I’ve had to call nearly twenty places! It’s mad. Not to mention they have to wait until they’re four now in some counties.      I understand completely, dear. I taught at a primary in Glasgow years ago, and I’ve seen things tighten up over the years too. I remember when we had space for thirty children in a class. Now you're lucky to have twelve. Didn’t it get worse after the big migration from Poland came through?      Oh, goodness, the Polish community has helped out quite a bit in the local supermarkets, bless them! But yes, it’s put pressure on schools and housing for sure. It’s a good problem in some ways, but then housing is now about as rare as a fresh breakfast on a Monday morning. I mean, house prices have gone through the roof, thanks to London people moving out, ordering online deliveries and expecting a place to pop up for nothing—ha!      I’ve noticed the influx of people from the capital as well. It’s understandable, really. London’s bloody expensive and crowded. My circle of publisher friends all moved out post-pandemic – Brighton, Bristol, the Cotswolds, you name it. But while the demand is high, the supply is next to nothing. If I could blame one thing for that, it’s the politicians’ obsession with ‘policies’ over practicality.      [mumbles with a mouthful of potato] Mama wants to go here!      Oh, there we go, about our little man. I’ve started trying to control the sugar rush with some diet changes. We switched to more vegetables and water instead of juice. Doesn’t sound too glamorous, but it’s better, don’t you think?      Absolutely. A healthy diet helps with the sugar spikes and any afternoon meltdowns. I tried cutting out processed foods with my students once. It had a  noticeable  effect.      I think it helps to have patience with the little ones, too. I remember my own children – they started their first proper go at computing on smartphones well before they even had a real desk! You simply can’t separate today’s toddlers from beards, blokes, or what your iTunes playlist was in 1998.      Haha! I think Jamie is more interested in dad’s beard than the iPad at this point.

Rather annoying the new car park rules, aren't they? I've had to get a pass for the local shops, and I've had no luck sorting it yet. I can't be the only one with a problem, can I?      No, you're far from the only one. Got eeny weeny passive-aggressive note on the windscreen saying if I wasn't in the allocated spaces I'd be banned from using the area altogether! Honestly, I thought I'd had enough of all that pulling in to do a bit of weekly shopping. You're never outside more than ten minutes these days.      It really does take the joy out of everything. What with all the other things on our plates at the moment, too. I remember you mentioned not feeling too well last week, are you back on your feet?      Pretty much. It was just a bug, really — better now. Felt old then, I mean. Not a week in the early spring, planting the garden and weaning, to not have a bit of energy to speak of.      My, yes, we must listen more to these signs of age. What with all the exercise and everything, and then still we go on like we are 25 again. Speaking of which, have you been for your usual cycle with the others?      Not recently. One of the regulars took to running and the whole group was after it, poor things! I made a pretence of going out with them one morning and collapsed within a mile. Walker time it's been.      Ah, well, better a bit of being stationary than pushing yourself too hard. I spoke to my parents last about our old school friend Ann — you remember the piano recitals she used to do? — what with the referendum and her family heading overseas now, she's moved out of the country entirely. My, time for her to play for us has gone passed.      Yes, the year after I was at sixth form. We haven't seen her for years. I hope she's well. Those were such exciting times though, weren't they? Sixth form was the big whammy for us, going out, meeting people, learning a bit.      Indeed. Looking back on it, I sometimes think I could go back for another go just for the experience, not because I didn't know what I wanted to do all those years.

Rather than share a text-based version of our request, I recommend we use this format to engage with the typist in the most efficient way possible. Otherwise, we’ll end up with something that reads more like a novel than a conversation.      Fair point — wouldn't want it to turn into een feuilleton, eh? Though I was actually wondering if we could use this as an opportunity to explore how we balance online professionalism with just having a bit o’ fun. You're da communications man, so you'll ken why I'm asking...      Aye, and well you should — I spend half ma day trying t' convince folk that a wee post o’ a drink guid nits in da office ain’t a PR nightmare. Crichton left a photo o’r team dinner on the main board. Roared o’r customers up! Half expected an inquiry for health an' safety!      I've been dae same — in ma university role, I deal wi' hides, academics who think da Twitter is a place to bleed opinions directly intae da public domain wi' no filter. One of ma colleagues recently put up a poll about whether students ken paraphrase. Hilarious ... but no in a professional way.      Aye, it's a knife edge. Ma view is that, like, it adds a human face t' an organisation — but ye've got t' have da tools t' control da message. I set up a dae-up group at work called #BrucefieldUpdate. Guidly a whitewash, but at least naeone's furyin’ in the comments sections.      I like that, Neil. We could do da same — though I'd be bolder. Think o' it as part o’ what we call ‘affective branding’ or ‘personality-driven marketing’ up yir way. My students like that kind o’ stuff — licht-hearted, human. They engage more, they remember it.      Och, but there’s a balance. I could see the bairns at the office being asked to post somethin 'funny' aboot da weekly team meeting an' takin' it a wee tae fur. Last man posted a photo goin' dae his eyes while sittin at his desk wi' a caption, “Thuressday team meetin’ vibe” — thirty reports an' a meeting summitted o’ it!      We've seen that, too. But, hey, it's part o’ da culture now, right? Social media is like that. Sae long as we ken where t' draw the line. I tell folk, it's like casting a net — y' can cast it as far as ye like, but ye’d better no期望 it t' catch fish ye dinnae want t' serve at da dinner table.

:  [currently chopping vegetables]  God, I am so grumpy. I had such a busy weekend with work... got home Saturday at midday and was already feeling down because I had to call off plans with a friend for a project meeting. Then Sunday, I had to stay in all day again. I haven’t een breathed properly since  sigh .     : Oh no! Sorry to hear. I’ve been working too. I actually had a night shift on Saturday, but I watched a comedy dump session once I got home and was decent. You should’ve called when you were feeling low. You know I like to help with project stuff if you need a second opinion.     : Yeah, thanks. My brain just couldn’t focus after that though. I’m not sure if I made the right decisions in the emails I sent today. Do you have a minute to glance over them?     : Of course. I’ll just finish my soup and be right over.  [pauses]  Wait, how did the team respond to the budget changes? That was your main project this week, right?     : Yeah, I think most people are okay with it. I only sent two rejections, but they were both strong ones. Honestly, it feels like I’m walking a tightrope. I want to stay friendly and approachable, but also prove I can be firm when needed.     : You're doing brilliantly, don’t doubt yourself. There are people out there who would flip a table over minor disagreements. At least you’ve thought it through.  [returns with a tablet]  Let me check the emails and be brutally honest, okay?     : Please do. I need to hear the bad news now to fix it. Oh, quick question—did you hear from Grace yesterday? I was trying to convince her to join a new book club with us.     : She said her mental health nurse told her not to overcommit. She mentioned being quite overwhelmed. I don’t blame her. You know how your schedule is these days—don’t overpromise. Even if it’s with people you love.     : Ugh, fine you’re right. I’ve made that mistake before. I’ll go talk to her again tomorrow about something more flexible. Maybe just a casual read-along? I really miss our group.     : Yeah, we should connect with them again. Maybe we can invite everyone over after next week? I can make some of that veggie stew you love.

Rather annoying this new car of yours, isn't it, Sarah. Handles like it's made of string and... Well, I don't know. I’m more used to the old model anyway. But hey, it is your cash, not mine. Look, speaking of things — our brother Andrew is coming in two weeks, and we should talk about the arrangements.      I know, Harry. We should clean the spare room, but I think that's all. He said he'll bring his own bedding, as it’s just for the weekend. And for the meal — what are we thinking? Chinese or Indian? Or perhaps something simple from Lakeland’s? I don’t want to make a big deal out of it.      Oh, you always talk like that, Sarah. But I’m not the one who flies off the handle if the lights go out. No, no, we’ve got to make it breakfast, no doubt about that. Like he used to — eggs, toast, and black pudding. Proper British, you know?      Good idea, Harry. I was just thinking, if we book the breakfast in, he might feel like we’re not as stressed. But I also thought, since today we’ve got this meal, why not have it in the garden? Weather is so lovely – no chance of rain. Fresh air and all that.      That sounds perfect. We did have quite the phone call with the travel company about his ticket, though. He wanted to change his travel date and they weren’t very helpful. Thank God I sorted it out. I can’t believe how difficult some companies make these things.      Aye, it's madness how everything needs a million clicks. I remember back in my days, talking to someone on the phone meant they actually answered you and not kept you on hold with some robotic voice. But I suppose it's to do with cost-cutting and the like.      On the bright side, he'll finally be home for something longer than a couple of days. It’s been far too long. We should talk about his voice. He’s doing a lot of singing with that band of his now, isn’t he? Wasn’t that you said, Sarah?      That's right. He really has found his passion again after all these years. I was at one of the gigs last month. He sounded brilliant, honestly. A bit raspy, but that’s just technique, I think.

Rather annoying this, innit? I’ve been tryin’ t’learn Spanish for ages an' it’s got me rather cheesed off. I’m more confused than helped with these textbook methods. Y’know, them conjugation tables an' all that.      Aye, it een't easy at all, love. I tried meself once, ages ago when I were workin' in Spain on a construction site. Got by with a few words an' a lot o' charmin', mind. But me grammar was like a dog's dinner.      You'd think with all them apps an' online courses, it’d be simpler now, but no. You can have like ten different ways t'say the same thing! Me Spaniards I’ve met, they look at me like I’m a right alien every time I try an' speak t’em.      Aye, I've noticed that too. I reckon part o' the prob' is we try t'earn it like a math lesson. Grammar over conversation. It should be more like, you know, talkin' t'someone in the market or in a café. Learn by doin', not book learnin'.      Oh, I got one o’ them apps that’s supposed t'be like speakin' t'a tutor, but the voice sounds like it's from 1940 an' it never knows what I’m on abou’! They chuck in castanets an' flamenco music like a bit o' background noise.  Bah ! Also, I've heard Catalans and Spaniards speakin’ to each other in different languages, and I about lost me head.      That’s right, luv. I remember walkin' through Barcelona an’ hearin' one bloke speakin' in that lispy, ‘castilian’ lot, an' then passed others switchin' to Catalan. One minute it's a land o’ scientists an' the next, you're in Aragon or Granada, an' words change again.      It’s a right whack! They're all supposed t'be in the same country, but it's like the North an' the South of England times ten! Why d’ya think they don't just choose one language an' stick with it? That’d make it easier for us foreign learners!      Well, history’s a bit messy, innit? I’ll not pretend I ken it all, but from what I’ve heard, religion, politics an' old grudges all played their part. But for our purposes, I reckon the best idea's to find a mate who speaks the lot an' try and chat to ’em.      Aye, I know some folks in them allotments on the park.

Right, I don't suppose we're going to get through all of this paperwork in one go, but let's try and sort it out by categories, yeah? I brought my laptop, so we can scan a few things in. Not only will it free up physical space, but it'll help me make a corpus for my upcoming assignment on colloquial British English spoken by older generations.      Corpus? Sounds a bit technical for me, son. Why don't you save yourself a headache and just chuck the old documents. We've nothing important from the nineties.      Dad, not everything can just be chucked. I mean, some of these old cheques or supply contracts could have historical relevance or at the very least, help with tax stuff. Plus, if you start throwing bits away now, you might chuck something that's still in use somewhere.      Fair enough. Though if we’re talking history, then I’d say your Mum’s kitchen in '93 was the most valuable document we ever stored. Still can't get that recipe for Christmas pudding right, even after over twenty years!      Hah, I remember that. You tried to replicate it and ended up setting off the smoke alarm. Still, maybe I should document it in my corpus. “Smells like – Mate, get out the fire extinguisher, it's not cooking, it's a chemical weapon.” That phrase would be priceless in a British idioms study.      There’s the cheek. While you're collecting data, maybe you can explain a bit more about how this scanning thing works? I’d rather not have a fire hazard and be left in the dark about modern tech in the same day.      No worries. Scanning the documents just means converting them to digital images so you can store them on your laptop or the cloud. It'll save you packing boxes in case of a house move or anything. Plus, it’s secure. If anything ever burns up, you'll still have a backup. Just like backing up my flight tickets before I go to Canada next week.      Oh yeah, off to Canada, are you? You flying with one of those low-cost airlines?      No, I’m flying with a proper service. British Airways. They have snacks and if you ask nicely, real coffee.      Hmmm, well I hope you manage better than when I had to cancel my online banking invoice with customer services because of some missing digits in my IBAN.

Rather annoying this, innit? Drove to the petrol station 'cos we was running low an' couldn’t get nuffin’ nohow. It were completely shut! Typical, innit?      Yeah, honestly, I’ve seen that more times than I like nowadays. I mean, I understand if there’s a shortage or something, but just completely out of petrol? It’s not like a petrol station only sells fuel. Do they even stock anything else anymore?      I know, it’s just mebbe the lads and lasses runnin’ round on bikes. You know what I mean? They’re mostly just lookin’ for a static to grab, drink somethin’, an’ maybe a fag. Still, who am I t’complain? I ain’t the one runnin’ the place.      Blame it on the bikers, then. I see 'em all the time in Herts; some are fine, others, you know, they just rev their engines outside for no reason and look like they're trying to scare everyone.      Aye, I get that. Out here in the North, you’re more used to trucks an’ lorries, but these little machine lads... it feels like they’re just lookin’ for a bother at times. Though I suppose it's all relative. Some of 'em are quite friendly when you get to talk to 'em.      For sure, I suppose it all depends on which ones you meet. But back to the petrol stations—don’t you think they should at least stock some kind of alternative fuel? Like, I dunno, electric cars are becoming more common now.      I know! I mean, the government’s saying one thing and the streets are sayin’ another. I know some stations down the motorway near York have started doin’ that. 'course, if you’re in the middle of nowhere, forget it. You’re lucky if you can even fill up.      It’s mad, honestly. I’m just wondering how prepared they are for a future where people drive less and cycle more. At least the cycle path near our place is getting decent, even if it does cut through the park by the go-kart track.      Oh, I know—still, better than nothin’. I mean, maybe one day we won’t have to worry about petrol at all. I just hope it’s not one of them 'one step forward two back’ situations.     Tell ‘em I asked when we get them electric charging points up near Sunderland so I don’t have to get stuck in a stalled car in the freezing cold.

Rather annoying when the grass isn't watered properly, isn't it? You can't get a decent first serve in and I've had to retrieve balls from more than one ditch this week.      I don't think we've had the tennis season as such yet, Martha. It was too cold and then the hail came last weekend. It was ridiculous. I reckon it played havoc with the court's surface.      Fair enough, John. But it's easier said than done to get a session in. We've been lucky to get two sessions in during the last three days. And you'd think the Wimbledon build-up would make people more enthusiastic.      I only got to play in the local tournament last Saturday. I didn't get to the final, but I did win the under-14s special Qualifier.      Blimey, Nicky! That's brilliant! When did you tell us this happened? I didn't even hear about it, love!      No, I told you a week ago over dinner. It was on the 8th.      Yeah I know, but I said it to you yesterday and only then did it sink in. It was brilliant, though. I mean, when I got to the final match – Mateo from Royal Grammar was absolutely pushing me, really making me prove why I’m there.      Mateo’s a good player, that’s for sure. His backhand is a work of art. But also, you adapted to his serve really well. I saw the match with my colleague, and he was impressed with your volleying through the match – said you looked like a seasoned pro at times about how you moved to the net.      Oh Nicky, I'm absolutely proud of you. You've been working so hard and it's really starting to pay off. That tournament result gives you the kind of platform you can use to aim for bigger tournaments next year.      Thanks, Mum. I don't know how long I can keep doing this. It's a bit of a struggle academically with trying to balance coaching with school work and homework.      That's true, but it’s not like you can’t manage it. Look at my cousins’ kids – they're doing both at the same time and doing just fine. You need to set a schedule and stick to it. It’s about time management, planning, and focus.      John's right, Nicky.

Rather skip the new pasta sauce, gran. That logo is just far too garish for my liking. We’d far better go with something traditional. I’m more than happy to take on the task of cooking this evening, as I haven’t cooked since the Easter fayre last month. Deer, it’s beginning to look a bit dry in this room, don’t you think? I’ve been thinking a lot lately about our holiday plans. If we managed to save a tad more, perhaps we could afford a bit of a journey somewhere fresh and green? I do miss the chase of walking through the hills.      My dear, I do so love a bit of holiday, but only if we can have a bit of turkey and all the trimmings to tide us over. Ten more pence from the co-op on pastry, and I think I could manage a rather astounding shepher’s pie.      Buckshee? I happened to read a bit in the paper about some planting initiative not too far from Kenilworth. Could make a worthy day out, and I fancied a spot of fresh air after the stress of this crop I’m keeping. A bit of insight might be helpful.      Sounds good to me, dad. I’m curious how the local market is faring?      Well, actually, the other day, while shopping, I nearly had a heart attack when the phone rang. It was one of the teachers informing me about the change in exam schedule. Spent my afternoon filling out emergency forms just like the old days.      Just the same as me, sorting through the paperwork for the farm grant. I did alright, but it remains a hassle.      I can see the pattern, but I’m just a project coordinator and not rolling in money. Still, I’m trying to keep up with both my job and this whole planning thing. Moments like these remind me how much I crave that bit more time to myself.      Oh, I hear you, my dear. I could use a bit more time and calm myself as well.      I think it's time we made some calls. My knees tell me I’m getting too old to sit on the fence forever. Let’s map out a weekend together. If we go tomorrow, I can line up the paperwork, and we could go from there.      Now that sounds like planning made simple!

Rather annoying I had to take the cat to the vet this morning. I was hoping to spend a bit more time working on my transcription project.      I know how that goes. It’s a shame, but at least we can finally have a quiet supper at home tonight. We haven’t had that in ages.      It was actually good I went. My blender isn't making noise like it should, and I thought I needed to fix it, but turns out it was just me imagining noises. Still, now we’ve got the cat and the blender situation sorted, I’m feeling more relaxed.      Still, I made sure I left enough time to pick up some Marks and Spencer food for tonight. They’ve got this new chicken dish I saw online, and I thought I’d give it a go. Rather than having the same old pizza for the third evening in a row!      That sounds promising. I’ve been wanting to try some of their new line, especially the ones with that 14-year-old wine reduction—just not over the £10 per plate.      I know, but I think if we spread it as part of the week’s meals, it could be worth it. I reckon the Marks and Spencer in town just got rebranded too – very clean look, fairly minimalist, and way more natural lighting than the old one.      It’s all very modern. I actually went in there last week for a quick lunch. They had a chicken and pesto pasta that was surprisingly good. It just reminded me of the one out in France—light, fresh, and delicious.      That’s a glowing review! I’ve been about to watch  The Walking Dead  tonight, but the  Trapped  vibes from a few nights ago have left me with that grim atmosphere still lingering. A bit of light cuisine to counterbalance.      Definitely. Although if you’re going to watch  The Walking Dead , it might be best to give us something hearty, like a decently sized salad with some protein. As good as  The Walking Dead  is, it’s not exactly appetizing.      Good point. I’ll set the chicken aside for after the meal.      Oh, on another note, how’s your appraisal at work coming along? You said you were due to go in last week.      It was good. I had a few points to raise, and the team appreciated my suggestions—there was even a new person to discuss delegation and workflow, which surprised me.

Rather annoying when the new boots don't fit right, innit? I was just in Chester ‘n all... got them dere, but they're nowt like I thought they’d be.      Aww, don’t tell me I got to listen to another moan about shopping then? I saw them on Instagram and thought “Aye, that’ll look good on ye”, but not if they’re knackered by the first walk!      If they don’t fit, just chuck ‘em back and go for somethin’ more comfy, don’t ye think? I saw Leah’s new heels in Derby and made sure I got me some the same, only to find me toes are black an’ blue by sunset!      Honestly, I go to the shops and end up feelin’ sad every time. I just spend an hour there and still come back with nowt, no matter if I’ve been wanting shoes or a new dress.      Nah, you lot’s always got so much fashion sense, I’d be lost without you girls tellin’ me what looks good. I always buy whatever puts me in a good mood, and if it goes with everything, bonuses!      Well, then, we should really plan a night out soon. Drink a few, dance, take loads of photos, and maybe pick somethin’ to wear next weekend!      That’s the spirit, innit? A proper night in one of them fancy places. I’d like summat classy but still a bit out there. Also, I crave a cheeky cocktail with something tropical in it —  maybe  a coconut because it’s about da only da ting I like about da summer!      I could be into that! Let’s meet up at some club and have a proper night out. I do need a ‘cosy up’ kind o’ dress ready for it. A bit more daring than the usual uniform we have on all week.      You mad, girl? We need heels as well. Comfort’s out the window when we've 'split shots and big plans!      Defo, I’m bringing my bestie along, she's got go-to shoes on lock and if she's there, so is the loosened-up attitude, innit?      Oh, what your lot sayin' is basically planning a night to remember, and I'm all in for that, don’t bellyache me to much on the way, ‘cause I might not walk at all!      Fair play to that luv, we're gonna be the ones they talk about, 'cos we've got the class, the heels, and the drinkin’ stamina to match it.

Rather annoying when the barista at my local café misses my name. I know it's such a common first name, but I always correct them. Otherwise I feel invisible. Not that I've been there that long, it's only since we moved to this place in Hungerford six months ago.      That is a bit frustrating. At least they didn't mix you up with Janet – that woman who comes in every morning before you. I once got a cappuccino with a hazelnut drizzle for her. She didn't mind, actually. Funny old thing.      You'd think the baristas would get used to regulars. I've had the same name since I was born in Kettering, after all. Still, enough about the café. I was reading this article the other day about imaginary timelines and how you could live the lives of different people in other centuries. Have you ever thought about it?      Mmm... I suppose if I could, I'd want to live during the Renaissance in Italy. There was so much going on – art, science, architecture. Not a pleasant place for a lower-level guy like me, mind you. But still, I'd be fascinated by the mix of culture and chaos. What about you?      Hmm. I'm not sure I want to deal with feuding families and toxic political intrigue. Maybe somewhere quieter. The 1920s in Paris? Montmartre, artistic cafés, and the roaring twenties. I could imagine sipping coffee with a French accent and smiling enigmatically.      Ah, now there's a real fantasy. Still, at least you’d be in a city that actually appreciates its coffee. Not like the monstrosity of my cappuccino from a few days ago. I ended up drinking it cold the next day.      My, you're quite the critic. Do you think you'd be cut out for imagining soul mates as well? I was thinking about it the other day. How you meet your perfect match, who just gets you, and that they've always existed in space or some weird quantum thing.      Some people believe in that sort of thing. I prefer the idea that the right person can go from being random to life partner through trial and error – and a few very bad choices in between. You know we were a total mess before we were a mess we could live with, right?      We certainly had our hours of earnest soul-searching, soul-baring, and soul-rouleaux.

Rather annoying the new tax rules, isn't it? Small business is getting more squeezed by the week. Mind you, I've been focusing on a few side projects lately—knitting patterns for a custom line of scarves. Nothing beats a bit of wool and a quiet afternoon.      Knitting? That's so different from anything I've ever tried. I reckon it's quite calming, though. I've been working from home this past week due to sickness, so I've had a fair bit of time to myself. Tried gardening, but I killed a basil plant in a day. Maybe I need some first aid kit to rescue it next time.      That's nothing, I can mend a broken fence and rewire a lamp with one hand. Practical stuff’s in my blood—from growing up around the factory floor. But I digress. Aunty Mary had an unfortunate fall at the old graveyard the other day, and I had to step in. Reminded me of when my old boss, ever so proper, fainted ordering puffin pie at a local pub. Classic culture clash—village vs city, maybe?      I can relate. A customer in Boston once got quite rattled by my use of the odd local expression. They asked me if I was from the “Dark Ages” – all because I said I’d be “up the creek” if the schedule didn’t sort out. All that language differences and stereotyping. It's no wonder people bring up the whole gun laws in the US at every dinner party—why not have a cultural exchange instead?      Some folks still equate guns with safety and violence in society with strength. I mean, it's as ignorant as thinking people about our generation don’t know the difference between the English lit syllabuses from South and East. My sixth form teacher was so strict with rho and sigma it felt like we were in a secret society.      Speaking of which, passed my test for that health and safety module the other day. Proper grueling it was, but necessary, you know. After getting your certificate, you feel as prepared as a professional firefighter. Next up: air conditioning systems maintenance and maybe even basic pet anatomy if the schedule allows.      Pets are a good idea—had a go at bringing one in life about seven or eight years back. Gave it away in the end, between work and the travel involved in sales roles.

Rather annoying this new tax thing eh? You know, me n mine we’un got cranked ‘cos we all got to pay some extra for local housing stuff. Blows! I thought uni would be cheaper!      I know, I know! It's  so  unfair. Me and een feller at uni, we were out for drinks last week and he said his mum helped him sort a grant but I haven’t got a clue where to start.      Honestly, I think it’s just another way to hit us students. Didn’t even get the full bursary because I was born abroad, even if I’ve lived here since I was three. Still treated like a foreigner. It’s turkey twizzle!      Oh you know! I had the same moan with Roxy and Gaz in our block last week. They actually rent out a room to a friend when it’s cheaper than paying this new housing tax... I’m thinking about doing the same.      You couldn’t do that, Emily! What if Landlord finds out? He’d chuck us all out. I’ve got it on good authority from Libs and Tom that he called the council on some fella for hiding a tenant.      True dat – Mate of mine got skunked and now he’s stuck trying to find another flat. Now don’t get me wrong, I like Libs and Tom, but they talk too much and never shut up.      Fair point. I reckon they just thought they were clever. Anyway, speaking of housing - did you hear that the uni is replying to all the accommodation applications next week? I nearly about wet meself when I opened the webpage the other week and it just said “processing.”      Don’t know why they’re taking so long, it's not like uni happens  next  year. Me and Danny applied ages ago, and his mate Max told him the system crashed a few times. Sounds like a bit of a dodgey mess frankly.      Yeah I know what you mean! Me and the lasses were on the message group the other day and almost all of us are still stuck waiting. Pissake, it's September goin' on October!      Honestly, I might just chuck in the towel and go home for a while until something sorts itself out. Cos you know how it is, if uni can’t sort housing we’d just be stuck, right?      Same here, ‘cause I’ve been working at the bar near campus and the boss reckons I got to be there at least two nights next week.

Rather annoying the queue at the supermarket, innit? Eh, least they had those crumpets in. I got the white ones with no holes this time, thought I'd try something different      Aye, crumpets are a fanny! But well done on getting the student grant sorted, dear. That uni place in Manchester was a good choice      Yeah, I reckon. A lot o' hard work but this project I’m doin’ on education policy is interesting as hell. Know you worked in the NHS for ages, Mu, so I might ask you some questions later       looking at his plate  What's a crumpet? Never seen one in the shops here      Yeah, no one back home eats crumpets as well. But this place is in Croatia, innit? So of course they’ve got something better      Aye, but still... I miss a good cuppa with some milk in it, you know?       smiling politely  Water with milk, you say? Well, in this country I can guarantee we have a very strong and very hot coffee for you. Have you tried it yet?      Be fair, I tried it at the hostel. It was fairly alright, but way too bitter      Then you weren’t asking for sweetened! You British are all ‘fix it with sugar’       laughing  Yeah! Like my man at home, he puts so much sugar in his tea it looks like a science experiment gone wrong       grinning  Oy, I did the same back in the day! But the doctor said my heart can’t take much more sugar      So you’re telling me it is uncool for my nan to be a ‘sugar monster’?      Aye and I told her the same! You lot are all scientists trying to grow worlds inside you       curious  What's a midwife do again?      Well, I’ve helped countless muggles into the world, luv. Picked ’em up by the goolies on day one if they were wailing too much      Ew! Never mind explaining further, I get it already       nodding seriously  Being in management roles, I know those challenges all too well—people problems, budgets, tight deadlines      Which one of us is gonna have the moped tomorrow then? Don’t forget, the bus is so unreliable once it's 80 degrees      To be honest, I swore I’d never let a child of mine ride a moped, but we’re all in the cycle, innit?       nodding  Just make sure to bring extra sets of clothes for all the dogs.

Rather a lot, I've got to say. That lighthouse we saw was just beautiful, real eye-opener after all these years.      Oh I know, I've seen a few pictures and it was quite somethin'. Was it the one at St Just?      Aye, that's the one. Light was shiner than the moon on a full Saturday night!      I think I know that place. I had a few kids tell me stories about pulling crabs off the rocks and nearly getting stuck by the tide during a class visit.      Oh, Horrors! I'd have nerves like a plate of jelly, I would.      My knees are still quakin', but it was well worth the walk up, I must say.      I think the lighthouse up there is actually one of the oldest working lights in the British Isles. Rather proud of that fact, actually.      And the scenery! No, you didn't see anything so beautiful in your time, Nancy. Just rolling over with green, and the sea shimmerin'      Like a gem in the sunshine, I'd say.      Sounds magnificent. I remember reading about a project where local schools volunteer at YHA places in Cornwall. I almost signed up but the journey was a bit much.      Volunteering at YHA? Oi, you should give it a go. Our group helped polish pots and mucked in with the cleaning, a bit of gardening here and there. Some hotter meals than this lot!      Still, at least it's a bit of light relief.      That's the spirit. I think the idea is to get more young people active and help out local youth initiatives.      And the youngster these days? Jolly, jolly lot. A few ones nearly pulled down the lighthouse on the first morning by trying to get a better angle for their photos.      You mustn't encourage the cheeky ones then!      Hehe, but it's the truth of youth. I took the kids in our road once for a cycle race by the coast, and the energy goin' on was enough to light up a town.      Oh, I remember you teachin' them all sorts, Tom. Must be nice to see all the changes.      Yeah, I'm quite proud of my time as a teacher to be honest. Got a few over the line into real places, even went to a few open days up near Cambridge.      I can believe it, Tom always was a dab hand at gettin' things right and helpin' others.

Rather skip the newfit sludge, innit? Eh, talkin’ ’bout las nights when we all got crashed out on tablets an’ now it’s all about smoothies an’ protein toast!      Chuffed if you like, mind you — I cannae be arsed een beginning the day with something that tastes like it’s bin scraped outta the fridge dreg barrel. Give me a plate o’ beans on toast any day.       laughs  Honestly, it’s just me grinding through another kale smoothie while you two are arguing over beans. You'd think the three o’ us who grew up eating processed meat would at least agree on breakfast, but nooo...      Listen love, I left Yorkshire primed for life, not for carb co-dependency! Qualify as a co-ordinator? Blimey, I’ve planned gig taller conferences breakfasts than whatever that thing is in your blender...      And I spent enough hides makin’ spreadsheets and qwickfire charts over full English that I’ve decided beans are the way forward, honestly.      Right, as if you’re choosing food for its nutritional content — no, love, it’s because you’re in a new relationship and want to show off?       laughs, swallows mouthful of cereal  Yeah, okay, you got me. Paul’s trying to win me over with his 'green juice principles'. Honestly, feels like I'm in a lifestyle show every Sunday.      Oh aye — you still seeing that Paul bloke?      Yeah, we’ve been seeing each other for a few months now. He’s a web dev living the healthy lit — green juice, vibes, and no sarcasm! Going stir-crazy trying to please him while still being  me .      Then just give him a bean on toast and a sarcastic comment — he'll know it's a pass or a fail.      You know, honestly? I think relationships are like events — you’ve gotta know when to take charge, keep the tempo, and when to just roll with it. Still remember when I got caught by a rogue queue system at that govt event I co-vordinated? It was a real organisational disaster!      Aye, but bloke, when what your actual job is to run events smoothly, and you let conference attendees eat in alphabetical order — well, I’ll not say anything to nobody, innit, ‘cause I was the last to queue!      Oh I love that story. Still, love, I think you’re romanticising it — did you at least feed the masses correctly and on-tide?

:  [currently chopping vegetables at the kitchen counter]  Hiya! I've just made us some soup — wanted to ask what you thought Barcelona was like this weekend. Blimey, I've been over here cleaning and suddenly it hit me we've not spoken since you left!  [pushes hair out of her face and smiles]      :  [sits at the counter with her mug of tea]  Hey! Aww, thanks for the soup! I needed it. Oh my god, Barcelona, though — it was  amazing . I wish you could’ve come with me. We went to this little beach-side cafe near the beach,  so  much better than the ones back here. Still, I miss you and the turkey curry you always make! So, what’s new with you?     : Aww, and I wish I could’ve gone! It must’ve been brilliant. How was the breakfast, though? You always hated the coffee here... I’m fine, busy, you know. Just lots of scheduling and team meetings. Also, I might actually go to Paris next month for a few days—my nan’s inviting me up. I’m seriously tempted.     : Hah! Tell me about it… I had to sneak extra sugar in my coffee just to survive. Paris – that’s awesome! I’ve not been, but I  want  to. I’ve been watching this French travel documentary all week, and I’m already planning what I’d do. There’s also this someone at work I’m considering asking out. He works in the office down the corridor.  [a flirty, awkward tone]      : That’s so  you ! Scaring off people about five minutes in. Just don’t try to touch the bandage on someone mid-conversation again, okay? Going to Paris is brilliant! I’m thinking of doing a bit of that freelancing gig I applied for while I’m there. Might earn some extra cash. And if you go on a date, you have to invite me out for a takeaway afterwards — or else I’m going to die hearing about it for a week.     : Hah, typical! Well, I took the bull by the horns and everything went amazing this time. I told him I was goin’ on a holiday, and he said he was going to Amsterdam. Thought it was interesting that we both had the same thing in mind.     : Ooh, big lives! So, what’s the next plan? Do you think we could go somewhere together?

Rather lovely to sit out here on such a peaceful Sunday morning. I confess, it's been a while since I got to enjoy some quiet with a proper cup of tea. Not much by the way of traffic this early, at least.      You said it. No better place than this for a bit of peace, especially with the view of the sea just out there. I actually enjoy these kinds of mornings. A lot less stress than the average Monday I deal with running my business.      Ah, business, was it? You're the entrepreneur type, then? I teach at a secondary school near home, so I’m used to the daily grind of the classroom, only with far fewer surprises like that one turkey who thought I was a fellow!      I had a few of those moments early in school too. But teaching must give you a nice routine at least. I, on the other hand, run a small digital marketing agency back in London, so the days are quite unpredictable, to say the least.      It must be interesting, juggling clients and campaigns. I used to work in corporate training quite a while ago, back when I lived in Dorchester. Nothing like this—it was all boardrooms and presentation decks. I left it all behind for the classroom: much more rewarding, in my opinion.      I can see why. Corporate life can be brutal if you’re not careful. I actually made a pivot from finance a few years back. Was in the system for way too long, and one day I just said— you know what? This isn’t for me.  So I took the plunge and started my own business. Not nearly as polished as I thought marketing would be, but it keeps me on my toes.      Going it alone is brave. I admire it. I could never quite step out of a ‘nine-to-five’ kind of life. Teaching offers autonomy, but I’m tied to the school year and the holidays, so it’s not quite as flexible. You must love having the freedom to make your own decisions.      Oh, absolutely. It’s the best part of it, even when things go pear-shaped. Then again, if you can’t laugh at goings-on on your own dime, who can you laugh at? Speaking of denting the budget, I might be in need of an honest critique.

Rather annoying me a bit, eh? Our new housemate. I mean, it's not like 'e's got to be 'ere all the time, but it's like 'e's always where we are. I don’t mind sharing t’ flat, but sometimes it's a bit much.      Yeah, I 'ave noticed that 'e’s always about. I don't know, I reckon I'd prefer if 'e was more... I don't know, respectful of our space, or summat. We've only just started sharing and it's already a right pain.      Right, I 'ear you. Last night I was tryin' to wind down wi' some Netflix an' 'e came in with bin bags an’ left ‘em right in t’ doorway. I 'ad to move the chair I was sat on just so I didn't trip o'er them. Ridiculous, innit?      Haha, yeah, that’s typical. I tell you, some folk move in and think the flat’s theirs. I was talkin’ t’ 'im the other day about t’ washing machine and 'e said as 'ow 'e only realises it's done when 'e takes a look. Ya'd think it'd be more polite to at least check it's finished before sneakin’ in 'is undies after me!      Oh, I know! It was the same wi’ the loo the other day. 'E just walked in an’ I 'ad to practically yell at 'im. I 'ope t' others are better at it. So far as I can see, 'e’s the only one, but we’ve got about five more people walkin’ in next week. Fingers crossed they’re more thoutful.      Let's just 'ope it's a case o’ one bad apple, ‘cos otherwise I dunno what we're supposed to do. 'ave a meeting or summat? I was ‘inkin’ maybe I could ask them about t’ rules when they get 'ere, like what they think of shared areas an’ tidyin’ up.      Yeah, that sounds like a good idea. Then again, if we started 'aving rules goin’ on, it might make it sound like we don't trust 'em. I’m just tryin’ to ‘old onto the peace, y'know?      Me too. I'd rather we could 'ave fun, maybe even like each other, but we can't have ‘im ruining our space or bein’ inconsiderate. I reckons I'm gonna 'ave to have a chat next week once they’re all 'ere.

Rather a lot, didn't we?      Aye, it's been a busy afternoon! What with the cold weather, I was glad to find a bargain on that coat. It’ll do nicely for the spring when we start going outside more.      Aye, spring’s on the way, though I don’t think I trust it just yet. My knees tell me not to count on it. What with this damp in the air, I’m feeling quite stiff. It was a dump of a journey back, but the bus service was running late again.      You don’t like the buses, George! Not when they keep you waiting. What I don’t get is why we can’t have a good service round here. The village got a new shop last year, but the bus still hasn’t improved. Still, at least the little place gave us a proper selection of vegetables.      Buckshee? I happened to like the old shopkeeper at the corner. She always treated me like a proper customer. This one? Young lass, all right—keeps getting things mixed up. I asked for tatties and she gave me a banana. Could’ve been a real laugh if I wasn’t on a diet.      Oh, you’re still dieting? Mate, you’ve been trying to drop weight for years. I’ve seen the photo of you in the army—still as slim as a pine needle then.      There’s old George. A full man now, but I won’t let a bit of bad fruit sour my meal. Though speaking of meals, mind the tea? It’s tea time now, isn’t it?      I did make a pot earlier. Decent tea, buttered scone with raspberry conserve. We can have some now. Need to put some colour in our cheeks after running around in that cold.      Sounds grand. Mind if I pour a glass of something? A little sherry won't ruin the day.      Not from me, but go ahead. As long as you don’t propose to me again. I've had enough of that in sixty years.      Sixty and still no takers, eh Mary? That's because goon is my best proposal, and even that's too much for some ears.      Darlings, you know I love arguing. Pass the scone. It won’t get better with sitting and gadding about all day.      It's a right laugh though. Still, over this and a glass o’ sherry I wouldn’t have my lot for no one else.

Rather chilly this morning, ain't it? I’ve just boiled the kettle and made us a pot o’ tea. You lot fancy one?      I'd murder for a cup, yeah! Got that maths homework due in Monday and the coffee at the library did nothing. But it was proper good on the cocoa there, I’ll say that.      My George used to say, a clean cup ‘o tea and a piece o’ cake, and you've got a right decent afternoon! That or a nice cuppa and me knitting. Those old jumpers, I still wear ’em you know, still nice enough even if they’ve seen better days.      Still, Alice, you always did have a steady hand wi’ a needle. I remember you mending George’s union jack scarf, careful as a cat with a saucer o’ milk!      Blimey, you two old lovebirds!      Now, don’t be cheeky, Ellie. You can have your tea and a biscuit, but don’t you go thinking I’m letting you off reading that algebra properly—there’ll be questions next week.      It wasn’t that bad, Miss. I mean, you’re not Mr. Beadle from chemistry. He’s the one who looked at me like I was some kind of toxic waste if I sneezed during a test.      Ah, now, back in me younger days, they didn’t give someone forty-three years for being soft! That was real discipline, not just a sour look an’ a red pen!      Oh, Ernie, don’t make your joints ache more by standing up about it! I’ve a mind to baste those slippers o’ yours.      That leaves me with the grim task o’ delivering the unmentionables to you two. But ‘course I do it willingly!      Now that’s more like a proper grandchild. Proper bloody cheeky, but I dunno what we'd do without you.      Ellie, what say we go to Malton market on Saturday? They do a ripping bazaar an’ there's always proper good tarts.      Oh Ernie, really, your life would be tart and nothing but.      Right enough, between you and the tarts, I'd say your conversation’s fixed. Alright, Ellie, if you’re heading there, we’ll come along—there’ll always be someone nearby to buy me a bun or two.      Aye, I’m game! Might be a good chance to get some new notebooks and maps for my geography project.      Likewise, and for me and the roses.

Rather annoying this, innit? We’ve been waitin’ ages for this internet company bloke to come fix the broadband. Never bin no luck since last week. I can’t even stream iPlayer proper!      I know, I tried to catch up on  Line of Duty  again and it kept buffering every five seconds. It was ridiculous. I reckon it’s worse in London than most places with how many people are crammed in one place.      It's all worth it once you get internet back, though. You lot never chase it, but once it's gone you can’t live without it. I mean, I still go to the café just to send a message on my phone if the Wi-Fi breaks down at home.      Probably safer to stick to café internet. I caught my nan in the hospital queue up for an appointment, just lookin’ better than breakfast, no doubt about that.      Oh don’t remind me of hospitals! My mums been looking for a home patch-up place for months now, like some kind of alternative to a clinic, you know—somebody that sells health products or one of them high-tech massage things. She still remembers the time I twisted my ankle at university and it was all just “just wait at the table” from the nurse.      Sounds like me old man. He tries to fix everything with a phone call or a “strong cuppa”. Once, he put me in a cast made out of plaster and bucket. That was just a pratfall at the end of the garden.      You lot and being hillside fitness gurus! Look, as someone who actually works about this sort of thing... the real story from uni wasn’t the lectures or vibes from professors—it was this one bloke that got obsessed with a self-made muscle-tracking device. He hooked it up to a speaker and it played Enya every time he flexed. Bizarre? Yes. But it worked for him.      Ah, uni stories always sort out the crackpots and the geniuses. I once wore a tuxedo to the open day—wasn’t invited, but I figured it would stand out. Course, I just ended up in goon bin with the crowd from the drama society.      I don’t see what's so different from blokes in tuxes to blokes in gym track-suit mats. You lot all wear costumes depending where you're going.

Right, I’m just scribbling down what we need for tomorrow’s shop. We need bread, pints of milk, some apples—oh, and more anti-itch cream, probably. That mosquito or whatever it was finally left Tom’s leg, but it looks a bit worse now.      That’ll be because of the bite, love. I tried to dab some of the cream on it a while ago, but I think he must have swooped off to play football instead. It was easier pulling teeth to get him to sit still than to slap on the cream properly.      It wasn’t  that  bad! I only did it ’cause someone said it might help if we left it alone and squashed the bug. I did leave it alone. Well, most of the time.      Squashed the bug? Tom, what are you talking about?      I, um… saw one of them buzzing round the kitchen in the early hours, so I… I thought, you know, if I smash it, maybe it would help with the bites? Doesn’t seem to have done though.      Oh no! Here we go. I tell you, that boy’s got more strength in his right arm than sense in his head. You can’t just –  ha!  – just smash one and think it’ll solve all our problems. You’ve got to clean that area up after, for goodness’ sake!       [chuckling]  Who said anything about solving problems? If you read articles like this, you'd know the best way to kill the insect problem is to kill them all and bring their bodies in a line to the desert!  [frustrated chuckling]  Or not. I’m just talking nonsense.      Honestly Ron, your sarcasm is brutal. Poor Tom won’t have it fixed up for weeks if the smell hits ‘em first. Let’s not add anything more to the shopping list unless it’s a deodoriser or something strong.      Honestly, I’m just getting distracted by the football talk as well. You blokes are always grandstanding with your stories. I mean, I’ve supported Bolton since I was 6 and I’ve got no idea how any of you even function in that world. But Tom, you’re not playing tomorrow. Not with that leg in pieces.      That bloke on the team said if we keep winning at 1-0, we might even get into the semi-finals! I don’t want to miss that chance just because of a ‘bad mosquito leg’ or whatever.

Rather annoying this, innit? I’ve been chuckin’ m’head for three days with this cold... got the sniffles and no luck findin’ any paracetamol left in the chemist. You’d think with all the luv we got for the NHS, they’d ha’ better stocks on hand.      Aw, blimey, that sounds rough. Have you tried a hot water bottle? I swear by ‘em when I got me gargle.
