An’ yeah, I know it’s a nightmare out there—ran out when me cousin was gettin’ bloated up from a dodgy takeaway last week! Not that I’m sayin’ the NHS supply chain is doin’ brilliant.      Oh, you know what’s on the telly tonight? That Professor Lloyd Grossman, he was sayin’ the government’s spendin’ millions on a new AI bodyscale recognition project—prob’ly to read everyone’s micro-expressions through CCTV. I’m bleedin’ terrified, Ken. It’s one thing havin’ a camera on me phone, it’s another if a screen can tell if I’ve got food poisonin’.      It’s not that mad, innit? I reckon the idea’s to spot when people got signs of cholera – especiall’ with all them vaccine checs that’re goin’ on. Though somethin’ tells me them algorithms might not know what to make o’ a sneeze from a cold.      Honestly, I’d rather just have time to rest up. I’m outta practice, and it’s gettin’ on m’nerve – all I wanna do is curl up and have about five misos. I don’t even fancy touchin’ the phone now.      That sounds blissful. I barely left the library yesterday. No time to step outside, let ‘lone check if the guest speaker was passed out or just depressed. I told ‘im it was a pass ‘n’ he said I looked accurate.      We should talk to someone at the hospital. Someone whose job it is to notice nuanced bodily signs whlle still doin’ the right thing. Though I expect even they’ve got their hands full with the vaccinated goin’ on about their symptoms and the unvaxed beggin’ for medics.      Yeah, blokes like Tom at your research lab—prob’ly got flu and feels guilty he’s not in Cambridge hospital hours after takin’ the jab. But I expect it’s better ‘n bein’ food poisoned again! I swore off homemade mulligatawny for a while.      Listen, let’s get this sorted out. Let’s call up and ask if they can send over some meds before Lloyd Grossman’s speech on ethical cameras ruins what’s left of me moods.

Rather annoying this gridlock at the shopping centre. I couldn't get the milk for tea time.      I had no luck either today. Drove all the way from the other side of town for a loaf of proper sourdough and came back with aching legs and a shopping trolley half full.      You'd think with all this technology we'd have lift-free parking by now.      Technology has changed many things, but not the way people park their cars. We've had the same struggles for generations.      You know what I like to do when I can’t get through the trolley queue at the butcher's? Make a visit to that new café on Oxford Road. They have the most divine quiches. I had one the other day with leeks and I think it turned me into a vegetarian for a while.      You're always trying to convert everyone to a vegan diet, aren't you, Rose?      I say the best thing to do is bring your own trolley and tell the person at the queue you're too tired to carry your basket. It’s unorthodox, but deadly effective.      I tried that strategy once when I got way too old for sprinting down aisles. I almost became famous because the cashier thought I was the Queen of England.      You know what else is lovely? We could post a photo of this game someone at the café played on Facebook. That way, the grandchildren will remember we had a life out of just walking and talking.      What game was that?      It was Scrabble. That game where you try to make the highest-scoring words. I lost terribly, but not because of lack of trying. I tried to lay a  quetches  on the board for 20 minutes until someone pointed out it wasn't a real word.      Ah yes, the elusive  quetches . A word I always thought was real, but as it turns out, it's just a beautiful failure.      That happened to me with  gleamers  the other day. I think the points I got go straight to my pride, if that's a thing.      Well, that's what we were doing earlier—playing scrabble. It was a proper contest. I made it to the final two roles before I was defeated by the word  geegle . Do you know what that is?      Is that a description of how my daughter talks to her plants?

Rather a lot of memories floating about today, isn’t it? I was just watching the lads string up those banners and I thought to myself—how times have changed since we used to schlep over to Hanover for the trade fair.      Aye, things were a little grittier back then if you ask me. I remember one time I nearly got run over by a forklift in Frankfurt. A German fellow with a mustache too big for his face told me sharply, “Wenn sie nicht rennt, arbeitet sie nicht!” Funny old chase when you think about it now.      Oh, you mean when I was designing that short-run litho press? You were in Frankfurt that day, weren’t you? I swear my left foot is still asleep! I had the Post-it Doodad, and I think I turned six corners wrong before I found the hall.      And then I showed up behind you after getting lost myself and nearly knocked you over! You looked like you were puffing out soot. Good times, those exhibitions—vast warehouses, stacks of printing samples, and endless coffee. I never did quite get the German for “limited edition,” but I understood it meant: “This thing will not work unless you write a check now.”      Oh, I remember, and how they used to line up for the paper samples! It was brilliant, really. Silky, beautiful sheets of press sheet after press sheet, and the inks—oh, they had a sort of shimmer to them. It made one want to invent an entirely new process each time.      And you pulled it off, didn’t you? That offset printing system about forty years back—Turnkey Offset-6000 or whatever you called it. I remember your Danish contact giving that frosty stare when you explained it didn’t run in 4-colour like theirs. Poetic, really. All that blinking machinery with that humming press, and the minimal setup time. It was ahead of its time.      I did what I could with a bit of brass and steam, and always trying to catch the right moment to whack the lever just so. I’d be lying if I said it wasn’t a bit of a gamble. But then I suppose life is full of those kinds of bets, innit?      And the box office bellowing at your exhibitions was you. I remember that voice! “Min kære kunder, come and try the new dry bellyprinting machine!”

Rather annoying driving down here, eh, Dad? I mean, I get why we’re doin' it— got to see some proper sea after all—but more than four hours in a car after school gotta be mad for y’r brain cells. Was school not enough today?      Aye een, I remembah me mam complainin’ about longer drives when I were your age. Though I reckon that was before all this “school stress” stuff got taken so seriously. So what was it today that made you grumble out the window like you’d seen a ghost, then? Still stuck on that geography exam?      Nah, nothin' like that. Though I still think "Worcestershire" is spelled wrong, you know? Like why is it Worcester and then "shire"? And what even is a shire in the first place? Like an area, yeah, but is it like a county or whatever?      Haha, you sound like me at five, naggin’ Grandad about etymology when I should’ve been makin’ a stew over the fire. A “shire” is basically an old way of sayin’ “county,” and it comes off Olde English, innit? Like, the land ruled over by a sheriff. So it's like – “where the sheriff is.”      Really? So “Worcester-shire” is like “where the sheriff was in Worcester”? That’s proper weird if y’ask me. Meanwhile, in London, we got boroughs an' none of them oddly named. Though what about Corn—Corn?? It's like “horning” in somethin’, innit? Cornwal? I about blocked the motorway announcer trying to work it out.      Aye, and not many know that it's derived from the Cornovii, a Celtic tribe. My, you're quite the language scholar today. Though I'd be more worried about getting lost than the etymology of any bloody county names.      Not when I got your GPS crackin' as loud as a bloke shoutin’ in the pub. Though I wonder what we do if it dies. I mean you remember that time Uncle Steve tried to find the farmer's market goin' on bike race about seven or so?      Yeah, almost ended up in pig pens in a bloomin’ field near your Auntie’s. Steve said it made for a good story though, after he was done with the pigs and all that grapplin.’ Still, that ‘quat’ pronounces “kin-wa” astonishes the m’lady to no end. My, where have you started, all this fascination with words?

Rather than chuck a bar of chocolate in the bin, I’m glueing it to the side o’ the cookie tray and calling it a flavour experiment, see? Blows minds, innit?      Div, we’re tryna make scones, not like some mad culinary art installation een Cambridge. Thought yer wanted to try out that new cuppa Aysha sent ye fer Christmas?      I swear Aysha got this off social media again; it’s got   20 steps  . Step one is chopping the raisins smaller than breadcrumbs. Step five is bloomin’ tea ceremonies like we’re in some Mary bloody Poppins film.      That’s what makes it posh, though, innit? The eccentric rich’s version o’ throwin’ stuff in the bin. But, nooo, Aunty Sharon says if she ain’t got a ‘proper culinary breakfast, no Bucks Fizz this year. Not a chance in hell she’s giving me the oversized 2024 calendar for wrapping paper again.      Right, forget the calendar—personally I’m just glaivin’ Aunty Sharon still didn’t tell us we’ve still got a cousin on the other side of Liverpool who’s a vicar. Absolute loony – Baptisms at Royal Ascot, cheffing for parliaments.      Nah, he gets invited for the speeches. ‘Balances the hills and toilets’ he calls it. Well, whichever, just don’t sour the lemon curd. Also, have   no   idea why it’s in a jar called  cream cheese . Prime betrayal right there about half the time.      Y’know this reminds me… my nan always said the secret to life was scorporately laying things out. No one mentioned that the bin, ‘cos she baked like 20 batches at once, stuffed 'em all into a freezer bag, told any ‘uns needing a snack to ‘just fetch from the Archeological Repository.      Right, but nan always knows the lunches of a couple of whippets in various orphanages. My grandad once opened a bag with three scones and called it go-to lunch on pond life if you ask him again      Y’ike that, but scones bloomin’ decompose your soul. Every time I have one I feel 30% more middle-aged.      It’s a sacred ritual though. Knows over half o’ Cuckfield were brought up on homemade scones and oatcakes and buttercups and chemical soft drinks.      Nah, we made our own adventure and our own ovenware. Still, you got that mixing, left long enough… sourdough, anywhere?   Speaker_3 :   Sour on what – the scones or the lemon curd?

Rather annoying driving instructor I've got. You know what they do. Just tell her it's ‘normal first gear’ and she’ll take it the wrong way. Blows me how someone can think shifting gears's that scary.      That is kind of funny. First lesson can be a bit of a shock if you're not used to it. Having done theory before helps, of course. You ever do a driving course before? Like one of those pre-driving school workshops?      Naa, just signed up with the instructor after the theory. Didn’t even want to test drive a car before getting in. My gran even laughs at me. She used to drive the Citroen 2CV and now I'm turkey on a stick with a Ford Ka.      I see what you mean, but maybe pick one of the modern cars? You know, with all the auto features. It'll get you more used to driving in town. Less pressure for the first few lessons, you know?      Could do. Just got the clanger of a bloke who thinks it's hilarious when I stall in a roundabout. I swear, half the time he counts how long I wait at the red light before going… watching for fun.      That does sound relentless. My Mate Laura had a fairly harsh instructor and ended up panicking so much she had to take a break for a month. Seems like a big deal to get over once you get the hang of it, though. How are your lessons going otherwise?      Better now. I got outta the area and focused on country roads. It’s calm and no traffic. No panic in the city, at least about rounding the corner and not seeing what's coming. She’s still a bit vibes off a clipboard, though.      At least you're getting out there. I bet the café here is a better break between lessons than sitting in the garage. Speaking of, have you tried the brownies here? They give it the full carb therapy!      Honestly? Not my first choice. I came in for a quick snack break with a mate a couple of weeks ago. Now I'm here every Friday for reflection and something sweet.      Yeah, go easy on the sugar rush if you've got another lesson soon, though. You'll either stall or zoom into the next box in the junction.      So true.

Rather annoying when the kettle’s still not boiled, ay? I was promising me a nice brew ‘fore p’raps adjournin’ to the garden, eh? Not a bad day fer a bit o’air.      Oh, George, you know well enough the kettle was boiling when y’went out, I was the one who boiled it just before! But I daren’t touch a thing without coffee in my cup or I’d swoon right here on the floor. It was quite a journey to the Gambia last time, mind you. Didn’t even get the chance to plant my little African violets right.      That’s because the roads are still potholed and they never told you, Elsie! I read about it in the Sunday Times – they had another flood in the same township last month. If I were you, I’d make a donation box and place it near the parish church for folks needin’ some supplies.      A donation box, Roger? You mean to gather spare coins so people can help others, or that newfangled thing where you get sent info you don’t really want? Bah, I’ve heard meself warned I’ve Münchhausen’s what they call it, fanciful things I make up from time to time. Ha – but it’s often the same with old stories, eh?      No no, not that Roger meant. Silly George, it’s just a wooden box with a slot for people to chuck in what they can spare. And speaking of boxes, have you thought about making a proper holder for the plants? I saw a nice design in a magazine recently – using an old tin can, painted and all.      Yes, Elsie, those can be very effective. I’ve a friend who turned some corroded water pipes into hanging planters. The twist was, she attached little bells, so that every time the breeze passed through, they'd chime. Rather surprising, actually. Thought it’d ruin the plant vibe, but it looked marvellous.      Bells, ay? Now there’s a word fer me: 've been meaning to do some ringin’ – not the church sort, but the rods with tings! The bell ringers go every Thursday on the lake if you like a bit o' action.      Oh, don’t go inciting George to anything near your age, Roger. It’s enough I have to help him manage the garden tools every week! And don’t forget, this morning you were late for break time over this very kettle again!

Rather annoying when a new app takes up so much space, isn't it? I deleted it like five minutes after downloading and my phone's already slowing down.      I've been telling you for ages not to download random apps that promise the world. You end up spending like an hour trying to set it up and then  boring —it never works properly.      Yeah, I remember that one from a few years back that claimed it could predict what friends you'd make forever. Cracked it. We ended up removing like ten people from our lives when it suggested they were toxic.      Honestly, who  chose  to listen to the dumb app? That was on us.      Okay, you lot talk like apps are this dangerous thing, but I like exploring what's new. It keeps things interesting. Besides, if you're too scared to try something new, when does the fun actually begin?      The fun part is usually the five-star awards we give, not the actual app. I still haven’t uninstalled that "viral recipe generator"—personally, it gave me three falafel variations.      And then we followed the steps religiously… ended up with falafel mix that looked like cat litter. Ha – Mate, you want to help me pick up these dishes?      No chance. I did mine already and now I'm happily watching this horror movie with subtitles in Swedish because the English version someone watched previously was too traumatic. Just trying to uncount the number of oddly dressed people now.      Don't you mean  intrigue , Margot?  Oddly dressed people ? I about wet myself laughing when the guy started bellowing liturgy at this haunted bus stop.      Oh that was you! I didn't know you could laugh in your sleep. But  please —I need someone to promise they will not start quoting the plot of  Hereditary  again. I think I had a nightmare yesterday about smiling figurines.      Ugh, that movie stays off my lips forever. I’ve been a little gun-shy about psychological horror since. My brain just  cannot  unsee that mask.      Honestly, I think it's more of a female phenomenon. I made my line of work out of figuring out what appeals to blokes—and horror movies tend to be more action-driven. Cannibalism, jump scares, exploding heads—we like those kinds of things.      Is it just me or does this make the food conversation from this morning even funnier?

Rather annoying this, having to rely on public transport when you get older. I’d much prefer a car like I used to have, back in the day when I was working.      Aye, I know what you mean, Arthur. I had a Morris Minor back in the sixties. Got me all the way from Costessey to Norwich and back on a Friday for the darts evenings with a few of the lads. Not that I do much of that now, mind.      Oh, don't give me that bleedin’ nonsense about the Morris Minor, Bernard. You'd leave the key in it even! And when I used to baby-sit your grandkids, do you remember that time the boot jammed shut and you couldn’t get the pram back in the car?      [Laughing] Aye, that was a right scene, wasn’t it? Still, it was a good car in its time. Hated getting stuck at the side of the road nowadays, especially with the lorry fumes and the clattering of those blooming Teslas.      Honestly, Arthur, I don’t get your fascination with cars. You and Bernard live on stories of decades ago. These days, I just rely on a little mobility scooter and the lovel – buses. Although, I’ve got a bit of a journey tonight back home. The last bus out of Harrow runs at half-past seven, and I don’t fancy walking three miles in the dark.      Why don’t you stay the night here then, Doris? We’ve got the spare room. Or I can give you a lift if I manage to get my hands on my key.      That’s very kind of you, Bernard, but I’m not a houseguest and I don’t fancy listening to you two reminisce about car models for three hours. My sister’s over the other way, and her son passed his test last week. He could give me a lift if I ask nice.      Aye, I expect your sister’s lad would be grateful for a cup of tea and a biscuit in return. Gratitude from the younger generation is the best way to travel these days.      Still, I reckon goin’ on public transport is more civilised. At least you get to see the world out the window instead of being stuck in traffic like when Doris drives.      I’ll have you know, I drive quite well for a sixty-year-old woman, Bernard!

Rather annoying this new traffic system on the M6, isn't it? I was trying to get up to Manchester last weekend and it took ages. I’m more used to navigating Dublin's clogged streets than this!      Yes, the motorways are such a maze now. I was trying to get to an airport meeting last month and got completely turned around. Makes me miss the old days of working on oil field development plans, where things actually made sense!      I’ve had some interesting experiences with journey logistics too. My job as a transcriber means I get to hear all sorts of travel anecdotes. Some of them make  this  motorway seem short and sweet!      Oh well, you know, I’ve only just retired last year, so I’m finally finding time for things I should have done ages ago. Like visiting relatives up North. I was thinking of taking the train, but, well… if I do drive, I suppose I need a car that’s more modern than my trusty, rattly old Escort.      Let me help you with that, if you like. I’ve dealt with enough development planning — even if it was for electrical and technical infrastructure on old oil rigs — to know a thing or two about specs and reliability. Tell me what you’re looking for.      I think it's important to take health into account as well. All that driving and sitting at home with the tea and biscuits can take its toll, huh? Our mum always said walking in the garden is better than sitting in a car, even if it's just out the back!      That’s very true. Lately, I’ve been feeling the old joints a bit more. I walk a fair bit, but it still catches up with you. Retirement is all very well, but it does mean you’re more aware of every ache and pain.      A little exercise certainly helps. I started cycling again last year — just short trips to the local shops and library — and it’s made a worlds of difference. You don’t have to cover great distances, just stay moving.      And speaking of moving — have you thought about where you might go? The housing situation in Dublin is so tense these days, with so many people leaving or moving in.      That’s the next topic on my list. I was thinking of buying a smaller house, maybe near your place, Speaker_3.

Mum, I just wanted to say sorry again about what happened with your bike. I know it’s been pissing you off for ages.      Oh, it’s fine, love. I’m just glad it got tracked down and returned, even if it took ages.      Got returned? Was it actually found?!      Yeah, it was found in town near the Boots on Friday. Somebody reported it just lying in a skip, covered in bin bags. Imagine that, dumpers probably thought it was broken beyond repair. But when the police checked, the GPS tracker was still on it.      Wait, you had a tracker on the bike?! That’s proper smart.      Haha, I did! When it got stolen back in September, I was gutted. But I thought I might as well be prepared if it happened again. So I got a tracker when I bought the new one this time. Cost a bit extra, but worth it.      No way, I had no idea. That’s like something out of a spy movie.      Well, I’m not in the spy game, am I? I just wanted to get my bike back. It was a bit of a struggle getting about without it. I’m used to cycle into work, you know, and with these roads in Hastings, it gets a bit of a grind when you’re walking every day.      I get that, but I also just walk into school. Although, I’ve been trying to use my bike more now it's not so hotter anymore.      That’s a good idea. I remember when you were starting out on your bumpy little bike, you couldn't manage round the hill past my old job. But look at you now—heading off to college and all.      Yeah, I just have to get into the hang of it. Geo’s been helping me practice. He’s got me on a WhatsApp group where we track all our bike rides.      Oh, sounds like the two of you are into cycling as well as everything else.      Haha, yeah, he's a proper biking guru. But serious, this tracker thing—should I get one for mine? I mean, if you've had it stolen once, could happen to me, yeah?      I’d say yes. Better to be safe. I’ll bring the one I used and we can look at it together after dinner?      Do you mean like, ‘tech time’ with Mumsie?

Rather annoying that the train’s delay’s cut short our time together. But at least it gave us a chance to play "Ticket to Ride". You all playing yet?      Oh, we’ve been hunched over that board for hours, Sarah. It’s a bit like teaching a bunch of bright eeny-minded students, honestly. Keir keeps trying to block me.      Please. You’ve only played once. I’ve got this all figured out. You draw routes, pick your colours, and watch the others trip over their own strategies. Didn’t even need the PhD for this.      That sound you just made, Keir, is the sound of someone thinking they know it all and then loosing unexpectedly. I remember playing it with Rhys’ boys over Christmas. One five-year-old shouted, “Blimey, this is harder than making a proper cuppa!” Made better tactical breakfasts, though.      Haha, honestly, the only strategy I’ve got is not letting the lads anywhere near the map. I like my wins simple. I do like the way it’s gone, though — I mean, we’re not in a classroom or griefing over something serious today. Just in a country cottage, with eggy soldiers, and humble “O okay” – “No problem” verbosity.      Hayley, you’re a support worker. All that emotional intelligence and you still rely on luck and blocking Liam? That isn't emotional intelligence, that’s strategic chicken.      Precisely, Liam. Hayley probably outmanoeuvred half your tactics and you didn’t even notice. Now,  that  is emotional intelligence at work. Sarah, I’m not bad at it, right? Or did I fritter my turn by trying to build another railway line to somewhere I didn’t need?      Honestly, you tried to route to Nottingham when you’d passed Manchester. It was wild. Like trying to teach a child something they don’t want to learn — all enthusiasm on your part, zero engagement on theirs.      That’s just how you learn. Or keep the game from being too straightforward, depending on who you ask. I did find this interesting parallel with the train derailments in the news the other week. It's not about how fast you go, it’s where you’re actually aiming.      Aww, Rhys, you could have just made it all about logistics and roles in society. Why bring the real world into it? But I’ll admit — the metaphor does work.      It's a game, so let’s keep it simple for now.

Rather annoyingly, I've got to do a six-hour train journey back to London tomorrow, so I wanted to make the most of being here. Otherwise, I’ll be staring at a textbook the whole way.      Aw, don’t remind me—get on with enjoying the weekend! You know I'm the sort who likes to leave things to the last moment, so I’m actually jealous of your planning.      Fair enough! I just got to be in a rushing job all the time as it is. So, anyway, what do you say we try out that co-op board game you bought the other day? Still haven’t made sense of it, but the box says it's "spooky"—and what’s spookier than being cooped up with a qualified educator?      Droll, but very droll. Alright, let’s take it out then. Cats are better at breakfast, but board games need to be devoured after dinner in my opinion. I’ve also got a couple of new ones delivered earlier this week—tentatively titled "Fiesta Feud" and "Cafe Chaos" — sounds promising doesn’t it?      Hmmm, only tentatively? Have you tried them yet?      Well, no. I’ve been too caught up preparing for that conference I’m giving on postcolonial theory next week. You know how it goes—there’s never enough tea or time. But we’ve got our weekend, and I want this to be full of fun and mischief.      That's oddly endearing. Some lecturers are all about academia, and some… well, they still like board games and curry and good wine. I do like that about you.      Reciprocated. Honestly, I’ve always found the idea of that academic world—lectures, research, meetings—rather dry. But, personally, I need the structure it gives me. Board games are my way of balancing it all. It's something removed, something playful.      You're getting your postgrad to talk about  balance  again. And also, trying to sound profound. I can see your students being terribly intimidated. But yes—games are something different.      Don’t go getting too smug. I do have a few glasses of wine loosened off in the evening, between planning and explaining box contents.      Exactly! So how many glasses can we manage before we start mishearing the rules of "Cafe Chaos"?      I’d say three—possibly four—depending on how drastic we become. I’ve also got that brandy they gave us in the Christmas party, so it can be a balanced drink-based evening.

Rather annoying the new council’s bins. You know, they do everything they can to make it harder than it is, don’t they? Just went through three bags of waste before I finally got the right bin for this week’s bin day.      Yeah, well, at least it’s not the beginning of the  move , then. I can’t believe we’ve already had all the furniture out. I’ve only just started working on the sideboard and I’m already cracking my knuckles.      You and your DIY. You always say you’re going to do it properly and then... well, let’s just say  this is going to need more than just a few paint pots.  You like doing it yourself, don’t you?      Ten out of ten for the compliment, A, but I’ve been co-ordinating projects most of my life. Cats, moving flats, even tracking down lost shoes – mastering organisation has been in my blood.      That’s Ken’s way of saying he likes the challenge. Or at least pretending he does. Come to think of it, speaking of organisation – I never did quite understand why they made you move the hob and everything. You’ve got a brilliant little kitchen, why mess it up just because “style” is the new black?      It wasn’t  just  style, Nana. We did have problems with the heat from the old one and the cookware we’d bought. Our food just wouldn’t cook properly. At least not to my standards. Besides, we had a  bit  of a fire drill a couple of years back. Still got the singed wall to prove it!      Her steak well done was a real problem for us. “Cooked properly” meaning black and not edible. But she insists!      Maybe I’ll do something less ‘well done’ tonight. To celebrate moving into the new flat. I have been planning a casserole. It’s been a long few weeks, you know. Painter, bin lorry, even a mysterious yellow sprite of a lady who always comes with a plan for the “hazards of location.”      You mean the health and safety man? Oh yes, that’s my day job if you don’t mind – avoiding the cold calls from the medical people that will come with the boxset binges and whatnot.      I seriously asked why we needed one in the kitchen. “Products” and “storage” – I had forgotten life could sound so ominous.

Rather annoying this traffic, isn't it? I mean, do we need this many cranes and roadworks in North London?      It's part of their grand plan, I think — to destroy every major road before rebuilding it. Look, we're making progress, though. Sort of.       laughs  Progress is inching forward on the 12th roundabout on a rainy day. What I don’t get is this obsession with carparks. They’re just going to dump someone else’s car in the space I needed for mine.      Still, isn’t it better to have delays than driver’s ed? I remember learning from the back seat of my dad's Ford Cortina. One time, I swerved into a lamppost — just grazed the front wheel.      I think modern cars are just too forgiving for that to happen. Though I almost got into a scrape last week — happened when someone tried to zip into a gap I didn’t see.      Road rage is a national crisis over here. Last month I was tailgated by a man in a老爷奔驰 I think he was quite drunk as he made several aggressive gestures.      Honestly, watching him reminded me why I prefer public transport. So — mother — –?      Yes?      Could I get a new set of car speaker wires next time you're at the electrical shop?      There are more urgent things at stake than your music system. Like why you haven’t thanked me for the magazine subscription — you know, the TLS.      Er — thanks for that! Look, it’s because most people I know are moving to digital — you can just touch the icon and it gives you the whole review.      Not like the physical one, is it? There's that lovely smell, the way the pages crinkle — no distractions. I actually read that cover to cover on the train to France last week.      Ah, France — I always wanted to visit to clear my head. Though being academically-trailed with lunches and wine and writing articles probably isn't your ideal holiday.      Then again, stopping at the village market and goading the elderly man who sells cheese about his cat was rather fulfilling.      Hopefully I’ll be in a position one day where I can go without lecturing someone on historical context.      Just don’t start writing earnest think pieces like your old editor does on the state of ‘the soul in the modern age.’ We both know what that really means.

Rather skip to the bar an’ get a pint, innit. I’m starvin’ mad! We’d got to adjourn this annual pub session at The Poacher!      Aw, hush up, Chelle. Look at us—half our group is gone abroad for uni again een Mumba’i and Berlin. It’s like   Viking   funerals without the bones, innit? A right laugh.      Yer bleedin’ right, Dan. When did we last all chuck ourselves into the boot of me cousin’s ancient Fiesta and drive to some grim seaside town to pretend it was Disney World? I still reckon that abandoned caravan park in Blackpool was some kind of coded MySpace message.      Oh, you lot! I ain’t forgotten the time we all thought we were in a   rollickin’ adventure   by going to Kendal for breakfast, and then turned up to a cafe with a sign in Welsh and a ginger charlady who thought we were ordering puffins.      That was iconic! I swear, you lot had me in tears—“We want two plate o’ banana toffee and a   jellyfish   washed down with… well, what  is  this then?”      Mate, jellyfish is not on the menu because they don’t exist in the Lake District! It was toffee   sauce  . Still, ‘Balloon Brex’ as she called me was someone who could read my name in Latin.      Bloke at the bar said something’d dropped out of his trousers into the soup—ain’t that the  best  bit?      I’m not even mad anymore. That trip was a chaotic fookin’ mission. But I’d do it again. I’d take it as a  rite of passage —turn up to Kendal like we were in a film called  Eat Sleep Worry Repeat  and then leave a positive review on TripAdvisor.      You mad or what? We were 18. You think TripAdvisor’s for folk trying to find puffin and chips?      Me grandad once said something unkind about a pie man in Doncaster goin’ on TripAdvisor. I think he  lied  for years. Thought it was a charity.      You know what your problem is, Izzy? You lot never settle down and start roles in accounting like moi! I’ve had to stop hearing tales like “lost in the ‘ooly shuffle of Cumbria” and   “  close encounters of the toffee kind  !”      Listen, Chelle, if you don’t cut the slang, I’ll tell everyone about the time you tried to wear slippers to the office open day and confused them for sandals.

Rather unusual to talk about wild winter camping in a conversation, isn't it? But it's a hobby that I got drawn into some years ago after reading a bit about bushcraft in an old field journal. You see, it's not quite glamping, I assure you! You wouldn't dream of having a tent and a generator out there. Just the essentials—and the   severe cold  .      Aye, now I can just imagine that! Coming from Oxford, I've done my fair share of reasonable countryside walks and stays in the occasional cottage, but never outside when it's  actually  winter. I like to keep a bit more  civilisation  near, if you know what I mean. On the other hand, you look rather comfortable living with the wild.      I do now, yes, but it takes some getting used to. The first time you're out in a blizzard with nothing but your stove and your jacket to keep you warm... Well, it’s a humbling experience. There’s something, though, about the stillness. The way the snow muffles everything and the vast, open silence. It’s not noise I miss in that land.      It sounds deadly quiet, but there must be dangers. I've worked in both psychotherapy and nursing. How does the mind react when you're out there in such isolation for days on end?      Ah, now  that’s  a good question. You see, it's not just the body you have to prepare. Mentally, you're constantly in a heightened state. I've done some leading in outdoor education, including a fair stretch in the Scottish hill country. The psychological  clarity  people experience out in the wild is... profound. Without technology, the mind starts to listen to itself.      That's very true. I've noticed myself becoming more observant, more in tune with natural rhythms. When the sun rises and sets, and the trees creak and settle, there’s a deep sense of being part of something far larger than oneself.      That’s beautiful, but what about the safety of it all? There've been stories of campers getting lost or suffering from the cold. Even you, Jack, as experienced as you are, would you recommend it to someone with no outdoor background?      I’d say start in the shoulder season, maybe autumn or early spring, and with a proper training course. You can’t take wild camping lightly.

Rather than going out for dinner again, innit, me an’ the lads down t’ Sunderland were thinking of making a meal at home. I’m more than happy t’ cook, but where d’you fancy eating? Not sure I’ve the right kind of things for a fancy supper.      Aye, I don’t mind if it’s just at home. I’ve been thinking about watching that new A24 film they put out this year, the one with that actor from  Parasite —the whole thing was set in London. Didn’t even get round to watching it yet. You like that sort of thing?      Oh, the Yeo-jun Ma one?  [corrects pronunciation] I liked that enough. Got a bit much of a gothic vibe for me, but the atmosphere was spot on. Aye, if you fancy watchin’ something after dinner, I’m game for it.      That’d be good. I’ve also been meaning to read that new Sally Rooney book— Jack Harrison . I’ve heard mixed things, but she’s a bit of a name now, I reckon.      Oh, I’ve started it. Didn’t get far, to be honest. Her rhythm in the dialogue got a bit much for me at first. But I’m not giving up on her yet—just needs the right mood. It’s got that introspective kind of vibe, innit?      Definitely. Like her work at first read, but I’ve not read all of it yet. I did do  The Conversations We Haven’t Had  and  Normal People . Made me think about things for weeks, really. Kinda about how people don’t always speak what they mean.      Aye, I can see that. Mebbe that’s why I’m liking it less up front—more used to dialogue that’s smoother. But if you’re after something that drags on and shows more than it tells, she's got that down.      Fair enough. I could stick to my good old  Tom Rachman  or  Eliot Turmen . Grabs me by the collar and doesn’t let go.      Now that’s the kind of thing go me bin on for—fine page-turners. Just give me a decent line in the first five pages and I’m hooked.      Aye, innit. Let’s get to cookin’. I’m blaming you for the washing up if I don’t help.      Sounds good. Let’s be them proper north-eastern cooks, innit—whack on the music, ring the next-door, and make a feast outta nothin’.

Rather annoyingly, I haven't been able to get anyone to talk about this typewriter I've been using... got it out of a charity shop for like 20p. I've been using it for little stories with the kids to try and help them with things like spelling.      Got eeny weeny stories!      [IN SEPARATE ROOM – LAUGHING AGGRESSIVELY AND CRASHING STUFF] I got a PCB in my leg... [LAUGHS VIOLENTLY]      Right, right, the PCB in your leg... Right, I'm coming!  Oh no no no, no no no no no, do not die now [LAUGHS]  You’ve already got a left foot in the box! I’m not letting you die on me now and I’m definitely NOT doing a brownie promise again about a cat!      He promised he wouldn't die!      [WHOOPS] I didn't mean to whoosh it. Also, the PCB is like directly in my spine bones.      I’m not even halfway through telling you about the typewriter and you’ve already started deadly attrition in the room… brilliant. Right, so it’s a manual typewriter. It’s – it’s been super fun trying to figure out because the instructions are in broken Russian and German. It took me like three days to work out what the ‘fix’ button did. It’s kind of like someone took Excel and crossed it with a PlayStation from like 1983.      Also, I just exploded and I want to be remembered for something!      You can have about five Legos to remember you by.      I have vibes from a PlayStation 1! I know that!      The typewriter’s got that same kind of ‘clicky’ response, you know? It’s not like word processors at all where you can delete a word and redo it. Here, if you make a mistake, you have to cover it up and then… oh, it’s also got ribbons that you have to change manually! So if I write a paragraph and then remember I missed a ‘v’ in the word ‘seven go’, I have to reach up and change the ink ribbon. Fun.      I had a typewriter box thing that we used at school to type out stories.      Typewriters are kind of amazing. They are like… like, boxes to magically write words in, and they are so old but super fancy! It's like the typewritten version of like… writing with a crayon.      That's probably the most accurate description.

Rather do this'n've rather than be scrubbed up for breakfast. I know it's not  normal , but after the conference, I'm bleeding knackered and I'd murder for a decent cup of coffee and toast with jam. Chuffed they allowed me in as a senior lecturer. Ten years I’ve been een academia and now I’ve got a proper title 'at last!      Nonsense, you’ve always looked fine to me, old bean. I’m the one who’s dressing as if I’ve rolled out of me own workshop. Bit of an old man in his donkey jacket. You'd fetch a better price in Bradford market if you tried. Now, tell me, what’d you think of the fruit farms they visit on the trip? I swear I left with a dusting of apples on me back.      I think it turned out alright. It's funny, the old place we toured looked eerily like a medieval village they’d studied a decade back. Me and me planting of oregano, rosemary, and thyme in the garden over winter has bloomed nicely—though I blame the frost for knocking out me crop last year.      Aye, the real deadly old folks might’ve known something about herbs—and living off rhythm of the seasons. You ever notice how the buses down here often seem to be in queue because of roadworks? I swear, somethin’s always going on and it’s slower than waiting for mail.      Honestly, I've been getting so much junk mail I’d read it like a dictionary for oddly-formatted letters—job offers, letters about my cat and then… here’s a curious one about  ANON’s  old house being about to sell. That house has had such a touch of tragedy, I’d almost be a bit sorry to see it sold. Not that I’d live there, but it’s history deserves celebration.      Aye, well if they’re going to sell it, maybe they will restore it a bit. Do you know, I tried using them modern little phones last week? Blooming useless as sticks. My Auntie Websites—she knows more 'bout Androids than me—was helping, but let’s say it's a learning curve.      Oh, go on then, tell me about your Auntie again—that one who made her own jam? I remember she once sent me a jar that turned out to taste like lavender and honey at the same time.

Rather annoying I had to take my paracetamol earlier. My back's playing up again since that first snow last weekend. Never mind, it is nearly Christmas after all! How's the cat settling in, Clara?      No, I mean—get in, Martha! Over here. Got a bit of a cold myself, so today was spent just drinking tea and reading the newspaper. The cat? She’s taken a liking to your Christmas tree! I swear she tried to eat one of the baubles earlier. We may have to tie the tinsel outside when we get the new tree up.      Oh,  yes , I heard about the cat and the bauble. Alice managed to film it and posted it on Facebook! The comments are brutal, by the way, Dad. I had to hide it from work.      Blimey, that’s typical of Alice. I still can’t figure out this whole social media thing. The other week, I tried to post a photo, and it showed up on the wrong timeline. I spent half the evening trying to delete it, and now I can’t figure out how to change the privacy settings. Someone might’ve seen me in a rather ... dodgy hat.      Oh, that sounds like one of my least favourite memories of you, Dad. Remember when you posted the photo of the “Red Bull and custard cream,” and then proceeded to use the caption “A man’s breakfast”? And, what did you say someone replied with? “Please don’t audition for MasterChef.”      Oh, that’s the one! It still makes me laugh. Anyway, speaking of breakfasts, I’ve been meaning to ask about the New Year’s trip. You mentioned the Lake District?      Yes, thanks for asking, Martha. I thought it’d be a nice unplug for all of us. No social media, no mobile phones, no emails. Just a quiet week walking, maybe a scenic train ride. Clara was quite enthusiastic.      Honestly, I need a tech detox. Between pitching copy for ads and constant notifications, it’s draining. I keep meaning to message my old uni friends but never get around to it. A week with no Facebook or the usual grind would go a world of good.      Just don’t expect me to leave the house without my green tea in the bag or my usual morning supplement. Can you pick me up from the clinic, love?      Of course, dear.

Rather skip the ales and go for a brew, old thing. I've just cranked through a typist shift and my innards are bellowing for tea. This place gives such a charming vibe, like we've popped into a time capsule from the fifties.      Got eeny weeny passive of me. It was either that or sit on my bottom all day making choices on programming that affects no one but me. Such a human existence, right? And yes, this is a reasonable little spot! So, what's the latest on your copywriting gig? Still glorifying socks on e-commerce sites or have you graduated to more profound subjects?      Still working on glorifying socks and promoting a myriad of mundane products. Fun stuff. It does rally well, though – I've been given some more architectural projects to dabble with. Living with inanimate objects is oddly fascinating. Wait, what about you then? How's Oxford treating you for your post-grad studies, and is there a possibility you'll move to London after?      Oxford is monumental, both the university and the town. My studies are in computational statistics, a rather niche area, but I thoroughly enjoy it. As for moving… well, I've got this friend, let's call her "O – Mate", who lives fairly close, and we've been making a huge hullabaloo about flat hunting in London later next year. You know what it's like – the hills are alive with the sound of someone needing to move.      That sounds absolute scrummy! I remember what it's like to weigh your options and wonder if being crowded out is worth all the hubbub in the city. I mean, I wouldn't mind you living the area nearby. We could have our tea parties in the park! Going back to work then, I've been juggling a decent side gig freelancing, but for the bread and butter, steady income is strangely comforting.      Oh, I assume you're right. Having a consistent amount of money waiting at the end of the month is as wholesome as a warm blanket. I've been living off of a little bit of student funding and some extra cash from part-time survey programming. Then again, I haven't met the vast goings of my parents’ expectations yet. If I work at it, I reckon in a year or so I could go further in the field I'm emerging into.

Rather annoying isn't it, how hard it is to find time to get any proper exercise these days? With all the deadlines and transcription work I’ve got on, it's like I haven’t moved in weeks!      Yes, it is. But you mustn't let it get to you, Mandy. I try to do a walk with the dogs every evening before it gets dark. It's not glamorous, but it keeps me going. Of course, it helps that I don’t live in a place where you can afford to ignore the price of houses!      You mean you can’t just skip walking around property inspections like I do? Still, I do get in a bit of exercise when I’m out scouting for properties. I’m not sure if I’m working out or just walking around looking for the next fixer-upper!      At least you're getting out and about then. I just wish house prices were in my budget! I know the area we live in, even if it's not a typical hot spot, still feels like property is getting out of reach for someone in a semi-routine occupation like me.      It’s wild when you think about it, isn’t it? For someone in a professional role, it's still a challenge. I often joke that the least expensive house on the market these days is my mother's kitchen!      If only! Last weekend, I spent the day in the kitchen trying out a new recipe for carrot cake. That could count as exercise, don't you think? Mixing and kneading is a full-body workout!      That’s cheating, Jan! You can't compare mixing cake to actual exercise.      Oh come on, James, what's your excuse? You don’t seem short on energy!      Fair enough, but for every baked good Jan makes, I can only eat so much. I'm sure the sugar is a workout in itself!      Well, I do hope you're enjoying the fruits of my labor. Also, if you two want proper coaching on both exercise and cooking, I do write about it sometimes for a living!      That's right, Jan is the writer in the family. If anyone can give us a schedule to follow, it's you. Although I'm not sure I'd read your book if you made me run three miles and bake a pie every day after work!

Rather annoying the Budget really, eh? You know, me an’ the lads down ‘ere in Sunderland... Well, I’ll not lie, I’m more than a bit tight on the old bob this month. I were chuffed to bits when the rent got capped wi’ the government sayin’ we’d een a bit more control, but then they go and chuck a big dollop of tax on us? I mean, I’m just starting out in this Corpus Administration lark, so it’s a right pain.      Oh, I heard about that! Here in Cambridge, the cost of livin’s like, mad expensive even without the tax hikes. I work in the civil supply side, postgrad and all that—y’know, roads, sewer systems, that kind of stuff. I’m employed for a building project, but now I’m fretting over whether I’ll actually be able to afford to stay here when it comes to rent and this new tax mess.      I hear you. Rent’s not exactly cheep near the uni either. Good job I’m still living wi’ me folks, otherwise I’d be in a absolute pickle. Anyway, what’ve you been up to outside of work, then?      Not much, really. I was just round Cambridge last night at the arts theatre seein’  Hamilton . Let’s just say, it was the cheapest night out I’ll probably have for a while. If I book ‘advance’ tickets that is, which I managed just before prices jumped again. Honestly, I’d die to see it again, but it’s not exactly in the budget at the mo.      Oh no, I  love  musicals! I nearly about got tickets for  Les Mis  a couple months ago, but I had to be a good girl and not overspend. Not like I’d get it outta me folks, eh. My sister ‘eard about it though, said if I wasn’t going she and her boyfriend were goin’ for it ‘at all costs’. I tried to stop them, but I could see the rebel in her.      Ah, yeah, that’s a familiar one with my younger cousins too. They want to experience  The Phantom of the Opera  or some classic like that goin’ on for life if you ask me. But at the end of the day, they’re still students. Who am I to say anything?      It’s the same for me really. Although, after I graduate, I suppose I’ll have more money to splurge on ‘proper’ stuff like musical tickets or a fancy meal.

Rather annoying this wet weather, eh, Pete? Thought we’d get a bit of a break ‘fore pittin’ on with this job. Still, more time to chat, I suppose. How’s the old cab business? Not too many tourists this time o’ year?      Aye, not like summer, innit. Light twitch o’ folk comin’ in fer the shops, but mostly just the regulars. Fair dos, this project, though. Not had a paintbrush in me 'ands since primary school. Thought me role was just supplyin’ the lads with tea ’n a fag every now ’n again.      You can have a bit more of a go if you like. I left the primers and brushes handy. I reckon you’ve got the eye for subtlety. Seen you take an interest in them old cars at the car boot, no doubt. Look at you, folkliife in repose!      Nah, you didn’t see that one, Paul. I fancied that classic Austin van with the scuffed paint, though. Cheaper I put it, the better. But still, I tell ya, that fancy bookshop on Bold Street, what with them second-hand tomes and art prints, I – Mate, I got a sneakin’ fancy actin’ in some film or film somethin’. Had me moments as Silas in the school ‘Romeo and Juliet’, innit?      Tales of the stage: a man of letters, a man of the telly, a man of the gutter. Er, no – the  guttering . We need to fix them gutters after this. Got a man in the building society who fancies a tidy-up.      Not you as well, innit. No one mentioned that. My sister ‘as put me onto some guest speaker thing at the community centre – urban development, they said it was called. ‘Bout the city growin’ too fast and all that. We lost my granddad’s pub to it. Always fancied trying me 'and at actin’ again. Not took the bull by the neck proper, mind.      That’s the go, Pete. Don’t be shy. If ya wanna give it a whirl, I’ll drop a word with the the box office gaffer at the little theatre. Paintin’s just a flukey pastime, mind, after I finished those degrees, never had the heart to start teachin’ full-time.      Thanks, mate. I owe ya one. Painter and poet, innit. Talk about goals in life, eh? You, me, we’re always lookin’ to patch up something somethin’ or other.

Rather annoying this, having to go through all these winding roads. I still can’t get used to Polish driving... What was the name of that hill we just climbed?      Oh, that was Kasprowy Wierch. Look, we're getting a bit of a view from up here on the right. You can see the Tatra Mountains stretching off if you peer through all the trees.      I think I saw one of those cute Polish hitchhikers down the side of the road earlier. We didn't stop, did we?      Oh, we didn’t... Not to worry, I mostly wave when I see them, but the last one only spoke Russian, and I’m barely turkey on that language these days. Fun to watch, though. They usually have wildly mismatched bags.      Fair enough. But I did feel for them a bit — it’s breakfast, isn’t it? I mean, here I am in my lovely campervan with milk and hides, and them puffing on the roadside. Good job we packed that cereal.      We need to ration, really. I know we said we’d do this trip on the cheap, but still, there’s something to be said for a little comfort when you’re out in the middle of nowhere. Speaking of which, have you actually worked out how much this is costing us?      Honestly? Silly question. I already lost count after the first three fuel stops. But someone said in one of the Facebook groups: "The cheapest trip is one where you don’t eat out." Also, I think the campervan comes with a premium price tag — which is, in my case, about half of what I saved in gold bangle money last year.      Laughs. Gold bangles aside, you’re a national treasure. And speaking of treasures — have you found  all  the hiding places you stashed stuff in?      Are you kidding? I was clearing my clutter last week, and I found a 1998 Polaroid of you and I at Cambridge doing something thoroughly idiotic with a goat. That counts as clearing clutter, right?      That goat looked terrified by the way the sun was shining in its eyes. But yeah, you've kept every memory. While I, on the other hand, had to give the box of old films away. Pass it on, like.      You and your roles in education. Always so earnest. Anyway, as long as we have each other, and this vehicle, we’ll be fine.

‘Mum, am I goin’ to be ‘ome in time to revise for tomorrow’s chem exam? It’s in the arse after the train strikes messed up all the transport plans again. Why are we doing this journey anyway?’      ‘Lottie, love, I promise it’s not that far, and we’re just making a few stops on the way to Preston. We need a few things for the house. And yes, this is a bit of a longer detour to get to Hay-on-Wye for the festival next weekend. We need to plan, don’t forget. You too, Dan, is it even open yet?’      ‘Nah, we can’t go that way, love. The road near St Anne’s’s is blocked off by some works – I saw the signs on the way out of the garage. We’ll take the back way through Blackpool if we’re going to Bucks. I’ve been there enough times for work, and the shortest way’s not always the quickest, even if it is the most direct. I remember when that new shop opened there, you couldn’t get in without queuing for ages!’      ‘Oh, for goodness’ sake, Dan, I don’t need to remember all of that from the last time. We just need to get to the Tesco and pick up the Hay tickets today. And, Lottie, you did say you wanted to visit the Queen’s Platinum Jubilee exhibition while we’re up this way, didn’t you?’      ‘Yeah, but I want to do that with friends, not with a load of strangers in a supermarket queue. Can’t we just download it online or something? I’ve got Legit essay to type up. And talking of friends, Charlie texted me earlier. She said her sister is back from school now after being away with a ‘flu-like bug. My sister’s got the chickenpox, didn’t she?’      ‘Yes, your Auntie Sarah called me last night. She said you’ll be fine, but stick to hand-washing and stay away from the little ones. She said your cousin’s on the mend now. Now, Lottie, when you remember, you come with us to the festival. I’ve go the tickets on order, if you don’t mind walking around for hours reading signatures in the rain, like I always do!’      ‘If you two are going to get lost in the conference centre again, I’m staying with the groceries and the trolley.

Rather annoying this newfit lot o’ toys, ay? I was tryin’ t’look up pedy-womfilms t’see if I’m more than I was ten years ago      Aye, we do try, but it’s such a maze. We could make appointments at eeny mental place, but we tryin’ t’do things online now. It’s not easy.      Nan, you  do  know what search engine is, right?      Oh, I heard of them! Looks like, but the bloomin’ keyboards... like, I juggle balls better than I type!      Grandpa left us like a MySpace, Nan. It’s still there. I can show you! I’m good at this sort of stuff, and I think it’s important.      Mm, we’re cleaning out old bits at this stage. Less clutter for the mind and the house. We looked at hides, stored bits, and the laptop was still chucked full o’ junk. I do tell you—personally, it was the meds that helped me out a lot.      Nan, we’ve got a funny thing going on. We’re making a humble website. It’s for memories.      Ooh,  humble ? That somethin’ to do wi’ Silly Stones? Or is that a different lot?      No, no—it’s more like a homepage for the family, with videos, stories, funny things. Also, some of the old photos and stuff you saved under the bed!      I did  not save any photos under the bed ! That’s where I kept my thimble box and some corroded nails.      You’re quite the haulers for trinkets, aren’t you? I did once find a baby shoe behind the bin.      Eugh! That’s why I always sort out me coat pockets first—don’t know what else I’d find!      Nan, do you remember the playhouse?      Course I do! That was a goon show on pond life if you ask me. And it was very active in the pond, between green frogs and box plants.      It was nice, though. You were really kitted out in that.      It was a cheap dress made of dolls’ overalls, but I was the star! I’m not entirely sure if I got any applause for that.      Grandpa kissed me on the cheek after the whole show. It was weird.      Yeah, we were Movember off, weren’t you?      Yeah, on stage he had one! But it was so strange once you saw it close—end of the face!      That was not Movember! That was like, overload.

Right, lads, here we go — I’ve just bought this brand new laptop, and I thought it’d be a good idea to show it off properly. Blimey, it sure does look sleek! Got it on a £200 discount from that site you recommended, James —DealsForBlokes, was it?      That’s the one! Glad it worked out for you. Let me have a look at the specs too — got an SSD, a decent Intel i7, and it’s light enough to carry around. You're gonna chase your friends into the past with how modern it is, Eddie! Still, did you back up all your important files?      Yeah, well… I did, kinda. I just copied the photo albums and stuff over onto the internal drive. D’you think I should’ve gone the cloud route? It feels a bit clunky sometimes.      Cloud backup is a bit more stable for long-term storage. I use Mega and Google Drive, you know, for different things. Maybe set up both for important stuff. I could help you get it sorted if you want — I’m in the middle of a quiet lesson this afternoon anyway.      Honestly, watching you two circle around it like it’s got a virus is pissing me off a bit. I’ve still got that old laptop from 2013 — don’t even know what the hell’s on it anymore, but it still works. Dunno what all this faff is about. Although, maybe you can show me how to clean up some unnecessary programmes — it’s running like a wheezing dog pulling a hay cart at the moment.      Fair point about the old ones. I love using retro tech — the charm of it, you know? But you really should update your OS and plug-ins regularly otherwise it becomes a security nightmare.      Okay, so lesson one: Don’t trust shady USB sticks that strangers give me on the bus. I was told all my life not to do that, but when I was out in the market last week and that sprite of a lady mentioned it comes with 'useful software,' well... I had to plug it in, you know?      Oh man, you got goon'd on the bus! Was it a virus or just a prank? Still chuckling at that.      Time to run a virus scan. Shawna at the cybercafé warned me this might happen after I plugged those “free” Wi-Fi USB sticks from the airport into my laptop.

Rather do this than sit at home, I suppose. Bit fancy for a midweek snack, but it  is  the first bistro in Tarnow, isn’t it? I've heard nothing but good things about it. Not quite Cambridge, mind you, but at least the coffee’s better than most places I’ve dragged my  ahem  tired bones into lately.      Yeah, it’s a real find! I actually came in last week and got a croissant that was  to die for . This place is giving me hope that the town might start developing a bit of culture. You know, aside from the Russian takeaway spots! Not knocking them, obviously, but the décor here is actually warm and kind of homely, which is rare for new businesses in Poland. It’s like they put some real soul into the place, which is sad in a world where so many businesses feel soulless.      Soulful or not, I’m more interested in the food. And the people, of course! No, you didn’t see the woman who came in just before us, did you? She looked like a book character—had this glaze in her eyes, dressed as if still living in the ’60s. Bet she’s on medication, or something stronger. Be a struggle if she's lost who she is completely, I suppose, like some kind of addiction to the past or something.      You know, that was what struck me about you as well, actually—this idea of someone being chained to who they once were. You used to have such drive, so many dreams—job hunting, teaching, whatever. Now you’re here, in a bistro in a town you never would’ve considered about five years ago. I sometimes wonder if the problem wasn’t the job market, but a kind of identity crisis. Have you thought about it?      Maybe. I do think,  maybe  I’ve always been chasing something. I used to dream about getting out to the world, going places, but I relied too much on other people for that. I don't know, it's like I waited for things to happen to me rather than making them happen. But I do have some dreams, even now—like maybe learning to shoot or taking up the piano again. Just wasting time on stuff that doesn’t cost much.      That’s the spirit! You don’t have to be working non-stop to have a purpose.

Rather skip the queue and just get us online tickets for the Dorset Steam Fair. Felt real busy on the weekend and I don’t wanna be hanging around with the crowd all day.      Oh, that’s a good idea, love. Be a lot easier than standing in a line in that heat. Mind you, I don’t think they’d have done if it wasn’t for them making it a wheelchair-friendly event now. Much better for old chums like me, easier to get about.      We can pop the tickets on for you both. Just want to make sure ’ere they’ve got the facilities right. Mary’s still got a dodgy knee and I don’t fancy her trudging about on the turkey legs all day neither.      Yeah, I’ll check the website again, but they did say they improve the access for the disabled last year, so there should be better pathways and even ramps for the stalls this time. They’ve taken in a lot more people using the fair for that, you know, for the community aspect.      Aye, it’s nice seeing them include more folks. Got one of them buggies as well for hire if need be, for folks like us who can’t walk far.      That’s good. Looking at it though, while I’m there I might take the chance to check out the local property market. All that talk about the fair’s success is making me curious—anyone been looking up the prices lately? Seems like Bournemouth’s gotten a bit pricier since we moved here.      You bet it has. I worked in a home in Margate not long ago, and there you couldn’t about afford a place even if you had a decent wage. Bournemouth’s not far off same now, really. Going to be tough to get a place if you wanna upsize.      Aye, I heard tell. All them new developments going up and all them students from the uni pushing the prices through the roof. I dunno how people manage anymore.      At least I’m not planning to move anytime soon. Just wanted a little more space for the cats if the market picks up for us. Mind you, it’s a pain trying to move the furniture when I do rearrange the flat though. Just don’t know how to make the space work between the sofas and box cat tree.

Rather annoying this wet weather, eh, love? Thought we’d get a bit of a break ‘ere. I got the seats polished for them scones at tea time! Thirsk does love a proper Sunday tea don’t it?      Oh yes, well, the forecast was iffy and all that. But I reckon the scones’ll still come out just fine – I’ve made a dozen. A lot for five people, but this lot never leave a crumb, bless ‘em.      Can I have the strawberry jam? The other kind tastes weird. Mrs. Porter says frozen is bad, even if it’s "flash-frozen". What’s that mean?      My turkey jam, perhaps? Canned though. I like mine slowrished on the back.      I’ll be the judge of that, dear, and let me tell you, breakfasts are better when you’ve been up with the lark! Speaking of, you ever looked at that Twitter, didn’t you say the other day? That chap from Middlesbrough with the pie-chart of inappropriate socks? Hilarious!      Oh, yes, the sock-gate scandal. Good on him for not hiding it. I saw a vicar post it too, – cheeky of him. I wouldn’t mind venturing a tweet now and then, but the parents of my class are all over me if I so much as email at the weekend, let alone joke about someone’s lisle knickers.      What’s Twitter?      Just the fastest way to get lost in the mouths of strangers, love. But it’s a good distraction most times. I’ve been trying to type up a short play for a local theatre group. Got a gig in Darlington next week. Not school plays mind you, more the kind for grown-ups. My sister’s planning on coming.      Ah, the Darlington players, they’ve done some decent shows over the years. I remember a time I played a madam at a dance school in a production of Cinderella. Got more applause than the lead, I think.      Was it the one where you forgot the line with the broom?      That one! The man playing the prince just laughed at me and I just said, “Well, sweeping up’s a bloomin’ chore!” and went on. The audience roared.      I think I’m going to start learning acting next term. I like doing voices. Can I help you with the play, Mr. Kendal? You can read all the lines out loud for me.

Rather annoyingly, I've got to take both of you to the dentist this week—the schedule they sent through... Well, I've had no luck rearranging it. I can take you both after school on Thursday, is that okay with you two?      But Thursday is my hearing test day at the beginning of the week!      Mine is on Friday. I wanted to go with Ashaad that afternoon—he’s got a skateboard in from his cousin.      Oh, who's Ashaad now then? Is he the one who lives in the conservation area with the big garden?      Yeah! He’s got a sibling with the same birthday as me, and they have like a My Little Pony party every year with jelly and stuff. It’s ridiculous! I’m turning thirteen this time!      Well, your dentist appointment is in the morning, and you better not breakfast on jelly then if you want to keep your teeth for teenagehood. And I know the hearing tests can be a bit tedious, but the audiologist says it's quick and painless—though she clearly hasn’t met Ashaad yet if I take two pre-teens in to her.      Have we ever talked about watching Monet's work on a school trip? I want to know if Baptistry of San Giovanni was painted in water because the pictures show huge reflections. I reckon the paints used water as a subject before anyone was doing it properly.      There may be food available at the gallery, but I wouldn’t count on a jelly bar. I can definitely buy some hotter chocolates—especially if your science teacher let you be head boy at Easter.  Sigh.  Prime time for sugar about now, I know.      She said something about “maths and light perception.” That sounds like that one school trip we had to the observatory last term—except with less time for nap time and twice as many light experiments.      Well, the one thing I was thinking about was the Easter chocolate—the way you can balance it on your stick while you do math and still have enough of a brain space left to draw radishes on paper with your free hand? It’s like, you remember that?      Oh, I remember. You were supposed to be observing light patterns through cut paper. Instead, you spent the whole time trying to make edible kaleidoscopes—and arguing about your findings with the older biology teacher.

Rather skip the queue and just go through the drive-thru. I've had enough of squinting at menus in the sun, anyway.      I know, I've been pacing myself with this heatwave. Not to mention, the dog's been barking at the postman for the last half an hour. Honestly, we need a bigger fence   or   better social skills for Harry.      Harry? That’s the best nickname you could come up with? Should’ve gone with Sir Barks-a-Lot or something like that. Remember when we used to get chased by Mrs. Whitley’s miniature poodle?      Oh God, I do. That little furball made my MySpace look terrifying because I posted an apology poem. It rhymed, albeit badly, and I still feel guilty for the dent in the front gate. But back to Harry, he’s definitely been a project—good and bad.      I’ll give you that. But seriously, we need to talk about this weekend’s budget. I'm fairly sure that grocery shop went into overdrive—personally, I just grabbed three smoothies, a loaf of bread and a few snacks.      Oh, I didn't count. I saw a markdown on fruit so I splurged. Plus, I bought some extra snacks because the Hayfields dropped off the twins last week and they somehow ate everything within four hours. I’m already foreseeing a similar weekend, and I want food that doesn't expire in ten minutes.      That's oddly endearing. Okay, but looking at it from a financial perspective… Any chance you still have the house budget plan I made last year in Excel?      You mean the green one with the chaotic number colours and a graph that looks like it was plotted during a storm? I have it. Still run into that weird error, though. Could just be the formulae expressing their discontent.      Sounds about right. Let's dock my allowance for talking about Excel, then. You know I could stick to my 9-to-5 as a copywriter if this lifestyle lunches and dog-related budget overruns gets too much?      No, come on, you wouldn’t. Don’t go wasting your copywriting life if you miss boring presentations or over-flowing meetings. I, for one, need your genius with words—plus your questionable taste in snacks—for the next post about fluency therapy.      As long as I don’t have to type case studies onarticulation therapy.

Rather skip the new bar in town, if I were you. A few weeks ago, it was just a dwindling old bakery, and now it’s supposed to be a bistro by day and jazz club by night. Though I don’t see how the acoustics would work with those high-backed chairs in there.      You’re one to talk, Margaret! You were all for that urban rebrand last year when they painted over the old canal signs. Still, I’d rather go there for a reasonable glass of red than to the High Street for triple the price when it tastes the same.      Speaking of property, I’ve been meaning to tell the tale of how my cousin bought a stone cottage in Provence. You know how you just left your lawyer to do the legwork? Well, Oliver didn’t pick up the phone for months and came back with a verbal agreement, and the sellers hadn’t even heard of him. He happened to visit a week later, and the old charmer just handed them a bottle of Armagnac and a handshake. That was it!      Nothing like some sturdy British sense of fair play in a land of chaos to make things work. Hah! Tell that to my local council. They tried to slash a solar project just last night. Said the panel angles were “charming, but not quite harmonious” with the local architecture. Now don’t get me wrong—Bletchley looks like a collapsed dollhouse most days, but even this someone at the planning committee should be allowed a dash of a modern energy system.      Ah, architecture. That brings up the town’s supposed “revival” plan. They’re talking about saving about half the 19th century shops from rot, but only if they let developers take what’s left. Going by that lot’s logic, the town hall should be turned into a hair salon, and the old cinema into a guesthouse. As if we need more of that.      Oh, I heard they’re fixing up the barn by the station. We’re to have a jive evening in there. Monica’s trying to get us a new band fromournemouth. Now if only the dancers could be taught a routine around this new lighting setup the committee is insistent about. I swear it’s more stage lights than a concert hall.      You’ll be the box office draw, Tom.

Rather than share a new sentence, I'll request relevant information. Could you please specify the characters or string related to the next interaction or provide further instructions on how to proceed? This will help me tailor the response effectively to meet your needs. If you have a specific sentence or continuation you'd like me to generate, please share the details, and I'll be happy to assist! 🔍📝✨ If not, let me clarify that I cannot produce or interact with this data format directly unless you give further context or instructions. Please let me know how to assist moving forward.     So, what do you think? Could we integrate video case studies into our learning platform? I’ve been thinking, with how visual learning is now dominating educational trends, it could really set us apart.      I’m with you on the value of moving images, but let me ask—are we thinking of it as a sales tool or an incorporated learning strategy? From what I understand, using case studies in teaching isn’t just about the visuals—it’s about depth and application for the students.      It’s both, honestly. We want it to be a core part of the learning experience, not just to show off but to actually  help  people retain information and apply it. Think of it like storytelling but structured around real-life scenarios—something teachers can use in their curriculum and learners can watch to grasp concepts more concretely.      That makes sense. I could see that working particularly well for teacher training modules. They could observe best practices, classroom management strategies, even cultural considerations. But how do we make sure what we’re offering is accessible and adaptable?      That’s where the social networking angle comes in. Imagine a community where teachers can not only access our case studies but also discuss them, annotate videos, or even submit their own. It becomes a collaborative space for reflection and problem-solving. We’re not just selling content—we’re building a learning platform.      A bit like YouTube for educators. But professional and moderated, right? We’d need to build trust and ensure quality. We could partner with universities or schools to co-develop some modules. That would add credibility and allow us to tap into educational networks.      Exactly. Then we layer in some communication strategies to promote it—maybe even run webinars or host live Q&A sessions with educators who have used the resources.

Rather lovely to be out here, isn't it? The sea’s practically whispering today, if you listen...      Yes, it's peaceful. Not a hint of the usual wind. You’d think we were the only ones allowed out.      Exactly. I always come here when I need to clear my head. It puts everything else into perspective.      I remember the first time I saw this coastline. I was barely 20, hitchhiking with Tom. We ended up sleeping in the car when the pub was full. Do you remember him? Tom?      Oh, how could I forget? The night he got stuck on the clifftop walk during the rain! He thought he’d found India.      D’you know, I think he turned round and started walking back, convinced the sea would have shifted breakfast somewhere near the dunes.      And yet he’s still the one who hides my wine keys when I have a row with you over the deadlines.      He always loved a bit of mischief. I suppose we all did as students. Did you know he got offered a job in Cornwall after we graduated?      Wasn’t he worried about being away from his family?      Oh, he said he couldn’t quite leave us all behind. Silly man. But he’s doing well now—teaches art in a coastal school. Claims the sea helps him think.      I do wonder what made us all drawn to different coastlines. You being from London, and me from Norwich, and there we all were, scattered from Lands End to the North Sea.      Funny isn’t it? Our little clique—none of us particularly fond of the sea as kids, but now it’s like it owns part of our soul.      I think it taught us the value of stillness. Do you remember when we tried to do a little study group out here while you were writing your thesis on coastal erosion?      I think it was the third time we met, and there you were, with a thermos of coffee, watching the tide go out. I asked you if you were going to work at all, and you said, “No, but I can see where the answers are.”      That was poetic or ridiculous?      A bit of both. But it stuck with me.      I always say that the sea talks to you—sometimes in waves, sometimes in memories.      And always, always in friends.      To be honest, I’d take this walk and these stories over a perfectly behaved day of work any day.

Rather annoying this newfit lark, innit? Me n’ the lads down ‘ere in Donny got used to calling it “straif” more than “shoise” or whatever. But aye, we’re all up with the topic o’ what you lot call  fashion .       laughs  Yeah, you know, I reckon fashion is more about self-expression than sticking with what's in, but I do side-eye most social media influencers these days. It's all a bit "O! me! My gloss-st.Fatalf!" Didn’t your nan always say somethin’ like “dress for the position you  want , not the one you’ve got”? That always stuck with me.      Oh, I like that. I tend to just throw on somethin’ practical for work, and I’m off the carousel. conferences an’ all that. But weekends – I get me spikes out if I’m going out with the lads. Me posh Leeds uni friends were always on about labels, but I was too busy clouting them for quad fees.      Oh, I listen to the occasional fashion pod, honestly!
