It’s wild how early you have to start planning for parties in the academic calendar, especially if it’s a themed staff social. I remember –  laughs  – I once wore chequered trousers to a Halloween event at my old school because I thought “pants” were for the bin. Embarrassin’!      Aye, luv, I’m with you. At a conference once, I had a tuxedo sent to me at a hotel and I thought it was a prank – ended up havin’ to make a run about five minutes before walk-in. Bloke from the bar said I looked “criminal”, so I figured that must mean it worked.      You're  definitely  edgy, Lucy. I mean, if you’re expressing yourself, why not lean in? Though I will say – I was at this vintage pop-up in Croydon a little while back, and the amount of queens in that room would’ve outshown RuPaul with a confidence boosted on glitter and digestive biscuits.      Oh, I  loved  that! I met an actual goth binman once who had more taste in denim than I’ll ever have in my whole life. You know – he was all bangles and whatnot, and you could tell he didn’t care if you liked it or not. That’s kinda the best fashion move, innit? Just  be .      Aye! It’s all well and good bein’ trendy, but at the end of the day, if it don’t keep you warm or let you walk in, and it looks good with your natural vibe, what’s the point?      Exactly!

So do you remember that time I got lost in Hastings old town and came home with like, ten awesome photos of those old cobblestone streets?      Oh yes, you nearly gave me a heart attack! But I have to admit, those photos turned out brilliant. You had a real eye for it then.      Thanks, Mum. I reckon it's what got me thinking about a photography course at college. I just love that feeling when I catch something perfect in a picture.      That’s amazing, I’m really proud of you. It's not an easy course, though. You'll have to juggle everything—work, school, and your photography.      It’ll be a bit tight, especially since I got that part-time job at the café now, but I can manage. I’ve been taking the train up to Brighton for some open days and stuff. They do a really good photography foundation course.      Brighton’s a lovely place. I remember we used to go there for the day when I was your age. It’s changed a lot, of course.      I know! There’s a new bookshop there I love called "Look Inside." They have tonnes of photography books. I’m thinking about getting one called "The Art of Seeing."      Sounds inspiring. I always thought you’d end up being an artist of some sort. You have that creative streak. And don’t forget your sense of humor!      Yeah, I’m glad you like my jokes. I thought I had a good one the other day at college. I said to the teacher, “I considered becoming a landscape photographer, but I couldn’t find the right filter!”      Oh, typical! You’re just like your old man—he always had a joke to tell. I miss him sometimes. Still, I bet he’d laugh at that one!      I hope so. I just wish he was around to see where I’m going with this. I tried showing you some of my photographs the other day, didn’t I?      Yes, the ones of the lighthouse from the beach? Some of them were really dramatic. I think you’ve got a good future with this if you work really hard.      That’s what I’m hoping. I just want to make it work. But I’m scared I might not get in. The competition is tough.      I understand, love. It’s natural to feel that way.

Rather annoying this, I've got to say. That lot down the end of the road, they let their cockerel go free at night. I’m up at four every bloody morning, thinkin’ I’ve got a sun strike or somethin’.      Oh, Frank, it’s bound to be  their fault  today, isn’t it? Bill just said they put up a brand-new fence, but by the looks of it from my back window, it’s shabbier than a Second World War bomb site.      Yeah, but don’t forget Mrs. Porter saw the cockerel herself! It’s dead certain it’s their problem, no doubt about it. You want me to visit again, Frank? I’m passing their house on the way home, everyday now I’m home from school pick-ups.      No, no, let’s forget it for a second—this form I’ve been trying to fill in online is driving me mental. Says I need a 3D-printed photo of me holding a ladder, or something like that. Nonsense, if you ask me.      Aha! Frank, you and technology—oh, I tried explaining it to you last week, remember? You need a scanner or a photo of the back of your hand. I wouldn’t mind scanning myself for that lot.      Mrs. Porter and Silas’ kids—do you ever see that nest in the willow at the bottom of the garden? I’ve been watching it a bit lately. I spotted a baby bird flapping its wings about ten times and then…  nothing . Can’t imagine  they  are going to look after about five eggs, though.      Oh, I had a thistle in my boot! Going to be telling you I’ve got it planted beside the pavement in my garden. That’s for the cockerel, Silas passed it around.      Oh, a thistle, eh? I don’t blame them for waiting till I’m out. Silas and Mrs. Porter’s constant bickering—it’s like watching a football match with no referee.      Football, Frank? You and your old man’s matches back in the 70s! You always said they lacked proper action—still do in my opinion, between you and me.      Now, you two! We’ve plenty bigger problems than football and cockerels. Did you know I had to send a birthday card to Frank’s niece from over in Birmingham the other day? Didn’t even tell me I’d been forgetting to water the tomato plants.

Rather annoying this, having my daughter living in Australia when I do everything I can for her, don’t I? Well, my James has offered to let her come and stay with us for a while. He said she’d be well looked after and he likes the idea of her being nearby.      That sounds like a sensible idea. It must be hard on you both, not having her around most of the year. What’s she saying? Has she agreed to it yet?      She hasn’t said one way or the other. You know how independent she can be. Still, I think it’s time she had some boundaries. She’s thirty-two, for heaven’s sake, and working some kind of tech thingy on the other side of the world. I miss her constantly. I’m not getting any younger, and I’d rather not be the grandparent who only sees her at Christmas and summer if we’re lucky.      I understand that. It’s emotional for any parent. I remember when my own kids were growing up—and I still miss them, even though they’re not so far away. This is a big change for your daughter though, moving continents. Did you talk to her about what she’d expect from life here?      Well, of course I tried. I told her it’d be fairly simple, and that it wouldn’t be long before she knew her way around Brighton and got used to the weather. I’m already foreseeing complaints about the cold and the wet. But at least it’s a chance for her to live a bit closer to the family. You and I had the good fortune of having our children nearby.      Yes, we did. I think it’s brilliant that James is supporting the move. He must really mean something to you two for him to take this kind of step. Not many younger men would handle it gracefully, let alone step up and offer a roof over someone else’s guest.      He’s a gem, as it is. But I think it might help if I spoke directly to my daughter. Maybe I should fly out and visit her for a few weeks. Just to see what she really thinks and what she needs from us.      That might do it. Face-to-face talks often clarify things that letters and videos can’t.

Rather annoying isn't it, eh, David? That Scottish referendum business has had me in two minds ever since it got brought up again. Just when I thought things were settling, now it's all over the papers and radio again. Not to mention the political chaos in Westminster at the moment.      Oh dear, yes, I’ve been twitching at the radio this morning. It’s not just a distraction—it's a proper scandal how the government handles all of it. And you know what gets me most? That same old political dance, like nothing's changed in fifty years.      I suppose part of it is also the uncertainty. I mean, we're just trying to get people to focus now that the turkey is cooked with Brexit, and now they’re throwing this back into the mix. I had a job interview last week I almost missed because of a teaching union meeting, and the agenda was all about this, too.      Haha, you and your interviews. I remember when you told me you were looking for a sabbatical lecturer post at that new campus over in Canterbury, yes? Well, listen—stick with it. You're a bright chap and you’ve got real promise. Tell me, was it anything to do with workloads in general? I find it's all getting too much for new lecturers, and I know for a fact some are choosing to leave the profession after their fifth year.      You hit the nail on the head. Our colleague, Lucy, left last week. Just handed in her notice. She's been doing a double-takeoring—PGCE and a masters in education—and she’s under so much stress. I spoke to her at a coffee meet-up last Thursday, and you could just see the exhaustion in her face. It's terrible.      Poor thing. I remember her as a bright gal—brighter, dare I say, than half the lads passed out at the bar last weekend. Tell me something—how's your daughter doing? Haven’t heard much about her recently.      Oh, that sprite of mine, Monica? She’s off to a new phase of secondary school this term, and it's a proper blur of excitement and nerves. She's into the sciences, so I've been trying to get her into some extra sessions at the college lab.      That's lovely. You're a proper dad and a proper professor.

Rather annoying to say the least. I remember sorting out a mousetrap game for the kids when they first came over and I thought I'd never get it sorted. I can't say I've ever been a fan of American children either to be quite honest, they're such a rowdy bunch.      I went out to New York with the job once and if it wasn't for the kids, I reckon I'd have liked it there. Such a big city, so clean and efficient. But, pulling someone to do paperwork at midnight was another matter entirely. Didn’t even want to know how things work over there.      Honestly, I don't get the fuss. When I studied in Chicago for a bit last year, I found them quite friendly and left themselves a lot of space, to be honest. Distant, but not unfriendly. They just didn’t want everyone up in their business.      I actually spent a summer working with a kitchen in New Jersey. It was the first time I'd ever cooked outside London. Everyone was great, but I still can't get over the lack of a decent cup of tea. They have these short, strong coffees that taste nothing like the real thing.      You always did say you liked a little bit of stimulation. Though I remember when we first got the mousetrap game together, it was huge. One time, Tom picked up that big spring and couldn't get the thing together for ages! Laughed so much.      That was also the time Kevin got sent a rush order for some sour marmalade from the States. It was vile. I still don't know if it was a joke, or if he really did like that stuff.      I still remember watching this man trying to make lasagna and not knowing it wasn’t necessary to cook the pasta first. No wonder he ended up with a pile of flour and treacle!      Parents were just more open to the whole learning by doing thing, I think. I tried to make them understand that I could stick to my own study schedule. Though being asked out every night by some 'British students' was a bit too American for me. Too much pressure.      Sometimes I wonder how we even go out of the country and manage to keep everyone else so confused by our weird habits.

Rather annoyingly, I've bought us a whole bunch of new pyjamas. We needed some new pjs, and I thought this was a nice opportunity to find a pair that we both would like.      Oh, do they have those kind of things in China yet? I was under the impression all the shops liked to sell the same stuff as British retailers, but just with all the brand names misspelled.      Some do, but honestly, the range is far more limited here. I had to go to the big mall and spend most of the afternoon looking.      Right, I assume you mostly just made a shopping trip of it and bought a few other things on the side? My instincts are telling me that you found something interesting while you were there.      Darcy, I was quite focused! I managed to buy us two sets of pyjamas – yours are the blue and white ones with the linen feel; I went for a more classic cotton style in a grey mottled fabric for me.      Nice, I was going to tell you mine are going to feel amazing next to my skin, quite a step up from the plastic-y stuff we’ve been wearing.      You'd be surprised, but yes, it's much better. I stopped at the gift shop and found these really gorgeous slippers while I was there. It was a bit of a splurge, but I got them for you.      Oh someone got full on dress-up mode on. You know, I noticed you came back with an interesting amount of shopping bags.      Well, I did find a few things in the fashion section at the bottom of the mall. I found you a couple of decent jumpsuits and some lightweight trousers.      Oh that was you! I was puzzled as to who left all that stuff on the floor for me to fold. To be honest, I did need some lighter clothes for summer. I'm going to have to take the wraps off soon, you know.      There we go then. You've got a new wardrobe coming with lunches and a new pair of shoes. I took the liberty of buying you some sandals.      Oh, so now go on then, show me if you've left them out.      They’re in the corner behind the box I brought the slippers in. I was intending to have them made bespoke to your specifications, but after two hours of fruitless negotiation with the cobbler, I gave in and went over to the shop.

Rather a brilliant game we had last night, wasn’t it? That try by Kelleher came out of nowhere, and the way they defended after that—well, I’d take that team over the All Blacks any day.      Yeah, Dad, it was pretty wild. I was doing my homework, and my iPad kept buzzing with notifications from the live updates. I actually had to put it on a timer so I wouldn’t miss anything. We lost, but it was easier watching than being there, I think.      I don’t get the whole point, but the passion in the room last night was something else. Mary stayed up to see the end, and she managed to explain the rugby rules to me better than you ever could, darling. Ten minutes, and I actually understood what a line-out was!      Well, dear, you’ve got to admit, when you see those big lads thumping into each other in cleats and scrums, it’s quite a spectacle to witness. And the shout the pack gives when they win a scrum—it just jumps off the telly, doesn’t it? Anyway, speaking of shouting, is Oisin still awake?      Yes, we’ve got a rhythm going with the bedtime story. He’s into tales of knights with fairly long speeches and dragons that just  happen  to be friends with pigeons. We’ve finished the first book, so he’s officially a knight-in-training now.      That’s so cool! When my school does sports, we just do a quick run and chuck a ball about. I wish I had a weekend tournament with sword fights  and  pizzas afterwards like Oisin. It must be epic.      Only you’d find that epic. To be fair, though, it’s better that he loves stargazing after his stories now—says he found ‘the little knight constellation’ last night after going to sleep. Sleeps better with a bit of imagination, probably.      That’s what I call a full head of steam to bed. Right, so as to what we were trying to sort out earlier—Mary and I have got the schedule set for tomorrow for the cards. I’ve ordered the boxes, and the printer guy said he can deliver them if you or Oisin can drop by.      Oh, don’t worry, I can drop by in the morning. It’s nice to do something for special days, and I think Oisin’s 5th is next month, right?

Rather annoying that the new house doesn't even have a spare room. I was hoping it would be easier once... you know, with a child coming. It's not  that  bad, though. Beans on toast is genius. Not quite gourmet, but I mean—      —You're een beginning to sound like my brother. He was all about simplicity before his wife had their first. Now? A whole nursery listing, and he's got this obsession with baby proofing cupboards. It's adorable, really.      Oh, I do hope he's still in love with her... like, truly, deeply in  love . I mean, we're talking supply tables, cribs and like  gender themes , you know? I swear my left arm is allergic to IKEA. I would've never thought I'd say that in a world where I spend most of my time sharing old clothes with friends.      Well, here's hoping in his case the love  is  enough to keep going even through those. Also, I might actually need your help—moving day is slated for a week from today, and I have way too much stuff. Want to come and share the pain?      You reckon I'd have time in light of the clothes donations I keep denying?      Why deny? It's not like you are the only one around here learning to be mortal through the use of large volumes of vintage fabrics! Though, let’s be fair, someone has to still dress like they’re auditioning for a time-share ad.      Touché. Still, I can’t imagine being able to part with all  that  without fully understanding the context about how I’m even managing all of it to begin with.      Exactly. Another person would've been better off barely surviving the housing crisis unscathed. I do wonder, though—have you ever thought about learning Spanish? I did with my niece, and man, it's a different world when it comes to relaying accurate context about your mad family stories while being accurate about conjugations.      Oh, I'm a little behind with my French these days, let alone any additional exotic languages. Then again, if it's good enough for goading my sister-in-law about her taste in romantic comedies, I might just pick it up again. Spanish could go a long way in arguing about your actual brother’s latest misguided DIY project.      That’d go down well, I’ll say that.

Rather annoying when people can't get my accent right, innit. I was in Cambridge the other week and someone got completely confused between "milk" and "smelt". Typical, eh?      Aye, we do have the strangest things in our accents. But it's also pretty cool, if you ask me. I use it all the time in the classroom when I'm trying to show my students the subtle differences in RP and regional English. I mean, you're practically a case study, mate!      I don't get the fuss about accents too much. I came from Luton, right? So it's not like me accent is the cleanest either. But I've been doing more turkey than talking for years! Gardening lefts me smell like compost, not like I need to risk sounding silly and I'll be the only man with an accent and a mulch gig! Ha!      I mean, accents are one thing, but what’s even the point in hides? They didn’t have any when I was growing up, and that worked for me.      Yeah, but takes one to know one, innit? I've tried the real stuff since uni trips in Cyprus… watching shows with subtitles. Still can’t get the hang of most of the Mateys ones, but I can still fake it till I make it.      Mate, you know you have to consider the nuance in everything! It's not just the words, it's the rhythm, the intonation. Ever watched a BBC drama and tried to do an impression? Just watch out for your gut, some of these accents can come with a  wind  as well as a vibe about them…      Haha! That’s true. Once I did a gig where I had to speak with a Brummie accent for a univalley board game. My eyeliner got all wet trying not to laugh after I said "I 'ave a dremit" instead of "I have a dream." I ended up introducing myself as Arty the Webley, as in… well as in a mess.      That’s what I do with my students. I get them trying accents after they’ve done some role-plays. Then go straight into the deep-v about linguistics and identity – it's brilliant! You’d love it, Arty.      Aye, but what’s the point in all this if we’re never gona live out where those accents are?      I mean, I’ve been over to Greece a few times, and I had a go at my Greek accent there.

Rather annoying driving today, isn't it? That car in front of mine was just moving so slowly. I had to wait forever at that red light on the way home. Honestly, I've been saving up for a reliable car for ages, and I'm not even sure it's worth it anymore.      Yeah, I hear you. It was ridiculous. I got stuck behind that huge van that clearly thought it owned the road. At least I managed to get back here in time to start cooking dinner, which is something. What are we making, by the way?      Chicken curry with rice. I thought I'd try that new seasoning I bought last week. It’s been on my list for ages now that My turkey curry was such a success. Wait, actually, you haven't told me if you've been driving at all this week. I remember you were supposed to pick up some documents for the project?      I did drive into town this morning. It was a bit of a commute, but I managed to do it. I took the train actually, since that car of mine is still off getting fixed. I’m not really one for saving, honestly.      It’s not like you to skip on something so important, though. I remember when we got together last month, we talked about saving for a joint purchase – maybe even getting a vehicle we could both use. Now don’t go rolling your eyes at me. I’m just trying to make our lives a little easier in the long run.      I know, I know. That conversation did happen. It’s just that at the moment, I’m overwhelmed with work. That new project I’m coordinating is taking up most of my time. I’m not even eating properly half the time. But I get what you’re saying. Maybe I need to be better with my budget and handle the car situation soon.      That would be great. I was thinking we could actually cut down on some unnecessary expenditure. I did a few calculations, and if we could just drive together or share a car, we could really save a bit of money on fuel and maintenance. What do you think?      That sounds smart. I’d be happy to contribute more with the budget if the proposal is aimed at getting a more cost-effective vehicle.

Rather do that than drink lukewarm tea with a grumpy Arabian prince and her crumpet in a palace with more rooms than sense. Although now I think of it, I do remember drinking something that categorically cannot be described as tea with a man I believe held the title of Royal Adviser — or at least, that’s what he told the porters as he tried to bribe his way onto the next ferry.      Ay, that sounds like a place where you’d find more names in interesting titles than you can shake a stick at. But what I’m still trying to figure out is how you two went to teach in Saudi Arabia  and  still ended up in the water, only to find yourself in a bit of a legal pickle with the cops. Seems like quite the plot for a short story.      Oh, I think the world might be better off if it was a novel — better character breakfast, no doubt. But to be fair, Hattie — and yes, you do remember her — told us to “just keep the boat going, it’s all mercy.” Water was fine, the boat was sturdy, and then suddenly I’m in a cell with a man who strongly believes the Ministry of Health only remembers dental magazines on Tax Day.      Speak for yourself — I remember the dental magazines more often than I care to, because they were everywhere. Magazines, brochures, leaflets. You couldn't even flush the toilet without a laminated sheet on the perils of someone not using an endodontist.      That's oddly precise. You’d think a sailing trip with a retired teacher, a former dentist, and a university lecturer would come close to a sailing school about half the time. I mean, I can teach the finer points of flossing — what you  can’t  teach is how to read wind patterns. Or how not to step on your own foot overboard while discussing the ethics of dentistry.      Well, the ethics of dentistry was all anyone wanted to talk about once you reached port. I honestly thought the security guard at the marina would arrest me for not quoting the proper amount of X-rays per patient. Not that I knew the answer anyway — I’m a man of books and the sea, not goopy holes in your jaw.      But it was the dentists, innit — they always go further than the rest when it comes to rules.

Rather annoying really, having to go through all that when you do everything properly anyway. But it's not like I got to pick it out myself. Otherwise I’d have picked a bit more specific      Well I don’t blame you, I mean what would be the use in it otherwise if it’s all the same? I don’t think they take that into account at all when they do these choices.      Not at all! I mean, I don’t think she was even there that long. We’ve had to change the set-up twice already when it was still within the first couple of months.      I don’t get why the teachers are still doing this to us like that.      The teachers left themselves in charge of picking, didn’t they? D’you pick and I’ll be the one crying because you’ve chosen far too easy something.      I just happened to like Histoire De Rien, you know, when we talked about France’s history. Also, the teacher excluded anything directly related to Watergate or any of those other political ones.      Right, as if you’re choosing only for yourself. I might’ve chosen something else, but it'd be a waste of time.      Well, I’m not sure, because the other day Anna was choosing something and she picked Ancient Egypt as her topic.      That’s not even a religion.      But also, you can read books and have your own opinion. I remember what you were saying at dinner when we talked about the politicians back in 2007. You said you didn’t understand how people vote for someone like that.      It was just a general idea and not about anyone specific.      You could be in that boat yourself, you know. Maybe you’d end up expressing more clearly what you were thinking at the time.      I mean, I tried once, but when I started doing all the research into queens and that type of thing, I got distracted with lunches and holiday plans.      Yeah, that sounds like a risk.      Yeah, go for it. But it might cost you a few extra hours in the library.      I don’t know, sometimes when I’m doing assignments like that I just take the route to conservation and then leave it at that.      True, but sometimes it’s better to overcompensate just to make sure you’re making the right decision.

Rather annoying driving up here in this traffic, innit? But I reckon it's worth it for truffle hunting tomorrow, yeah? I’ve never tried proper black truffle before—only the fake stuff that comes in jars in chippy shops.      Aye, truffles are somethin’ else. I met a chef in Bolton once, proper mad he was—used to grow his own herbs in his back garden, but he said truffles were a top-notch ingredient. He even had some chefs from America come and interview him for a telly show.      Mummy, what’s truffles? Are they like mushrooms?      No, love, they’re a kind of fungus that’s really expensive and only grows in certain places. This part of Istria is known for 'em. Some chefs and foodies fly in just for the truffle season.      I still can’t believe you knew a chef, Hattie! Me and Josh have only ever been to places where the chefs shout at the people behind the counter.      Can we eat a chef?      No, love! You can  taste  food made by chefs, but they’re people—just like us. Although I will say, some chefs do smoke a lot of cigarettes while they cook, and that does smell a bit like burning food.   Speaker_4 :   Smoking in the kitchen might be a common habit in some circles—but in professional kitchens, certainly not. Health and safety standards have come a long way since the 80s.      Oh, Paul, you sound like one of those telly chefs who about five syllables to say the word “flour.”      Speak for yourself, Hattie. Paul was at Oxford, remember?      I was at University College for econ—had no aspirations for the kitchen.      Well, you would’ve told any chef with a cigarette in their hand to bin it.      As a matter of fact, yes. And also to improve their knife skills. Watching someone whack steak with a cleaver in some road-side restaurant in Bolton once made me think the NHS was away goin’ on holiday.      Okay, okay—no one in the car is a food critic today, bloke.      What’s NHS?      Oh gosh, I’m startin’ to sound like your granddad now, innit?      C’mon Josh, I’ll explain it all when we get to the guesthouse. We can watch some of that cooking telly once we get internet back.      Better still—get your mum to rustle you up a few things.

Rather lovely day today, isn't it? That sun is making everything feel a bit more bearable than usual... What with the cold often hitting Cambridge this time of year. I mean, sure, Aylesbury's not exactly sun-soaked either, but I do miss a bit of brightness now and again.      Definitely, I’ve got to say I haven't been this grateful for sunlight since, well, probably last year when we had that unseasonal heatwave. Oh, and congrats by the way—I remember reading you work in language research. That must be fascinating, don't you think? I can't imagine keeping up with how fast everything is changing, especially online.      Thanks! And yes, it really is. I love how new technologies and platforms are constantly shifting how we communicate. You'd be surprised how much subtlety goes into understanding even the smallest shifts in meaning. Though honestly, I envy people in more 'applied' roles... I spend most of my time poring over data and writing reports.      That does sound like quite the brain workout. I, on the other hand, spend most of my time keeping things moving on the ground. As a projects assistant, it's more about organisational skills than linguistics. Still, when it comes to languages, I'm very much a practical learner—up and down the road at the press, everyone speaks somethin’ these days.      Absolutely, we’ve had to become multilingual in business just to keep up. Our clients are all over the world, and digital marketing is so global now—piece of toast is a different type of bread in many countries. Can't just make assumptions anymore, or you risk a public relations misstep.      Oh, that's gold. I remember a campaign where they thought “biscuit” and “cookie” were the same thing in Europe. My, what a disaster that turned out to be in Belgium.      Haha, biscuits are a landmine all their own. I tried once to impress a German client by saying I'd had a  Lebkuchen  for breakfast. Turns out I said  Lackhund , which apparently means “shitty dog” in some parts.      Oh no! That’s one for the history books.      You’re not the only one, I promise. I’ve got an entire folder full of misheard and mistranslated marketing snippets.      That’d make for one hell of a book, wouldn’t it?  SuccessListenerFail: A Guide to Translating Your Company's Idiot Slogans Abroad .

Rather annoying that the satnav's gone off again, isn't it?      Oh honestly, Mrs. Thompson, you're doing it more than I am. I've fixed it three times this morning already. Not to mention when the wheel came off at the motorway service station.       laughs dryly  Not helping, young lady. But seriously – are we going to Tarnow? I think that's where this road leads, isn't it? It was on the map that Adrian sent me.      Yeah, it's the second big town north of Kraków. We should make it in about an hour, depending on the roadworks.      I still can’t believe you lot talk like this in the North – I’m from the South, for goodness’ sake. "T’town". Blimey, you’ve really shaken it out of me.       giggles  Well, I didn’t teach you that, you picked it up from the other teachers. I reckon your attempts to learn Polish are ten times worse than my accent.      Right, as if you’re not the one who tried to say "dzięki" and ended up sounding like a cat being strangled. I already foresee a situation where we'll be stuck in this van with four people who also can't speak Polish, and none of them want to speak English out of principle.      Oh here we go – the revolution against your beautiful, unaccented English about to begin.       laughing  It's not a revolution, it's linguistic solidarity. Not that I mind staying up all night speaking French to my boyfriend just to avoid conversing with someone who's only expressing opinions I already agree with.      You're such a teacher. Always trying to twist everything into little life lessons.      I'm being academically honest. It's alright, Mrs. Thompson, you were doing pronouns properly at least.      Oh I did? Blimey, I thought I was just accidentally romanticising things by saying everyone is "piękny".

Rather annoying this, innit? They’ve got the telly on but it's muted, an' we're just stare oot at them players runnin' abou’ like their socks are on fire!      I know, I know—some people wouldn't know a decent kits design een their face if it kicked 'em in it! But I reckon this new sponsor deal… what's it with McDonald's now?      Yeah, McDonald's? I'm not sure, y'know. It feels a bit… cheesy. Didn’t they get axed from some team in the Football League a few seasons back?      Oh, I’d heard that rumour too. My mate who works in marketing says it's got nothin’ to do wi' the quality of the food, more to do wi' the brand image—like, it’s a bit ‘incongruent’ with football values or whatever.      Bloody charades o' corporate speak, innit? All the big fast food chains jumpin’ in wi’ their golden arches an’ neon gloves—look at it! The strips are as flashy as a bingo caller in a smart suit.      You'd expect a little from the way it's gone – Mate, have you seen Liverpool's new strip?      Yeah! Someone tries to sell me them and I will laugh in their face! It’s like they’ve dressed the lads up in full Premier League but with a Kevin McCloud vibe.      Some nutty graphic designer got a grant and ran with it, I reckon. Look, it's not all bad. I mean, McDonald’s is a global brand. With their money, they can get teams th’ kit they need.      I get it, innit? It’s the funding, ‘cos the football development stuff costs. Binnie here got all kinds of schemes funded by companies too. Still, I’d stick wi' good ol’ hoody’s or something—keep it local 'stead of Louis Vuitton flags flyin’ o'er the pitch. It’s a bit of a shame, though, innit?      Yeah, I’m not sayin' it’s not necessary. But I mean, I’d rather see a few local businesses get a chance to be part of it, y’know? They could put on a half-decent burger, an' no one'd be flashin’ neon shoes at ’em before kick-off.

Rather annoying to be honest. I’d rather be hanging out with mine or just chilling in peace. But anyway... What's been going on with you? It's been a while since we've caught up properly.      Aw, don't even get me started on eBay. Just sent an order that I'm pretty sure doesn't exist anymore. Not like I've got spare cash to waste on dodgy kitchen items. A lot worse things to worry about these days, honestly. Benefit applications are a nightmare, pulling teeth it is. You wouldn't believe the amount of paperwork for a bit of JSA. You'd think the government could afford better bureaucracy if they can afford a new national rail upgrade, don’t you know?      Ooh, you still claiming benefits? Well, I can't see you working anytime soon with the way you’ve been moaning about the state of everything for about a decade now. Wait, is it still JSA? I remember you saying you used to live off universal credit and then switched back, or was that just a dream?      It's not a dream, love—personally, I'd take universal credit if it wasn't for the stigma. I tell you, it's like they want to make us feel as low as possible when we apply. And no, I’m not talking about the same thing again, because really, if I was the one earning pin money, I would be the one saving up for holidays and not you! Though, let’s be fair, someone’s gotta pay for the George Forman grill dinners, right?      Oh yes, the George Foreman—nothing says luxury like grilling undercooked sausages in a heat-retaining pan about five minutes before they smoke the entire living room. But yeah, I get it. I’ve been trying not to worry about that too much. I have mine, but I still worry. My sister’s got little ones and she constantly texts me about train times for day trips. Honestly, the state of public transport is depressing—ever tried catching a train from Chatham to London without arriving an hour early as a contingency?      Mate, I live in the dystopia of the National Rail schedule. My sister tells me I should take my kids to somewhere nice— if I had money I bloody well would . It’s not like I have kids, but I would do that.

Rather annoying when the sat nav goes wrong, isn’t it? I was driving up to Chester last week and it got me completely lost in some muddy field.      I nearly hit a cow and thought I was going to die. That and the children shouting in the back—it’s a wonder I made it anywhere at all.      I reckon it’s not as bad as flying. A few years back, I nearly died in a plane crash, so don’t let me anywhere near a machine that’s supposed to tell me directions.      Oh dear, a plane crash? That’s awful!      It was 1974, and I was flying to Mykonos. The pilot lost his head and tried to land back where we had taken off from, only it was foggy. A good 200 of us were injured and one poor gentleman breakfasted with the sky. I happened to be a bit in front and saw the tray tables go flying like shopping trolleys.      I still can’t eat toast without flinching.      I never thought about it like that. So grief and trauma, it really sticks with you, doesn’t it?      You’re telling me – I once had a fairly large warts, it really bugged me.      Oh, warts! You know what cured me back in the old days? Dabbing them with vinegar every night. Strictly bedtime: read a book, dab them up, preferably with something hotter than the coldest vinegar in the world and be sure to sing a rhyme!      I did something far more modern: laser treatment. Paid good money and had this man looking at my hands like they were rare artworks. Not that I mind, it helped a lot with my confidence. My account manager role depends on being rather put together after all.      I don’t really have any such problems, but I do meet some odd people when I’m doing the shop run for Mrs. Alderson.      Oh, I heard about that! She asked if the man in the aisle was delivering something for her by the way he was looking at her. I said: well if you don’t mind walking over your shopping, just follow him out the door.      Family can be such a world. My husband’s sister lives 3000 miles away and never comes to visit. But send her a Facebook message and she’s ‘Can’t you meet me at the airport?

So nurseries, right? My teacher was saying they used to be super strict. Like, they’d make you stand in the corner or something if you misbehaved. I asked what they were called, and she said “nuns,” and I was like, what even is a nun?      Oh dear, yes, they were a bit scary when I was your age. Proper no-nonsense. They wore those grey habits and would walk around with a ruler, ready to give you a clip round the ear if you wasn’t quiet. I used to be terrified during maths class.      Ma needs to go! Ma!  claps excitedly, stomping out of the room.       Okay, okay, I’m coming! Don’t run off like that, love.      Wait, I think I read something about them in a book about the Matrix. The Matrix is, um… like a system that’s fake? I’m not entirely sure, but the book compared religion to the Matrix, kind of like a programme people follow without realising it.      Oh, I’ve heard of that film! It’s a bit sci-fi, but I suppose, in a way, religion  is  a kind of rhythm in life. It gives people something to follow, something to believe in. Though I think it’s important to question things too.      So like, you don’t have to believe in everything? I mean, religion kind of feels like it’s just rules and stuff. Like why do you have to say grace before a meal?      It’s more than rules. It’s about being grateful for what you’ve got, and connecting with something bigger than yourself. Not everyone believes the same, of course. Some people like stuff like Scientology, which is kind of like a religion but it also has all these expensive courses. My sister read about it once and thought it was nuts.      What, like a religion you pay for?      Yes, exactly! You start off doing one course, and then you end up being asked to pay for another, and another… It’s whack. Not everyone’s going to agree on what’s true, though.      That makes sense. I think it’s cool that there are so many different beliefs, even in the same family. Like we go to church sometimes, but I also like learning about other stuff. I mean, even Santa and Father Christmas are kind of like made-up figures people follow, aren’t they?

Rather annoying driving up here, eh? You know, me n’ the partner was discussin’ when we’d got the seats sorted out whether we’d do more than just observe at this folk dance thing we’re goin’ to. Y’know, like, proper learn summat.      Right, so, you meant to take an ac-tual lesson this time? Because last time, I remember you were listing off every North Eastern folk dance tune you could remember in your head.      Aye, was me n’ this old lecturer from the uni. He was big on Old English, y’see, so he taught us a few songs and such, only I’ve forgotten half of them.      So what made you want to start takin’ lessons then? D’you miss the old uni days?      Nah, more ‘cos we’re goin’ on this holiday in a month or so in the Lake District, an’ they’ve got this massive folk festival near Keswick. Me n’ the partner thought—why not do a few weeks of proper practice? Y’know, instead of just turnin’ up and griefin’ everyone with our dodgy step…      Well, from what I’ve seen at the last one, you two were absolutely in your element. You were the only people not sommat like… clapped out after the first hour.      That’s because I’m still got the stamina from my Corpus admin days. You’d be surprised how runnin’ a database all day still equates to a fair bit of energy being left at the end of the day.      I suppose. Anyway, the real story from the last trip was this fella from a charity walk—he thought he was doing the dip and the step correctly, but we had to step in and show ‘im the proper way.      Aye, I remember that. Thought he was gonna cry, he was so disappointed in his performance. You ever think about stickin’ with that and teachin’ folk a bit?      Nah, I’ve got enough on with work. Still, I did run into an old uni pal the other day goin’ on about his new PhD in medieval metrics and imperial units—still line in the sand, between ‘em he said, like yin and yang.      I’ll be honest, sounds a bit poxy. I mean, even the new True to Life on iPlayer or LoveFilm is better than that, innit?      I dunno, they said the guy’s got a theory that the old ballads shaped our legal system.

Rather annoying this new roundabout eh? You’d think in 2023 it would be easier to get from A to B without getting stuck in a queue of Range Rovers staredown      Aye, we do love the view though—sea on one side and olive groves on een-a. Proper idyllic if it weren’t for the traffic.      I reckon we should’ve driven to one of them music festivals. They said there’d be a stage by the sea.      Music festivals at the peak of summer? That's a recipe for a heatstroke or a queue for the loos so long you forget your name. Still, I do love the idea of the olive groves. I read Istria is the best place in Europe for artisanal oils—probably true too, and I’ll be the first to spend £40 a bottle on something better than breakfast margarine.      Haha, you and your oil, Dad. You lot never miss ordering the most expensive bit of the menu.      Nonsense, I know what I’m paying for. I’m a professional, as they say. And tell me, what would you buy if you weren’t risking it on something called ‘silver humble sauce’ from a market?      Right cheery thoughts for a long drive. Let’s talk about something more heartening—did you hear about the new restaurant in Poreč? Word is the chef was someone who appeared on a TV show. That sort of thing is big here oddly.      Mom, did you watch  Sons of Anarchy ? I heard people are into that type of about motorcycles and tattoos. I reckon you’d like it.      To be fair, luv, that lot were barely more worrying than your uncles on Sunday after the 12 pints.      Honestly, I’m just worried about where the campsite is. I don’t fancy sharing a caravan with you boys when it gets dark and the crickets start.      Relax, we've booked a campsite by the coast with electric hook-up. That means you don’t even have to cook. I’ll get the barbecue goin’ on day two if you promise not to go exploring in the woods with a camera drone again.      Fair point. Last time we were in Croatia, I made it to the top of one hill and ended up with a trespassing notice from a shepherd who had a better arm than most Premier League players.

Rather annoying I’ve just got a notification on TikTok ‘Anal’s got 3m likes on that pedy dance again. Never mind. Y’know, I were thinkin', like we could start a little YouTube thing? Just us four, like filmin’ games and stuff. We could make a bit of cash and it'd be fun while we're all still young and about.      Oh my gosh, I think that's brilliant! I mean, we've all got records of some interesting times anyway. We could just be ourselves. Cambridge's never had a vibe like Doncaster. You know what I mean?      Aww, that sounds like real fun. Although do we have to do the turkey dance again? I still get a bit self-conscious about that video, to be honest.      I think it could be really cool if we approached it the right way. Like, maybe we focus more on the games and not just random daft dances. I know some uni students that have massive channels based on games and challenges. We could do something similar—set up a few concepts and try to get consistent viewers.      Yeah, innit. I dunno, like, we’ve got a proper little group. We’ve been through all the weird crap together, and that’s what gives us a bit of authenticity. No one else is gonna come off as natural as us.      For sure. And we don’t even need to be all posh. Let people hear us in our own accents. That's part of what makes us unique. Some of the best content out there now is real and comes through as genuine.      Ooh, I do like that. We could even show our journey! From daft kids to trying to make something of ourselves. Like, that’d be kinda powerful, innit?      Definitely, and for the games, we could invite some of our other mates. The more, the merrier. Let's make sure it's accessible and funny, you know? Like, maybe a game each week and then vote on what to do next.      That sounds whack. I say we set it up for next Saturday after the shoot by the park. That's got goin' on usually, if we start there, we can get some views off the goin' past. And if it goes well, we might get some of you older lasses to get in on it too!      I can setup some editing software and help produce it.

Rather hungry I am, ain't I? That last coffee they serve here was as thick as wallpaper paste. I got to get some proper food in me before I go back to teachin' those bleedin’ spreadsheets.      Oh I know what you mean, like the coffee was brewed in eenywee  bawks  somewhere. Honestly, I reckon it was made in the lift with a paper cup and a prayer. I’ve got this craving for a massive chip butty right now, or maybe something a bit healthier. Wait, are those slimming pills in your bag, Dave?      You two are united over the tragic coffee, as always. I, on the other hand, brought my own turkey sandwich. You know, healthy and stuff. It’s not like I’m one of them kebabs-in-the-car every night sort of fellas. I was at a takeaway place yesterday and breakfast, no less. I swear they threw in a bit of goat and a teaspoon of regret.      You always say that, Paul. I reckon your sandwich is fresher than the kebab chef’s idea of clean towels. I’m with Dave on this. I’ve tried to be mindful with my diet but if I don’t eat proper food, I’m just got one cuppa and a cheeky Mars bar by lunch, and then it all goes downhill from there. I’ve been trying to find good vegan places round here. Found one in the city called Green Bean, but the coffee was just  awful . Honestly, they might as well have given us motor oil.      Ah, vegan, right. I thought it was supposed to be all leafy greens and good stuff. I did this ‘Meat Free Monday’ a while ago, and I ate a salad for a week so gloomy I ended up buying a chicken sandwich and crying. I mean, I was just trying to  be  healthy. Dave, you’d probably eat a concrete wall if it was on the menu.      Fair point, but I did manage to switch off the deep fryer at home and that’s a start. My missus went vegan last year and it was a warzone in the kitchen. The only veg I got around then were the ones the kids hid in goon socks on the landing. It's not about goin' cold turkey, is it? I mean, we can’t all be saints.      So Dave, what’s for tea tonight, then?

Rather annoying when people pop in out of nowhere to ask about social networking, you know? They think it's all got to be Insta or TikTok these days. I mean, what happened to just a good old inquiry at the desk?      Ah yes, well, you'd be surprised how many students still don't understand the difference between research databases and Facebook groups. I had a lad come in a week ago, all wide-eyed, asking if we'd got a WhatsApp for books. Imagine that.      You're never surprised when it happens, though. You just fetch the books without a page!  Oh, no, that's Facebook, I don't do books in there.       I find it fascinating—from a New Zealand perspective, things are pretty similar. I used to work in a library in Auckland, and the questions would generally be "Is there a group for this?" or "Can I post my essay on social media and cite it?" You'd think they’d be so much more clued-up now, but no.      Well, it's up to us to keep up, as much as we despise it, innit? We ran a workshop last week on LinkedIn and its importance for academics. Half the session was about how to prevent your gran from commenting on your published work.      Now there's a nightmare! You don't want to go searchable and then have your aunt Fiona from Liverpool in your references section. That’s a bit much.      Oh, you mean the awkward relative who shares your childhood photos with their 300 friends? Yeah, I've had that about Twitter. Someone once sent a screenshot of the timeline of my library card number going viral.      Honestly, I think I've lost it. I Facebook-message my stepdad just to check for reading recommendations. It's gotten so bad I actually friend his pet hamster.      Oh, I've gone full Australia, mate. You know I joined a Facebook group called "Mums Who Read 1984 with Their Kids." It's just been quizzes and passive-aggressive book comparisons since.      Sometimes I wonder—will social go the way of snail mail and end up obsolete or just evolve into something even more baffling? I genuinely don’t know if I want to be your digital virtual academic ghost at 10 am on a conference call one day.      Just make sure your virtual ghost is wearing appropriate socks.

Rather than going the traditional route of buying land to build a new hospice from scratch, would it not make more sense to adapt some of the local properties already lying vacant? I’ve spoken with a few estate agents in the area, and there are a few nursing homes being sold — well-maintained, in good locations, and at a more attractive cost than building new.      I heard you. That’s a logical suggestion. But before we go anywhere near estate agents, we need the business case pulling together properly. We can’t just react quickly and lose sight of the bigger picture.      Right, I understand. But surely consulting estate agents is part of the bigger picture? You’ve stressed the importance of the location being accessible for both patients and families. The one I mentioned in Tunbridge is right next to a bus stop and within half a mile of a hospital. It’s far more central than the farmland site we discussed last week.      The point isn’t just about the location being accessible, though accessibility is key. We have to consider the full rationale for where we place the hospice—person-centred care, the impacts on local health services, as well as how we integrate with existing organisations like the local hospice network. We’re not just building a building; we’re building a new model of end-of-life care, and that needs to be backed up by the consultation and the data.      You're absolutely right. And don’t get me wrong—I’m in favour of a full consultation. But I’ve been looking into the existing health budget allocations, and there’s a significant portion specifically for community-based and integrated palliative care. If we don’t act fast, there may not be enough funding left to even start the project properly.      That’s a fair point. We should start compiling that data now and factor in the proposed changes to local organisational structures. The NHS has made it clear that they’re moving towards multi-organisational partnerships, so the business case must show how this project supports that.      Absolutely. And while we're at it, I’d propose we include a space in the proposal to keep the hospice running even if funding is reduced in the future. That might come with the building—nursing home goers are used to life-care nursing and can be real assets in supporting our line of work.

Rather skip the newfit slippers, love. That lot tend to go flat after a week.      Never mind them—look at that photo I found in the back of the drawer! There we were at Royal Ascot in '99—remember the hat with the feathers? Ruined half the event when a gust of wind took it!      Lmao! No I didn’t—they should've made that the theme this year, "Lost Headgear". Imagine what the Royal Family would do!      Oh, don't get me started on hats. Mine just needs to stay on during these bloody Zoom meetings. I've got the thing clamped tighter than a clinic trolley.      So eccentric! I'd be terrified of falling off the screen mid-pitch, but then I'm more the hoodie type.      Speaking of, breakfast, what's for dinner?      Stirred steak, charred tomatoes and that feta cheese puff you love so much.      As long as it's not the mushroom and tofu one I once had in a landmine.      That’ll still be there in a couple of weeks, trot it out then.      Mate, I got a job interview and I need to eat something that doesn’t taste like cardboard.      You're the copywriter, you should be used to those kind of feels.      Just trying to stay professional. Besides, I've got an ambition hotter than the stove—prove to them I can be their next big thing.      Sounds exciting, doll. My tip: don’t try to impress the panel with your lingo. Keep it civil and crisp.      Exactly! And if they ask about my previous projects, don’t mention the meme stuff. Keep it professional.      And don’t let them assume you're just the student who stared at them for 5 minutes before sliding the exam paper back.      He knows the 'stare and memorise' method. Some people call it cheating—others call it a ninja mind.      Look, I remember your first day of work, you practically prepped for six hours, but that was because you were nervous blooming about it.      That was flu, not nerves, and I still had the hours to spare. Just like your first interview for nursing—stood outside for over half an hour just pacing and filing your nails.      Nailed it, didn't I? They hired me on the spot 'cos I spontaneously cried over a tomato. It was deep and moving.      Yep, then you cried again when we couldn’t afford the rent, and then cried once more when you found out about the new tax bill.

Rather skip horror films me an’ my gran used t’watch A Night at the Museum, real mids... got scared once, proper jumpy now I think about it! Any idea wot ye fancy then? I've got £6 t spend, so probs Netflix or summat.      Right, cos  A Night at the Museum    ain't   scary at all… come on, you’ve gotta have a bit more guts than this! I’ve brought along a couple of films, dumpier ones. We can chuck sommat on and see who screams the loudest.      Right, fair enough. What've you got then? Don't say  Hereditary  or  The Conjuring 'cause I definitely won't be watching them. I like jump scares more, the usual ghosts an’ ghosts, not proper sad stuff.      Nah, don’t worry – we’re starting with  The Grudge . It’s alright for a bit o’ mild horror. Proper spooky but not, y’know, so traumatic that you wake up at night thinking you heard something. Might get under your skin a touch, I reckon.      Yep,  The Grudge  I might go for… watching it with you probs makes it better. Remember when we watched  The Shining  at your gran’s and you made me skip every scary part? I didn’t want t’tell your gran I’d lost the film ‘cause you rewound fifty times!      Oh ha ha ha! Cos you didn’t like it, did ye! I remember cos you were all, “It's just real loud and people are acting like they're mad in a hotel.” Not a fan of Jack Nicholson clearly! But you can man up now – watching this together, properly.      Oh that was you! I thought it was the sound went out! Jokes, jokes! Alright,  The Grudge  it is then. Betcha me and the biscuits will be on the floor at the end.      Biscuit? Not scared! Though I’ll admit to doing a double-take with that creepy kid in the first one. Not the same with the voice-over and everything. Proper freaky. I’ll get the popcorn goin’ on then.      Just don’t expect me to not scream when that green lady with the box walks in… I might run out of the room at that bit. You’ve been warned!      Fair play. Just don’t blame me if you talk about dolls with creepy smiles in the middle o’ the night. Now, I reckons I'm gonna crouch behind the sofa when it kicks off, so we’re even.

Rather than going out for take-away, I've decided to do something a bit more fun tomorrow — I've found a listing on Airbnb in Exeter for a weekend stay. It's an old farmhouse, and there are reviews that say it's really atmospheric.      Oh, that sounds nice. I always find the idea of staying in someone else's home rather than a hotel intriguing. Is it far? I remember that Aneurin’s daughter used to visit Exeter every now and then. She loved the place.      It's only an hour outside of the city, so we won’t get too far from home. I’m still trying to get used to the idea of booking places like that, but well… you know, I’ve met enough eccentric people through friends’ stories to consider it part of the adventure!      Aye, I suppose you do, at that. I still prefer breakfasts made by someone I know, but still... I suppose there’s a certain charm to it. I never did get into it myself when I was working, too busy, I suppose.      Well, you should try one of these next time we’re in the area. It'd be nice to book a room and spend a bit of time without worrying about all the cooking. And while we’re preparing for that, I was thinking, I really should get an iPad. I’ve been trying to manage emails and school notices on my old phone, and it’s getting tedious, to be honest.      Oh, an iPad. Now, those are expensive, are they not?      Yes, and I want something solid — maybe a newer model. I spoke to my sister today about it, and she said the best ones are touch-screen friendly and can be used for cooking or watching videos. She even recommended buying it online from one of the big websites for a better deal.      Aye, well if you’re going to buy something online, be sure it's a reputable site. I once tried to buy something from a little-known company, and the parcel didn’t arrive. Took me weeks to sort it out with the bank. Things are easier these days, but the risks are there.      Thank you for the heads-up — I’ll make sure to check if it's secure. And I think I’ll line it up with the purchase of a new box set of films from the same shop.

Rather than share a new book last night, I found an old one I had in the attic — it was a gift from my Gran when I was a lad. Dug it out by accident after Ailsa mentioned it in passing. Title's  Brave New World  — wouldn't say it was my fave, mind ye, but it's got some fascinating stuff on society.      Oh aye? A classic, but tends tae polarise folk, doesn't it? It was one o’ the first books we had tae read for English at uni. Remember the class dissection o’ it? Some o’ them wee  philosophical undergrads  were convinced it’d guid up in the future.      Och, aye — well, I wasnae convinced at the time and I’m no’ now. Still, I was thinking aboot it while we were on the trip tae the Highlands. Reminded me o’ how much I missed the silence oaf being out in the moorlands, the way time just... stretches oot.      Aye, that really impacts you if you’re not used to it. I tell me students that travel isnae just watching new places — it’s about seeing the same things in a different light. Or nae light at all, mind — the starry sky above the loch nearly blew me mind.      Dinnae weet? I’d never looked at stars like that — full skyline, no blight or trees in the way. Had the sourdough baking hotter than the fire going. Soakin’ in it through the window as I baked.      I about cried at that wee hill near Eskdasie — the wind had this peculiar howl oot there and the sheep were bleating like they were in a film. No’ in a dramatic sense, jist the way it sounded lone. Brought back memories o’ Gran’s stories o’ the old folks and their superstitions.      Aye, I could see her there, as clear as day. She’d have taken one look at that hill and said somethin’ about the fair folk, for certain. Mind, she’d have told the kids tae go back tae the house if they heard that wind.      Which, interestingly, is why I’ve started infusing Scottish folklore intae some o’ the tutorials I run for postgrads. They think it’s whimsical, but there’s real cultural analysis to be made in the way traditions evolved in the landscape o’ this place. It’s all so... rooted.      Just like books, once they’re under yer skin, they root yers.

Rather annoying to be honest. I’d rather be hanging out with you both anyway.      Well, I’ll let you finish this letter, and I can take a look after you’ve had a rest. You don’t look too happy about it.      I don’t want to sound like I’m being difficult, but I   really   need advice on how to present myself. I’ve only applied for this because I got this call from an old client who used to work in planning. He said he’s working in the government and might be able to get me an interview.      That sounds brilliant! Why so hesitant, love?      It’s like that old turkey again. You know, the one left over on Sunday and destined to live on the sandwiches the following week. I’ve been sitting on this application for weeks, and every time I start writing it, I feel like it’s just going to be a bit inedible.      Oh, don’t be nonsense! I know you overthink too much—especially when it involves big steps like this. Who is the company again?      It’s the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government—somehow it feels quite imposing when you just read it out loud.      Right, now that does sound important. I imagine they’re quite conservative about their wording and structure. You know what I always say: make your points, keep it factual, and don’t try to sound too clever. They just want clarity and proof that you can manage what you say you can do.      I know—I just get so bogged down by trying to flatter them with words I don’t even know!      And there you go—that failsafe old charm of trying too hard. Remember, if they like your background, your education, and your eye for construction, then expressing that clearly is more than enough.      But how do I show my experience without sounding too modest or too arrogant? That’s my downfall as an architect. I’m good at space, not people.      Now, love, no one is asking for a poetry recital. Just the facts: what projects have you worked on, where you were placed, and what your role meant to the company. Also, don’t forget to mention any software or design tools you’re confident in using. That’s seriously impressive.      And your client—does that help me to mention?

Rather annoying this new council tax regime, innit? Seems they've gone and hiked it up 'gainst all logic. Never mind me never working, yet still I’ve to cover this extra bill!      Aye, 'tis as bad as it can be. I’ve 'ad to use my pension more than I’d ‘oped. Still, at least we’ve got each other. You’ve ‘ad any trouble with the old place, George?      To be 'onest, t’roof’s started to leak again. 'Ave no idea how long it’s been like that. 'Ave to sort that out before winter. What with supply and demand these days, builders are 'arder than ever to get.      And I’m hearin’ the same, dear. I tried gettin’ a roof check done for my niece’s place – she doesn’t 'ave a 'ousehold. Cost a 'arm and a leg, even with Government grants. They say the lads are so short. Good 'eaven, I nearly went into a 'orror when I 'ead up about that two-year land registry backlog.      Oh, that’s on another level. My neighbour ‘ad a will all got drawn up, and the land’s been tied up since last May. It really is a mess.      Aye, and the government promises what it can’t deliver! 'Ow’s the 'ousing someone who ‘as never worked? ‘Ow are the 'eads wein’ manage with all this added 'ostility? I say the politicians ‘ave no grip on the future.      It's sad to see the younger ones 'aving to move out of the area. I’ve lost touch with a few of the school friends I grew up with. ‘Ere to the bin, ‘eck. The prices are well outta reach for the 'arsher crowd.      Do you think there’s a way for people like us – retired and long-term unemployed – to get a better say?      I think it takes ‘olding on, lad. My grandchild’s a 'ealth worker – she's 'ad to go work in Manchester for a 'igher wage.      I say let’s not lose our 'eads over it today. ‘As Mike fixed the windows yet, dear?      Not yet. 'Im ‘as gone over to ’is son’s in Cambridge ‘cause they’re ‘avin’ them fitting. I’m goin’ over tomorrow to see if they’ve got an ‘our. Least, it’ll take 'is mind off the news. ‘E’s been 'andling it all, you know?      Good idea.

Rather annoying to be honest, the amount of work needed in that old warehouse space. We’ve only just sorted the last lot of fire hazards with the fire escapes, and now we need to figure out where we’re going to store all the new furniture we ordered for the children’s area.      Yeah, it is a bit of a maze with the layout. But if we use the old staff room next door as a temporary storage area, we can clear out the main event space for rehearsals. We’ve got that drama group coming in next week, don’t we?      That’s right. I spoke to Helen last week, and she’s excited about it. We just need to make sure the lights are up and working by then. I’m still not convinced the tenant from the second floor isn’t going to complain again about the noise.      I told them it’s a charity gig – we’re not running a nightclub up there! Anyway, I’ve been thinking about the marketing for the new season. We should consider doing some social media shout-outs for the upcoming events, like the poetry night and the weekend book fair. We’ve got some decent numbers following us.      That sounds like a good idea. We could even do some stickers or little brochures. You know, something for people to pick up when they’re in the café. We need to be more proactive about getting our name out there.      Absolutely. And don’t forget the toilets and the coffee bar. We need to get the bulbs replaced in the ceiling there. Those flickering lights are not what you want when people are meeting up with friends and being ‘artsy’!      True. I’ve got the electrician coming in on Friday to touch up a few things. Oh, and what about the holiday cover arrangements? I know Sally mentioned she’s going away next month, and we need to make sure the maintenance schedule still works out.      I’ll have a word with Tony – he was quite keen last time. He knows how to handle the basic stuff while the real contractors are out. Though to be honest, it’s the lunches we need to plan better. People have been complaining about the delays in the canteen.      Yeah, go talk to the canteen staff. If we can’t get them to speed up, maybe rethink the food options – box meals or something.

Rather skip the newfit trend, Joshua. That’s my honest opinion.      Oh, come on Claire, she’s only doing it to find a bit of motivation.      Look, I can do a bit o' continental breakfast for you. But it’s gotta be eeny weeny, yeah? Or I’ll be handed over to the health and safety police.      I think Ayela’s too much of a perfectionist. The guilt will get to her if she can’t manage it.      It’s the worst. You start with the best intent, and then  wham . I did it once, and only lasted a week before I craved turkey and mash. Still dream about it.      We should just cook what we feel like and say no to the guilt. Living healthy is one thing, but you better not breakfast on leaf and water if you want everyone here after 9am.      That’s what I’m saying. We’re not in a full-on detox retreat. We’re here to get away, not listen to Ayela rattle off calories every time someone opens their mouth.      Her excuse is always the same – it’s about being humble and setting a good example.      Well, it’s not like she’s the only one of us who worries about what they eat. I’ve cut out gluten for a while. It’s kind of just someone needing to feel like they’re steering the boat, whether they actually are or not.      I say, if she doesn’t want to eat the sausages, she better make her own about five eggs and walk a mile to grind the beans.      Honestly, you could make a documentary about her diet and the self-punishments she goes through to maintain it.      To be fair, I did cut sods of porridge the other day for any ‘vegan warriors’. I tried to make them taste like a spoon of crack to make up for the sprite of the cereal.      That was you? No wonder we ran out in five minutes.      I told her early on go easy on the guilt trip if she intends on using mine. I made her line in the sand, between food and guilt, and let her know what your actual body will tell you.      You want to avoid making those kinds of moral judgements over toast, right?      Precisely, and this is supposed to be a holiday. I think we all forget that sometimes, and let the expectations of one person spoil it for everyone else.

Rather annoying advert just popped up on my phone ‘bout a holiday to三亚那啥—the Chinese place. D’ye fancy a trip out there?      Sanya, you mean? That's in China, right? Sounds alright—I’ve not been there before. What made you think o’ it?      Just felt like an adventure. I reckon it'd be easy to get a visa with our EU passport, but I'll have to check. Y'know, seeing as we might not be in the EU anymore. Leeds to the airport's a bit of a trek.      Right, I get it. Not like we're near Heathrow. I'm still likin’ the sound of it, though. When were you thinking of heading?      Maybe around the end of next month? I’ve not got any meetings planned then an’ it’s a nice time o’ year, no doubt. I've been wanting to try some o’ that northern Indian food ever since Ellie went, you remember?      Oh yeah, she said it was one o’ the best trips she’d ever had. I mean, we did a road trip last summer and ended up drivin’ through the Lake District—it wasn't exactly exotic, but it was good fun. Though I can’t complain: got a chance to film some footage for the project I was working on.      Aye, that was quite the drive! When I saw the car lights whizzin’ past in the fog, I was fully convinced we were gonna end up in a ditch. Some o’ the villages near Keswick were real pretty, though.      Yeah, there’s something peaceful about them old-stone walls an’ rivers. Anyway, back to this holiday—have a look into flights an’ hotels an’ let me know the details. I could probably clear my schedule.      Aye, I'll do that. Hey, while I'm on the phone, d’ye think it'd be a good idea to catch up with Tom while we’re there? He’s got a cousin in Sanya, or somethin’ like that.      Tom? The one from uni? I’d love to! I owe him money goin’ on for years from that poker game. Just don’t expect me to pay him back, will you?      Aye, well, you could at least take fluoro to dinner and see if we could rope him in for a visit.      Sounds like a solid plan. Might as well be them two together. Now—got any suggestions for films to bring along?

Rather annoying the queue at the surgery this morning, wasn't it? I had to get my blood pressure checked... got the results back this afternoon. Nothing too bad, I suppose. Still, it's worrying when you hear your own heartbeat echo in those cold rooms.      Oh, I can imagine. My sister went in last week about her sore back. They reckon it's not as serious as she thought, but I know she's just put that off for a year. You know how she gets, pulling herself together and pretending she's fine. It makes me cross sometimes when people don't take things seriously.      I couldn’t agree more. I've had to deal with that in my job too. It's easy when you're living with others to think you can hide things. I had a pupil who lost her brother last year—just out of nowhere. It hit everyone in the family hard. The parents, the siblings—they all dealt with it differently. Hiding in silence, shouting, even laughing at wrong moments.      That sounds tough. I lost my uncle a few months ago, you know. He was in his sixties. Poor thing, it was quick. We tried to be as careful as we could with the arrangements. My mum insisted on a little funeral. “It's the least we can do for him,” she said. It was strange seeing the family come together like that. All that emotion in the air.      It must be. I remember the day after someone in our family passed—my cousin. He was a chef, you know. Funny thing was, the night before he died, he was still being his usual self: witty, cracking jokes, even joking about his weight. I always admired how he kept such a good sense of humour. It made it a little easier for the family to talk about losing him.      Maybe that’s the trick, isn’t it? Keeping things light. My sister tried going on a diet after her brother’s funeral. She was trying to take better care of herself, I suppose. I always told her the best thing you can do after losing someone is to keep moving with your life. It doesn't mean forgetting them, but going on with things.      That’s the spirit. Of course, it's never easy. It's not about pretending everything is fine, just about finding a balance between grief and the everyday grind.

Rather skip ahead a bit here. So I sat at my desk glueing wires for hours, real string spaghetti... got to the end and thought, is this more art than tech? But sure, where are we off to next? I'm alright for food, though. I char the toast 9 times outta 10 so I just pack sandwiches. But that skiing trip over Christmas, you remember? I fell over 20 times in the morning! Yes, the art of improvisation is golden when you’re doing freelance. Last month, had that sprite of a lady from London who insisted lunches include a new dish from the Michelin list each. Me?
