Rather skip to the part where we chased the badger down that garden path? I swear it came out like it had a vendetta against me after I nearly stepped on its cub.      Oh, don’t start with that story again! You nearly frightened half the street out of their wits and then cried when  I  told you it was just a mother looking for food.      A mother with  teeth , as I recall. And besides, I was terribly flustered. You were taking photos the whole time and didn’t chase it off or anything. You just stood there like you were on assignment!      Well, excuse me for thinking capturing a moment like that might be useful. You know I’m studying nature photography, right? And I had the perfect shot of you, legs flailing in slow motion like a flustered windmill.      You should’ve edited that one out! Hiding in the pantry for ten minutes after is not a good look for a man of my editorial renown.      Let’s just say it’s one of my favorite photos I’ve ever taken. You’re so unguarded in it.      I prefer the photo of me at the little shrine in Kyoto. The one where I’m bowing politely and not looking like I just ran into a wild animal.      That was the best trip, wasn’t it? Everything about the temples and the food. Remember when we got lost in the alleyway and just followed the smell of grilled eel?      And then we ended up being adopted by this old lady who insists we are honorary granddaughter and grandson about five times a day. Her goldfish watched us the whole time like it was judging our terrible Japanese.      I think the goldfish liked us. It followed the old lady like she was the queen of waters. Though I don’t think it expected us to leave a shrine to a land crab as a thank you.      I still stick by my story that it was a safety precaution.      Yeah, because clearly Japanese ancestors have strong opinions about British badgers.      Look, all I’m saying is that I never want to see a badger again. But I  will  admit that that trip to Japan beat it all by a mile.      Well, I’ll make sure to print that photo out and frame it, right next to your pantry survival shoot. For posterity.

So, I heard you lot were in Ireland last summer, Sarah. What was it like? I passed through Dublin once and thought it was mad—like, more pubs than houses.      Oh it was amazing! We stayed in this tiny cabin outside of Clogher in County Monaghan. I mean, there  were  no pubs for miles. But we had this insane night… we decided to go skinny dipping in a muddy lake at midnight! I swear, Tim, you would’ve   loved   it.      Oh god, don’t remind me—it was  freezing . I went in up to my knees and immediately regretted everything. But Sarah, you were the one who made that My Photo app collage afterward, remember? You left Tim in the water by himself because you were too busy editing photos of your sad face.      Well, the lake was better than breakfast, anyway. The landlady’s "Irish stew" looked more like charred oversized mac and cheese, to be honest.      Let me guess—no-one knows Claudia Roden recipes in Ireland?      What’s Claudia Roden got to do with it, Tim?      She’s this legend from the UK who writes amazing – but mostly Jewish – food stuff, like, rich stews and spiced pastries. I was just reading her memoir and thinking about how cool it is that you can connect food to religion, family, all that.        Yeah, yeah, I've definitely never tried anything like that. Down under, we stick to more basic stuff—steak, vegies, lamb, and a few good pies. Nothin' fancy. But I've got to say, I'm a fan of your Jewish jokes Sarah. Not that I've heard any.        My,  you  just showed off that you can make grammar work for you. Classic Tim. Speaking of which – any updates on the café? I tried your new sourdough last week and it was good, but I swear it gave me nightmares.      Ohh! Tim had such an interesting night when you  snored , Sarah. I think the ceiling tiles got goosed. I mean, if you were a zombie apocalypse survivalist, I'd suggest separate sleeping bags.      Oh come on, Sarah’s snoring doesn’t rise to the level of a post-apocalyptic issue. In fact, maybe we should have a survival strategy? I say poetry is overrated in the food shortage, but you can’t go wrong with a good oatcake and butter.      Listen, if it's a zombie apocalypse we're talking about, and the only food’s stale bread and you’re scribbling poetry in the dust, you've already lost.

Rather annoying when a bar of peanuts finds its way into your drink. I was just trying to decompress after a shift and nearly choked mid-sip. It's not like peanuts are banned or anything, but there's got to be a proper serving system, innit?      Aye, it’s all about expectations, yeah? You’re expecting a drink and end up with a snack. Bit of a slap in the face when you're halfway through a pint. Still, easier to handle than what I got last week. Tried to play an online computer game with some mates from uni and the bloke from Germany had like three Russian characters in his name—made no sense, couldn't even load the game. It's like everyone's turkey on border security these days. Fun got put on hold just over some dumb alphabet soup.      I hear you. I mean, you’d think by now they’d have something a bit more streamlined. I've been doing some research into data verification processes for border checks and it's wild how much room for improvement there is. They use overcomplicated systems—vast warehouses of info—yet still can’t tell if I’m shortlisted for a job or still trying to get in on my uni application.      Sounds like something outta a film. You ever see that one where the hacker’s trying to get into a government system and the passwords are all somersaults and clockwork oranges?      You mean  Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy ? No, that’s more suspicious characters and conspiracy theories than algorithmic mess. Though I can see the connection—there's a fair stretch between data encryption and shadowy state secrets.      Not nearly about as exciting as the time I took a mate down the coast to Alton Towers. To be fair, the rollercoaster was more dramatic than the security check. Still, I'd have preferred less time queuing and more time enjoying. All that scanned rubbish. They make it sound like the whole place is under constant threat of an explosive.      I reckon it’s just security theater—those yellow lines and constant foot exams always make me want to reach for the peanuts again. Not that I'd want to set off a metal detector with a snack.      Nor do I. If I wanted risk, I’d just hop in my car and go for a spin.

Rather skip the mushy peas today, love. Thought I’d go the whole nine yards and order the pikelets and whitebait instead. Going rowing down at the Cam this weekend, and I need to make sure I can keep up with the lads—get a bit of heartburn otherwise. Got eeny weeny wisp of a rowing club at the uni.      Oh aye? A lot of starting now, aren’t you? Still, easier said than done. I know someone once—can’t recall the name—nearly capsized when he tried the kayak at the weekend. Rain came down like it couldn’t decide what to do with itself and he had only a pair of old socks and what you might call a bin liner for a raincoat. Classic. Probably woke the entire river.      I’ll be the same. Living with assembling a kit of waterproofs better than breakfast, honestly. You need to look half like a garden gnomish posh astronaut and not a total muppet in the water. Also, the wind over the Cam can pick you up like a child—personally I’ve had enough of that since yesterday.      I tell you, since November we’ve been bowled over by it. Still, when it got to spring, I remember Matey talking about planning a trip with the kids to Hayling Island. One time he nearly picked up and flew like a doddle when the kids left the sails untethered and the old man wandered into the wind. Strictly sailing: read climbing a cliff backwards.      Ugh, don’t mind the wind as much as the rain. I mean, when it’s coming straight at you, you at least know where it’s going to touch the ground. When it’s thundery, and the leaves are doing that zany dance and it starts snowing sideways in April, that hits like a slap. Moments like that remind you that others are going on and on with their lives. Last week was bloody awful—had to meet my cousin for the first time in over a decade after hearing about her engagement. Auntie had mentioned it passing with 'Oh Jane and Paul—you know the cousins? Anyway, no point telling you, you’re not interested.'      go on then, what happened?      Well, I just said, “Actually, yes. Who lives in York?” And what comes out of her mouth? “I’m seriously Jane,” and then proceeds to tell me that Grandpa never even mentioned me.

‘Mum said we’s better get a move on ‘fore we’re late for nan and gramps. I got the text ‘bout twenty mihutes ago.’      ‘Right then, we don’t wanna keep ‘em hangin’. By the way, did you manage to get that eenvelope from the uni yet?’      ‘Not yet, dada. I’m waitin’ for it to come through in the post. They said it’d be here by Results Day, but it ain’t shown up yet. Is it me chase it up or what?’      ‘Aye, if it’s not here by tomorrow mornin’ you give ‘em a bell. I know ‘ow it is - universities left and right, and sometimes they get confused who’s who. But I’d say make sure you’ve got it ‘fore you start choosin’ halls. What’d you apply for this time?’      ‘Just Leeds and Liverpool. Nah, Liverpool didn’t shout out so I’m not expectin’. It’s Leeds I’m hopin’ for, though. Y’know I like the North.’      ‘Smashing. Leeds is a good un. I went t’me first year there way back. Back when we communicated with each other via letters and Morse Code, not these phones we’ve got now.’      ‘You was what? ‘Ow did you survive, dada? I couldn’t survive one day without emojis!’      ‘Aye, well, you had to be a bit more creative. Wrote ‘em letters, drew pictures, sent photographs in the post. I even ‘ad to send a telegram once to tell me mum I’d passed me exams!’      ‘That’s so old school! Can you believe people still use WhatsApp and Messenger ‘nd every other app for that?’      ‘I can, believe it or not. ‘Ere, talking of messages, you’ve been on eBay again, ‘ave you? Yer Amazon thingy came yesterday, didn’t it?’      ‘Eh, no, it was a pair of shoes from eBay! The ones I ordered goin’ on uni. I wanted some new ones so I ain’t look like a greengrocer’s reject the first day.’      ‘Fair enough. I made me own shoes when I was in me teens. Properly stitched ‘em, took ages. But they lasted for years.’      ‘Blimey. I ‘ad mine for five mihutes. I dropped em in the queue at Tesco once and they were dead.’      ‘Aye, times ‘ave changed. But while we’re walkin’ we might as well make sure you’ve got everything. You need a refillable glass bottle, a couple of pens, maybe some extra e-numerics in case the laptop says otherwise?’

I'm just grindin' through the last few essays. Still got a load to do. You on a break now?      Yup, finishin’ up next week, thank god. Today just me and the PC. You know me — when I get stuck in front of the screen, I forget to even eat.      Bro, same here. I've like lived at my laptop. Honestly, I swear my left hand is gonna forget how to do anything else but hover over the mouse. I think I turned my sandwich to toast by accident earlier.      Now  dat  a tragic tale, Dann. I pity the sandwich!      Yeah, but once I finish this lot, I’m off to Tokyo. Just booked it last week — I mean, Japan has been on my bucket list for ages. You’ve still got time to join me, you know.      No disrespect, Mate, but I’m not sure I’m ready to fly halfway across the world and somethin’ go sideways like when you tried to make sushi and set the kitchen on fire.      That was a blunder. But man, they’ve got  amazing  restaurants in Tokyo, and it's cosmopolitan as hell. Unlike someplace I once  regretfully  visited where I about got food poisoning after eating street meat.      Yeah, that was you barely leavin’ your hotel bed for two days. My sister had to put baked beans on toast for you like it was some kind of therapy.      Yeah man, but I made it through. But I might see if I can volunteer somewhere or just travel for a bit before I commit to full-time work. Y’know, live a little.      Bro, that sounds like a plan. I mean, I’m just figuring it out too. Maybe I’ll start with a job in the tech industry, learn the ropes. You got my kind of brain for all that computer jargon.      Oh, I do. Just not in the way you want. I got the vibe you got no idea what a firewall is.      Ask me again once I’ve survived this next week.

Rather annoying when a phone’s on silent and you only notice once everything's gone. Felt real guilty piling all the parcels on top of it this morning.      Oh, that's probably it then. Not to worry, the postman brings such a mixture. But it was nice of you to clear out the post tray while I was out. Still, it seems odd they'd send a medical brochure that early in the morning.      Bother? I’ve had worse. When I was still at work, I got once sent a chase-up letter about a delinquent invoice... Right to the sorting office! Spent weeks bouncing around the post system like a hippo in a hatbox. My postman nearly retired on the spot laughing.      You had Postman Pat moments, Dad. I think he turned down a promotion at the Royal Mail just for you!      I wonder if it has a signature in there. When’s the last time we thought about re-in-surance? Should have been sorted over the summer, but somehow it’s slipped off the radar again.      Funnily enough, I had a call off David Cameron today. He was pointing out how the tax system is a little generous these days. Not much – just enough to make a chap with a savings account slap his head and mutter, “I don’t know where I did wrong.”      Still, if he’s chasing people out of the back door, he might as well read them a checklist of tax rules first.      Tax avoidance, eh? Mind you, I had a patient once – colleague, not actual patient – about to fall off the back of a lorry in the office. I had to reconstruct a whole story about why he was there to plug the insurance gap. The lad was so flustered he didn’t stop to check the form was even right. Said he was there to learn about expenditure effectiveness.      That does sound like something you might say on a rainy Tuesday.      Let’s not talk insurance. I’ve been mulling over that ferry trip to Ireland – you know, the one via the South Devon coast. Might be good to set goings on it before life gets more complicated. Any chance of persuading you to chuck in a cruise between us?      I’d say we could. It’d take the pressure off navigation and give someone else the chance to wrestle with the tide.

Rather annoying driving up from Kent last Sunday.      That's it, no SAT Nav... got to follow some maps from the internet.      Oh, where did you go again pop? Not Belgium or something, I hope!      No, it een't dear. We went to Belgium. Not 'something'.      Yeah, I said that I had a flat mate who went too and she loved it. She used Google Maps, easy as that.      Not when you're in another country with slow wi-fi. Get lost three times! Still, it made us talk a lot more and we found some lovely little markets in Brussels that Myra hadn't even heard of.      Oh, tell me about the food. I know how you love a good market.      Mmm! Wait breakfast, no doubt about that. Found some Flemish waffles, and lots of different roasted meats! No, you didn’t have to get a saddle of lamb, we shared like proper grown-ups!      Haha I can imagine, quite a contrast to the high-tech food in London. Have you tried any local dishes we can try?      I’m more curious about the cycle paths. I know you, Brian, always trying something new. Did you do any cycling?      Aye, we hit the hills in the Ardennes for a couple of days. Bike hire suspiciously cheap. Used a mix of car and cycle.      Sounds adventurey. I thought being abroad would be easier, but your colleague said driving abroad was a nightmare with the tolls and all that.      It is. To be fair, not all roads take tolls and the SAT Nav helped a lot once we got the app working.      App? I had a basic phone and used me old Nokia. Unreliable bloody thing!      Oh no! I told you about my new phone and how much better the apps are.      Brian, I do suggest if you're going abroad you get a phone with updated travel apps! Maybe get a Sim go that works on your own phone.      You’re all in the future, I’m behind the box! Time to catch up your lot.      I’ve been looking into European bike trails. Maybe we can all go next year? Less stressful than driving.      Mmm, cycling sounds better. Less chance of getting lost, at least.      And less chance of getting fined for driving in the wrong lane or wrong way up the motorway.      Yep, last time someone in our flat drove backwards up the cycle path for ten minutes.

Rather annoying when people from the South make fun of our accents. Sheffield lasses can get quite strong when they're warming up in cold weather.      I can well imagine. I come from Manchester and we've got our own set of words and phrases as well. People like to act superior if they come from the south, but we're just as capable. I reckon it's not all that different from a place like Bristol in the West Country, where I've got a cousin. She used to travel quite a bit to Queensland in her youth, she said the warm climate suited her, but the blokes there dress... well, very differently from us.      That's true, I've had colleagues from Australia and the way they speak is quite melodic to our ears. But back to accents, I've lived in Sheffield all my life and every now and then I get an accent coach breaking me down to better understand when I lecture universities about dialects in Anglo-Saxon literature. Though at my age, I suspect I'm not going to lose it. Also, the way they describe their banking system is interesting.      I remember when I retired I thought, "I'm going to Australia and enjoy the sunshine." I did go on a couple of trips, and it was lovely. The way the locals wear – very practical: often just a singlet, thongs, and a floppy hat. Doesn't quite appeal to my sensibilities, but I suppose it's the sensible choice.      They've got to in a place with such extremes of temperature. It's different from here, where even in summer, you have to have at least a jacket when it rains – which it does daily, doesn't it? I did business there once for the company I was in, and had to get a loan from what they call a local bank that was more like a savings society. Rather informal for my taste.      I once guest lectured at a university in Queensland and was told by the students they could cope with my accent better than their professor from London. You mustn't knock the North too much.      No, I've taught in a couple of places in the South myself and let me tell you, delivering something as complex as EFL grammar with a Southern goody-two-shoes tone was suffocating.      I suppose it's all about respect in the end.

Rather annoying isn't it, how everything these days seems to revolve around your internet presence. I know  some  people rather like it—that sort of attention, don’t they? But forgive me, I much prefer to keep my life quite quiet online.      Oh, totally get it. I mean, I use my socials a lot for my teaching job and stuff, but I also have a dark side that only watches too many niche podcasts in the evenings. They’re easier to binge guilt-free, if you know what I mean.      Didn’t you say you teach English in some international school? So your profile must be  visible  online regardless, whether you want it to or not.      Yeah, I’ve got an Instagram and a bit of a LinkedIn, but I’m lucky in that I pick and choose what I share. But then you’ve got TikTok and Reels and all that—there seems to be a new platform every week!      Honestly, I try not to even look at the news too much. I just tune in to Waterstones or BBC if I need info. These days, I prefer short, quality content. Did you hear that podcast about vegan cooking while we were on the train here? That was quite good, actually.      Mate, I binged that last night! It was  excellent —so inspiring. It makes sense, what with us being in a vegan restaurant and everything! Though the reality is never quite as appealing as the online version—haven’t you read about the chef here? He had a  massive  following, but now he wants to go back to non-vegan recipes.      I did see that. Seems a bit dramatic, but I can imagine the pressure. Not everyone can be into this kind of lifestyle forever. Speaking of which, have you managed to switch to entirely plant-based, like us?      For the most part. Though I have been stressing a bit lately about not being as dedicated. I still scroll through too many influencer posts about protein-shake recipes and then end up being  so  hungry by the weekend.      That happened to me with the podcast you recommended a couple of weeks ago. I started watching the TV go along with it. The show is pretty good, but I think I watched six episodes in two days without even eating.      Tell your story! It’s all so easy to get pulled in, isn’t it?

Rather annoyingly, I haven't got anything to do this weekend. I was just wondering if they’re going to be alright on their own with the babysitter yet?      Let me see that picture you said you drew! She’s beginning to get used to it. She was actually really excited this morning when she found out they were going swimming. A lot more excited than I managed to be, to be honest.      She's the one always talking about when we get the swimming tickets.      Tomorrow! Not this weekend. I forget sometimes the detail of their schedule. On the other hand, you know, I’ve already got to pay for the tickets and the babysitting – I’m not upset about getting them extra pocket money for doing something fun with their friend.      You know, they were so excited about getting a picture to send for the Blue Peter badge, they even showed it to the babysitter. I think she was quite flattered.      I showed her the one I did last time and she thought it was amazing.      He may not be a professional artist, but he’s imaginative. I suppose that’s part of the value of the badge, really – the idea that people don’t have to be brilliant at drawing to win it.      When I was their age, I always tried so hard to draw my family properly. I remember I had a picture accepted once. Also, I think the badge involves collecting stickers, so maybe they need more passes in the passport holder...      You mean you had the Blue Peter pass?      Wait, not that passport. Not the actual government one. The one they send out to collect with each badge. You know, the ones with the laminated card. They used to stick on the TV Guide.      She tried to make me understand once that the stickies come from different shows. You can get them from space shows, lunches, or the big one— the circus! We almost managed to see  The Travelling Circus  once.      I remember that! I wanted to meet the real lion tamer! She said, no, it's just a box in the tent.      She said that? That's unusual. She’s quite against any animal stuff, right?      She was, but over time she’s become more open. It astonishes me how kind she is to them, how often she checks in.      Speaking of patience, did she tell you that story again about the Chinese people eating old eggs?

Rather annoying to be honest. I mean, I understand it's normal and all, but it's been like... off and on lately. Like, one minute he's  rock solid  and the next, he's suddenly gone all squidgy and seems like not even as frightened by a bear in a nightie as he should be.  laughs       Ugh, that's  so  frustrating. I’ve only been with Alex for a few months and I’ve already noticed it happening. It doesn’t help that he gets so anxious about it. You’d think blokes would be more chilled about the whole... like, it's not like  every  sexually active man doesn't have it occasionally!      My turkey still gets all twitchy about it. I tell him constantly – I ain't obsessed with the boner, and I don’t care if he goes limp in the middle of Netflix and chill. I just want him to enjoy it and not be a total stress doughnut over it. But o’ course, he still frets. Like, it’s like he’s walking around with one foot out the door of PD Land.       snorts  PD Land, love that. Honestly, I think men feel so much pressure from all the media and whatnot. Like Matey: “This chap, he needs it big  and  bendy and he needs it every time.” And when their willpower and anatomy don’t match the narrative, they panic. Like, someone said in one of them medical magazines: it affects a million blokes over 40— obviously  it's a thing.      Aye, and it ain't always down to about age neither. Stress, health, fookin' diet, even fookin’ what you've had to drink that day. My mate's dad had a near heart attack because of anxiety, ‘cos he was like, “Oh my god I can't sod up at me girlfriend’s house”. And it was all because he thought it was a midlife crisis or something!       laughs  Right. And also, some firms are finally talking about it more—my uni had an ED awareness day last term! I mean, it's still really awkward to talk about sometimes. If I was to say "Alex, I think you might wanna go see a doctor ’cos y'know your downstairs man’s acting all shy sometimes," it feels really personal and weird to say out loud.      True, but it's better to get over the hump and be open.

Rather than going the usual route of booking a swanky resort for our holiday this year, I've been thinking... What if we try something different? Like road-tripping through France? I've always wanted to take in the countryside at a slower pace. What do you think?      Road-tripping? That sounds like a nice change of pace, but I haven't driven there in years. Plus, I'm not sure about all those narrow country roads and language barriers.      It would be like a journey together rather than just another trip. We could chase the sunsets, visit those little villages you like to talk about. I'd write a bit, you'd set up your portable wi-fi, and we'd just... live in the moment for a bit.      I see the charm in what you're saying. I think I could handle a few chaotic cafes and confusing roundabouts for the weekend breakfasts and whatever. But this conversation makes me wonder — in your perfect day, would it include a holiday, or even a holiday at home?      It would include us, coffee, maybe reading in the garden, and I don't think location matters as much as the company. For instance, today — just finishing this book, you making me something to eat from your experimental recipe list — that's perfect.      And that's why I married you. You make perfect out of simplicity. But hypothetically, if we could go back ten years and tell our younger selves something about work-life balance...      ...I'd tell them to stop worrying so much about getting ahead and start enjoying the little moments. Both of us had our heads in future goals, never looking at what we already had. That rush for promotions, the pressure of performing — it distorted our priorities.      Definitely. I know I pushed myself harder than necessary, partly because I thought that's what success looked like. And honestly, if I had a tattoo that read "Stop stressing," it'd be on my back right now.      You always did have a flair for the dramatic. But seriously, doing something like that — with a funny message — it would probably make you feel liberated. Like, you remember that time I had that rash on the back of my gothic tattoo on my neck from that antiseptic cream I used? I thought I was making a stylish statement.      And what your employer thought was even less stylish.

Rather lovely to have you here again, David. That postcard from the Highlands was a nice touch — did you manage to visit some of those quaint little villages mentioned?      Thanks, George! Yes, we did. We took a side trip to Plockton, near Plockton Bay. The fishing village there is picture-postcard perfect, with those little white cottages and all. You should go sometime. A change from your usual tutorial regimen!      Laughter. I wouldn’t mind a nice cup of tea by the sea instead of marking essays, but the coursework has been piling up. I’ve even fallen behind on birthday arrangements for the weekend. I had planned to do something special for Sarah — you know, my niece — but between the postgraduate seminars and committee work, I haven’t had a spare minute.      Is she turning ten again?      Nineteen this year — I mean, she’s practically in university herself! I was planning to take her, her mother, and a few friends for a meal at The Coach House in Mitcheldean. Nothing too raucous — I don’t fancy another call from their parents about early closures.      Sounds good. You know, we should make a weekend out of it. My partner Jen would love to meet them, and I could really do with some peace away from spreadsheets and technical support calls.      Absolutely, we could make it a family and friends day out. Let me just get the RSVPs sorted. Now, by the way, did I tell you about the latest fury going on in the news? The Scottish independence nonsense — it’s taken on a life of its own again. I’m disappointed to see so many young people still clinging to this fantasy.      Yeah, it’s been on my mind too. The whole thing leaves me cold. My father was born in Glasgow, but I was raised here in the Midlands. I have no idea why it keeps flaring up. I mean, I understand national identities, but I see little advantage to splitting the United Kingdom.      Precisely. I think it’s partly the Nationalists milking sentiment, and partly a distraction from pressing issues like education and healthcare. Of course, I get that life improvements are often incremental — but at least Scotland is part of the solution, not a separate problem.      True. Anyway, back to the planning — if we’re heading to The Coach House, I’d suggest maybe doing a little walk to the Blaenavon Industrial Museum in the morning?

Rather than a new chair, Arabella, I think you meant a different kind of chair, like a typ... What was it, Thomas?      I think she said a "suspension chair", Miss Elise. You know, like the one Grandad has on the porch?      Oh, yes! A suspension chair, Thomas. That was the one — the kind with a rope that you can lean back on and swing gently. But Arabella, you were talking about drawing a chair to help Syrian refugees. How do you imagine that works?      Well, I saw on the telly that they don't have much, so we could draw a chair that people can make like that at home, you know, with sticks and left-over rope or something. I made one for school, Miss, and Mrs. Holland said it was very thoughtful!      Oh, Arabella, that's brilliant! It's very kind of you to think about what people might need and how we can help even through simple ideas. But tell me, how did you come up with the idea of a chair?      I don't quite remember. We read a book in class, and ... someone there was sitting on the floor because they didn't have chairs. So I thought maybe if we shared chair ideas, they could make one.      That’s very kind of you to care and share. You know what, Thomas? When I was your age, I also used to draw things I thought would help people. I once designed a desk for blind children. It was made from cardboard and had different textures and sounds. But Arabella’s idea is more personal, and chairs make a home about five times more comfortable.      She’s right! Once I sat on the floor and thought it was so hard to draw or even write. So, a chair to sit on, like for reading or playing, that’s really important.      Exactly, Thomas. It helps give a sense of security and comfort. Now, Arabella, I could help you make a proper drawing of your suspension chair, and if you want, we can explain it clearly so someone else could try to build it too. Would you like that?      Yes, yes! I want it to help someone else. Maybe one of the posters on the wall could show it. And I could write the words.      Great! We can even make a small model with some items lying around the house, maybe some old broom handles and a spare bit of string from the kitchen.

Rather lovely day today, isn't it? I needed this walk. The university has been such a whirlwind with all the publicity from our recent initiatives.      Agreed. There's something about being out in the countryside that just clears the mind. By the way, did you hear about the old superstition in these parts about crossing the road if you see a hearse?      Oh yes! A lot of people still take that seriously. I remember my grandmother swearing by it. She used to say if you don't, the deceased soul might take chase when it's your time. Rather grim, but I suppose it adds character to places like Norfolk.      That's not the only one. My uncle still believes if you drop a spoon on the floor, it's a sign someone is about to get married. Rather sad in a way—he lost his wife last year, and still clings to these old tales.      It can be comforting, though. I know the lecturer in the comedy studies department told me a story about the time he performed at a pub in Yorkshire and a policeman turned up, thinking he was up to no good. Everyone just laughed it off, and the audience got even more into the show.      That does sound like a funny story. I remember when we first got together, we went on holiday to Hay-on-Wye. You were set on buying that obscure comic book, and I spent the entire weekend looking at your back, muttering in your ear about the cost. Honestly, you were a stubborn one.      Oh, you were the one complaining when the bookshop ran out of the premium edition. I had to wait until we got home and ordered it online. You even brought it up when we were watching TV that night. "Still waiting for that book, are we?" I've never heard anyone unashamedly nag quite like you.      Well, you passed it on. Though I have to admit, it was a great holiday overall. There's something about being surrounded by little villages, bookshops, and good pubs.      Definitely. It reminds me why I took up teaching in the first place. Not just to be part of something bigger, but to make the world a little kinder and more informed—superstitions or not.      I think that's what makes you a good lecturer. You're always one to explain the meaning behind the madness.

Rather annoying this new phone of mine. You know, dad, everything's just internet-based now. You can't even turn it off sometimes without it doing something more annoying. I swear, it's designed to distract you every 5 minutes.      Aye, technology moves quicker than my old een can blink now, luv. Back in 'my day', we just had a landline on the table and a big TV. If the TV was off, it was easier to think.      Well, nothing was moving quickly for you back then when you were still using a payphone to ask someone out! Still, I made sure I explained everything about the new laptop to you last week. So you shouldn’t be struggling with that email setup now.      Aye, you did. But I still find it funny how little buttons can take you miles away. By the way, when's the old place up for sale? I tried to arrange them by era, but I lost my head halfway and just ended up doing a rainbow order by the color of the glaze.      That's you alright, luv. Prettier the mess the better go the photos on your Pinterest board. How're your plans at the Great Dorset Steam Fair shaping up by the way? That bloke on the radio said it was going to be something else this year.

Rather annoying isn't it, this business with the library? I was reading the local newspaper online and it says it's facing threats of being knocked down to make way for a new supermarket or something. It's a shame, really. Not only do they have a good children's section, but the place was built in the fifties, and has a lovely modernist look to it.      Yes, I’ve heard about it. The council's too focused on short-term financial gains. It's all about building something flashy and commercial to appeal to the tourist trade. Places like that don't last long if they fetch the right price on the property market.      What I don't get is why they can’t just restore it. Surely, with enough grants and community support, they could keep the library alive and even expand it a bit. The modernist architecture is quite an asset, you know? It gives character. Not everyone wants ultra-modern steel and glass.      Absolutely. I looked into that, actually. Some property developers have a façade policy, where they keep the front of the building and gut the inside. But the library in question — well, as it is, it only qualifies as non-historic. The council would probably say it’s not worth the cost.      That's precisely the problem, isn't it? Things like that are the soul of the community. You know what gets me? If the building is gone, the only record we have of it is someone's photo online or a suspiciously clean government report. It just dissolves into the air with no trace.      I get it. I was trying to research whether people are doing anything about it. There's a campaign group trying to gather signatures. But you know how it is — a few hundred signatures don’t count for anything with these big decisions. The problem is, local action rarely has a big voice against big development firms.      Well, I suppose we'll have to do what we can. Speaking of development, though — I found some nice fabric online while I was browsing for the library campaign. Rather soft and earthy tones. Would you like to see the pattern I had in mind for the settee?      Of course. I can go and get my laptop. I wanted to look up something about pre-war libraries as well, just in case we could find a precedent or something.

Rather annoying this new Spotify algorithm, isn't it? Seems to think I like pop songs by Ed Sheeran or some lightweight bloke with a bad case of vowel stretching! Honestly, I prefer jazz or classic rock, not this upbeat pop claptrap.      Oh, you haven’t tried that “Genre Dive” feature yet, have you? It’s where you pick specific artists or genres they don’t know about, and it actually gives you more interesting stuff. I use it all the time to discover new bands to play in the car. Music makes the drive so much more bearable.      Yeah, I’ve even used it to find throwback indie stuff and 90s alt-rock. Being a bit of a music hoarder helps though. I’ve got playlists for every mood – like this one for when I’m sad but want to be nostalgic. It rules, by the way.      I’m more of a radio guy personally. The classic FM station’s got the best 80s hits. I can’t get into all this streamlined digital blooming nonsense – it just jumps from one inappropriate track to another too quickly for my taste.      I tell you, old-school radio has its charm, but the algorithm – it’s like it gives you what it thinks – not what you want. I almost had to take the battery out of my phone trying to switch it off.      If you’re looking for a tune that sets the mood for the drive, though, I’ve also got a few playlists I can share with you. Nothing fancy – just my personal ones with some chill instrumentals and a couple of acoustic covers I like.      That’s about how I stumbled upon a whole new appreciation for Renaissance lit music, which is vibes. I’ve been trying to convert Sarah into that too! I mean, it does sound strange at first, but once you get into it…      I think I’m just more into rhythm and minimal instrumentation – something you can move to or sing along with. Give me a strong beat and a good vocal track over that sprite of electronic jabber.      That’s what I do with haircuts, actually – set the mood with the right music. Clients sometimes get so relaxed, they almost fall asleep! I’ve even had a couple of them ask for specific songs, which is nice because it means they trust the vibes.

Rather annoying this new car tax eh, lad? Thought me old Escort would've lasted another few years 'fore I got to splash out agin.      Nah, I think it might be worth it in the long run. My mate said electric cars cost less to run in the end. Got eeny weeny bills and no road tax if 'e remembers rightly.      Oh aye? A lot o' expense t' me just t' save pence on fuel. An' besides, do y’think somethin’ like that’d hold up wi’ all ee carin’ needs? I mean, you've still got t’ insure it and all, don’t y’?      Well, I did a bit o' research. Car insurance fer electric is actually cheaper in some cases, and I think the Government gives grants for charging points too. Maybe we could put een charging point in the garage? Cheaper if ye charge yer own battery at home, innit?      Eeh, so I’d not 'ave t’ go to the petrol station, then? That’d save me the occasional trip in the rain! Still, I were worried ee'd not hold as much gear in it—what wi' ee always bringin’ bins and shopping from school –?      Nah, I looked up a few models. One like the VW ID.3 would be alright, but if we go for somethin’ bigger, maybe the Tesla Model Y or the Kia Niro. They say they’ve got good boot space.      Tesla, is it? Sounds fancy. Mind you, I were brought up with a De Stijl and a Ford Cortina. Not a bad thing, but I still like the way an internal combustion engine purrs. Nothin’ like that plug-in whirr, if y’ask me.      I reckon it’s all about future-proofin’ though, gran. You know, with the ban on new diesel and petrol cars comin’ up. I don't wanna be stuck wi’ a car that’s out o’ date.      Aye, I suppose ye’ve got a point there, luv. Just like I told ee when ee goin’ on that maths paper—look ahead, don’t just solve the question in front o’ ye. Although I ‘ate that exam when I were younger. All them summin’, I lost me head and got a D.      You gave me a C on it once, ‘cause I didn't show me working! It wasn’t fair! You lot just like paper and writing things down in a weird order, old school.

Rather than share a recording of this, I think I'd prefer to just have her in the house when we're talking and see what she makes of the whole thing. I'd be lying if I said I wasn't anxious about being recorded.      Grandad, can you imagine how interesting it would be if we could go back and listen to all these little moments again later on in our lives? I reckon that would be so cool!      Tim, you are far too young to be talking about wanting to listen to your present self when you're considerably older. That's a rather grim thought, to be perfectly honest!      Now now, no need to go on about that. My turkey curry definitely beat Marco's effort though. His chicken lacked flavor altogether, to be honest. D'you know how I make mine?      How do you do it, grandad? He doesn't use any spice, which I suppose is kind of the point of it being chicken, but even so it's so bland.      Ah yes, Chicken, Chicken Curry, Chicken Curry—there are three short words quite casually squashed together. I think that's what makes it go down so well.      No, no. The trick is adding a generous helping of cinnamon, and then making sure the chicken is broken into bite-sized chunks before you add any sauce. Silly Marco, he probably didn’t cook it for three hours.      Marco also doesn’t have a real wind pipe, he’s had a tracheotomy. Also, he's 89 and still works as a taxi driver! Can you believe that?      That is incredible! I can’t imagine what he thinks about most days. I bet he fails to know that the world barely works the same way as it did in his youth.      Enya, you passed the test with that. I could see the concern in your face when you said he had a tracheotomy. You mustn’t worry about such things as he manages just fine. Rather annoying this wet weather, eh gran?      Aye, it’s been pissing nonstop since woken up. I’m more used to it in Bolton, but where we are now is a different story. You took it so hard.      Aye, well, it was a difficult time. He was a good man, even if he didn’t agree with me on religion or anything. Though I’ve never taken to church myself.      That’s your difference, Nancy. Still, I’ve got my tuppence worth to say — go to church on your own if you like, but don’t impose it on others.      Who’s Terry Wogan? I saw some old photos online at school — I didn’t know he was famous in Bolton.      He was a Northern lad originally — from Bolton over where I’m from, actually! He became a massive radio and TV presenter over here and worked with Bear Grylls for a while, apparently.      Oh aye, he was a legend. Still, nothing before Wogan, who was the original.

Rather annoyingly, I haven't been able to get anyone to talk about this for weeks, but when did you all start becoming semi-vegetarian? It's not like we need to eat a cow every day to survive...      Look, I’ve never fully been vegetarian. I was vegan for eeny weeny bit of time last year, but I just got tired of not having meals that made a bit of sense in the middle of the week. I mean, I don’t eat red meat, not unless it’s a special occasion anyway...      Yeah, but the worst thing isn’t the meat, it’s how they  get  it. All the slaughterhouses, the conditions. It's like that one turkey on Christmas Day who you watched grow up and then you just... serve him up for dinner, right? I used to think eating hunted meat was better, but now I’ve learned how horrific factory farming is, I’m just not interested in eating meat at all.      I agree that factory farming is pretty awful. I mean, why would you treat an animal that way? Like, yes, we can survive on vegan food, but we’re not as innately violent humanely as we like to pretend we are… watching animals being tortured – it’s deeply unpleasant.      Mate, I don’t think people like watching it either. But the fact is, unless you don’t eat any animal products at all, what else is left? We might as well be eating people at that rate. I think the real future is cultured meat, right? That  lab meat  stuff? They're making it taste the same as normal meat, but no blood, no suffering, and better for the environment about tenfold.      Interesting! But what about taste? I mean, what if they make meat that doesn’t taste like meat? Or if it  does  taste the same, but for some reason you feel less fulfilled eating it knowing it's artificial?      Honestly, if I can’t tell the difference, I don’t care. I just want to know that as few animals as possible are involved in the production of lunches and dinners.      Yeah, but it's not  just  the animals, it’s the environment. Meat production is really bad for carbon emissions and contributes  heavily  to climate change. Imagine making that same food with no land usage or methane.      So are you planning to go 100% plant-based then?

Rather annoying to be honest. I’d rather be sunbathing on a beach in Majorca than trawling through the archives of old legal cases this week, don’t you think, Sophie?      Absolutely. True enough – but it's precisely that kind of local variation that makes our jobs fun. Though I have to say, working as a co-ordinator does make me nostalgic for holidays! That was one of the more chaotic Alumni Day sidesteps, if I recall.      Yeah, go back to my parents’ place and end up at a rammed camping event with a guy singing Frank Sinatra with a kazoosh—unforgettable. Though, honestly, I’d have to say it's been nice catching up after all the hours we've spent in meetings this week!

Rather skip the new recipe, eh, love? Thought we’d do something a bit different today. Tried pikelets and lamb shank from the Middle East, actually picked it up from the TV. Reasonable, I thought. There are real lives at stake, and while we're making tea and pretending the world is stable, there’s a camp in Calais where people are starving, and the media pushes it to the back of our minds like it's some kind of myth.

Rather annoying this, isn't it, David? That grout’s still cracked in the bathroom tiling. Angela? Oh, of course. Her always had the eye for a good finish — probably the same mind that let her write a thesis in three drafts. Pity she's all the way in the West now. If she was in Reading, I'd have made her line up the tiles in  my  kitchen.      I’m not sure she’d ever forgive you for it, Tom. Rather a lot’s happened in the last few weeks, hasn’t it? That Storm Fergus battered the place when I was out with me horse. But it's nice to give them the chance to express themselves. They get so excited about it.      Express themselves? I say let ‘em dress up in a big old coat and say they're a ghost. It’s the flu that's really to be scared of out there, with all them muddy boots in the classroom.

Rather annoying this, isn't it? You think they'd have decent roads by now in such a popular area... What was it, five minutes of crawling at 10 mph? Now it's all holidays, all the time. Got more fairs, more tourists, but not enough housing, not enough road capacity. Put people in the car for no reason. Eat, sleep, drive. No thanks. Now don’t get me wrong, I'm grateful for the bungalow you found, but isn't the system just someone sitting in an office saying, “We can't do this, we can’t do that”? Even for disabled people? It shouldn’t be this frustrating!      Look, when I was your age, I thought housing was a right. Everyone gets a decent home, depending on their needs. But now they make you fight for it like it's some bloody competition. No one in that office has ever had to put someone like your mother in a wheelchair.      Exactly. You know, I was at the surgery last week, and there’s a waiting list for a physio to even assess mobility. You think of all the disabled people with no support, and it's just the same with housing. My Ma’s got a blue badge too, course she does. But even go there with one, and if you don’t get a Disabled Parking Space, you're in trouble. I was at the fair last year, and the one space was occupied by someone who didn't even seem hurt, just wanted it because it was “convenient.”

Know where we’re at anyway—ain’t gonna half        Nope, not going half—good plan. Lotteries, CBUs, casting calls for plots. Just make sure to keep the dirty work split evenly.      You have my word.
