I won't mention the time you told me you were  definitely  going to try to understand Arnie’s accent in  Terminator 2  again.      I  did  understand the first time, you young sprog. But where's this heady desire to get the scones? I'm not about to risk burning them by waiting for you!      Alright, go on, then. I’ll zip off and bring the tea. I might get pastries this time, not scones. I think we all agree scones were a bit much for yesterday’s film fest.      S’all right if I start tidying the room? I may as well make it romantic for our 'date night' of watching action movies and snacking on cakes.

Rather annoying the new DVD player we got isn't working, isn't it? I mean, it's like... barely a month old and already it's skint. I can't even watch the new boxset we got in the £2 trolley the other week—  Lovesick  , it was. Got eeny weeny passive-aggressive rating on the back. Still, better than  The Undateables —I only watched one episode and I had a migraine by half ten.      Honestly, if one more person tells me "cancel culture" is ruining TV I might scream. You'd think the people who moan about  The Undateables  haven't seen  Love Island  with their own two eyes. Speaking of, I met this eccentric couple at the spa last weekend, they had the most bizarre dynamic, like one of them was the manager of the other's emotional baggage. Cats and dogs, breakfast at Tiffany's.      I’m not even going to touch the TV subject, I’m still reeling from the interview I had over the weekend. I mean, do people truly get sent inappropriate questions in 2025 or is it just me? The human resources manager asked me, "If you were a magazine, would you be  Grazia  or  Men's Mate ?" True story.      Oh my gosh, no! What did you say? Did you pivot gracefully or just blame the universe?      I said  Grazia , obviously. That answer alone got me thanked for coming and the door was flung open at about ten past ten. It was like they were trying to make a point, "We value people about as much as we value our coffee mugs."      I feel you. My fails were more... diplomatic. I once accidentally replied to a Facebook ad in Welsh. My grandma proofreads for me. She's well high on grammar, you know. Still, I edit. It's not like my day job is confusing.      Honestly, while you two queens were dodging professional academies and spa-dwellers, I was analysing board game stats last night. My sister set us a board game conundrum—she’s convinced that go-fish is played differently if you add  I Spy  features. I tried to explain that that was like making a boxset by rearranging the plot of  Friends  with post-it notes.      I'm confused—there are people who don’t already know how to play Go-Fish? I thought it was the modern version of a Socratic seminar—just one person asks for "2s," and the rest of the room falls in line.

Rather annoying this new washing machine eh?      Aye, it's a real mither, isn't it? I swear it's more fiddly than a gym machine after a gym class. I tried to programme it t'other day and nearly frightened the cat.      Right? Thought I’d lost the use of my eyesight for a minute tryin’ t’slice through that instruction manual. Like they wrote it from Mars or summun.      Honestly it’s a wonder we still use the things. Didn’t your mum use the one at the laundrette until she married yer dad?      Oh aye, that was a proper beast. My nan still talks about boiling everything in the sink and hanging it on the radiators – back in the good old days. I think she turned 90 last year, by the way.      God, that’s brilliant! Tell her I said “well done” from me. That’s some innings. She must’ve got the knack for seasoning too, by the way. My gran didn’t have a clue—used half the packet, no seasoning, innit.      Aye, I can imagine! Though I’m not sure how much longer I’m gonna be able to afford to cook real food. My budget for the next month’s already gone somethin’ awful.      What’s the emergency? Did you pay those fancy coffee roasters at the uni again?      It’s not that! I buy out the bake-off at the local farm shop sometimes and it’s all premium cheeses and butternuts and… you know, about five square meals walkin’ about.      Alright mate. I’ve been trying to cook more at home too. I made this lasagna the other night that was just, like, flour, treacle, and despair.      Aye, it’s a hobby ‘at can ruin y’r liver, innit? I did see the trailer for that new Ryan Reynolds film though. Sounds like it’ll be right up our street with all the bombastic nonsense.      Right? He’s like the English James Bond goin’ on holidays. I’ve seen it all before. But I’ll line up for it, I’ll be honest. Nothing beats films when the house goes quiet and the washing machine’s in the corner pretending to be a courtroom.      You’re a larrikin alright. Though I’m still tryin’ to convince me folks that living near Cambridge is all that Cambridge-y and they just say “we’re fine, thank you very much.”

Rather annoying this VW thing isn't it? I suppose anyone with a car these days is affected somehow. We’d got the house sorted out in Dublin, you know, but prices fell by such a margin we had to rethink everything. Not to mention those emissions frauds—  what a shambles!         Yeah, it’s bizarre really. I remember when the scandal broke years ago, I worked nights transcription and I swear I heard more about diesel emissions than I wanted to. It was all over the headlines. We moved to Birkenhead for a change, though, but the cost of housing north of the Severn is even more  volatile  than I imagined!        If you ask me, it's not just VW. It's the whole system. I was in the technical side of planning, developing for the oil industry back in the Midlands, and it was a mess from the top down, no doubt about it. Moving up here to Hunsonby seemed a safer bet, but you can't escape the economic tides—and prices still bite like anything. The south’s overpriced, yes, but it’s not the only way short-sighted property schemes end up backfiring.        Words to live by, Seamus. When we got offered that flat in Dublin, it looked like a gift, and then boom—value plummeted. You couldn’t move for people scrambling to offload their flats. I understand the press were calling it the "Dublin property crash" at the time. Honestly, I’d read about it and thought,  what a comedown  from the heyday when people were buying and selling through word of mouth like  they were trading in precious metals.  I daresay even a maths teacher can do the sums when it finally hits the fan.        Still, you’re in the housing market long enough, and you start thinking,  what do I really need?  A flat in Dublin with a million memories, sure, but if you can’t afford it now, it's gone. I remember passing a friend who lost their place as well. They had to split and move up here too, a little more affordable—though not by much. I’d be lying if I said this VW thing didn’t hit the economy in every way, including property values.        And let me tell you, I’ve seen this in the industry—when big developments promise all sorts and then fold, it’s the regular folks left holding the bag.

Rather annoying when a new housing estate goes up, isn't it? I was just reading in the paper—what with the new building project on the outskirts o' Norwich, they're sayin' it’ll change the whole look o' the place. Look like we're losin’ yet another bit o' history een our hometown.      Aye, I reckon so. I’ve been around these parts long enough to see too many ol’ buildings go and not many come back. Mind you, I wouldn’t mind a nice cuppa and me pension once in a while when it's all done. You'd think the Government could sort out these bloody pensions so we don’t live hand to mouth.      It’s not just buildings changing, love. I left my last B&B over in London and came back home for a bit o’ peace. But now I spend most of me time lookin’ after me grandkids—good fun they are, but no one pays me like they used to. I miss being a childminder, I really do.      It’s a laugh, innit? We used to work—some of us never did quite make it to the high fliers o' this world. I was a civil engineer, so I seen a thing or two. But no matter—retirement's got a sting, and none o' it’s softened by the system.      You and me both. I was never one for education beyond school, and look where I've ended up. But I’m not grumpy about it—at least I can still do me crossword and chuck the telly on in peace.      Aye, but it’s the upsettin’ about things changin’ that does it. New houses, different people, computers everywhere. I’ve tried to learn how to use that plug-in o’ mine, but it’s more to do with websites ‘n' messages rather than what’s happenin’ in the world.      Don't get me started on the computer business! I tried to learn once, but all the buttons and clicks and that—"delete this", "-spam this", '—it’s whirrin’ like a beehive in a box. Mind you, it's a wonder how the younger generations manage it all day.      Just don't click on anything in the morning, love. And don’t let the estate developer near your bed and breakfast. It won’t be long before we’re all one big poxy housing block, I’ll warrant!

Okay, so I've just watched this documentary about evolution, and I'm trying to get my head around it... Like, how exactly did humans develop from monkeys? Is that even how it works?      Honestly? I feel like a lot of people get that wrong. Humans didn’t come from monkeys; we and monkeys  shared  a common ancestor. It’s like how you and your cousin have the same grandparent, but you don’t actually come from your cousin.      Yeah, that makes sense. We had to do a whole project on that in science, but the internet made it infinitely worse. All these TikTok videos act like evolution is a conspiracy theory and people are still arguing about it in 2025. Honestly, I’m just left confused on what people actually believe.      I know right? The funny thing is, even if you watch videos arguing against evolution, they’re still using scientifically advanced things to do it, like microphones, computers, social media algorithms… You can’t even argue against science while using science!      Haha, fair point, Wemb. I mean, I guess it’s also about how people understand their own human experience. Like, I asked my best friend—she’s a year younger than me—and she said she didn’t get why it matters if we evolved, and I kind of get her point. If I’m me now, why would my past matter?      That’s actually a really good question. I guess it matters in a way that understanding where humans come from helps us understand  why  we think and behave the way we do. Evolution explains a lot of our instincts and biases, which can be good or bad.      Yeah, but it can also be misused. Like, some people say things like “that’s just how humans are,” and it becomes a reason for things like racism or sexism. Which is totally not fair. Just because something evolved doesn’t mean it’s right.      Oh my god, talking about this is making me remember that argument my brother had with our aunt over dinner last weekend. She mentioned that women were 'better suited' to being mothers because of their "natural roles," and he was like, “So like, the cavewoman go-to?” I choked on my drink trying not to laugh.      That’s funny, but serious too. I mean, it’s one thing to talk about biology, it’s another to let it define roles in society.

Rather annoying to be honest, I've just come back from the hospital – had an operation for an infection. I got prescribed tablets, but I’m not sure yet whether I will need something stronger      Oh no, that's not nice at all! I picked up yet another cold last week – I'm like a sponge these days. It was ridiculous really.      Yeah, I remember that awful cough you had last Christmas! Honestly, I thought you'd never shake it.      You young things, always picking up the silliest things! I'm more concerned about my friends. My dear George who used to play rugby with me is now out of action due to some kind of knee problem      So what are you doing this week then,George? I mean, assuming you're not convalescing?      Well, I’m not going to give up altogether. I've been thinking of trying some acupuncture – heard it’s good for old age aches, even if it's a bit strange.      I do like the way you're taking it all in your stride! Sometimes I think as people get older they only worry, worry, worry.      But it’s natural, dear. We all remember – we had our lives. I, for one, had a long career in the kitchen, and don’t you know what? Cleaning’s a killer on the back! Still, we live and learn.      Saying that, I read about a new treatment for infections that's coming out soon. Also, I arranged a hospital appointment next week to follow up – just to be on the safe side.      That's responsible of you! I’m watching mine closely too. I’ve already skipped some tablets because I thought I was better, but it didn't last      Burgundy, you always were the light-fingered type. I remember you used to try to sneak any leftover vitamins from the medicine cabinet!      Ha ha, you didn't hear that from me. And also, trying to catch up with friends wears you out. I took the car out for an MOT, and now I need new tyres. That's going go cost a pretty penny!      Yes, MOTs line the pockets of garages. I had mine done last month – what a shock it was. It reminded me I seriously need a new car      I never had to worry about that sort of thing. Retired over thirty years ago, and I never went job hunting again!

Okay, luv, bedtime's almost here, and before we get ready for bed, I'd like to... talk to you both for a moment. It's about something important—something that happened in history long ago, but that still affects people today.      What is it, mummy?      Is it about bad people? Are we going to hear about war again?      War is part of it, darling, but there's something else too. It's about something called slavery. You might not have heard of it before, but it's the worst kind of injustice... when people were treated as property just because of the color of their skin.      But why would anyone do that? That sounds really mean.      Yes, it was extremely cruel, and it happened for hundreds of years. Some countries—like Britain, America, and others—participated in the trade of human beings. They were taken from their homes in Africa, put on ships, and sold to work for no freedom and no pay. They built things like sugar plantations, and many of them died because they were treated so badly.      Did no one stop them? Did people just watch?      That’s a good question. Some people did try to stop it, but it took a long time for laws to change. And even after slavery was officially ended, the effects have stayed with us. People who were enslaved and their descendants still suffer from discrimination. And in some parts of the world, it unfortunately still happens, just in different forms.      I didn’t know that. But what about wars, mummy? Why are people always fighting?      War is about people having disagreements, often over land, beliefs, or power. Sometimes, it’s because of greed or fear. People think killing each other will make the world a better place, but it always makes things worse. Innocent people suffer the most—children like you two.      So, what can we do to stop that?      Well, first of all, we always try to be kind and respectful to others. We stand up when we see someone being treated poorly. Then, we learn about the past so that we don't repeat the mistakes of our ancestors. And finally, we help others as much as we can, because we were all born equal—and that should never be forgotten.      I think I understand now, mummy. We should all try to make the world better.      Yeah, and we can be the good ones that stop the bad stuff from happening again.

Rather annoying isn't it, eh Harry? That Christopher Dean character’s still on telly, doing his penguin dance and smiling like he’s never touched a worry in his life. I've seen him three times this week on some £200k for a garden programme — wouldn't know where to start with half of the plants he mentions.      I reckon his wife's the one making most of the decisions these days, if you know what I mean. Still, easier watching someone else deal with their garden than my own! Speaking of which, Viv, you're still tending the roses at the back? That’s your pride and joy, isn't it?      That's right, and they're looking lovelier than ever! The new horticulturist boy, Matthew – the one Oliver brought round last spring – gave me the goods on pruning and feeding, and the results are better than breakfast, no doubt about that!      I'm not much for planting anything oversized! I mean, who’s got time to care for a rose bush when you're trying to write ten-quarters-worth of blog copy for clients by Friday? Sometimes I think I’ve traded plants for paragraphs.      Make something of it, Claire – it’s all just words and weed. Back when I was running that café, people still came because they thought I used homegrown mint and sage in the tea, even when I bought the stuff in big plastic bags! Truth hurts, huh?      That’s the sort of thing my missus used to give me sour looks about— “Harry, it's not mint from the garden, it's the stuff from B&Q!”  Not that I could afford anything else back in those days. Anyway, what's this luv from earlier about TV and dancing? I reckon that Billy Connolly bloke is doing better these days; I caught a clip on the news about him guest-hosting something.      Billy’s a legend, but he was always more of a stand-up man. Not that I’d mind a crack at gardening as long as I had a good brew to hand.      More importantly, have we heard from Ann? Still chasing after that tabby cat of hers? That James fellow go back to visit her again? Something about him being engaged now, or is that in the papers again?      Oh, I read your cousin’s page online — something about James and Jessica?

Right, who’s up for helping me unload the dishwasher? Lucas, I know you like sorting things out like... well, like James Potter from Harry Potter did with his books! Amelia, you can find me a tea towel, yeah?      Is it the one with the wand shaped like a stick and all the magical trains?           The magical trains? You mean the Hogwarts Express? Dad once told me about a real train, but it was not magical, just lots and lots of engines and big wheels and steam! George Stephenson invented the first big one, I think. It was even older than Grandpa!      Oh no, George Stephenson’s trains weren’t _that_ old! He lived in the 1800s – back when Oliver Twist and pick pockets were in the world! But Lucas, dear, about the dishwasher... better not get distracted by trains or wizards just yet. Let’s get in there and sort out the plates and cups first, then we’ll have time to talk about magical ones, okay?           I’ll dry everything as neatly as Aunt Karen does. Are we going to make toast after?      Mate, I want to help, but I need to find something that’s not a plate or a cup. Is this a phone charger? It looks like the thing Professor Dumbledore used to carry!           That was a wand, love, not a charger. Though yes, Dumbledore was a bit like a mobile phone – he had all the answers when you needed them! Now, about George Stephenson – he was from a place near here, did you know that? Or no, he was from Northumbria. Either way, it helped connect up the country to the railway, like the express route between London and Manchester.      Is George Stephenson the one who told the stories about scientists and talking trains?      He did? I didn't know he could talk to trains. Professor McGonagall could do that with frogs! Maybe he took the Hogwarts Express when he was a kid?      That would be gothic of it! But no, he was a real inventor, made real machines. Imagine making a train go from one city to another without stopping. No magic, but still pretty amazing. The railways were the wizardry of his time, you could say.      Do we have a book about adventurers on trains?      I’m not entirely sure if I like magical trains better or real ones. I like both, but real trains go _toooochoo_ and magical ones go _hocus pokus choo-choo!_

Right, I just texted Jess to see if she fancied coming over this Sunday for one of those supper club things again. Her flat is way nicer for that vibe than mine. I've been humming songs from  Hamilton  all day, and I swear I saw a pigeon outside my window doing a jerk routine. Hashtag tragic.      Yeah, Jess is always good fun at those meals. Though I remember last time she tried to roast the potatoes too much, and they ended up more charred wads of roadkill. You might want to bring a side dish for backup, or just invest in a meat thermometer like a real person. I mean, I baked a Pavlova last night and still got it perfect.      Oh, you did not! I tried making a Pavlova from YouTube and the meringue was sad in the middle and collapsed like an deflated balloon. Cats would have been breakfast, not dessert. I just stick to cakes these days—no cooking required, you know?      You Aussies and your Pavlovas, right? I grew up with lamingtons being the gold standard of baked goods. Honestly, your Pavlova is nothing on a real, proper Lamington dunked in chocolate. But I digress. Speaking of desserts—I’ve been baking for Mateo’s new café opening, and let me just say, the schedule is a nightmare. It’s enough to make you want to quit and go back to Melbourne with your mates, huh?      That’s rough. I work my shifts at the shop every day, and some people think I’d just hand them a croissant and be their friend for life. No, I’m fully aware most people about five minutes in. I mean, “How do you take your espresso?” is a loaded question.      Honestly, I’d take it with a side of peace and quiet. But I’m off to uni for guest speaker thing next week about Words With Friends addiction. Sounds like it’ll be eventful. I once used a triple word score to make “quixotic” to win a game. My player of the day.      That’s better than the time I competed with someone who just used “aa” repeatedly and thought it was their version of go-to-war on Word-via-Text.      I just started a supper club group on Facebook—call it “Fancy Meals and Fake Snobbery.” We take turns hosting, and everyone brings one dish. It’s fun, gets people out of their houses without the pressure of going ‘properly’ out.

Rather skip the new salad bar today, aren't they? I've had one for three days in a row... got to my throat with it. Going for a good old-fashioned chicken tikka sandwich instead — a little bit of spice does the world of good, don't you think?      Honestly, I couldn't eat the chicken tikka if my life depended on it. I've been trying to go plant-based, actually. Found some hummus wraps and a side of roasted vegetables. It's surprisingly filling.      Right? That makes sense. Looks considerably healthier too.      Yeah, I guess. Though honestly, I mostly do it because the toddler at home tends to get nosebleeds after turkey, and I don't fancy being left with a damp handkerchief on the back of the sofa again.      Oh! You're a mother already, are you? That must be somewhat of a whirlwind.      Oh absolutely. I have a daughter, Masha, she’s two and a half. Sweet, determined, and louder than one should expect, all at once. How about you?      I’ve got two boys. One at primary, one starting secondary this September. They’re a little bundle of chaos. You wouldn’t believe – this morning one got a sneaker tied to the other’s chair. I had a hard time telling which one to blame.      Oh, don’t get me wrong, I love her. But full disclosure, I’m seriously auditioning for a time-share in a convent when school starts in September.      I feel it. I still remember packing lunches when I was at primary school in Aylesbury... though back then, our school had the kind of canteen they showed on TV—that kind of retro charm.      A bit of a galactic comparison with what we've got here. Our guest speaker last month called Cambridge the 'food capital of Eastern Europe,' which sent us all into a fit of giggles, I must say.      Well, we can’t all be dining in London or Cambridge lunches, right? At least we’ve got the company. My day tends to get serious around this time. I started a bit of go-karting again—fine hobby or madness, you be the judge.      Go-karting, blooming brilliant! I can't do sport myself—it's like I lost all fitness when I decided to work from home last year. Though I have taken to reading Russian novels in the evenings over tea.

‘Mum, am I gettin’ confused or is tha’s the third shop in ten minutes that sells baby shit and fluffy blankets? It’s like they run out and smuggle their stock into another shop!’      [chuckling] ‘Aye, love, it’s ’cause eeny shop in Preston likes to think they’ve got the best baby stuff. Almost as bad as the bread aisle. A lot o’ shops think they’ve got a monopoly on pitta bread. It’s a conspiracy, if you ask me!’      ‘You know, I think the ones with the baby monitors and sound machines are the ones that sold me my first fridge freezer back in Slovakia. It’s like the same stock, just rebranded!’      ‘Told you! D’you think these shops make a survey? Or do they just watch customers pick things up then vanish when you try to check out?’      ‘Maybe they’s planting the idea in yer mums to move house. Start takin’ over the town, like. First it’s blankets and baby stuff, then it’s kitchens and full renovations. You’ll end up living in a hobbit hole with a spa in the roof!’      [laughs] ‘That’s actually not bad. I could deal with a spa in the roof if I was movin’ out of London. It’s so cramped there. I’d probably just jump in and not come up for air. Who’d miss me for ten mins?’      ‘You’d definitely need fresh water piped into it. Or installed into the bath, at least. I remember your grandmother spoke about moving out o’ Bolton decades ago—said the tap water tasted like the sea had wandered up from Morecambe Bay and gone to her kitchen!’      ‘That’s righ’! She ‘ad to buy bottled stuff for her plants. Said they grew better and more suspicious o’ her!’      ‘She always made them grow like mad. My nan could talk to plants and they’d blooming outgrow the Gardeners’ World shots. She told me once if I spoke to my homework it’d get done faster. Course, I told it to get goin’ on its own if it liked that style so much!’      [snorts with laughter] ‘You’re a chip off the old block. I remember visiting Bolton once and your nan gave me a tour o’ the garden while we were planning her renovation. She made me hold a trowel while we discussed flooring! It was a very green decision—second to her going for hardwood.

So do you lot remember when we used to play that old internet game ages ago? The one with the typewriter text and the creepy forest? I was just thinking about it, and I've been trying to find it again...      Oh, you mean that one with the talking ghosts and the puzzles? That was a  bore  with the controller. I reckon it was about as exciting as washing a clean ladder. But I suppose younger folk like puzzles and all that science-y stuff.      Oh, wait! That was me trying to get you all when I was younger. I coded it... like, sort of. I mean, I used a basic generator and spammed creepy phrases. It wasn’t that scary, but I thought I was some big computer genius back then. Probably messed up half the school website while trying to test it in the first place.      Honestly? I think it was way more frightening then than it would be now... I used to lose sleep over it. I remember one night thinking the ghost’s message was a real person, like, actually messaging me over the internet, and I nearly screamed myself into oblivion.       Laughing  And that's what happens when you leave a child unsupervised with a web browser. Mind you, most kids – even though they don’t admit it – were terrified of it themselves. Some of us still are of the dark web and all that psychological nonsense.      Truthfully, those kind of things helped spark my interest in psychology. I mean, what's scarier than the unknown? That’s the whole point, right? Whether you're looking at online games or social situations, your brain creates its worst-case scenario about people or places. It's kind of the human condition: we fear what we can’t control.      So you’re telling me it helped you  learn something ? That’s like saying falling into treacle waters was good for developing a sense of perseverance. Still, I totally get where you’re coming from. I fell in love with psychology when I started doing it at university. It was way more interesting than I expected.      Gracious me! When I took exams, I’d be  pleased  if it was just the weather report or go-kart routes. But if you lot are going on at me about college and heady stuff, I might just go raid the biscuit tin and leave you to it.

Rather annoyingly, I've got to do a bit of sewing. But you’d think it'd be easy... What's the difference between linen and hemp anyway?      I dunno! It sounds like fancy grass to me. Look, Mummy! I made this new sword in my game and it's made out of  emerald !      Why isn't that a real thing?      Emeralds  do  exist, but they're not used to make swords. We mainly use them for jewelry and stuff. Now, can I borrow your tablet to show you the difference between cotton and wool?      What’s a hippo do? It’s that Myths and Legends game you told me about last week, right? I told the class I invented a story about a magical bird in school the other day. It pecks at the sun to make it breakfast, and then it throws fire eggs.      That’s brilliant, sweetheart! Maybe one day you’ll write a story that’ll be  real . It’s actually interesting how people, way back, made up stories to explain natural things — like volcanoes or the size of the ocean.      Can we play that game where you make up our own legends? I want one where zebras protect water, and they live in the clouds.      I did already! I have a secret cave under my duvet at the weekend, and I wrote down all the stories in my book.      That's amazing! I remember being you age and making a whole fantasy world in the back of my sketchbook —  long  before there were games and about five billion apps.      But what's this about vitamins? I’ve been taking some orange little pills that you told me to have every morning, Mummy. Are they like ‘super energy’ balls for adults?      A bit, yeah. They help your body grow, fix things up, and keep you strong when you’re doing all the important kid stuff like climbing over the sofa or fighting space dragons with your brother.      I do that too, you know. I run with my snack and fight the dragon away go bad guys on the tv if they come too close      I don’t see why we can’t fight  real  bad guys.      Maybe in the stories we create today, we’ll come up with something even better than emeralds and space dragons. How ‘bout this — why don’t we invent a new metal that’s so magical it floats?

: Right luv, I’ve been thinkin’ ‘bout that thing you said last week ‘bout like... those nutter ‘paedophiles’ runnin’ around. I've been readin’ articles online and it's honestly doin’ my head in!     : Yeah een? I know, I don’t like it either. But if yer gonna read stuff like that, do you have to scroll so far down the comments too? Half the internet are just shoutin’ abuse at no one. Makes me wanna chuck me computer out the window.     : I know! It's like even talkin’ about it is enough to start a debate. Still, I’d like to think our mates are all alright sorts. Fun to be ‘round, innit? I mean, Darcy and Liam and the lot—remember when we all used to watch videos of them gigin’ when we were younger?     : Aye, they were alright. I remember we used to go to those little gigs in the village hall, sat on the floor with our ‘grades and everything, shoutin’ along. I never did quite make as much of my guitar playin’ as they did though. Me frets never quite worked out right.     : Mate, you got the same one I did, the Hayman thing. You weren’t nearly as bad as you thought you were. If I could ‘play’ at that age, which I couldn't, then you were alright too.     : That’s because I got outta practice! Still, mind if I ask… you fancy bein’ in a band or nothin’? I about considered it for a while but then uni just took over my life.     : Nah, I don’t know. I mean it is a fun hobby but I do get a bit over it. Sometimes I just sit down and mess about with that old chord me mam gave me—only it was my gran’s before I got it. It’s got a split stick on it but I like that. Feels a bit like a proper 'thing'.     : Yeah, I like things like that too. You know, like the 'stuff' goin' on in life, like our mates, or just messin’ about in the garden, growin’ a bit of veg. It might not sound exciting but it keeps me grounded.     : I know what you mean. Just not stuck in that headspace talkin’ ‘bout this stuff. We should go see Darcy and Liam again so—shake things up a bit.     : Yeah, why not? Invite the lads.

So did you guys hear about the new exhibit at the Slough Art Gallery? They’re doing that Montenegro photography show again. I’m telling you, last time it was wild—these incredible landscapes and people there are totally unique. I’m thinking about going during half-term.      Yeah, that’s kind of cool, I guess. But you know I haven’t been there in ages… not since I turned vegetarian. They always have that sausage sizzle at the event. Not really my vibe anymore.      Oh right, I forgot. Funny how things change, isn’t it? You remember when we used to juggle hotdogs during breaks at school? That was dumb, but also hilarious.      Yeah, I remember! Mike nearly got hit in the face by a skewer once. Oliver shouted, “Blimey, that’s a spicy situation!” and we’ve never been the same. Anyway—vegetarianism aside, are you actually going to the gallery, Josh?      Actually, I kind of was thinking about why I like those exhibitions—makes me feel like, I dunno, part of the world. You know what I mean? Like, humanizing other places. Like we’ve got poverty in Slough, and then in Montenegro or somewhere else. It’s all part of being human, right?      Honestly, that’s actually deep of you to say. I think about that too. Last night, I was watching a documentary about humanitarian efforts. It made me think—what if I did an EPQ on global inequality or something? Ideas are still jumbling.      That’s intense. I’m stuck with my EPQ because I wanted to make it about travel marketing but then I realized it just sounds like I’m bragging.      Oh that’s funny! I mean, if you could run your own travel blog, wouldn’t you?      Maybe, but I’m just worried about grades. I’m told the EPQ can actually help with uni applications, so I need to get this crackin’. Like, I’m literally doing a starter project trying to find a recipe that counts as “authentic” but also vegetarian. Still trying to figure out if it’s even possible.      You could do Thai green curry without the fish sauce! My mum taught me, and I swear it tastes amazing with coconut milk and lemongrass. It’s all about technique, seriously.      That sounds delicious! I think I’m going to try that next week. Oh, by the way, have either of you thought about what you want to study at university?

Rather annoying this newfit, eh? The heating’s broken again. I had to put on two jumpers just to make a cuppa.      I know, right? I swear we’ve reported it at least three times this term. I mean, it's  Lancaster  in November and it feels like  Liverpool  in February—and trust me, that ain’t a good thing.      Honestly, if I’d known this flat was gonna be this cold, I’d have taken the other place. My rent was cheaper too and at least the internet worked there.      Yeah, I’ve been freezing  every  night. Mum keeps texting me, saying, “You in a shed Mylo?” I’m like, “No Ma, it’s just a leaky window frame.” D’you think they’ll fix it this time?      Probably not ‘til we’re all frosty dormice. Which brings me to another thing—how are we even paying rent again?      Oh God, the student finance is late again—again! My gran’s been covering some of it, but I can’t keep asking.      I’m on benefits, so it’s… well, it works. But it feels like we’re all surviving on – Mate, have you seen my sister?      She’s into that new bloke from the uni radio station. You know what she’s like—always chasing the next drama.      Ugh, yeah. That Emma just wants to be famous  already . You’d think getting a degree would be sufficient, but no… she’s got to be  everywhere . Prime Club, Apple about, even doing walk-ons in theatre trios now.      I feel sorry for the lads. One minute you’re a student, the next you’re in her WhatsApp group, ‘cos she’s like, “Oh you passed my module?” Bazzinga.      I asked her once why she liked blokes from the Archeology dept. She said, “Oh they’ve got a nice earthy vibe.” Whatever  that  means.      Honestly, you don’t even need to go to uni to get drama— go to her flat for tea if you want  proper  stories.      I’m not even gonna go there bloke. I’ve had enough of that. I’m planning to go to Liverpool this weekend, mind. My nan’s birthday. Just need to find a train ticket I can actually afford.      Aint no money in the cupboards up here, so if they’ve got a stew pot, you’re sorted.      Likewise, I’m heading to Manchester at the weekend.

Rather annoying when the bar’s out of anything stronger than lager. But anyway, it’s only a pub... What's been happening with you lately, Nanny?      Oh, don't mind me, love. I'll stick with my usual—half a pint of Ten of Clubs. Got a bit of consultancy work lined up in Brighton next week. Still, it's not as exciting as your job teaching English abroad now, is it? Where are you off to next?      Antalya. We've just finished the school year here in Muğla, and I'm due to leave in three weeks. Still mostly online these days, though, post-pandemic. Less exciting than traipsing the turkey bazaars with you lot back in the '80s, I'd imagine.      I'll be the first to say you're far braver than me! I breakfasted with old Winnie this morning. She told me in no uncertain terms I'm not getting any younger, you know. She's still got the knack for sarcasm, by the way.      I hope she doesn't take that from your side of the family. I only live two hours from Torquay and I reckon I've got wrinkles forming from all the eye-rolling at my nan’s tea parties!      Ha! Good one. Anyway, her sonPhilip is moving out next year. You know what he's like—never settled. Briefly tried farming, someone said in Iceland. He wrote me a letter once saying the cows liked him because he didn't flinch when they stared.      Cows? I thought he was in the city somewhere. I did meet his cousin Anna a while back. Interesting thing, she had this job in document management in Manchester and thought it was the bees’ knees. Doesn't sound too glamorous, but to each their own.      To each their own indeed. Still, I have no idea where I’d be if I hadn’t relied on family for guidance. Remember when I convinced your mum to come with me to that rural safety training out in Dorset? She came back with spots from the lice in the simulation tent.      Don't remind me. That was one go at Christmas I didn't want to attend. But you two have made quite the team, really. You're always dragging her into adventures—and I'm your unpaid photographer at the beck and call.      Only because I know those snaps are going to make your holidays to Antalya feel that bit more envy-inducing.

Rather annoying to be honest. Loads of speed cameras going in. I've had to get my license renewed like... What was it, five times since I last saw you? Not to mention the number of people I've driven mad trying to process applications. That and the fact that half the towns in Bedfordshire now look like building sites since they started expanding the motorway.      Yeah, I heard about a few places being redeveloped. Got one next to my place where we're seeing scaffolding go up like it’s a city in the States. Still, you're in Brighton now, aren’t you? Get the sea air and all that.      That's the plan, yeah. It's like a breath of fresh air after living in Bedford my whole life. Though I do miss the hustle back home, even with the building works. A bit of a cultural shock actually, breaking free and working with students. I never thought I’d be an English teacher after I left university.      You always had the right way with words—and people. Good for you. It helps that I do customer service—person-to-person skills, really. I never thought about teaching as a job, but I do like helping folks.      Well, we're both in services, then. Though I remember you once told me about a guy in Tanzania who tried to scam you while you were on an out-of-country trip.      Oh yeah! That guy with the dhow boat in Zanzibar. He claimed it was a government deal, but it was just a scam. Some guy had the nerve to pretend he was real and still got upset when I called him out.      I would've laughed while I walked off. But talking of different cultures... have you seen any of the new Danish dramas? I got into one the other day.      Not really, but for TV I still go back to my old standbys.  Game of Thrones , it's a classic. Do you still play those board games you loved when we were younger?      Yeah, but now it's always English with ESL students. It's whacky how things change. Earlier in the road trip, I got caught by a camera on the way here. Miserable day it was.      You always had a knack for making that happen. But you’re blooming, son. Pass some of that weight onto me, I’ll manage it.

Rather annoying day today, wasn't it? That meeting about public relations for the new module schedule — it felt like we were talking circles round the same point for two hours. I swear, someone needs to start categorising these things alphabetically or we'll never make sense of it all.      Oh I saw the meeting minutes — honestly, it was ridiculous. I reckon half the people in that room don’t even know what public relations actually  is , from a practical point of view. I watched one of the session assistants do a whole PowerPoint slide on "perception versus action" without once touching on real-world application. Ridiculous! Still, at least I had a break in the afternoon, right?      My break was definitely not as nice. I left the university and just needed some food, so I went into that deli I told you about by the train station. God, the wait was unreal. I ended up standing there for fifteen minutes, with a queue in each line. I even asked the barista, “Excuse me, can I check which one is faster?” and she said, “I don’t know, listen to the people in the queue.” It was either grief or ham on sourdough.      Sounds like it was a lost cause. I’m surprised – weren’t you supposed to pick up something for the store room? Or was that me?      No, that’s on  your  list. I’m the one who said I’d get the music samples for the seminar tomorrow. You know, the ones for the PR campaign on music-based branding.      Oh right! The music one – I  love  that part of your lecture about how branding works. I was listening to the soundtrack of  Whiplash  during my commute yesterday and thought about it. There's something powerful in the way music defines a brand’s personality. Case in point: the new Apple ads. All that ambient, minimalist vibe. Signals class, effectiveness. It works.      I tried to make them understand that sort of thing in my presentation, but I swear half of them were thinking about their lunches. I think I told them the same point five times in five different ways, and they still looked like I was talking about tax law or something. But yeah, maybe tomorrow I’ll go over it again, just in hopes they remember it. And I’ll pick up the music samples today after lectures.

Rather annoying isn't it, eh?      Aye, it's such a mire... What was I supposed to be doing now?      I've nearly finished this bean bag, it's £20 worth of wool and what you see is what you get, if it stands up to being sat on.      I reckon it'll stand up to that, aye. A lot worse things would happen in this house than someone squishing a bean bag.      We've nothing to eat. Is this fish in the freezer or the washing-up liquid?      Fish! Not everything is fish, love. What d'you fancy? I've got that lentil soup you like, or I could throw something on the pan.      D'you know what I fancy? A little of your attention for once instead of you working on something when I'm trying to talk to you. Honestly.      I'm sorry, love, I didn't mean to be so thick. What did you say?      I said I'm fed up of us always cooking in the kitchen.      It's not like we've got another option is it? Our living room is stuffed from wall to wall with knitting – Mate, I don't know, I think it's a good thing we had a flat packed kitchen because if you carried on at this rate we'd never find the door.      You've got a point. Although I don’t know what's wrong with the shower curtain. It’s floring me is what it is.      Can I speak plainsmith here, or is it a floring metaphor?      No! Flooring me, Floor-ing me. I keep getting this damp patch because that godawful shower curtain is always unzipped.      Oh for god’s sake, well if you’re going to sod up the whole bathroom décor then at least give me a hand cleaning up.      I will when I'm done with this.      What is this?      More importantly do you remember the last time you took a shower?      I think so yeah go on then I'm all ears.      Did you ever remember to close the curtain?      Well, I might have if it was in fact something that I could manage.      Well you're going to have to, because unless you want me to start knitting over this bathroom floor again, I'm afraid I’m not entirely willing to sit there for hours letting this seep in.      Alright love, alright, let's make a pact and try not to flay each other for at least the next hour then, yeah?

Rather a gray day, isn't it? That sun ain't shone much this week, ‘as it? Got me in a quiet mood. I’m more used to the countryside, you know. Livin’ in Costessey all my life, I had windswept fields and the sky was always clearer een here.      It was lovely there, if I recall. Quite peaceful. Though I’ve always preferred the city. Not that this place isn't nice, mind you. It's cozy, ain't it? Just feels a bit too quiet at times. I remember when the garden was buzzing with children running to-and-fro! Those were the days, weren't they, Arthur?      It was lively, definitely. Still, enough talk of the past. What do you think about the weather forecast for tomorrow, Eunice? They're predictin' showers again. I've got a shipment coming, and I’d hate to see it soaked.      I expect the sky will weep, as it always tends to in the morning. You’d better bring in the outdoor things, Arthur. You’d think老爷 would have given you a better property as a proprietor, but no, we’ve still got a shed like it's 1912!      Ha – no shortage of humor there, Eunice. Still, I'm more concerned with tea and scones than shipments and forecasts. If the world is goin’ to weep, then by God someone should give it a handkerchief. Ever had a plum scone, Arthur?      Fairly often, though I prefer being able to match it with something stronger than milky tea. I did earn a university degree once, you know, and still found time to run my own business. Not that I need it now, but it gave me a sense of purpose for quite a few years.      Yes, well, I had a different path. Sixth form was as far as I went, but I had my own worlds to shape through little ones. Being a childminder gave me something to do. Even if it ain't 'managerial and administrative' by the book, it certainly shaped characters for a living.      Aye, and goin' on about life improvements and degrees does get a bit much at our age. I’m just glad we’ve got each other and a bit of tea to talk about. It's the little things, innit? The scone, the rain, the garden not growin' roses worth talkin' ‘bout this year.      I suppose so, old friend.

Rather annoying I know, isn't it? That Christopher, he’s promising one thing then dashing off like... Well, rather like a child, really.      Yeah, he promised he'd help wrap gifts and all he does is pop off to the shops  again.  Honestly, if it een't the holidays, I don't think he'd know where to put wrapping paper!      A lot worse than just Christmas! Why I got to be in training and watched a patient’s vital signs misread 'cause the guy got distracted by the smell of his lunch.      Right, but enough of that. I've been meaning to ask the two of you, do you think you could pop to the supermarket for me? The oven left bursts on this morning – I’m not sure what the problem is, and I’ve no head for gadgets.      Oh! Wait breakfast, no doubt. I've been wanting to try some of these new almond-based pancakes ever since I read about them in the health notes the GP gave me. So we can pick some up for me, yes?      I'll keep your health as top priority, Nurse. For now, fancy trying some of this Moroccan lamb I've got on in the oven? It's from one of those foodie blogs I follow, and I swan it’s gonna be the talk of the block!      If I weren't still on a diet, I'd be in heaven. Honestly, I miss the days when a meal was a rush of chicken and chips at the corner shop. Also, have either of you worked out if you’re going to Margaret’s for the Christmas do?      Not yet. I’m just trying to rearrange this job schedule. I’ve already skipped my sister’s birthday to plug some extra shifts in.      My sister’s over in Poole, guest speaker thing at some university. She’s always dishing the culture stuff – something about British values and how they meet global stuff. You’d think she'd crack from such a tight speaker schedule!      Do lunches cost a little more these days? I took the kettle out of the socket after the bills this week. I swear the EPC goings really need to see if savings or not!      Yeah, I’m trying to teach myself the box thing – y'know, all virtual groceries. It’s faster, and I can live without the automatic potholes of the supermarket car park.

Rather lovely to sit out here on Sunday mornings, isn't it? The sun's just easing through the pines, and the coffee's warming through the handle. I do enjoy how peaceful it is here, even in the busiest of towns.      Indeed, very agreeable. Bushey in the old days couldn't offer this kind of view, but I haven't been there in years. Still, a clean cup of coffee is a clean cup of coffee anywhere, wouldn't you say?      Oh, I suppose. Although I have to admit the coffee in Northern Cyprus has a bit more of... I don’t know, character. Richer. I've had the odd debate with students about whether it’s well worth the gritty bitterness, but I’m partial to it myself. What about you?      Heh, I think I turned my stomach to most of it by the time I retired. Wife, bless her, always said I’d ruin my palate in my old age, planting myself by Turkish cafés day-in, day-out. But the memories I have from that time?      Oh, I’d love to hear about them. You said you’ve spent time here before?      Oh aye, several years. I was a gardener way back when — just about managed a living through horticulture, but the winters were long. One time, during a particularly cold winter, the whole town was covered in dust and wind, and the toilets wouldn’t flush properly. I found myself mending the system in my wellies and a gardening gloved hand. Some Christmas Eve, that was.      Good grief! I can only imagine the smell! You know, I just came back from a weekend trip to the Kyrenia mountains with some colleagues. The roads were quite difficult to navigate — narrow and barely marked. But the views up there are to die for.      Yes, well — passed through those mountains once. A young man named Yusuf told me he lived at the very top of a cliff, waiting for a tour bus. As it turns out, he disappeared the night before the bus arrived. Never explained where he went! Of course, the next morning, you remember, the sun comes up like it's watching the whole goings-on on your life, and there he was, at the bottom of the hill, making tea between two tourists.      Oh your stories do make for nice tea-sipping! I’ve had my fair share of minor mishaps, too.

Rather annoying isn't it? The amount of pollution hanging in the air today.      I know, I could really do without this today. I could have sworn I left the windows open this morning, and I can honestly say I have not felt as bad in the lungs in a while.      I've been meaning to say this for a while now. I actually have been considering a sabbatical from my lecturing job in a year or so. Not that I don't love teaching, it's just... I was thinking maybe taking a gap year in another part of the world.      That sounds brilliant. I can see you thriving in the sun, giving lectures on some tropical island surrounded by palm trees. You’ve always had a bit of a knack for persuading people – I’m not surprised they pick your classes every term.      Thank you, and you better not get too smug about your own lectures. They're not bad either. People usually leave your lectures in quite a thoughtful mood, I have to say. Good for them.      To be fair, some of them just shuffle off looking like they've been in a deep introspection. Philosophical by nature, aren’t they?      Well, from what I hear most of the students are incredibly bright. I was speaking to one of the students today – the one you saw me talking to by the stall at the college fair. She's doing exceptionally well in her biology modules, and someone at the university is considering putting her forward for an exchange program to Australia.      That’d be a great opportunity for her. Any chance I could speak to her about it as well? Not in about pollution or university news, but about our friends. She’s very keen to meet some other people who've gone beyond their studies.      You're up for introducing her to your sister’s group of friends?      I am. They're always open to a new laugh and any fresh perspectives. If there’s someone as bright as your student getting out there and meeting new people, that’s to be encouraged.      I think it would be amazing for her – and maybe even for us, something different.      Yeah, go on then. But let's make our way home – I think I saw a head of smoke that was genuinely from the incinerator on the corner today, and you know how that can get.

Rather annoying the new oven’s taking so long to preheat. I blame this damp weather, it kills everything! What d'you think, love? It's not like we need an oven hotter than a tin pot for a simple lasagna.      It's been like that all week. Got me thinking we might need a new one, but with the budget we’ve got on— sigh —I don’t fancy starting another argument about this. I’ve had enough with the boiler last month pulling through to Christmas!      Oh come on, it's not  that  bad! I’ve been watching this show  Obi-Wan Kenobi  on Disney Plus, and it's like watching Mycroft Holmes fall in love with his eccentric cousin’s stories. Ten minutes, and I’m in love with the past and sad about the present! But then you two start arguing over appliances and it’s breakfast, no— not this again !      Blooming typical. Just when we’re starting to wind down. Still, the pasta’s ready and that’s something. By the way—personally I think we should have put the photos up by now. I’ve been meaning to ask what you did with the ones from last year's trip to Brighton, Mark?      Mate, I got distracted trying not to lose the kids in the huge crowd. You know how it goes when they start queuing for the trams and the donkey rides. Lost one of 'em for forty full minutes. Honestly, I thought my heart might give out. But yeah, the photos are still in the box under the kitchen table. Any chance you two could sort through them?      I’ll do it after I’ve had a quick wash-up. We could have a memory lane night sometime this weekend—you know, choose the best ones and frame them. Would be fun to have something to remember for the grandkids, right Dad?      Kid, you'll be the one holding the grandkids while I’m still fixing something. Not waiting till I’m past 80 for that!      He knows the drill, Jane. At your age, you’re the perfect ambassador for nostalgia and delivering the odd plate of snack! Still, I reckon go for it. It'd be nice to see them properly appreciated.      Yep, I’ll get on with arranging the photos after dinner. Now, about lunch—should we get fish and chips from Haz’s again next week?

Rather annoying this new bus route eh? D’ye think they’ve sorted it out yet? ‘Cause I’d got to get from Magdalene to the press shop on Kettle’s Yard, and mebbe lost me hour ‘cause of that chaos.      Yeah, honestly it was absolute madness on Tuesday. I met this student runner with an 'I CAN'T STAND ÇAPITALISM' slogan on a A4, shouting at the side of the bus, begging for attention. Imagine what would’ve happened if she wasn’t ignored. I mean, what’s the point, arguing with blokes stuck in a queue of buses?      I reckon she'd’ve shouted at the sky if no one listened. My lofe, I’ve met enough eccentric lefties in this uni town, but I’d never seen a protest picket dressed in a patchwork of khaki jackets and hand-painted trainers. Wait, does your old uni up north have all that? I mean, don’t get me wrong, I quite like Cambridge, but I hear York isn't quite like this.      Yeah, it’s fair to say Cambridge takes itself a bit seriously. York as in the city and the uni, it's got a vibe… it's less... trotting in little tweed caps. Though I remember Mateo from Royal Holloway, and he swears by his university’s ‘cultural inclusivity’ and ‘decentralised campus’ – all very buzzwordy.      Aye, but aren’t the libraries here brilliant? That bookshop just down the alley at C.U.P. has this dark wooden furniture and real leather-bound books. Can’t fault the decor in a city like Cambridge.      Absolutely. I picked up a lit review there this week. Though I’ve got to say, it’s not like Oxford or even Edinburgh. There's not quite that old-world, ‘cosy and treacherous’ feel here.      Well, the biscuits they give out at the café there aren’t half accurate too. You ever had those scones with clotted cream they serve up at the grand English firms lunches? I think the one at the bookshop is almost as grand.      Pfft! Don’t get me goin’ on scones again. If I go one more day into the day trippin’ with scones, clotted cream, and all that, I swear I’m gettin' a conference seminar just to debate the virtues of earnest afternoon tea.      Oh laddie, this is why we should’ve gone north when we'd got the chance. Least we’d get true hearty eats and not this… élitist, faintly condescendin’ feel to the whole town.

Rather lovely day today, isn't it? I suppose it's a shame we can't take a walk first, but the lunch appointment is in a bit more of a rush, ay?      Oh yes, it's alright. Look, we’ve got our scones and jam in the car, we can eat them on the drive if we get hungry. I just wanted to get over before the place gets too full.      I’m so excited we’re meeting up, honestly. It’s been months since the three of us could just chase the day together. Mummy, you’ve been far too quiet since you finished teaching. You need to get out more, not just for us but for you.      Oh, left well enough alone, thank you. I like the peace. But this place I hear has the best fish and chips in miles — a bit of a treat doesn’t go amiss. Now, are we alright for money?      Mummy, you didn’t have to bring that up. I’ve got it sorted. I do tell you all the time — I earn my crust now!      Well, I wasn’t suggesting otherwise, dear. Just watching the pennies.      Mummy, for heaven’s sake, just let her treat you today. You’ve been a good girl all retirement.      Very funny, Selina!      Honestly, this is why we need to get together more often. Now, have you thought about whether or not James is still coming up for a visit over the next couple of weeks? I mean, he’s been there for most of your crises, right?      She’s had three job interviews and a house viewing this month alone. James is like her project manager now.      My, my! You lot certainly do put words in my mouth.      No one is holding any punches, love. We just want to make sure when he gets here he doesn’t have to deal with a full-blown Monica-trauma.      Well, I do love the young man for trying, even if he does talk too fast for an old goth like me. But if you insist on using so many strange phrases, just pace yourself, eh boy. English is a lovely language, but I can only take so much at once!      I think he says those phrases just to show off, honestly. Do you ever catch him without overcompensating?      You know my point of view. Always acting like he’s in an English class, trying to impress people with his vocabulary.

Rather lovely this, isn't it? You can’t beat a walk along the Thames in the evening when it’s got that golden light. Just the two of us and the river. I've always thought this stretch was underrated compared to the West End or the City.      Agreed. Got a bit of peace and quiet here. It’s nice just to sit back and not be rushing from one meeting to another. Though I still can’t get used to not seeing a car tailing me. I know you said you haven’t missed it, but for me, it feels like I’m gloriously car-free... like part of a cult!      That’s quite the put-down. Honestly, I haven’t missed it at all. It’s ridiculous how much London is obsessed with cars. We live in the capital, for goodness' sake, and it’s harder to get a car here than in a major city in most other countries.      And the thing is, I’m not even evangelical about it. I just like the idea that I could get places without the hassle of hunting for a parking space. I remember when your brother asked to borrow my car last week, and I had to tell him I didn't own one. That was awkward. “Um, no – I don’t actually have one, and I barely remember how to drive.”      You know what I found awkward? The size measurements on those American coffee mugs at the campsite last summer. Like why do they have to measure in cups or ounces? I had to constantly weigh my coffee and milk in my head. “Is this  actually  a small or a large about to fall off the table?”      Oh, yes. And cooking in the States! Going by cups is madness when I’m used to grams and millilitres. My sister nearly overcooked the whole ham guest for your family holiday last year. I’m surprised no one was rushed to the hospital.      I miss that holiday, honestly. We were such a tight group. Even though we were always trying to find directions or debating what size glass to use, the memories are there.      Sometimes I wonder—will we go back? I mean life gets busy. If we go on holiday as a big group, it becomes a logistical nightmare. But I can see myself at your age retiring and taking all the kids to Rome to sort this out one way or another.

Rather annoying this wet weather isn't it? I mean, I love the occasional rain, but it's like it's never going to stop now. I’m so ready for summer proper, you know? I've been stuck inside all week, trying to keep my little one entertained. I did take her to Build-A-Bear this morning – I think she's now obsessed with bears and fluffy things in general. I remember when all we needed was a cardboard box and a sock to make a dummy bear, and they were happy as larks. But I don't mind spoiling them every now and then. Besides, you never know, she might be in a dressing-up phase one day and need a new bear to dress up.      Some days I’d rather have a Build-A-Bear and tea in bed – no promises to ballet, swimming, and sport about sports days. Honestly, the energy required to get the kids to everything is exhausting. I’ve barely had time to tidy the house let alone cook something other than lasagne for the third time this week!      I know right? I did Parents' Training at uni on the whole potty-training thing, and it still doesn't prepare you for when they’re doing it while you're holding your shopping bag full of wine and bread! And honestly, I miss swimming with my sister when we were kids. We used to sneak off around the estates and go for a dip even in cooler weather. But kids are more risk-averse now.      Oh yeah, I don’t go near open water these days.

So, I’ve been doing a fair bit of thinking since we got here, and it’s real easy to see how the time could just drift away while we're stuck in the same rhythm.      I know what you mean. Look at us—house-sitting like a vacation, but it’s beginning to feel passive. I think both of us are ready to set some clear goals.      Exactly. Maybe not full-time forever, but I was thinking—like maybe part-time teaching with some creative side hustle? You know, as long as it connects with real growth for me.      That’s something I’d like to support. I remember back when we first got together, you were writing these really fiery letters about changing the world through education.      You know what—I could try mentoring at that youth center in the next town.      And I can promise a bit of peace when you do. Some goals for the kid—like, maybe starting a shared weekend ritual with the family back home in Dorset?      That would be gold. I’m still blinking at this whole part of "family planning," though. You meet your people, I meet mine. We crack on with our separate things but as one team.      That sounds doable. Now, the next step—it’s calling for something around this week. I’ll get the calendar goin’. You make it about your clients or whatever work. I’ll focus on the mentoring gig and figuring out this mentoring course I heard about from Dorset.      Make it happen. And we take it together—like we always do.

Rather annoying when people can't get through a request without grumbling. I was in Costa the other week and I got the barista to add after-eights to my latte. Such a simple thing, but she made it sound like we were fighting over the last biscuit in the house!      Right? I swear people don’t use the 'please' and 'thank you' as often as they used to. Half the tent flew off in the wind!      Bucksy? I happened to still be in the loo at the time and looked out the window, thinking it’s the apocalypse! I came running out all dressed like I was going to the ball! Championship level of panic.      You did? I didn’t even notice, I was too busy arguing with my brother over Pokémon. He said Beedrill is better than Butterfree. I said he was wrong and now it's a long-standing grievance.      Speaking o’ Pokémon, I've been trying to catch 'em on my Fitbit app. Silly thing keeps thinking I’m sitting still even when I'm pacing the flat. I tried to scan my payslip into that accounting software and it misread every bloody number. I nearly had a breakdown ‘cos I was like, “Are you trying to fight with me?”      You lot are all scientists trying to decode aliens! I just came back from the shop. Got us fresh crisps and more of them After-eights. 'Cause I heard someone whinge about chocolate last week. That's how you know I care.      Oh, goody! I’ll see if I can talk about you at the camping trip next week, yeah? You’ll be the ‘unreliable brother who always goes to service stations at 1 in the morning’—not that it’s a crime, innit?      Is it Friday or Saturday ago I asked why Mogs wouldn’t talk to me?

Rather good to have you all under one roof, what with it being the first Sunday in ages that we've all got the time! I've rustled up a bit of bangers and mash, seeing as there's not much else left in the larder.     Deary me, I'm positively starved, George. It was lovely of you to invite us over without warning. Though I must say, Sunday diners tends to be a bit more posh in our day.      We've been spoilt by restaurants when we're in London or Cambridge, but nothing feels quite like coming back to Norfolk and having a proper no-fuss dinner at home, don’t you think?      I’ve just been thinking the same thing. London life, for all the buzz, can feel a bit alienating. This? This feels like coming back to the old country. And breakfast, no doubt, at this time of day...      And the Queen's Speech, ha! Still have the old habits. Good for the digestion, I find. Though tell me—personally I’ve never trusted people who never skip a meal. They must be grief stricken, or fancying a shilling on the bookies.      Excellent point, George. I must say I agree with you, though I do try these days. More tea, don’t you think?      Actually, Liam and I were just talking the other day about how our students barely remember the Queen. They just consider her part of the background noise. Some even think the monarchy is a recent invention. It’s wild.      They’re not wrong in about half the world. But the Crown’s the touchstone of this chaotic place. Though I suppose you could say the same for the school of hard knocks.      Aye, ‘knocks’ being the operative word. I remember when the Queen came to open a new school in Costessey all those years back. Properly decked out in a red robe. Feels like yesterday. Though of course, young folk probably take lunches delivered by Grubhubs now.     Hey, I take my opposition to that on principle. There's still room on your plate if you'd like another slice of pudding, George?      Aye, bloke, I might just take you up on that.      Father’s been blaming the youth of today for just about everything since I was ten. But, Liam, I asked the students to debate modern monarchy last week—surprisingly sophisticated opinions came out of it.

Rather annoying to be honest. I mean, I only dragged them in the front entrance, and they’re like...  shame , they’re browning at the bottom already! These were brand new, you know. I did go in and drop out during my first term. It was just... too much pressure for no reason. I mean, I still ended up getting a job, but the idea of sitting in a lecture hall like this every day was killing me already.      Honestly, I've been thinking about it too. Just not knowing what the rush is for. I mean, what if I’d dropped out when I was 16, gone to work in the cafe in St Michael’s? I did loads of jobs while I was growing up, and the craziest thing is they paid  more ! Going to uni was like barely a step up.      My grandma always said I was like a little sponge — passed out on the tiled floor at 6 a.m., holding any bloody book I could get my hands on. My little brother, though? Total rebel kid. Named that sprite of evil after our grandad? 'Cause he walked like one! My nan took the liberty, but you try delivering a pint with a kid like that watching you — go straight to shithouse if you don’t get it right!      Oh, don’t go boxin’ on your family — we’re all bloody peculiar. I mean, me mum and dad decided to give my brother and I names with like, zero coherent logic behind it.

Rather skip the starters and just go for the main, old habits die hard, dont they?      I hear you there. I’m more of a straightforward kind of gal now. Beans on toast is genius. Not quite Oxford Castle, but it brings back memories.      Has it really been  this  long since we last saw each other? My goodness, years of separate universes and careers have really carved us apart in this strange social circle.      Honestly, it’s shocking how different our schedules got once we hit the big, bad corporate world. You as a project co-ordinator and I as a Pearson marketing executive, we must have been on another planet.      Touching base with you though left me feeling nostalgic. Remember how we used to moan about university assignments and yet somehow get the best marks? It feels like yesterday.      Absolutely. You always knew just how to help me in times of panicking. I looked up to you, to be truthful. And now we’re sitting here, blooming grown-ups with real, challenging jobs, and still retaining the occasional sense of humor about it all.      Honestly, we’ve got to commit to meeting up more rhythmically, like monthly. It's too easy to fall into silence. I know I've been buried in project deadlines and the like, but don't you miss the depth of a conversation with someone who knows you?      You couldn’t have said it better. And not to mention the chaotic energy of oddly-timed catch-ups in random spots, like a muddy park café and here, Oxford Castle – all corners of England are fair game for us, it seems.      Speaking of which, I had this idea a little while back. Going back to university to do a masters. The thought has bobbed around the edge of my planning for the last six months.      Wow, that’s a leap! What sparked such a move?      You know me, I get restless if I'm not learning. Also, I've been thinking about coaching or management long-term, so this feels like a solid step forward.      That's fantastic! I go back to my parents’ place sometimes and there are so many stories lingering in the air, but I suppose it's the background blooming blossoms of your career and personal development that have been blooming all along.      On that note, what do you say we plan our monthly meet-ups over this one’s food and drinks?

Rather than going out an' getin’ swamped in tha shops, why dontcha hop online 'n see ifcha can get a better bargin on tha computer? 'Specially if yeh keep a look out fer “buy it now” on second-hand gear what’s still in good nick.      Right, but I ain’t too sure what t’look for. If I get骗ed , Gran, Mummy won’t breakfast with me for a week!      Aye, that’s the deal o’ th’ day, luv. Yer gotta read the details real close—check the ratings, see what other buyers say. An’ if yeh don’t feel good 'bout a product, yer always got a right to bide yer time. Another thing—always use a secure wi-fi. Don’t be doin’ yer shoppin’ on public ones in cafes.
