Okay, so I’ll set up a sort o’ shoppin’ list and maybe even log off once in a while to 'split up' big payments—cos I’ve ‘eard that’s safer, too.      That’s yer go, lad. ‘N ifcha ever feel lost or confused, I’m just a call away. I might be a bit older, but I’ve ‘ad me fair share o’ cyber fluency over the years—tryin’ to navigate all them GCSE exam papers online!      Thanks, Gran. I’ll be sure ter pop yer a message if I get stuck. Maybe we could do a “pair shop” once in a while, 'cos I think yeh’ve got the breech-tide knowledge to bee me way better at this!

Rather a cold day out, eh, love? Thoughtful of you to bring in the mugs. That coffee’s the only thing keeping me from crawling back under the duvet.      It is a bit chilly, yeah. Looked like rain at one point. But it was nothing, I just popped out and brought the drinks in. You look a bit tired today, Dad—are you not sleeping well?      Oh, I’m not much for sleep anymore. It’s not like it used to be. You hit the hay when you're considerably younger and wake up feeling right as rain. These days, even if I do manage a couple of hours, I'm still knackered by morning. My knees are playing up again too.      That sounds familiar from the stories you told, Dad. I think it’s time you gave the doctor a call again. They better do something about those old bones of yours. And for goodness’ sake, don’t just sit about so much. You should go out for a bit—just to clear your mind.      Doctor? I’d rather not be sitting in that waiting room with all those other grumpy old bones, thank you very much. Besides, I’ve got work to do from home today. I’m helping my Mate Reg with sorting through some of his old papers. Found a few letters the other day that reminded me of my youth. Silly old things.      Oh, did you? Who was in them? Maybe you can read them to me tonight, give me a bit of drama while I’d rather be mindlessly scrolling through my phone. I still find it fascinating how people wrote letters when most people about our age don’t even type properly anymore.      Ah yes, old Reg—he had a tidy way of writing. I remember delivering those letters up for him to the postbox. Funny little route it was, down toward the river. mulher that sailed past me on the river used to give me all kinds of cheek, but I suppose she was mad in her own way.      Is that right? What with your stories, I can almost imagine the old path and the views. Still, I’m happy with how things are now—bit more goings-on on my own street than yours does in a week! Speaking of, I was hoping I might pop down the box office later on today.

Rather annoying I say, having to fly on Christmas Day. Like they can’t just give us a bit of a proper Christmas. I’m flying to visit family in Manchester. Not a huge fan of airports on a normal day, let alone Christmas.      Yeah, well, at least it’s not on the 24th this time. Last year I tried to drive up to York on the 23rd, and I hit a massive tailback after a deer had been hit. It was a dump of roadkill and everyone grinding to a halt for an hour. Disgusting.      Oh, I had even worse. Last Christmas I was baking shortbread slices, and my van wouldn’t start because the turkey had been in the oven for too long. It was ridiculous! I had to phone around, shouted at the microwave I think, turned out the thermal fuse had just about died. Made it back in time though—just.      That’s rough. Nothing’s more annoying than being stuck without food on Christmas Eve. Out here in Australia, we don’t even really get the roadblock drama. Though I’ve seen plenty of foxes sprinting across the highway once or twice. Kind of awe-inspiring in its own weird way.      Speak for yourself. I remember my nan’s fox story. She swore she saw one slap a chicken off its perch and run off with it. We used to always leave a plate out for the fox at our old place in the countryside. Silly but sweet, right?      Definitely, I always left a bit out for them—especially near my cafe. They’d be queuing up like regulars. Though, there was one ugly about five years back. I think he stole the baubles off the tree. Classic.      Oh that reminds me! I’m thinking of doing up the bakery with some Christmas fox decorations for the theme. Got a few vinyls I printed. They look quite dapper. Thought it’d give the place a bit of festive charm, you know?      Sounds good, and I’ll come say hi if you’re serving lunches. I’ve got flights to do today, but let’s arrange for after, yeah? I’m stopping by the cafe to pick up a cake on the way if you don’t mind.      Course, no probs. I’ve just done a fresh batch of gingerbread. Can you pick up some cinnamon sticks for me on the way?

Rather annoying driving a stick in Cambridge. You know, with all the tourists and narrow streets, it's like... What's the word? Like a pressure cooker, innit?      Hilarious, Rob. Not quite a pressure cooker, but I agree — motor cars can be a bit of a nightmare if you're not used to them. Having said that, I still prefer automatic. Far too many times I've stalled when trying to reverse in a tight spot.      Yeah, dump-shifting and handbrakes was the bane of my early life, but once you get the hang of it, it's not bad. Though I still much prefer manual for real driving — you’ve got that control that an automatic just can’t give you. Fun fact: My first rally driving was on stick, and I can tell you, I'd be lost without it.      Cats, rally driving? When did that start? I mean, no shortage of creativity there at the dev studio, but rally?      Haha, it's actually my younger cousin's thing — he drags me into it every other weekend up near Milton. It’s a bit of a bonding thing. Kind of like ... dodgems on a country lane, if you get me. But yes, it's competitive – very precise driving with fairly large, and sometimes barely roadworthy, vehicles.      Mate, you've got the best of both worlds, eh? Console by day, rally by evening. Who am I kidding, I’m more of a footwell-to-helmet kind of a guy with my tractor-chase racing. Or as I call it, chicane-free zone cruising.      I about blocked you there after tractor-chase. But okay, different cups of tea. Speaking of which, and not to change the subject too suddenly, but have you managed to sort out that Jell-o-flavoured baked potato voice you've been using since we arrived?      Oh, you mean my nice crisp Birmingham lilt? Give it a little context, Alice. This is Cambridge, and I'm being academically accommodating by adjusting my accent a little.      Adjusting it? Rob, I swear you’ve done a full BBC News 2 go. I've never known you to sound so… so posh.      I will have you know, bloke, I’ve had to modify my dialect to impress the big wigs down this way. I'm not pretending to be anyone else — it's just more professional for the company meeting over this afternoon’s cod and chips banquet.

Yo lads, you’ve gotta hear this new album I downloaded the other day—the bass hits so hard it feels like my earbuds are vibrating through my skull. It’s by this band called   Middle East  , genius stuff. You into indie stuff like that?      Middle East? I’ve heard their name floating around the sixth-form common room. Yeah, I’m all about that vibe. I’ve been listing to Phoebe Bridgers and a bit of Wardruna. It’s interesting, right? Especially how different the sounds are from what most people listen to today.      I’ve been jamming to some orchestral stuff, actually. Like, classical rock hybrids. You know that Mychael Danna soundtrack for The Banshees of Inisherin? So good. You ever watch that movie, Izzie?      Yeah, I saw it last weekend, and I was totally blown away. The acting was so intense at points I felt like I was sitting on the island myself. Caspian and Martin, legends.      Caspian is brilliant, but I still can’t get over the way they made the grief feel real, like, cinematic but also… personal. I mean, it’s dark but humble. Kinda like the physics we were doing in class earlier today, right? You trying to bend the emotional logic of the world to fit what you see on screen.      LAUGHING Honestly, what someone said in physics today about gravity was blowing my mind. It just felt oddly similar to how emotions work in the film—like, you can’t see ‘em but they pull  everything  together.      Yeah! My physics teacher mentioned the   Einstein Field Equations   and stuff like black holes. Like, that movie with Greta Gerwig, she uses space-like silence the way a black hole would swallow light. It’s nuts how real it all feels.      Tell me about it. I’ve been trying to wrap my head around quantum entanglement, and it’s gotten so confusing. Websites just say things like 'particles influence each other over distance.' What if the next James Bond movie is a physics thriller? Imagine like a man with a particle go-kart zooming across dimension lines.      I just started reading this science blog. It’s got this post about quantum particles communicating faster than light. It said it’s like they’re writing notes across the universe using invisible ink, or something like that.      Not overcomplicatin’ it at all. I’m more into how all of this intersects with music.

Rather annoying I had an email last night from Elise, Lucas’s mam, her house is being done up... got a big swimming pool installed and now they want to do their garden, apparently there is going to be a manmade waterfall. Lucas seems over the moon as it's exactly like the one in the park on the edge of Newton Rave.      Yeah I wanted to have that on my birthday but Aunty Phoebe said too expensive. I did an assessment in Balanceability, and the teacher said I was in the top 10 about how I move. I think I’m the best at my class at doing the standing balance on one leg! I remember in my PE classes at school we were told all the time – what your body can do expands with time and practice.      We were also told never to dive belly first into a pool, because you could get hurt. Lucas’s friend at school tried it last week and got so blamed by the teacher.

Rather annoying this game, isn't it? I mean, how do we know if it's ‘normal’ difficulty or the ‘impossible’ one? It's all about whose turn it is, really!      Charming as ever, Sarah—get on with it! Okay, so I've just finished my first year at university. I can't believe it's real! It's been so weird, but also kind of amazing. I miss home a bit, though. Rather lovely to sit down and have a chat, isn't it love? That rain's easing off a bit, got the seats dry at least. I’m more than happy to take a walk after dinner if the heavens don’t open again. I’ve seen those fells on the motorway and it was a real eeny weeny bit of hill to trudge up. Still, it kept the legs going.      Yeah, but would you walk from here to there Missus? I watched a clip online of that journey and you’d be doing at least ten miles. I can’t imagine doing that every day... like, without a car! Not when you could just hop in the Citroen and do it in like twenty minutes. Even if the traffic’s a bit left-right on the A12.      But that's the fun, innit? Living with no wheels at all. Got better for breakfast, no doubt about that. Walked to the local in my old trainers, bought the milk and hides, came back puffing and sweating like the clappers, but blooming fresher than a daisy. Cycle if it's up near Cambridge if the land's not to slippy and the hobnobs still in the bag.      Cycle? Be careful on them roads, young man. I see you lot cycling down Horncastle with your earphones in and a phone in your hand and it gives me the willies! I blame the universities for that — they put all sorts of ideas into people's heads!      Auntie, it’s not that bad — you just need to have a red light aware and be looking out for the reversing Teslas in the car park. My sister does that every day between Enfield and Bicester.      Well, as it is I was thinking, I might get myself a bike for the little ones. My missus wants us to pedal them to the park instead of always trying to catch the 704 bus. Not that the 704's a bad run — it's just the wait is longer goin' on for than if you just clip along on two wheels.      Oh, don’t go getting all wheels on wheels, your legs'll be like jelly by the time you get down to the river path.

Rather annoying isn't it, eh? You've only just arrived and they've herded us into the first floor of the Law Faculty by association. I’m more of a history kind of gal myself.      Not to worry—I read somewhere that things start to get interesting in a few hours when the guest speakers arrive. I understand one of them is from the Basque Country.      The Basque Country? That’s right in northern Spain, isn't it? I’ve done some linguistics research on minoritised languages, so that might be interesting. Did you know that the Basque language is unrelated to any other language family—completely unique? That's pretty wild.      [Chuckles] Yes, I remember studying its phonology in the 60s. I was in Shropshire then, in school. Basque had an entirely different way of marking cases than anything I’d heard of before. Now  there’s  a language that’s proud of being different.      Wow, that’s fascinating. I actually studied Mandarin in university. I found it very challenging initially, but after a while I began to really appreciate the structure. Though nothing like the inflections in Basque, of course.      Oh, Mandarin gives you no room at all for inflectional verbosity. Everything’s tonally precise. I’ve been there a couple of times for research conferences in Beijing. You know what struck me the most? The contrast between the formality of someone like a professor using classical Chinese versus a local in a market just down the street. It’s like speaking to two entirely different people.      That’s a good observation. You know, most people I meet from London—especially the younger ones—don’t even consider languages beyond French and a bit of American slang. But that’s changing now, isn’t it?      Definitely, I think part of it is education. My generation are much more exposed to language learning than the one before. But I think it’s also because of travel. I recently went on tour with the Lincoln Girls’ Rugby Club to Wales. Even though it’s the UK, I heard Celtic English being spoken quite often, almost like a third dialect.      Oh, the Welsh dialect goon really gets me—the use of  “I go on”  instead of  “I’m going to,”  it feels so archaic. But also kind of charming. I’ve made it a small personal mission to collect every minor linguistic deviation I can find across the UK to contrast it with studies from further afield.

: Right, so am I the only one who still scrolls through Facebook every day for no reason? Rather annoying this new coffee machine, isn't it? Seems like everything sticks and it's always coughing up bits of debris. Now, Brian, you know I’ll back you up, but not when we’re thinking of clearing out the kitchen again. One time, we moved a table and it looked like a bomb had gone off. I still can’t believe your mother managed to sit in it when she came for her birthday dinner.      Honestly, when it comes to removing things, the cost is one thing, but the mess is another. Still, I think someone with real skill could clean up the mess. Look at how much life improvements could happen if someone was just a little braver in the manifesto.

Rather annoying really, but at least it means I get a few days off before Christmas. I’ve been preparing a couple of workshops for some trainee teachers, so it’s all going on at once. Me, my boyfriend, and his extended family in Norfolk. It’s turkey, parsnips, and eccentric aunts all around. I hear you’re still co-hosting with Dad and the in-laws? Is Aunt Betty coming again?     Oh, heavens yes. I swear she’s still convinced she’s running a dinner party for five hundred people every year, ordering way too much wine and insisting on Christmas caroling in the garden at 8pm—personally, I start regretting it two minutes into the first song. I know what you mean. It's one of those things that are a bit of a chore, but in the end, you wouldn’t want to miss it. I’d miss being home over New Year, but it’s not like I need to plan weddings or anything.      Still, I’m proud of you. Teaching's a tricky gig, especially when it’s far from your own classroom. Just promise me you’ll line up a proper Christmas dinner before you go, and maybe send me a postcard with a wink.

Rather annoyingly, I haven't seen anything to suggest anyone has bought the wine. Should I chase up first thing tomorrow?      I’m more than happy to take on the responsibility of chasing up and doing follow-up with them. No worries at all—get on with things you need to do at home, and I can handle it. It was lovely to see you.      Oh, yes. A lot of wine tends to disappear from my social circle. Oh, and she was joking, of course. We've had to chase up once or twice before when people don't say anything.      That's mostly because when wine is involved, people tend to supply only wine. On the other hand, you know, if you're giving wine left and right, bottle by bottle, you know you're going to pick and choose what you want to buy. It's a far harder sell than if it's, you know, food or something else.      People usually expect the odd discount as well, even if it's a gift. One time, we were doing a wine tasting, and someone had come in with a bottle I had never seen before.      It wasn't even as if there was something wrong with the wine. She said, “Oh, is that available for discount?” I said, “Well, actually, no, but if you come and have a wine tasting,” as if that would entice her to buy the wine at full price, which it did.      Honestly, I think my friend's problem is that we are a buy what you like, drink what you like, share and be merry sort of social group.      Yes, about wine. I think if it was a language class, she wouldn’t mind going and buying what you wanted. Going into that is like paying a fee to have a fun time.      Oh, I like that. “Paying a fee to have a fun time.” You know, I was thinking about it the other day—the way I teach language makes me feel like I’m doing a bit of a professional version of what you two do with your wine.      That's a really nice way of looking at it.      Yeah, go on then. But tell me more about your French or Spanish classes.      I actually teach Spanish in a secondary school, and what your conversation reminded me of is the importance of practice and immersion, even outside the classroom.

Rather a lot of activity in the garden this morning, old chap. I was out there with a pot of tea, and I saw one of the robins building another nest by the shed.      Aye, we do see the same sort of thing over here. We've put up a few feeders since wintertime. It's fascinating really, watching how they swarm in every morning with a bit of sun on their backs.      I love watching the birds as well, dear. Today wasn't just the birds. I also spotted a couple of the kids passing by with makeshift puppets. It reminded me of  my  childhood, with those puppet shows at the summer fairs in Harrow.      Puppets, is it? Probably the grandchildren from the Wood family next door. Their little girl has turned into a proper puppeteer, far more than any civil engineer I've ever been.      Speaking of which, what’s for tea, love? I saw the plate near the kettle—didn’t expect anything too sweet with me and the sugars, but hope for something fruity.      You’ll do fine, Arthur. It's just a slice of Victoria sponge—very light, and I’ve put a humble fruit cup beside it for those of us with a bit more care to take than others.      Bless you, Edie. Silly old man—used to chew through hills of jam and never give a thought to the consequences. Now I’ve got to count the grams like a squirrel counting acorns.      Well, let’s be fair, Arthur, I  wouldn’t  call it consequences about you. I’ve a type of diabetes myself now, and it’s an education learning how to walk and talk with it. Not that I’d trade it for a younger, ruder bunch of nonsense.      You young men are all the same. Invincible when the blood is young and fresh, and once it’s a little too sweet waiting on the spoon, the world changes as quick as a season.      That’s the truth of it. Now, the more I think of it, the more I’m feeling nostalgic for the old days. Looking back on being young, you'd think it was ages ago—practically separate lifetimes between us and the lives we had before grey hairs and stiff joints.      There's no denying it, Henry. Time just gallops by like a wild horse nobody can catch. But I’ll be hanged if I wouldn’t give up a few years of my age to have a go at a decent cake like yours once more, Edie.

Rather skip the starters, don't you think? This grills everything quickly and it's such a muggy day. Just go with the chicken souvlaki, and I'll take the same      Aye, quite alright. Look, Susan—get the tzatziki with it. Got eeny harm in that, more'n just garlic and dill if you know what I mean.      I think I know more'n I should, Tim. You used to keep me up 'til the small hours telling me about the Greek priests who chase the black cats outta taverns. Get the tzatziki.      Allrighty then, drink? You know the beers are best turkey brewed. I remember you saying once you heard a Cypriot doting on the ears of his pastry chefs and I think he turned out a sourdough for about a month after.      I've been thinking about Hellen in Crete. I hear her shaman hides fennel in spare wine so that the clairvoyants can chew on it and tell you your reading is misplaced. She takes meds for short attention now. Still walks her dogs early. Hellen always said we were on a watching brief, that we'd been drawn from the same spring.      I remember, and I take her seriously when she says the stars have been telling her to check her shadows at night. I tell her that's the hills. She says the hills are someone else. That's what scares me: knowing she's right and not sure which hills. Some hotter summer nights, I've seen her up and being calm as a ghost, slipping along in her socks because she reckons the binding threads walk us all sideways. Interesting thing, Susan, is that most of my old ones—that failsafe cab that used to barely listen—are now listening.      That's strange. Maybe it's that her shaman insists on sundown and candle dowsing. She told me once that it's not about hearing, it's waiting till the spoon trembles to tell you what's beyond being. And also, trying with lunches to keep the dizziness at bay.      Gobsmacking. Proudest man alive when she go's her map of life from a daffodil. Gave her line in the sand that she's always go to return by. And what your husband Mike said to me once about flu and hearses and Romans, it was like those jokes that never end belly-laugh to belly-laugh.

Rather annoying to be honest. The living room needs a bit of love – you know, new wallpaper, maybe a couple of new sofas? Just to make it more... I don’t know, functional?
