Silly grin on my face for the rest of the day.      Oh yes, I saw the score! That's brilliant – well done. I remember going to a game at Twickenham with some friends a while back – it was  freezing , but we had a whale of a time. I think you'd have loved the atmosphere, Nanna.      That sounds smashing. Not that I’d know much about rugby, mind you, but I like seeing the family enjoying themselves. Speaking of family, are we all on track for Christmas? You know your mum – she's already trying to get us all to meet up at the same time.      You mean  on  track? I’d be amazed if we survive the day with all the presents and nibbles and everything.      Haha, yeah go easy on the snacks, Dad. Not everyone can work off a Christmas dinner like you, but I suppose we could go with traditional gnomes and your usual thing with the carols. I’ll help with the tree, if that helps.      Oh, that’s kind of you, love. And if we start to think about the renovation a little... You know I'm not exactly into DIY, but I can manage the colour chart.

Rather annoying when people just ain't honest innit? Jeremy Kyle’s the one show where it’s like—basically, people lose their heads over the lot o’ stuff, ay? My gran watches it every week, says it’s proper telly, but I reckon it's a bit much.      Aye, I used to trawl the internet watchin' the best bits on YouTube, but I’ve stopped now. Like, yeah, it’s got funny moments, but seeing someone get humiliated ain't really me cuppa. I got more issues than people on that show.      Right, but it’s mostly people who’ve been catfished and then taken on another person for it. It’s wild, innit? I watched one last week where this bloke thought he was back together with his ex, and turns out he turned up at the wrong person’s door. Cats ‘n’ dogs, no doubt about it!      Aye, catfishing is so common these days, even online group chats get a bit dodgy. One bloke I went out with, turned out he’d catfished three of his mates. Got him to admit it when I sent a photo of my friend in a wig and glasses, and he said, “Blimey, is that Matey from university?” I was like, nah, it’s my best mate, and he was gone.      Oh, that’s classic! I’ve been catfished once, someone said they were my age but they were like ten years older and thought I’d do anything with them. Sorted out quickly mind, I just blocked and bin their messages like a house on fire. Scammers out there, innit?      Yeah, but what worries me is how much stuff you can find out about someone online these days. I mean, if you Facebook stalk enough, you can piece ‘em together. I once guestimated my flatmate was catfishin’ me by the biscuits in their DMs. He once said, “Hey, I’m mad into cricket,” while my actual flatmate goes to every Derbyshire match.      Grin! I’ve got a cousin whose partner turned out to be a whole other bloke! She met him through goin’ on Jeremy Kyle, and after the show, she said she wasn’t sure, but he came over with the boxset and said, “Let’s settle it like adults.” She made him watch it and then he ran out the room! Proper mad!      Blimey, I can’t imagine watching that and them tryna string it out!

Rather annoyingly, I've got to do a presentation in an hour about bees for my university course. We're studying the biodiversity of insects in urban areas, so London's got a few surprises      Fascinating! When I was in Paris, I saw a group of French scientists doing something similar on the Montmartre hill. They told me bees are quite resilient, actually.      Oh, cool, but I'm more of a Classicist than a biologist. It was easier pulling together quotes from ancient Greek texts than biological data for this report. Although, I did learn a few words in German to help with some older research—Managed to get through the first six pages before my brain rebelled against me My lectures are fine, but I swear my computer’s trying to backfire on me constantly I had to reboot it this morning just to get the email system to work again, and now the printer won't do anything—      Technology... I remember when all we had was the phone and the radio, and even those were a luxury. My son, your uncle—God, he'd have a laugh hearing you say that—used to drive me nuts with all the gadgets he tried to buy me for my studio. Eventually gave in and got a tablet, and then of course I had to learn the language it spoke with presses and swipes, because nothing’s ever as simple as a paintbrush.      You know what I miss the most? When we’d just sit in this kitchen and have discussions like this. I think my generation's rush to multitask and do seven things at once has somehow made me less able to pause and talk. Like, I had a colleague last week who couldn't even make eye contact while eating his lunch. But talking of which, this lasagna is amazing.      Thank you! I made it yesterday after sending a postcard to your aunt in Burgundy. She always sends her son over here for Easter. He’s into modern art. Doesn't have a clue about the old masters, but I suppose that’s fine. We all have our passions. I remember being 19 once, with your mother, and speaking English to the wrong waiter in Florence. We ended up eating something that looked like dog food, but we still go every other year for a weekend.      You’re always in the Italian frame of mind.

Rather annoying driving today, isn't it? That man nearly drove into the back of us on that roundabout... What was he thinking?      Blows me away, the number of people who can't drive. Not only do they have no respect for speed limits, they can’t make proper decisions on roundabouts. I remember when the rules were simpler. Faster if you just had to stop completely before a junction.      That’s because things changed, Tim. They redesigned the roundabouts in Harlow to make them more driver-friendly. But obviously, people still get confused.      Yeah, I had my driver’s test back when roundabouts were the real terror of the road. You had to signal, look around, and everything. Fun stuff. Honestly, I think I’m terrified of driving in a city now. I stick to the motorways if I can.      Well, if you're going to travel in peak times, drive in the early hours, you’ll avoid 80% of the mad lot out there. Good for the scenery, too.      We need to avoid cities altogether. I never understood why anyone would choose to live in a real city like London. The noise, the traffic, it’s unhealthy in every way.      Mate, I got a lecture last night on urban development and how huge cities attract people because of opportunity. But honestly, after living in London for three years, I’m not surprised so many people want out. The hospitals are overcrowded, the furniture is tiny, and half the people are on their phones all day.      I’d be surprised if most of them  actually  looked at the Sat Nav about five times to get to the same roundabout! I’m watching this man trying to get to Bicester yesterday, circling that roundabout three times while listening to a podcast.      Oh yeah, I always tell people if you’re going to use the Sat Nav, read it before you start driving. I once used it in the middle of waiting at a red light while my kid was in the middle of doing a math equation. Rude move.      Not to mention, no one tells you in the Mot tests how to fix the points the ass go out of their way to be difficult. If I was building a car, I’d just make the lights green always.      And your health isn't helped by all that stress, either. I see more people blaming high pressure jobs, but I’m betting most of them would complain about the same stuff if they were working at the post office 10 hours a week.

Rather a gray day, isn't it love? Thoughtful weather for a bit of chinwag, if you ask me.      It's not doing much for the mood, is it? Got me stuck inside with no enthusiasm to read or even watch the telly. But I was just about to make a pot of tea. Would you like some?      Tea would be most welcome. I've had a cup or two already this morning, but what's a day without a proper dump of it, eh?      Funny you should mention it. I've been thinking about my tea habits. When I used to run the childminding business, I had to make sure there was always a fresh pot going. You know how children are—they’re either asking for more or they’re obsessed with the lemon slice I used to make.      Sounds like a proper old gig! I must've been in my late sixties when I finally gave in and sat back, planting the odd bit of veg, ordering the telly soaps. Good ones, too, like Watercress, if I remember rightly.      You're quite a way from Harrow and the real city life, aren’t you? I always fancied a little trip out of the way. How's the countryside treating you?      It's a riot, if you like peace and quite a lot of fields and ducks. I've got a garden out the back where I grow some salads and leeks. Nothing too grand, but it passes the time. Besides, I can always point out the stars—there's a fair stretch of sky here when it's clear.      You know, I miss being useful. I used to look after such lovely children, chaotic but brilliant. I suppose you and I are alike that way—both laid off our jobs long ago, both never quite found a ‘proper’ route back in. But I like knowing what I did made a difference to someone else's day.      I hear you. I haven't always been one for talk, but when I do, I reckon I've always been a bit of a character with the lads and the telly. Still, I wouldn't trade the peace for the noise of the goings-on I used to be stuck in.      I think we're both living proof that you don’t need the pace of the world to still be content.

Rather annoying this wet weather, eh? You’d think in Cambridge we’d know if it’s ‘goin’ to stop or not by now. I’m more used to the blasts of wind we’d get in Sunderland, at least with them you could tell what kind of mood the day was in straight off. Got plans for the weekend? I’ve been thinkin’ about gettin’ the garden in order again, a bit ambitious I know, but I’ve got this new bud pot I’m really keen on tryin’.      Aye, and what am I supposed to be? The weatherman? Get the spade ready then, I’ll lend you me secateurs and we’ll get stuck in together. Though if it’s still chuckin’ it down by Saturday I’m not sure I’ll be able to bear the drizzle for very long. Fair enough though. I did actually plan to do a gigin’ breakfast, no doubt about that. Found some folk musicians playing in a café down the road the other day, fiddle and lute and the lot. Good stuff, real authentic—set me thinking ‘bout all the tunes I listen to up in Birmingham.      Oh yeah? You always listened more to that sort of thing than I ever have. I was all about pop bands most of my youth. Remember that phase I had with Massive Attack? You used to mock the deep beats and say it did my head in. You know what it is though, I’ve been revisiting some old tunes lately. Spent a while talking to a few of the mates from university the other evening—haven’t had the chance much with the work as Research Manager ramping up so quickly after my postgrad days.      That’s all well and good, but you had taste back then. I’ve been trying not to fall back into that academic era of thinking everything has to be overly complex. My PhD’s on plant response to stress factors, can you believe it? A bit more scientific than the music business I was originally all fired up about. Guess it’s just waiting on me to stick the landing. Still, I do miss the old chats with you and your mates.      Some of our best conversations were after a couple of drinks and a muddy man’s hands from goin’ on pond life improvements. Not everyone could sit through that and still have a decent chat about art.

Rather annoying to be honest, eh? You've only just started your PhD and here it is, another round of stats on youth unemployment coming out. I’m more than a bit fed up with the whole thing.      Aw, lass, I know you’re well aware how it was for me een beginning. Still, I suppose it’s one o’ them things people just keep dishing up for a bit o’ headlines. At least you got a job outta uni, y’know?      Aye, and I were lucky. Didn’t even get into the uni I really fancied the look o’ first go ‘round. My folks were gutted, but I grabbed a job in a lab straight away, helped me get my foot in the door. But back then, the fees weren’t what they are now. I think it turned out for the best in the end, really.      Bucks ain’t much better now, are they? I remember when I were bleedin’ paying m’ way through uni. Still, I got through, and that’s what matthers, innit? But I’ve got a cousin in Manchester, quite a bright lad, and he just took a job as a barman… watching him go through that was a little heartbreaking.      Mate, I know the deal, and I know the system’s not exactly fair. But there’s more to life than work, innit? I went and saw  West Side Story  the other week. Now there was a proper show! All that dancing, the energy, the costumes. You’d think something’d sparkle a bit in the world of dull ‘prioritising objectives’.      Sounds right about it. I’ve not been to a musical in ages. We were luvver o’ them when we were young. I still remember the time we both managed to sneak in to the matinée for  Phantom of the Opera  at Manchester Empire. Busted at the end, of course – was bloody hilarious.      Aye, mad we could stick it out for as long as we did. Even if it were the wrong show! It were  Cats  if I recollect rightly.      Pfft! Still, we got goin’ on that life o’ our own, didn’t we? I just wish the lads and lasses coming up now could get through what we went through wi’ summat o’ that charm.      Aye, innit? But as long as we can talk about it and help where we can, that’s somethin’—even if all we do is luv our musicals and keep the dream alive. 80s kid, remember?

Look at this! The pictures in this book are amazing. Like, they've got this dragon with loads of... What's the word? Like, sparkly things?      Sparkles, darling. Or magic. Not sure if they have technical terms for it in children's books, but yeah, it’s nice.      I remember reading books like this when I was your age, Aimee. Back in Glasgow, before I moved here. They had pictures but not so... fancy, as you'd say now. The ones I had when I was a child were cardboard with crayon drawings.      Naa, that’s not as cool. I found this book in the charity shop that Myla took me to after you dropped us off. It’s about a boy who finds an old family photo and goes on a journey to discover who he really is.      Oh, that does sound lovely. I wonder if he finds himself in the end. People usually do in stories.      Aye, and that’s the best part, isn’t it? Finding who you are, or remembering where you came from. Sometimes both.      It made me think today, though. I was looking at my own little book, the one you made me when Myla was born with all the family pictures, and I was trying to remember the stories you used to tell us as children, Silvia. Like the one about Liam’s great-uncle who climbed a mountain in full Highland dress and got lost because he forgot a map.      Oh yes, the one about my brother and Ben Macdhui. That was a tale best told when there was a fire about. I always told it with dramatic flair, didn’t I?      Yeah, and you always ended it with “and that’s why it’s important to carry a map and a warm coat”.      Exactly. And now with Myla getting into stories like this, I was thinking, maybe we could do something like it for her. A little book about our family—stories from our lives, old photos, maybe with illustrations.      That would be awesome. Like, you could write the parts with Myla and the baby, and go back to my nan and granddad or something. Maybe even your stepdad, Dad? I remember you used to go up to his farm when you were younger.      I’d be happy to help with that, love. I can write some of the old tales I used to tell, and maybe even make up new ones about modern times.

Rather annoying to be honest. I finds it so much more easier to sticks with her own ‘look’ like... What's the word? Like natural? I mean, I don't see the point in going through all that hassle. Not to be rude, but it's such a faff! Deer:       laughs  Yeah, I get that. Some people just really like their hair clean-shaven. A lot of people tends to do this stuff because it's easier or because of what they see in advertize and social media and all. But yeah, honestly when it come to body hair – specially under the arms or legs – I'd rather not bother. It's the same for me!      My mam still tries to push for me to have it all off. Says I’m lookin’ “presentable” and I should be the same as all the lasses at uni. Blimey, it’s old-fashioned at this point. I mean, in my opinion, I’d rather not have that razor near me if I can helps it. Oi, I once cut myself and it looked like a crime scene in the bathroom! I don’t fancy repeatin’ that!      Oh, I’ve been there. I tried it once and it was a struggle. I’m more of a person who goes for a depilatory cream, but even that’s not my cup of tea. I just feel like it’s such a waste of time when I could be doin’ something more productive with my afternoon. Honestly, I’d rather just walk out of the house with a bit of fluff and not have a care in the world.       laughs  Oh, you and I are on the same page there. I just roll with the fluff. It’s not like no one else got it. I mean, some people even have it untrimmed for bits like the legs, ‘cos they says it’s less irritatin’. I did read somewhere that it can be a choice between shavin’ all the time or growin’ it naturally. I prefers the latter. Feels more like me, y’see?      Yeah, it's all about what feels comfortable. I think it's a personal decision. Plus, I started watching a few goenvironmental videos lately and I’ve been thinkin’ more about sustainability. You know, all that packaging for shavin’ cream or razors... Passes me by. I’d rather not contribute to all that plastic, if I'm being honest.

Rather annoying when a barista can't spell ‘chocolate’ properly, innit? I swear, typin’ the alphabet backward often helps m’remember things. I were teachin’ a kid last week who thought it were alphabet soup with a bit o' mind control tossed in.      Right? I  hate  bad spelling. At least if yer gonna be bad at it, do it creatively. Y’know, like in this one social experiment where they had people list names o' drinks in the alphabet... and som’un wrote "Lagavulin, but with less vegan."      Hah! That’s a good one. But honestly, drinkin' can make things worse. I still can’t believe I spelled my own name wrong on a drink order once – I wrote Oliver instead o’ Elinor. They screamed ‘Olivier’ at the waiters like it were a foreign dignitary.      Aye, and I’ve had my fair share o' ordering errors. One time I thought I was getting a  Gin and Tonic  and ended up with a G&T written in short-hand – a “G and T” – which, when I asked fer it, they thought I wanted a “Gin and Tea” instead. Made for a weird conversation at the bar, leastways.      Yeah, but don’t get me started on the  real  alphabet stuff in universities. Y’know those fancy people at someone’s thesis viva who go “Is it Bourdieu, Baudrillard or Bataille?” and everyone just stares at them like they’re speakin’ Martian.      I about wet meself once at a lecture when the prof said: “This is most defiantly related to Butler.” And another student pipes up and says: “Which one  is  that, Doc, ‘cause I’ve got six ones.” All the others burst out laughin’ and I were tryin’ not to cry I was so disappointed in the state o’ higher education.      I know what yer mean. It’s like people think a PhD makes you fluent in alphabet code-breakin’. Reminds me o’ a time at a conference where someone called another guy out on his racist slur about a football player.      Oh, yeah, I read about that. I dunno if it were all them big mouth louchers in the stands or managers who think it’s funny to say certain words in different languages. But I were talkin’ ‘bout this with my mates at the fights down at Hyde last week – all of ‘em were shoutin’ about how it’s time to box that racism right out o' the game.

Rather annoying isn't it, how some people think they can do a bit of internet research and call themselves a heritage expert. I've been meaning to talk to you about that grant bid for the old Redgrave Hall. I've got a contact at South East Historic Buildings Trust who might be willing to give us a nod if we tweak the proposal.      Ah yes, Redgrave's a beauty of a job. I remember working on those Elizabethan side wings back in the '90s. It's interesting you mention the grant—our figures still look solid when you run the conservation costs through the Heritage Action bidding model, but I'm not overly confident when it comes to the short-term repay plan.      That's the snag, isn't it? You can't just pitch a ten-year works plan like you're building a multi-use car park. They want something with an immediate return, a legacy project if you will, and that doesn't quite fit our historic building context in Dorton. I've had to tell one funder to puff up the 'community benefit' angle, even though we're just reinforcing vaulted ceilings.      I can relate. A few years back I had to tell off a council planner for suggesting we install electric heating in a sixteenth-century domestic façade. It's absurd – we're talking about a structure with more value because of its lack of modern intrusions. Now don't get me started on their new digital submission portal for grants. Half the time, they don't even read the full application. Just scan for keywords like 'sustainability' and 'community impact.'      Exactly my point. I've been through their scanning algorithms. I had to re-word my most recent about five times to get a green light just to attend the first presentation meeting. Honestly, it's more about the buzzwords than the work. I've even had to hire a PR person to help me ‘rephrase the language’ so it generates more sympathy.      That’s one way of putting it. I once used a grant to commission a little performance piece by a local drama group as part of a restoration of a 17th-century coaching inn. They told me the show took the visitors back in time and positively influenced community interest in the building's context. Of course, it didn’t cost nearly as much as a real conservation project.

Rather annoying I know, innit. You know what they're like – always thinkin' they know better... got to pick some tablets from the chemist yet?      Yeah, gotta pick 'em up later. Chuffed they allowed me in as a student, mind you. My coordinates were eeny weeny, I swear. But they didn’t seem to mind.      Aye, fair play. I know one too who got in off a stretch. Imagine what it’s like to do a PhD in sommat like linguistics – chase your own ideas.      Right, I'm working mostly on dialect variations. Bit like your home, in fact. You know, like that 'yin 'or 'ai' talk they do in the North. I’m lookin’ at how these regional shifts bubble in modern speech.      Oi, you better not get too cheeky then 'cos I'm still a doc in rep at the uni. Got a bit of weight, even if I say so meself. I reckon we should invite some pals for tea, maybe try some of them fancy leaves I bought in York.      Do tell – York? I did a project on Yorkshire dialects once. Absolutely fascinating, the way certain pronunciations – cheeky ones at that – linger in old families.      Yeah, an’ not to be rude, but you know what the ‘ Midlands’ accent sounds like, huh? Like a someone who found an accent in the library an’ just tried to mimic it.      Fair point, I suppose. I worked in Birmingham through my undergrad – all right city, but there’s a bit about the speech there that makes you wonder if the English lit books had finally caught up with real language.      Not to be mean, but it does sound like they’re lisping, ‘cos they just keep sayin' things like “rught” and “binnit,” you know? ‘Course it sounds very relatable, too. You ever been up North?      Once or twice. Stayed in York 'cause I thought it was posher, but the next night I was trying to get around with a cabby and he called me goonie on account of I couldn’t pronounce “muller” properly.      Aye, ‘cos up North we say ‘moughlur,’ innit. You’ve been to Scotland, haven’t you? Talk to anyone there like that and they’ll laugh at you for ‘being posh’ or whatever.      I did go to Edinburgh for a conference once. Gave a paper on Midlands syntax. One of the professors asked me where I was from and I said Birmingham and he just looked at me as if I said I came from another planet.

Rather annoyingly, the school dinner service has been raising its prices again.      We... got to pay more? But why? It wasn’t that bad before.      I don’t wanna stop eating at the canteen!      I know, love. But if we don’t bring you some extra money at the weekend, they will have to charge you a deposit now too.      So what are we meant to do, dump our packed lunches and go hungry?      Eat, but not well.      No, you can still have a packed lunch. What I was thinking is that on Fridays they do what’s called “Granny’s Day”, where you can bring in food from home and the school offers a special pick and mix stall. They say it’s an added extra to the usual school dinners. I could pop over then and bring you some supplies... and in exchange, you’d be allowed to eat at school, even if it's not the canteen.      Like, a kind of tuck shop or something?      Yep, and they actually let the kids design the layout and decorations for the stickers and stuff on the chairs. So it's a –      Fun school activity!      Yeah! Now don’t laugh, but the whole theme was meant to be about the circus. And, they wanted people to dress up in red and black.      So what did you do? Some nutty clown costume?      Er, no – I had to come as a lady circus barker. I’m disappointed I didn’t win the prize for best costume this time. Overall, though, they had clowns that wandered around and gave out lollipops, and there was even a ‘Ringmaster Moment’ for guest speeches toward the end. Parents were supposed to come to the event, but it was quite chaotic.      You must have told me about this earlier...      No, probably not explicitly. I think it was related to the school tennis tournament. The money from the tuck shop and snack boxes the kids made up go toward various school extras, like the tennis gear or extra sessions for kids who struggle in the team. You know – the ‘sportier’ kids get your leftovers.      But we’re not sportier than them!      It's to give everyone a fair opportunity, love. Anyway, the main point is that I’m allowed to go over and bring you food once a week, kind of like a little cooking project, so that we don't have to pay the deposit, and you can still eat at school before it goes completely posh on us.

Rather skip the new Disney one we saw weekend? Thought it was witty yet had its fair share holes in plot... What say you, David?      I agreed with that, Joan. The plot was hasty. Not to mention they skipped key historical events! I wouldn't say it was outright detrimental, but if you're going to dabble in history, do it properly. I've been thinking a lot about that debate in Cambridge — how to best teach history, especially to younger kids. It was quite interesting.      Aye, and what good are these films if they glorify one moment and overlook others entirely? Still, I’ll give Disney a chuckle every now and then. You know, like that one turkey film I caught years ago. Fun to watch, even if it was a farce.      I think the real issue is how history is approached in the curriculum today. I've noticed my pupils are more familiar with Anglo-Saxon myths in stories than the actual facts. It's quite worrying, given the new national curriculum in England. It's all well-intentioned, but if it lacks depth, we're really not giving them the skills.      And that's what I've always said… watching history through a screen is no substitute for learning it in school — and doing it properly at that! I still remember my days at Reading Grammar School. More facts, less fluff.      That brings me back to the discussion about linking higher education to industry. As someone in advertising, I see the gap between theoretical knowledge and real-world application. You can teach someone all the theory in the world, but if they can't apply it — whether in a museum, a school, or even a campaign — it's not the most effective education.      Exactly. We often overlook the fact that school is the first platform to connect learning with experience. I think, personally, we need to bring guest speakers in more often, let students analyze real case studies. Doing so helps contextualize all those dates and events.      I could see the value in that. I remember being asked to write a report on 'British Politics and Everyday Life' when I was your age, Joan. Gave it a whirl by talking to the local MP even. Though he didn’t share much more than a few policy pamphlets.      Hopefully, these days the box ticks off something more tangible than just writing a report.

Rather a damp day we've got, innit? Seems like we've had more rain this April than roots in a puddle! I remember when the weather more or less stayed in its place. Now, it's all 'boutups and doownset and finkle-faddle.      Oh, don’t listen to him, love. Not all good things come from springtime! Though I must say, I do prefer a bit of warmth in this old back of mine. If only the sun would grace us once in a while. You know, like when me and Harold first started.      Right, love, I won’t argue that. Though, I must say, I can recall some real wild weather back in the '30s. My folks lived through the War, you see, back when things were far more grim than just a bit of drizzle. I was about 10 then, breakfasts often consisted of bread and jam if we were lucky!      That is a lot, Ken. My father told similar stories. One time, he was taking coal over the road, and the police came after him for not using short cuts. Ridiculous! It’s only ten paces more, but in those days, the police were always on about something trivial.      Oh aye, I remember that, because they were trying to scare the people out of their homes to make them pack their bags and run. Not that they needed to — we were all in a state of near-permanent fear. My grandfather was in the First World War, so I got all the tales from that lot too. You can’t be born in Norfolk and not hear about horse and cart logistics and mud about waist high!      Now that sounds dreadful, Charlie. I can’t imagine having to grow up hearing that sort of thing. I was more fortunate, born in Harrow and, well, never really left. Harold was my employer back in the '70s — a proper gentleman. Children adored him.      A childminder, you say? That takes real patience. I’ve seen children grow up with lunches of sandwiches and chips from my younger days, but you folk must be used to something a bit more… elaborate.      Aye, well, that's not to say I've led a quiet life either. I had a job in quality assurance until about five years back. Checked educational standards all over the country! Made me see a fair bit of the UK, really gave me bellyache from driving more than talkin’ ‘bouts.

Rather skip the new house’s garden for a moment, dad. I need to know—the state of the flat... What's the condition? Have you touched it yet?      I haven't been near it. Not since your mum moved out. It's frozen, like the place was burgled and left empty. I admit I felt bad about it. But if it's not your cup of tea, you’ve only got to say so, son.      So what was it worth as it stood? You said the agent called and said the price was undercut before.      I think it was originally valued at 340K. The supply and demand dropped it by about 20K. I’ve already sold it. The lawyer said the money was on its way.      Actually, the agent called me last week, about the Catsfield house. I called back and then... I mean, I didn't sign anything yet. I wanted to check with you, you know, before anything was final. I'm not going to buy it over your head, dad.      I know, son. I’ve made peace with the idea, since I know how much you wanted it—and it’s not like we've got hundreds floating about. My share of the sale will help, and I know you'll cover the rest. You’ve been telling me that already.      I’m not doing it for you, though. I just think the house is right. And not to mention the garden—it's oddly massive. You can fit a football pitch in there, and I want it filled with green vegetables, not weeds. You know, try and do something productive with it.      You mean like your first garden in Birmingham where you tried to grow watermelons and ended up with nothing but weeds?      Hey, I had one lone tomato that passed for a sundae. Come on, don’t laugh. But this time I’ll get it right. I’ve read up on permaculture—      Well, if you're going to do a new start with your own place, I wish I’d done that after the divorce. Picked a place with a garden go-to rather than just a place that cost less per month.      Y'know, we were talking last week about nan and your brother. How he doesn’t take calls from her anymore. She’s been blaming you for holding her back?      He’s changed.

Rather than going out, I thought we could have a little do at the house for your nan’s 80th next month. Maybe just the family and a few close friends. I've been thinking about a Sunday roast — probably with all her favourites like Yorkshire pudding and stuffing — you know how she relies on that!      That sounds lovely, actually. I reckon she'd much prefer being at home. I’ve been listing out the guests in my phone — I’ve got about ten people down. Would there be space in the dining room? I don’t want the layout to look too cluttered. Would you mind clearing the shelves of some of the bric-a-brac we’ve been accumulating?      Yes, of course. I’ve already emptied the left-hand side of the bookcase to make space for the table, and I’ve bought a set of candles to make it a bit more special — rose-scented, her favourite. I happened to see a recipe in  Great British Bake Off  for a Victoria Sponge, and I thought maybe we could bake one for her.      Oh, yes! That’d be perfect — I can help with the baking as long as you don’t mind me messing things up in the kitchen. I’ve tried following recipes in the past and… let's say the results were a bit questionable. But I think it’ll be a huge hit. I’ve been trying to find out what kind of tea she prefers. Last time I visited, she was telling me about this someone at the local hospice with early dementia who’d forgotten her own name.      That’d be a shame, wouldn’t it? Still, at least she had a sense of identity because of those small reminders. I’ve pulled out some old photo albums for the birthday too — I thought it might be nice to display her life story around the room. People always love looking through old pictures.      That’s a thoughtful idea. I’ll bring some of the ones from the attic — I was going through them last week and found some I’d completely forgotten existed. We could run them off and put them in frames. Oh, by the way, I’ve already told my colleague at the office about the party — she’s a great fish buyer and can get us the finest gofion on the coast if you'd like to go that route.

Rather annoying me a bit, me wijsdoomtheeth. I've got a bit o' a headach and me face is all bobbled up on one side. I've been thinkin’ 'bout gettin' 'em out, but I don’t fancy spending another bob at the dentis een Frenchie land.      Oh no, that sounds proper bad. You should really get that looked at, if they’re that sore. I had mine out a couple o' years back, it was a nightmare, but I got it on the NHS when I was back in Cambridgesh. It was a bit daunting at first, but much worse when the infection kicked in!      My mam keeps saying I should phone up the local NHS one here and sort it out proper, but I don’t know how I’m supposed to find a dentist with a proper queue, let alone one who doesn’t speak a hundred words of English. Not that I’m bad at it, but bleedin’ mouth noises, y’know?      I reckon that’s a fair point. Moving here for the uni term was one thing, but keepin’ up with dental and all the other stuff... I miss goin' back for the holidays. My mam was all “at least we know who to trust with your teeth!” last time I had to go to the surgery. You know she don’t trust any mortal surgeon who’s not from the village.      True. Our parents always think they know best, even when you’re in a foreign country. I had a proper laugh last week—there was a hole in me sock and me moither phoned  me  and said, “Av about da holes in yer socks?” I nearly dropped the phone. She thinks I’m living like a king and not noticing little things.      That does sound like her! I bet she’s planning on coming to visit soon. My mam’s been asking me about rent and where I’m staying. She was all “I’ve heard houses here are a little mad, but I hope you’re not overpaya?"      Oh, we  are  overpayin’. Some arsehole landlord set us a price for this titchy room with a window goin' on for life if you ask me. But at least it’s got Wi-Fi and that’s a win in my bloomin’ eyes. Passin' on the PSU invoice to me brother to help, though. Uni fees are startin' to look like a life sentence now.

Rather than going out and doing something extravagant for Chinese New Year, I thought we could do something a bit more... meaningful, you know? Like random acts of kindness?      What kind of things would we do? Give out sweets or… like, write nice notes?      Or maybe we could leave some of Mummy’s very tasty   lactose-free cakes   on people’s doorsteps? A lot of people can’t have normal stuff, so maybe we can make it   extra yummy   to surprise them?      Oh, that’s brilliant! Let’s do that. I’ve actually been practicing some   lactose-free cake   recipes and I found one that’s quite good. It uses a mix of almond and coconut flour—it’s not like the usual stuff, but it still works really well, and it keeps in the fridge for a few days if we dress it up nicely.      Can I decorate them? Maybe draw some little dragons or   Chinese symbols  ?      Absolutely! You can even help pack them in cute little boxes with red and gold wrapping—  Chinese New Year   is about red and gold, right? We can add a little note, too, saying something like “Happy New Year! We hope this little treat brings you good luck!”      And I can carry some of the boxes to the next-door house! We don’t have to go far at first. I’ll be the delivery person!      That’s a great idea. Let’s start with a few houses and work our way around the village—  Comberton   isn’t too big and it’s nice this time of year when people are out and about.      Mummy, can the   cakes   have sprinkles or icing like what you normally make?      Yes, if it’s vegan, we’re all set! I can show you both how to make the icing too. It’s just aquafaba and sugar—no dairy at all.      I bet when we do this, the people we give   cakes   to will be so happy! Do people do this kind of thing in   China  ?      Some of them do, like giving out oranges or红包 for good luck. This is just a different version made for   our home kitchen   and our own community.      Maybe we can make some   Chinese New Year   craft activities and give one to each person too—like maybe   Draughts   pieces made like gold coins or   Chess   pieces to them so they can play games later?

So, I just read  Alice in Wonderland  at school. It's kind of weird, but in a cool way, you know? Like, the whole time she's going into this dream world where nothing's normal. Our English teacher said it was about growing up and making sense of things that don’t make sense. Do you remember reading it when you were a kid?      Oh yes, I read that book when I was your age. Such a strange but beautiful story. I used to read it over and over. We had a hard copy at home—my mum even knit a crocodile costume one year for the school play! Still, I never did anything with it. What did you think about the Alice in the version your teacher used?      Yeah, we tried to do a bit of the play in class, but no one had the courage to wear the costumes properly, except for James. He dressed up as the Cheshire Cat and refused to take it off in the car on the way home. His mummy was not happy when the fabric got soaked in rain. But that’s not why I tell you—my teacher said she used to write songs about the characters.      Songs? That sounds like a nice way to remember the book. I always liked when people got creative with it. My nan used to sing a ballad version, but I don’t remember the words.      We tried something like that too! I got stuck on the part where the Mad Hatter is all confused with time. It made me think about real life, actually. Like, do you ever feel like the rules just change without notice?      Believe me, when you are driving and trying to get somewhere on time while a seagull pecks at your leftovers on the pavement… it definitely feels like the rules are written by madness! I had a near car accident last week that was just ridiculous. A little seagull flew in front of me, and I had to slam on the brakes. The kerb was  very  disappointed.      I hope you weren’t hurt! Scars are always the clue that something interesting happened. I keep meaning to ask—was there anything you got as a present after that?      Haha, no goody bag on that one, I promise. But you know, lately I have started reading quite a lot. I go to the library sometimes when the house goes quiet.

Rather annoying isn't it, how they just keep coming in with these planning applications for wind turbines? The first one got turned down, but now there are more proposals down the road from me.      Aye, we've had the same sort of thing in our neck of the woods. Got een wind farm proposed right where we used to go walking. I reckon it's not all about energy—they're making money off grants too.      They're certainly making money alright. I know someone involved with one of the energy companies. Sums are astronomical when it comes to government subsidies. But tell me, how did you make out when you were advising that local group last night?      My advice was simple: do your research and plan your actions. They approached the meeting with the committee without a shred of evidence. If you don't know your stuff, you're just noise at the back.      That’s true alright. The other week, I showed the group a couple of case studies where local opposition was successful. One was in Kent, where they demonstrated the visual impact and the inappropriate location.      Aye, it’s all about location, location, location. We in Manchester—well, it’s quite a different story. You’re bound to see more solar panel proposals there, given the way it's flat and urban. But even there, they're trying to sneak through turbines in places where it's just not viable.      And don't get me started on the appeal process. The council just rubber-stamps a lot of these things, and it's the local people who end up fighting for their rights. We need more people who know the planning laws. Someone told us the other day the appeals can take over a year.      Precisely. And while they’re dragging it out, the developers are already lining up for the next one. What troubles me most is the politics. The planners have ties to the energy companies. You know, it's not always obvious, but it's very real. We need to be careful and stay on the right side of the law.      Ah, I remember the good old days when you could get a nice opposition campaign together with a bit of go-fund-me cash and a few hand-painted posters. But now, you need digital signatures, social media strategies—proper campaigning.      It's all very well, but we also need proper energy storage solutions.

Rather annoying this, having to go through all the hoopla of learner's permits and whatnot. But I suppose it's a necessary evil if I'm going to visit my sister in London regularly without relying on the train.      Dad, I know it seems a bit much at first, but it's all for safety, really. You've got to get used to it. I've helped quite a few of my students through the process—there's a lot more to it than you think.      And don't forget the insurance business. That'll run you right into the ground if you don’t shop around properly. I've seen some surprising quotes, dear. You just have to ask around.      Insurance, yes, I'd forgotten about that one. Ten more bits to worry about, what with the tests and the instructor. But I'm not about to let a few hurdles stop me. I've driven for decades without this nonsense!      Well, I'm more than happy to help you prepare, Dad. We could go over driving theory or even help you find a good, patient instructor. I’ve got contacts I can tap into.      And while you're at it, there's something else we wanted to discuss. We were thinking about taking a holiday at the end of the summer. I know you've never really had a long break unless it's been for Christmas.      A holiday, is that what you're calling it? I might just call it a week wasted on the beach. But I’ll admit, a bit of a break from the daily grind is pleasant enough. What have you got in mind?      There’s a great caravan park near the coast—close to Bournemouth, I think. We were considering going for a week in late July or early August. We could take the family along too, if you're up for company.      Bournemouth? Aye, I’ve been there once on a school trip long before your time, love. Good place, I suppose. I’ll have to crack on with the learning then so I’m ready to drive us all down there.      Now, love, no pressure—just a suggestion for now. We can talk about the actual goings-on on another day if you'd rather focus on one thing at a time.      No, no, let's lay it all out.

Rather annoying the new Facebook app eh, Dad? I keep missing messages because the notifications don’t work properly. I got to check it often manually. Otherwise I miss messages from Uni and whatnot.      Yeah, honestly I don’t even use it that much anymore. Too many pop-ups and I find the new design cluttered. It was simpler back in the 1950s with a clean interface. Back when things just worked!      Haha, yeah, I bet it was! You always romanticise the 50s though, don’t you? You'd fetch water from the well even if it was bucket rain!      Well, it wasn’t that bad, love. You had more time to think and no distractions back then. We had to survive, didn’t we? I remember walking miles to buy fresh produce in the morning before attending school. And breakfast, no doubt, always proper tea and biscuits after getting in.      Mmm, you didn’t have the choice of processed food like we do these days. I do try to get my kids eating properly, but I swear if we land a week with no food bank food, we’ll still be in trouble…      Well, healthy eating shouldn’t cost the earth. I used to grow my own vegetables, you know. There’s something about fresh produce straight out of the soil. You couldn't get that in supermarkets back then!      I know, but it’s so hard with everything being so expensive. Moving to Brighton to study was supposed to make it better, but the rent here and being self-employed is a mess! And parking is impossible!      That’s the same story the area had when I was your age. I used to park my old cab half a mile away and walk it. These days, I bet the politicians are too busy cutting their own bonuses to sort anything like that out.      Oh they’re not busy, they’re very busy fixing tax breaks for the ones who don't need it! At least that’s what I read every day online with my morning tea and biscuits!      That's where you get the source of your sarcasm, isn’t it? Anyway, I remember life was more about working for a living, and I do support the people that can’t anymore—especially with the disabilities benefits helping your lot. It's all part of the bigger picture of survival and support in society.

So, I swear I just watched my cousin describe Shakespeare in a job interview like he's some kind of  business guru  or something. Like, “Oh, he wrote all these plays about emotional intelligence and workplace dynamics.” Honestly? Not quite how I read  Macbeth .      Haha, yeah, I can picture it. It’s like people just think his advice on leadership will help with a spreadsheet. A lot of people just  win  at social nonsense, don’t they?      Win? You mean  not  win. Didn’t your cousin get the nickname “Mr Shakespeare” at the golf club even though he still can’t tell a bunkered shot from a bunker? I mean, that’s a skill, I guess — skilling up while golfing?      You're stealing my punchline. That’s the thing about nicknames in the family, eventually they’re stuck with you no matter if you've mastering the skill or not. My aunt was called “Stiffy” for, like, 20 years just because she once sat rigid like a statue.      I feel for her. I used to be called “Exeter Express” when I was at uni because I was always on the first bus. Then it was just “Express” no matter where I went. True story, last night, I was at this coffee shop and a bloke tries to start a conversation with me by asking, “So, you the Express, eh?”      Oh no, what did you say?      I said, “Depends what’d you like delivered.” He looked so confused. Made my day.      You’re a legend. I respect your sarcasm game. But honestly, what’s with people trying to be funny by referencing anything? “Express” shouldn’t be the handle of a student who can’t do basic chain differentiation.      Honestly, I don’t even know why I used to go to those early buses. Maybe it was a weird determination to be on time or something. We all have our quirks. Some of us work in places trying to 'win', and others just end up with ridiculous nicknames no one remembers the origin of.      That's the spirit. Work on your own terms and let everyone else work on nickname-based reputations. Just don't end up like my uncle, working at a sandwich shop and still being called “The Breadwinner” 30 years later.      I’ll take that as a life lesson: choose your nicknames wisely, avoid working at sandwich shops, and maybe—just maybe—reconsider trying to Channel Shakespeare in an interview.

Rather than share a beer in the pub tonight, I fancied a glass o’ wine ‘ome. We’d got the seats, tablets out, and I’d actually  shout  someone      Yes please, I'd kill for a glass of wine after this week. Has anyone even got a normal job anymore?      My job isn't exactly normal. I’ve been working double shifts just to keep this flat afloat. You’d think being a labourer you’d get paid enough to not worry about rent. Didn’t even get the full overtime check last week... like, jokes on them!      That's harsh, love. You know I’m always working event after event, but I swear my pay’s barely keeping up with inflation. I’d rather be on the picket lines in the rain than coordinating conferences with people who dress like they’re born for breakfast, no doubt.      I used to live for the production schedule and 4am starts to meet delivery deadlines—and I still do, but now I’m thinking maybe it’s time I try something less... intense. I mean, don’t get me wrong, I like the adrenaline, but I miss having time to actually live my life.      Tell me about it. I’m at the opposite end of the spectrum, barely making ends meet. I’ve been telling myself to just save up and move back in with my parents, but that feels like failure. Like, someone at my age should be independent!      That’s so unnecessary pressure—look at me, I live in a tiny studio with two roommates and a  schedule  as chaotic as most people’s crises. I’m not even eating properly half the week.      Same here. I’ve been doing that juice detox thing every other week. No sugar, no carbs... like, for like four days and then I cave and eat a pizza that’s more crust than cheese. It’s exhausting being all  wellness intense .      Honestly? I’m just trying not to live off of ramen and bread with lunches delivered through Grubhubs. I took the 50% off voucher for a nice salad course—which I basically just ordered go and ate on the loo like some kind of work-weary sadist.      I tried box sets last week to distract myself from my cravings. I watched three in one night and ended up raiding the fridge hours after pretending I had gone cold turkey.

Rather annoying this new TV licence regime, isn't it, George? I had to fill out a form like I was still in school or something.      Oh, I didn’t have a problem with it. Not like I’ve seen telly in a year, mind you. My coordinates were on the form anyway, I suppose. It was all rather bureaucratic if you ask me.      A lot of people just think it's all a bit much these days. It was easier when you just had to send in the sixpence every month.      You'd think the BBC could afford it these days, what with all the streaming and such. But perhaps we should be talking about the turkey on the table instead of bureaucracy!      You're right, Frank. I bought a whole leg of it today, for the eclipse viewing party! We’re streaming it live on Skype this time.      Oh, you're not actually moving, are you? I heard the news the other day, and thought—      We're not moving, George. I was just saying it as a joke. But serious question, what do you think of Marcus watching us during it?      I think it's very important to show the younger generation these things. Though I imagine some are choosing not to join because of that whole politically correct nonsense.      Everything's politically correct these days, Ethel. Spoken to the vicar last week about a new owl box we’re putting up—everyone had to sign a form in triplicate and be ‘sensitive’ about birds of prey.      I agree. I think I prefer the good old days watching “Cosmos” with Ron. At least he talked about black holes and the beginning of space without sending out impact statements. My, what a programme that was.      Speaking of black holes, Frank, I saw a programme on the scientists trying to grow worlds inside them. You’d love it.      You've all seen more space than me recently. I’ve been watching my own garden instead. Added a fence where the neighbour’s bamboo had taken over!      That sounds brutal, George. How’d they react?      Well, I don’t know, I wrote them a letter and told them politely. It was only bamboo! Eventually, we compromised and shared some.      It's a pity we can't have compromises over everything, especially on topics like this. I’m trying to get all of you to paint the shed.

Rather than going up The Metro, I reckoned I'd do mine the ol' fashioned way an' drive... got the seats, maps an' all that sorted ready. Not a bad call if you ask me, it beats chockin’ up the quay as far as the uni in a bus full of eeny-minded types passive aggro tryin’ to get where they ain’t wanted anyway. Yeah?      Mate, I got this all mapped out. Oh, and you   didn’t   mention you were coming in the car. You just said 'I’m meeting you later at the café... like, near the library.'  Obvs . That’s 15 minutes’ drive away from the cafe you’re meeting me at. I’m not even gonna start on this map nonsense, because if I do, I’m gonna scream.      Blimey, sorry love. Got a bit breakfast-crazy and forgot I said that. Not a problem in the car though, you ever looked at a map, or do you rely on that voice in your head telling you which turn to do when you get lost?      I do, quite a bit to be honest. It’s not that I’m lost in general—it’s just that maps confuse me when they got way too much detail – buses, cycle paths, sidestreets, and  hills  that weren’t there before. You know what the worst is? When the ‘voice’ tells me to take a right turn just before a full-on roundabout. And not a roundabout with just one exit, a proper  job lot  of them. So I have to be like,  right ,  now ? Where?      That’s the same roundabout problem we had outside Tyne Bridge th’other week. Sat there for five minutes trying to find the housing estate near St Nicholas Cathedral that the café’s ‘supposedly’ in. You’d think they’d put a sign at the roundabout. Or a billboard sayin’ “  THIS IS WHERE YOU GET LOST  .”      Yeah, but at least there’s always a solution. You keep the conversation going while the voice is doing its thing, you remember a place around the corner or a place you remember from goin’ on your own. It's not perfect – but it makes the journey more of a story than just a list of turns.      Exactly! So instead of feeling like it's navigation, it’s almost like we're writing the next plot of this adventure to find a decent sandwich or a overpriced coffee or whatever.

Rather annoying this newfit alarm clock o’ mine, is. Keeps goin’ off ‘fore m’ ready, and I’ll often jolt up like a startled bairn an’ nearly spill me cup o’ tea. Not to mention, the bird outside me window started singin’ straight after it. een-a-meen, een-a-meen, like that little dicky bird.      A dicky-bird? Ay, that’s a chaffinch, if I’m not mistaken. Always sounds as if it’s in me garden first thing in the mornin’. I reckon feedin’ ‘em makes a heap o’ difference. I toss out some sunflower seeds and peanuts. Course, they come at turkey time too, but you get the gist.      Aye, I’ve bin meanin’ to start a patch for ‘em an’ all, but with me sprained wrist, gardenin’ has been a tad hindered. The doc at the surgery said it’ll take a fookin’ age to heal, and he had me sat in a room with three other elderly lasses, all listenin’ t’ stories abou’ their fillings and griefs.      Oh, I reckon I saw ‘im a little while back. Poor chap lost ‘is collar button, I heard, and now he’s starin’ at the ceiling somethin’ awful. Mind you, tha’ Dinah ‘ad a nosebleed so bad the other day someone said she looked like a blushing radish.      Nosebleeds—’e’d better watch ‘imself. Me cousin ‘ad a bout o’ throat cancer, and it all started about with a noddin’ off and the odd bloodied hanky. Not th’ cheeriest of lark, that.      Aye, well, that’s life, ‘asn’t it? Enexpected things happen. I was at that EFL class yesterday and one o’ the lads said he used to teach in Bangkok. You’d think learnin’ to talk as he does would’ve saved ‘im from ‘is lunches, but nooo!      Slang, you mean? Aye, but like feedin’ the birds goin’ on ‘ere, sometimes it’s about the give and take. Still, I’m enjoyin’ this bit, bloomin’ breakfast and your company. It’s nice to take time and chat.      As long as the toast doesn’t go black again like it did Friday, ‘cause I nearly bought the farm with that bitter stringhanger I ‘ad to eat. Always forget to flip it ‘fore the smoke alarm claims my ears.      Oh, that’s the spirit. ‘Appy, content and as light as a leaf in the wind—so long as my teeth don’t betray me, that is.

Rather skip the new book, eh? You've done a proper switch-around with your life, haven't you? What was it, five years since we last caught up properly?      Yes! It is rather different now. I sold the flat in Bury St Edmunds and bought a smaller house on the outskirts of Newton. Gives me more space to write and meditate. I’ve actually been working on a book — fiction, but set in Cambridge too. I thought it'd be a good setting, pulling in local characters and places.      Didn’t you want to keep doing social work? I thought you loved it.      I did — and I still do, but I wasn’t well. Burned out, really. So I left the job and gave myself a year off. And during that, I thought: what if I tried something different? I’d always fancied writing. So I did a creative writing course online and then, after some soul searching and lots of yoga, I started penning this book. Honestly, the change has done wonders for my mental health.      That sounds brilliant. I’ve always admired people with the guts to do something like that. For me, I’m still in teaching, but I've started IVF treatment. It’s been a bit of a rollercoaster. I’m still working full time, trying to keep the kids and staff in check, but also trying to stay on top of my own emotional situation.      Oh no — but aren’t you glad you're not alone? It must be oddly lonely at times — you know, not having a partner to share the journey with.      Yeah, there is a bittersweetness to it all. I’m the kind of person who always had a partner — or so I thought. Life doesn’t always go the way we plan. At least I've got family, and for the most part, friends. Though I find it funny that I have 200 people on Facebook ‘friend me’ but I only speak to about 10 of them. It’s as if we use social media to stay updated, but not to keep in touch with people the same as we used to.      You're not wrong. That's one of the themes I'm developing in my book — about real human connection in a hyperconnected digital world. I’m also looking at exploring the lives of women your age who've made major life changes — career shifts, new relationships, parenting on your own, all that messy stuff that life throws at you.

Rather annoying isn't it, how some people think they can do what they like just because it's the weekend... Our next door neighbour had his barking dogs yet again last night. I've nearly lost my mind by now.      Oh I know what you mean, Martha. Over here in Birmingham, it's like everyone thinks they're on holiday all week. Someone even played a full rugby match on a Sunday afternoon only a few streets over. Such a racket!      It's quite interesting you mentioned Birmingham. You grew up here, and I never did when I was younger. I came from Hitchin, near Hertfordshire—very quiet, very different to this place.      Oh Hitchin, I've heard of it! A bit more leafy, I imagine. I've been meaning to pick your brain about the education system up there. I was a teacher myself for several years. What made you go into teaching languages?      Well, I've always been fascinated by how people communicate across different cultures—and I suppose growing up with a large family taught me the importance of clear expression. I ended up doing a postgrad in modern languages as it made sense to me.      Sounds like a good fit. I was a Geography teacher. You ever consider swapping – I swear I could fairly well teach French now, just from trying to remember the weather terms!      You never know! I could probably teach you a few phrases, and then you could teach me some Geography. Although I’ve not read a proper map in years.      That’d be a fine idea. I’d be happy to set something up! We could even do it at my place—nothing fancy—just a few stories from the past and a bit of learning. I’ve been quite fond of reading lately, you see. It helps me feel as if I still have something to do with the day.      That sounds lovely. I have a few students who’d benefit from a nice informal setting. I always thought you should mix conversation practice with a bit of good storytelling.      Exactly! There’s a reason I loved teaching—you learn how to keep the attention of even the most distracted minds. Just by telling a good story!      Well, if you ever need a real teacher in the house to bring in some structure, I’d be more than happy to lend a hand.

Rather annoying this wet weather, eh? You’d think in Cambridge we’d know if it’s ‘ere first... got the cow parsley growing in the dining room more than I’ve seen on the fells round Leeds.      No, I mean—get in, James—it’s not like it’s  standing  in the room. It’s just   drizzle  , not a tropical storm. Though I suppose that cow parsley is starting to look more abundant than the cutlery. Honestly, someone should invent a cup to collect the rain and pour it outside when it drips off your hoodie.      Lakelands is no Cambridge, but the real debate still tends to be whether you consider the turkey a vegetable or not. Honestly, I think I’m the only one in my family who used to think it was a meat. But in all seriousness, James, if we’re talking food—maybe I can bring some homemade Hefeweizen bread over later. My Nan says it’s the best way to keep the damp out.      I do like Hefeweizen bread, yeah. I mean if we’re going down that road, I’ve got a shepherd’s pie in the oven—want some, Sophie? Though I can’t promise it’s traditional—my version involves swiping the topping off and just eating the meat.      You know what—go on then. Though if you carry on like this someone’s going to report you for abuse of a cultural icon. Though speaking of abuse—what about the way people still insist on watching  The Office  in the UK when it’s about nowhere near us? I mean, bleeping the word ‘sh’ out… it’s so  absurd .      Honestly, if we went by that logic, we’d stop watching the US  Friends  version too. They bleep the word “Damage” out as if it were a swear. I mean bless. But honestly? I think the best thing that came out of that show is Justin Bieber.      Justin Bieber? Wasn’t that you calling him a “baby pop machine” the last time? I think your real contribution to  The Office  is merely watching the David Brent “meatball” arc with a face like a lemon.      I mean seriously, why was everyone’s first instinct to start with the meatball bit anyway? Surely we start at the start where David’s walking up the stairs and everything else is a  build . The meatball was a red herring, and now people just watch it to see if it happens again.

Rather annoying the wet weather, eh? You know, me and mine were trying for a trip to the gym... got nipped off by the rain and had to call it quits. I've been meaning to get back into it. That’s cool, man. I’d love something like that—putting it in a game, waiting players to explore a virtual forest, solve some problems, and doing a bit of cardio with it. I think it's the younger generation’s version of the camp experience.      Now you're talking my go-to buzzword: gamification. Rather annoying that the ref’s still not given a red for that foul – you’d think it’s obvious. I swear, some of these officials’ve got more chance of callin’ it right than a goose! At least you know that your Easter egg hunt won’t be a full-time job to collect them all ‘cos he’s hiding them in the lightbulb sockets. I once found one behind the TV—only discovered ‘cos it rolled onto the floor mid-match.      Sounds about right. I swear, the only way to truly test your patience is to have a child. Now, the films—what you think of the one with the dog and the astronaut?      The one rated seven on IMDb or the one made in the Sahara Desert by a group of filmmakers who hate oxygen?      The latest one. I mean, it looked alright in the trailer, but those_ratings never mean much, do they? I had a look at ‘Interstellar’ when it came out and thought I’d go blind halfway through.

Rather skip to the front of the book, isn’t it? A few hurrahs for when the first one got the big boots on. You remember that, Dervla? I've told ye a thousand times, we were up to our necks in mud outside the fun fair near the park. Ruairí wouldn’t stop wakin’ the whole town with that little toy his mammy had given him — a police whistle from a fairground tuckshop.      So what was it like, Grandad? Did you and me mam and Granda chase him through the park with a net or somethin’ like in Disney?      Now the cheek of you, Liam — and you well know you were a bit of a terror! When’s the last time you were to the fun fair, Aiden? Eamon in the park? Or was it in the GAA field one year when they brought the rides there? Oh yes, the time you lugged the pram up the side of that slide because ye couldn’t push it and hold Eilís as well. It was watching that mess that made me give up being a “relevant mother” – no chance of being a part of the action with two jobs and a kid. But oh, don’t ye remember the London marathon, Dervla? The week after our Eilís was born, someone said to me, “But you won’t run a marathon again.” I said, “I’m running the marathon of motherhood and I intend to win!”      That’s amazing, Granda. Did you run the actual marathon?      Oh aye, back in '08! Going into that frosty cold beside the Thames, a sandwich in my pocket. My sister had to put me on dialysis for weeks after — all the salt and strain. But the day before I was running, I had Eilís strapped to my hip. I told the volunteers to “never fear, I’ve got a future here wrapped with a nappy and a whinge.”      You set the bar high for us, Aiden. That Eilís is a wild one, if you ask me. Just like your mam. Still, I’m thinking between us we’ve given her the best of what your mam and I could sum up — fluency in tech and stubbornness in equal measure.      It’s a pity we can’t take ‘em all to the cinema at once!

Rather skip the new TV show last night. That dumpling recipe I tried was just the ticket. The first time I ever attempted it, ages ago now, my mother-in-law nearly stared me out of the kitchen. But we finally came to terms over the years.     Deer, that's delightful. I liked the dumplings as they were handed over to me. I've never been one to cook ambitious meals from scratch. Not that I don't want to, but you know how it is when you're managing a whole team and household. Still, I do love to get the knitting going after dinner... like to keep my hands busy.      Oh, I still knit. It's like that old locket I have - you know the one with the tiny bottle of rummy from my wedding in it - I used to make Fair Isle sweaters for most of the family when times were better. I still remember those board games we used to have... I used to absolutely love the charades as a child, you know, those old ones with the flimsy cards that would crease and tear, but we loved them none the less. I never thought about it as much as now when I see grandkids today.      My parents used to play games like dominoes most of the time. But we'd sometimes manage a game of cards or something. I remember my mother saying quite often that “It's a small world after all.” Little things like that made sense in the context of someone who had four kids and two jobs.      I can definitely understand what you mean, and it's quite the way of being philosophical in a practical sense. We all are in a way, about our little worlds. I sometimes wonder if the next generation even comprehend this saying.      Going back to toys then... I remember we had a classic Little Tikes dollhouse, quite the showpiece. My sister and I passed hours making imaginary dramas and creating new stories. I used to assume being the queen of my own worlds, you know.      As for books and such, I’ve taken to reading eBook versions recently. I find it easier to have various titles on my tablet, you know, something around with travel or a relaxed dinner by the go. But I still love paperbacks. There's something tactile in them, like in the way that you might savor a traditional meal.

Rather fine day today, isn't it love? Thought it’d be a bit damp, seeing as it piddled all weekend.      It is nicely dry, dear. I think the sun's finally made up its mind to come out this week. I made us some cold chicken sandwiches — proper good on the crusty loaf I got last week.      Aye, that does sound a spot of cheer. I’ve just put the kettle on, if you don’t mind a nice cup of builder’s. We can sit in the sun for a while — it’s always the garden at this time of the year that makes me feel alive.      What a lovely idea. You know, I always think of the old days when you used to have bursts of green fingers. I remember you once grew the biggest parsnips I’ve ever seen — came straight out of the earth like old sticks taller than breakfast forks.      Hah! That was me and old Mr. Timpson from next door — showed those city folk how it’s done, real Suffolk soil under the Norfolk sun, luv. I still try every now and again — well, as much as my grief and painkiller fog will allow.      You work too hard, dear. You should take more time to enjoy yourself, not trying to prove yourself to the parsnips. Let’s have some of those sandwiches and enjoy the day for a change.      Right, right. Our garden. Our day. Though I do say, it’d be nice to have some visitors occasionally. Some of the ones who used to pop over have all but vanished — Margot’s in Bognor now, and Gerri’s taken up travel clubs with her brolly and all.      Aye, some folks are like that. I think age makes it a bit harder to step out of the house for many of us. But I do like it when you speak about the village — the Costessey mentioned in those old maps, I always thought you must’ve been brought up in the very heart of somewhere that time forgot.      'Tis the truth of it. I took the air in that little place, where the reeds whisper and the sun sets away goin’ on for ever if you let it. But I think I’m just in love with that part of the world, bloomin’ marvellous all of it. It’s got character.      Like you, dear.

Rather annoying I had to take the bus in to work this morning. My car's decided it doesn't like the weather and conked out on the way outta Bristol. Not a good start to the week!      Oh no, I felt for you on the WhatsApp message. My mince eeny is always  just  reliable enough to get me where I need to be — until it's not. I swear it’s reading my diary!      If only cars were easier to fix than a typo in a copy edit. You’d just chase it, hit the undo button and you’re good to go! We were just going to take a walk around the park after this. Summer barely gave itself a hint, but it's still quite doable. Burgers and treacle scones at the food truck on the corner too. Okay, but you remember my cousin's wedding last summer? The proposal was classic goings-on on the lake, and our nan got so emotional, she hugged the goose in the gift basket. Rather annoying the new developments in this area innit? Seems like everything's getting choked full o' 'igh prices and naff building projects. Rather annoying the new free school meals system isn't it, Mary? I know Richard—the head cook at the local school—said it's all about variety these days. I can't say I'm entirely convinced though. I keep wondering how we'll know the kids are being fed anything nutritious.      Oh dear, Eleanor, I do worry about the lunches too. When I was in primary school, a "lunch box" was just tinned tomatoes and a slice of cheese. Now, it seems like someone is inventing gluten-free, dairy-free and nut-free versions of everything! Do you think the children can even enjoy their meals anymore?      Honestly, the only way I can manage is by bringing my own turkey and quinoa wraps! The new food fad is ridiculous! I made one for Alan the other day, and I think he turned pale. He said he was far more used to sausages, no matter if they’re a bit dodgy for the gut.      That's typical of Alan! I still remember the time he tried to cook a stew and it looked like a crime scene. Honestly, he might have been better off relying on the dinners from the Farm Shop, like the Village Shop in Berkeley—it always has proper local stuff. Speaking of which, have you ladies heard about the new bike race passing through our way?      The Tour of Britain? Oh yes, it's going to run through High Wycombe! Have you decided where to go?

Rather annoying I had to cancel last minute innit, me n mine lads got cranked up for a minith weekend conference inn’ Cambridge. The feedback was really good, and we’re kina thinking about putting on a smaller, more team-focused gathering in a few months time. Rather annoying isn't it, eh? The council wants to knock that old library in Plumstead. I couldn't believe it when I heard them talking about tearing down such a lovely building. It's where we used to study as kids, remember?      Yeah, well things have been moving fast in the borough lately. I mean, the council says they're cutting costs, but c'mon—that's a functioning community space! I think they just don’t see the point of books anymore. It's all apps and videos these days.      Exactly! We need to get the word out. I saw a leaflet on the noticeboard at work. I've been thinking of starting a petition. It's amazing how many people still use the library, you know. The children’s section alone gets loads of use.      I think it's brilliant. I’m in for sure. But do you think breakfast, lunch and then late shifts will be enough time for me to help out, especially with my 9 to 5 admin gig?
