The brain needs training, just like your biceps at the gym. Brain training, if you will.      And the more you recall something, the stronger the memory gets. It’s like when I practice your favourite word to remember you by. “Plumstead—book—brain.” That’s the one, right?      That’s the beauty of mnemonics. Visual, rhythmic or go back to my pond life if you like. Anyhow, we could even line up a few teachers from local schools—word might spread fast through the community if we reach the parents directly.      You’re on to something. I can ask Sarah from the nearby primary school next week.

Rather annoying lot, them Jehovah's Witnesses. I used to get 'em knocking on the door when I first moved in to Mattishall. Always asking me to come to their meetings, like I’d have time for that at my age. Still, the view from our garden is well worth the peace it brings.      Aye, I’ve 'ad 'em too. I tell 'em I’m not interested, but they still keep coming back! I don’t get why anyone would go to all that trouble to convince people when they’re not wanted. Funny thing is, I don't even know what they talk about half the time. Mary over the road used to listen to the lot of 'em. She’d brought up the family by 'erself, you see.      I didn’t like their leaflets, the way they make people feel like they’re making a choice about the end of the world when, really, it’s just a pile of papers and a hard sell. I remember the day my eldest got married, the local witness was outside the church door, trying to hand out one of those big books. Rather inconsiderate if I ask you!      Aye, that sounds like her. Good on you for not engaging, by the way, Jean. You’ve always been the calm one of us lot. Still, I suppose they’re trying to do the best they can in life somehow. Just not the method I’d choose.      Speaking of best in life, have you been to the café in Manningtree lately? It's one of the few places with a decent meal and a proper scone. Mind you, parking at the coast is a ballet unto itself these days. I swear I’ve spent more time trying to find a decent spot than I have looking at the sea.      I know! I tried it last week, went in to have a drink and realized I’d left my guest list in the car. Backed up at least a quarter of a mile before I found it again. I ended up sitting on the grass with a biscuit while the rest of them waited!      And 'aving a new dental bill to top it all off. My ghastly visits to the dentistry these days. They charge more for every breath I take it seems. Not that I can afford it.      I had a root canal done last year, and what a shock it was.

Rather annoying the new developments next door. You know, the one where they had that log burner installed? We can feel the heat from here on a windless day. I’ve asked them nicely if they might use gas instead, but you can imagine they weren’t overly impressed.      I don’t get all the fuss about logs. It’s an older house; if it wasn’t for the heat, I’d probably be listing it up for sale. Of course, it’s easier said than done with the market as it is. Did you hear about the new restaurant that opened in town? That place has really shaken things up.      Oh, I heard about the new place, and I’ve been in twice already. It’s unexpectedly good, especially for what they charge. But back to the topic – I was meaning to ask, how is the school progressing? We had an in-service about the move to academies. I must say, I’m a bit uneasy about it in general.      You and I, old love. Academies have been a mixed bag for everyone—especially when it involves the budget being shuffled around. I’ve written to two different committees about it. You’re not the only one who feels uneasy.      You two should consider moving from the UK. How much prettier it is in Japan, with all those little temples and neat roads. Though I reckon the salary there would never be as high for a teacher or administrator.      There are pros and cons to every place. I’m glad you didn’t consider it, Alan. I do miss out on a lot at times, but I can’t be split from this country. I heard from a colleague last week who about to make the switch to India. That man had the balls to consider outsourcing.      That leaves me with frostbitten hands worrying about the future of decent local jobs. My, I do hope the new restaurant will survive if they are going to attract international talent into the area. It could give the place a better look.      I hope your colleague is not too brave. I remember being sent out once to Moscow with a conference. It was one of the worst experiences of my life, and I positively froze. You know, I once met an American guy in Tokyo on a work trip. He had a cat and a dog, just like us.

Rather annoying this new tax they’ve brought in, isn’t it? I was just reading it in the  Eastern Daily Press —something about local authorities having more power over property taxes now. He bought it from his brother thirty years ago.      Oh dear! You’d think the government would be more considerate, but no. I mean, I like to keep things sorted,  yes , but I don’t need people tellin’ me what to do in My own house. I’ve already thrown out the plastic bottles this week! I ain’t like the kids now, pickin’ every single bit of litter to recycle it for a bounty.      Bucks ain’t much these days, Hattie. A few pennies for a bag of bottles, even if it is environmentally sound. Good for the planet, I suppose—but do tell, have you used your Sat Nav up near that remote village land? I’ve still got grief with mine, it only works in Norfolk…      Oh, I got one from my granddaughter—says it’s newfangled, and smarter than the other one. I’ve tried routing fer my sister in Norfolk and it always seems to work. Last time, I even made it to the old manor at Spixworth without gettin’ lost once.      That’s a relief! I got stuck in marshland and a hill once—had to  literally  follow a farmer in about five inches of mud to the nearest road.      Not surprised. We civil engineers thought about roads that go that way back in the day, but the council cut the funding, ‘cos they said it’d be cheaper to let the lanes remain. And now we suffer the consequences.      At least someone knows how to whinge properly. We should talk about  buying property again . I read somewhere that with inheritance tax keepin’ on creepin’ up, it’s far easier to get something transferred with a pension plan.      I think it was that chap on the telly, made a dent in the estate,  didn’t he ? Time to get the Financial Times out and see how much planning I can manage before this whole tax mess lands on those of us never had a job.      ‘Tis a right pickle, innit?

Rather than money, I often say to the children at school that happiness is more about the little things in life... Like rhymes, or having a comfortable home, or even just a warm hug. Then what about Daddy? He’s always being money money money, but he says   LJL  , and we all do it. So does that make him happy?      Hmm. Going by that, then yes. But it’s a bit strange, because the older I get, the more I wonder if having money will make us really happy. I remember when your father used to say he just wanted to provide a better life for us. Well, if that’s true, then I suppose being a teacher, a mother, and living in this beautiful little house isn’t too bad. After all, happiness might just be a few rhymes, a couple of little hands on your shoulder, and a   LJL   echoing in the living room.

So we'd focus on schools to start, then rally up some interest online—YouTube maybe.

Rather lovely day today, isn't it? That sun gracin’ the garden just made it real cheery... got the seats out agin. I’m more than a bit proud of that lil’ table I built meself. Not quite up to the quality of what you lot get now in them shops, but eeny bit more personal, don’t you think?      Oh, yes, dear. A personal touch always adds to the charm. I rememb’er your hands used to be firm and sure as a craftsman's, even when you weren't working properly, but still, you gave it a good go. That table does look lovely. I reckon it'd suit real nicely with sommat on it like that Myntia vase I’ve got. Fun wee bursts of blue and white, ain't they?      I think it's amazing how your table connects with storytelling, Dad. The character of it—like it has this lived-in quality... I was thinking about narrative art today in my lecture, how some pieces tell you a story even without images. Your work, like this table, tell you a story too, don’t they?      Indeed. Narrative art is a real treat when it's subtle. It's not just about stating it in your face. You want the observer to find meaning in what they see, and sometimes it's the memories attached to the object that do the talking. It's something you can’t quite teach in lectures, but it's important they learn to look deeper.      Well, my stories are mostly just bits and bobs of what I had—bits of wood, nails I found here an’ there. I had to improvise most o' the time. Not like now where you can just buy it all ready to go. But th’ effort you put in leaves its mark.      And the mark leaves something to remember. That’s why I took to childminding in my time. Parents would bring all sorts o’ bits an’ bobs, and I used to knit wee tales for the kids based on what they brought in. Made them feel as though they were part of the story.      That’s such an interesting perspective, Mummy. You’re teaching by incorporating imagination, which is really powerful. In my lectures, I sometimes talk about using real-life experiences as material for creative pieces. It adds a sense of authenticity.      And it’s authenticity that resonates.

Rather annoying isn't it, how even simple things like having a decent coffee or internet in the morning takes like... ages to sort out sometimes. You'd think more people would just take a bit of time to think first, rather than reacting to things straight away like it's a competition.      Yeah, well I suppose that's where the difference between common sense and intelligence comes in. You can have a PhD in quantum mechanics but still not know when to stub out a cigarette inside, or how not to spill a coffee on a nice pair of shoes. I once met someone called a "quant" bloke – brilliant with numbers but wore a scarf inside out because he thought it looked different the other way round!      My God, I’d probably have thrown my hands up in despair and told him to look at the floor. But anyway, I think it's funny how even with all the options we have now – mobile breakfasts, laptops, tablets – people are still... I don’t know, slower at some things. Maybe they’re indulging in vices too much? I see far more people smoking and drinking coffee, or both, than ever before.      You’re probably right. I think for some people, routine is their comfort zone. Smoking, alcohol, scrolling through their phone – it's all just background noise to prevent thinking too hard. I mean, even when we are at home, do we not find ourselves reaching for something to do rather than just being present? It's strange.      Oh yes, and I’ve often read articles saying that multitasking is a myth. But nobody ever listens to reason. Or wants to pause and look at something – like analysing people, or even their own habits. I mean, I sometimes wonder if the problem is different cultures... or just different ideas of what “progress” is. For instance, I was reading something the other day about how some cultures, like Scandinavian ones, have such rigid equality between men and women – that even at mealtimes it's a democratic discussion about whose turn it is to do what!      Ha! Like queens and commoners being asked politely whether they fancy the lunches of a king or common folk. Now, I don’t know if that’s something I’d want to live with personally, because go on then I might well be stuck heating up a saucepan for six while someone else is out living it up.

Rather than going out and taking a walk in the park, do you both know what we did today? We had a trip out to a farm. I’m so glad I agreed to do it after work, because it turned out to be quite fun. Look at the children! They wouldn't stop talking about the pigs and chickens the whole way home. Did one of the lambs sit on you, Sophie? Or was it a goat?      It was a lamb, Miss Sarah. The lamb was wobbly and soft and fell into the hay. It hit me in the tummy.      I fed a pig lettuce! It made a silly noise, like the squeaky hippo we have in the DVD My turkey friend didn’t fly away. I left it a crumb! I made it my friend, Miss Sarah, and I think it turned into a horse!      Oh, Liam, it was a pig, not a horse! Horses are big and live in stables, remember? You saw them too. But the farm was a lovely size for you both. I do think, though, we might need to take special food in next time.      It wasn’t my fault we had to feed the duck crumpets! Well, it got messy. Any plans to make a proper dinner, or will we be scraping the bin for ‘leftovers’?      I did really well at school today. Teacher said I told the story all by myself. I even showed them my little pig drawing!      Oh that’s great, Sophie! What about you, Liam? Any big stories to tell from today?      I did a drawing too. Mine was a dragon with goos on it. The dragon is friendly and lives on the farm.      How lovely. I think you might need to show your drawings to your dad when he gets in. Maybe we can frame them and put them above the DVD player?      Do we have more dolls from the farm?

Rather lovely to be out here today, isn't it? The countryside looks particularly idyllic with that light mist over the hills.      Yes, I can't say I've ever seen a more peaceful place. Norfolk really has a magic to it—very different from the buzz of London.      Definitely. I remember when I was younger and we'd come up here every summer with my parents. A lot has stayed the same in this part of the country; it gives you a sense of continuity, you know?      Funny you say that, because the villages we passed on the way here seem like they've barely changed. I love that sense of time standing still. You can almost imagine thatched-roof cottages living in the same ways for centuries.      I think what makes it so special is the slow pace of life. It's a far cry from our daily routines. As lecturers, we’re used to ticking off assignments and reading lists. Out here, it's just us, the wind, and the occasional sheep!      Ah yes, the sheep—there's something very English about them! You don’t quite see their equivalents back in the city, where everything is in such a rush. Over there, time is money; here, it's tea and tales.      I think it's important to step back into a setting like this every now and then. It’s grounding. Particularly useful for someone like me who spends most of their time buried in theory and textbooks.      And it helps to reignite creativity. Some of my best ideas have come to me while walking these kinds of quiet trails. I was actually reading about village enclosures about an hour ago—can you believe it's such a different world out here from the 20th century projects of enclosures?      Absolutely, it's like the rural landscape here has made itself into a living museum. The hills, the hedgerows, even the minimal signage—it's all part of the charm.      I always find it ironic that such a beautiful place is also academically rich. Between your historical studies and my English literature research, we could almost write an interdisciplinary paper together after a day like this.      Mm, that's not a bad idea. Maybe one day—on condition we don’t exhaust our stroll with too much academic jargon.      Deal! But only as long as we keep the conversation as natural as those villages, never too artificial.

Rather than going out tonight, eh? You know what, I’ve bin thinkin’ ‘bout that new James Bond film. ‘ave you seen the trailer yet?      I have! It looks proper good. Chased by the bad guys through a dodgy-looking city, classic Bond. I saw the preview at the weekend while I was down at the cinema.      Aye yeah, I dinnae get that far. I just think he’s got skills people want 'round here.      So, back to films—Do you think this new Bond will be the best one in years or yet another let down like Spectre? This one, though… I reckon they’ve got a cracking cast, and the plot lines look ambitious.      Objectively, I think so, yeah. But I still can’t get over the fact that casting that actress was like choosing someone for the cool eyebrows rather than the real acting chops.

Rather lovely to be out here today, isn't it? The spring has been so kind with colour in the fields.      Yes, it's perfect weather for a walk. I saw a bunch of hawthorn flowers by the hedgerows as we came in. It's like the countryside is beginning to bloom anew.      Definitely. There's something so calming about being surrounded by greenery. It’s a far cry from the urban setting, where you're seeing blocks rather than blossoms.      I take it back then — when football season starts, I'd rather fetch chips from the corner shop than go to a match. All those crowds, no vistas!      My lectures on economic theories are more calming than a packed stadium, I can assure you. I was just explaining to a class today about the structure of local agriculture and cash crops — how even something as mundane as potatoes can tie into global economics.      And yet, I'm the one who hides behind novels to avoid intellectual debates about trade deficits. I lectured on language acquisition today, oddly enough—there's a link between crop impacts and linguistic shifts in rural communities.      That's interesting — there probably is. Climate change, migration patterns, all of these influence languages. I remember doing research on how evolving economic strategies in areas dependent on farming affected language use. More international trade often meant more multilingual exposure.      You're not wrong. It’s kind of poetic that the people in this part of Norfolk speak a dialect rooted in old English but are now farming with techniques from all over the world. It’s a blend of tradition and trade all woven into daily life.      I agree. The market up North in Manchester buys them, so that local economy has kind of shifted toward niche exports.      Sounds like it's a balancing act. I mean, I tried growing herbs on my balcony once. Weeds sprouted faster than I expected!      Ha! You tried and failed with your botany, but let’s not forget you still managed to pass your course on the fundamentals of semantics. Though I daresay if you'd had to grow metaphors instead of herbs, you’d have had a green thumb.      Okay, fair. But at least I can still quote obscure poets and misinterpret them in hours of earnest conversation with you, which to me is the same as understanding agriculture.

Although the other day, I saw what must have been a fox circling the outside.

Rather annoying I heard from my cousin, innit? Seems like that tax firm her nan uses got in a spot of trouble for launderin’ moolah. Blows me mind what folk would do for a buck. If you can’t explain where the money came from, it’s up for grabs to the system, ‘cos they look fer stuff that’s irregular. And if you’ve got kids, teach ’em early. My youngest asked me once why I kept accurate accounts for little bills, and I told him because you never know when Auntie Websites is gonna start lookin’ a little closer at your doings.      Genuinely, teaching the next gen the importance of accountability goin’ on early is key. It’s not so much about money as about how you treat it. It could go either way — prosperity or a proper slap with a fine.      So, like, we’d better start with the paperwork even for little things now?

Well, whatever path you take, good luck with it. Family-wise, the big news is the baby’s due next month. Still trying to decide on names but we’ve got a shortlist goin’. You two fancy having a guess?      We? Finally, you’re involving us in the name game then?      Oh come on, I can't help but want to suggest a few!

Rather annoying when the vending machine eats your penny, isn't it? I was just trying to get a sandwich... got nothing out, just a penny lighter and more grumpy!      Aw, I've been there. Honestly, I’m starting to wonder if the vending machine is one of those noble experiments from the 1960s that was doomed to failure from the off—like some misplaced piece of the ICL mainframe land.      It’s not just the machines though. The production schedule here is practically rhythm and blues. You never know when the copy will come in, when it will go, and whether the cover image is finalised. Someone tries to print “Page 42” and then realises the typo comes from three drafts ago.      Honestly, I think my coping strategy is just to oddly cosplay a production editor and ignore the chaos. Not that I’d drink it if it  didn’t , but... at least it doesn’t keep your lone penny hostage. Although, once it gave me 60p change for something that cost 50p. Honestly, every time I come down here, I’m reminded of one of those posters from the printing house that says “Do it right, or do it again.”      I can live with that motto. I think I'm going to start carrying even more sandwiches from now on.

Postdated cheques, signatures on the documents, dates for collections—no bloomin’ mistakes. Last time we planned a charity run, I lost me sums and we ended up out o’pocket by fifty quid.

It's what you make of your surroundings that counts. I've always felt it's important for both children and adults.      Definitely. Although I must say, when I'm at my desk all day, I do sometimes miss the outdoors. I tried gardening once, but I think the plants just rebelled against me. I suppose we all find our own escapes, don’t we?      Indeed. Whether it's writing, carpentry, transcribing, or managing people—each person has their way of contributing and coping.      A fitting summary from a former headmistress.

Rather than going out, I thought we could spend the day together. Maybe start with breakfast in bed? We could all make a card or something. Rather annoying to be honest. I’d rather be hanging out with you anyway.      Oh, come on! You're telling me you're more annoyed about missing a gym class than seeing me?      No, not annoyed, just— you know, things are getting busy. Got a timetable to sort out for the students today, and I haven't even looked at all the lectures next week yet. A lot of topics to cover in this semester, including language acquisition and semantics. It's interesting, though. We've been doing some research into how different languages influence thinking. Burgers and treacle sponges passed down through generations. And now we’re supposed to strip them of their voice just to fit some arbitrary academic frame?      Not to mention, we can’t ignore how language connects to identity. Family, culture, even your region. I took the students to visit a local library where they had archives of old manuscripts—documents written in the 1940s or so using real regional features.      I imagine they’d go mad if they could hear what your 20-something-year-old fluency feels like to you now.      Totally. But anyway, to get back on track, I’m planning to meet up with them this weekend.

Coffee to start with, though. Black and treble shot. All that caffeine, innit?      Aye, got you. Tea or coffee for me too. You ever been to that shop down the side of that park? The one with the pink door? Bits of the countryside whiffs in there, and the scones are positively  legend . Pipping hot, butter melting away goin' on your fingers if you don’t watch out.      Right, that’s the one. That bloke behind the counter always says “rightio luv” in that posh, un-understandable way. Properly gets under your skin after a while, innit?      Crickey! It's a proper vibe. Half the time I feel like I'm in another world.

Rather nippy today, ain't it? That wind off the fen sticks to yer bones, it does. I got me a cold brew on the go—always find I can take it hotter than most, mind yer.      No, I ken what you mean, dear. It was proper bright een window this morning, but once the sun ducked behind the clouds, it turned as grim as a wet Sunday. A shame, really—might have had a spot of gardening if it’d held up.      Gardening, bah! You're never outside when it's the least bit chilly. Get frozen to yer bones even inside if you don't take enough care.      That's like you sayin’ water's wet! The chill goes straight through you when you're this old, you know. But I’d say the worst of it is my knees again—goin’ ‘click, click, click’ if I step wrong. Reminds me of me mum when she was ever so.      Honestly, I don't know how you two endure it. I swear, if I had to choose between cold weather and Wi-Fi, I’d pick the Wi-Fi and hibernate. Honestly, my heating went out three times last week. I thought about just moving to Cornwall. At least it’s warm and sunny all the time, right?      Yeah, but don’t get me started on heating. I spent all last night wrapped in ten blankets, and the coffee machine someone gave me last Christmas— eep! —keeps turning itself off. I think it’s had it at this point. I swear the only thing that still works in my flat is the kettle and the Apple Watch. Everything else is a ticking time bomb.      электронику? Bah! That lot are all ‘blaggable’ and no substance. No, I ken the smell of ‘proper’ gear. My radio’s been going since ‘62 and it works better now than it did then. Not like them newfangled things you gents carry ‘bout in yer pockets, eh?      Ah, yes, but we do miss out on the odd thing if we don’t use it, don’t we? My granddaughter showed me how to set goin’ on that thing about sending messages through the sky. Still, I reckon it’s easier just to pop down the road and say it face to face.      Honestly, it's been ages since I’ve seen my parents just pop by for a chat.

Okay, I just wanted to say congratulations again to both of you. I know it's been a week already, but I’m still so starry-eyed from your joint engagement announcement. I've been over this a thousand times in my head, and honestly, I can't believe it.      Thanks, Steph. I  am  still a bit stunned myself. It was actually quite spontaneous. We were on a day trip to York and just got so caught up in the moment. Chris proposed right there by the Minster. We've been planning the wedding for months now, though, so the nerves are starting to kick in.      Oh, no pressure, then! I'm still waiting for "the one," but you know, I’ve met enough eccentric characters recently to last me a lifetime. I dated this guy last month who thought I was a vegan because I had an herbal tea at a café — it honestly doesn’t bear repeating.      Haha, Jo, that’s gold. I remember that guy, didn’t he say he was into survival skills and built a "treehouse" out of lollipop sticks in his tiny flat?      Exactly! I didn’t even live with him, and I was already watching for emergency supplies. Honestly, when are we going to meet someone who just…  gets it ?      Oh, I totally hear you. It’s so hard when you have high standards and then you’re hit with that whole, "well, what someone  should  be versus what they actually are" thing. But for now, at least, you still get to have your sisters and your friends being excitingly chaotic.      Speaking of friends, about this dinner Steve and I mentioned you girls to — the one at this Italian place downtown — what time does everyone want to meet up on Friday? I'll send a reminder email.      That’d be great, Geo. Friday will be perfect. I just have to wrap a project by Thursday. And Jo can come with me to pick out my little black dress!       Oh , as if I’d want to do that alone. I’ve told my younger cousins I’m going shopping with you and Jo, so they're expecting a report with lots of goings-on on the way home.      Well, I just hope the Italian restaurant lives up to the box art. If it’s one of those places with "Steak Tivoli" and "Vodka Lasagna," I’m bringing a belly dancer just to contrast.

Rather annoying this newfit laptops an’ all. I tried to get onto one of them photo albums m’grandson showed me, but it went all crashy and I lost a few pictures of the ponies. I don’t rightly know why they have to make things so complicated.      Oh, don’t worry, dear. It’s the same with me if I try to use them fancy phones. I’ve only got a basic one, so I just ring up Miss Alice or Miss Sadie, who live round the corner, and we chat. But what ponies were them? Do you still have the old one, Horsey?      That’s Princess to him, only now she’s in a bit of a field near Wymondham. The vet says she’s well, but I miss her company. Still, I’ve got the granddaughter round today—she brought her two young ones to play. I don’t know if I’ve mentioned them before.      Yes, the ones in that little green tractor costume for the village fete? I remember seeing that—charming.      That’s them! I don’t rightly know where they find their energy. It’s like having a couple of ponies on mini-speed.      Tell me about it—he does remind me of my days as a childminder. You’d think I had a couple of arsonists and a war vet under one roof! Bless ‘em, they keep you on your toes, though.      This is just the time of day I like. Cuppa in hand, and a bit of peace between the children’s energy bursts.      I do try to get out at this time to play bridge, but it’s been hard this last few months with the lack of funding at the school. We barely have the resources to keep up with the basics. My wife’s been cutting back on things too. Supermarkets are all cut-price and offers, but the prices are still high.      That’s how it is with me. We get by, but not much beyond. I used to grow a few vegetables back in the big garden—now I’m lucky if I can water them a couple of times a week.      It’s the same for me. I had a real ramshackle garden full of herbs and flowers when I was active, but now it’s more of a jungle. The cats have made a nest in the laurel hedge!

Rather lovely to sit down and have a chat, Christopher. Life’s been a bit full-on with work and all, and I haven’t had the chance to pop down properly in a few weeks. How are you holding up?      Oh, I’ve been very well, dear. Living in retirement on a nice little passive income has its perks, I must say. Of course, as self-employed most of my life, I never actually got the best from the social security system, but I’ve managed.      You always were the savvy one when it came to running your business. I remember you used to talk about it even back when I was a teenager, visiting the house for family dinners. It's amazing how your instincts paid off for you.      Thank you! I had good instincts yes, but mostly I was lucky in the world of competitors. It was a far harder sell back then than when you're in your late thirties with a teaching contract like yourself. I hear the school awards quite a few to young teachers now.      That’s true. I do feel very lucky to have this consistent work. I mean, with the pandemic, it wasn’t all rainbows and butterflies, but there was something to be said for working from home then. I got so much done – lesson plans, new curriculum ideas, and actually had time to rediscover my old sketchbook hobby.      Silly of me to forget you were artistic back in the day. Our youngest niece said she found your landscapes in the attic a few years ago – thought they were a bit out of place, but now she says wants to frame one!      That’s so sweet of her. I did quite a few back in Hitchin, when the sun would slip through the thicket on the Radipole fields. Not that I’d ever call it a classic masterpiece, to be honest.      Well, modesty passed you by with that one. Speaking of landscapes – did you get to see those hills in North Wales as you had planned?      Yes, over the June bank holiday. Took the train with a few students and their parents to do a weekend tour. My students adored it—loved the mountains and the castles even more than I thought they would! It's always nice to give them a taste of something different.      That sounds splendid. I might try to do a day trip to Cannock Chase to breathe in a bit of fresh air myself—there's always that new walking path I've been meaning to get over to.

So did you go out for dinner on Valentine's or what? I was like seriously cringing through that first date with Adam at some overpriced dining place off Edgware Road. The waiter thought we were on our first date and kept hitting us up with questions—  what a vibe  .      Hah, yeah, I got the 'Valentine's special' vibe as well. I went with my sister though, to this cute little Italian place in Leicester. Oh my gosh, it was like something out of a film. Flickering candles, red roses, the lot. But the meatballs were so dry, even my sister made a face. Still, the décor made it worthwhile.      Aww, bless your sister. I left Adam halfway through the main course because I couldn’t take his constant pick-up lines anymore. Honestly? Half the evening I was just checking my phone to see if my Thai takeaway had been delayed again. Not a romantic in me at all, you know?      You always say the wrong thing, don’t you? I mean, it’s not a crime to be awkward on dates. I remember when your uncle tried to impress my mom last year, he said "I read a brilliant article on... trotters," then just got really quiet. Ha – Mate, I laughed so long, I think I cracked a rib.      It was a   medical condition  , for crying out loud. You don’t talk about trotters at dinner. Who does that? But anyway, I ended my evening with popcorn and a movie. I watched  Barbie  again—repeat offender, I know. Still better than trying to make awkward small talk.      I respect the dedication. I binged  Exorcist: Believer  and  Wait Until Dark  because that was the theme I set for myself— scary movies only . But I got so scared I ended up screaming in the sofa. My cat ran away for a solid ten minutes.      Okay, that’s terrifyingly British. I could see the cat hearing you and just being like  “Oh here comes the weird shouting again.”  At least the chocolate melted fairly. My takeaway bag was delivering something around Thai basil or lemongrass or whatever that is on the menu if you don’t read properly.      Oh no, I genuinely like Thai box food—should I be your takeaway buddy? We could have a monthly takeaway night. Thai on one week, Chinese on the next?      Only if we can have soundtracks from romantic comedies and a large bag of M&Ms.

Rather annoying isn't it? The amount of people who support policies that they know nothing about. I mean, I got to pick some really flavourful chicken noodles, and I can already tell you're over-thinking your buckwheat ramen.      Buckwheat is healthier, Sue. Got to watch the carbon footprint of my diet as well as the policies I write about. It’s not just a choice—it's a stance. Speaking of which, I got to send in that article on housing in London by tomorrow. Know anything about the council house conversions going up in your neck of the woods?      Oh yeah,  those  buildings. Looked at the designs before they went to planning. It’s a mix of affordable and high-end properties. The problem is, by the time the affordable units are even finished, the high-end ones sell out. It feels like it’s just delaying the inevitable.      So typical. They tick the boxes, but the real issue remains. There’s no serious reform, just window dressing. I read a report last week—something like 80% of new builds in inner London are sold off or rented out as second homes. And the real housing crisis is in the suburbs and outer municipal areas, not where the media look.      Exactly. And the political class still promotes that narrative about London as broken. Meanwhile, people in places like Watford are getting pushed out too. There’s a real divide in how they label 'unaffordable' and who actually gets to live in these places. Racist undertones definitely there—look at the housing policies in the northeast versus the West Midlands. Marginalised communities are always the last to be considered.      Don’t even get me started. I had to interview a tenant in Tower Hamlets last week. She barely spoke English, but managed to tell me that the rent company had tried to repossess her flat after one missed payment. The system’s engineered to disadvantage people who already have less. Capitalism with a veneer of compassion.      Ugh. I sometimes wonder if we’re even trying to fix the problem or just survive within the system. My recent project—it’s a housing block for artists and students—which the council called ‘an experimental model’. But it’s still subject to market rents. Gave me a head ache trying to include green spaces in a 999-unit zip code.      Maybe we’re fighting a losing battle against the system, but at least we can contribute to the conversation.

Rather annoying to be honest, eh? You know, me going back to work next week and Emily having to start nursery full time. I've been up half the night worrying about how she's going to cope with it all.      Look, Mums! You'll both be fine. Emily’s een beginning to wean, so that’s one less thing to worry about. And as for me? I’ve been working from home this past term so this is a bit of a stretch seeing you two in action like this. We’ve been through the nursery options, the routines, everything's sorted. She won’t miss you, honest! Or won’t show it anyway, as babies are real divas!      My word, you say that like you've got experience, young lady! I’m the one who remembers your first day and how you screamed the house down for an entire hour while I tried to leave for breakfast, and then turned up at the front gate after I’d driven a mile, didn’t I!?      Well, I was three, and still have a strong memory of it, yes! But this is not the 1990s. Emily is going into a real, proper, professional nursery. The others are all getting used to it, from what I’ve seen at the open days. Plus, I’m still living at home, and I’ve said I’ll pick her up and check in through the day if possible. And we’ve already booked the childcare places for any days someone has to work late!      That is true. I had a word with my boss, and he's been helpful as hell being flexible. Can’t promise I won't end up early most mornings, just in case. I don’t want to leave her blinking at the ceiling looking for a familiar face and not finding it. Not that I’d blink it out if she turned up to the office, like you did once when you were in high school.      Oh, I was bloody adorable! Pink cardigan, smiling like a little madam. We had to rush her out of the boardroom after Jake from finance asked 'Is that the receptionist? Cos I do love a Manchester lassya.'      Oh, go on then! But enough about that. If we're at full capacity at work and in nursery, what's the plan for holidays? You know what your dad was like with all the planning.

Rather annoying day today, really. I had to give a statement to the police for the broken window in the kitchen. Just couldn't work out who was responsible, and I ended up talking for nearly an hour! It is such a £ugh.      That does sound like a drag. I had eenough stress at work myself. Made a few calls for fund-raising today, and one of the guys I’ve been working with flatly refused to support us again. No idea why, but it put a dampener on the whole day. Still, what can you do?      Honestly, I just want to avoid even thinking about work. I had to handle the EE phone bill complaints again at the store today. One customer was convinced they’d been double-billed, and I spent ages on the phone trying to get it sorted. I think I turned six shades of red by the time we eventually got it fixed. Not sure if it was me or them!      Blooming typical. I had a stressful day ordering equipment for the office and the guy at the supplier kept missing calls and getting things mixed up. Eventually I ended up having to put two different orders in as separate shipments. Honestly, sometimes you wonder why we even bother trying to manage people.      Tell me about it. My Mate Laura stopped by the house earlier and mentioned that her Hay-off today was the cheapest her flat had ever been. I can’t help feeling I’m missing out on something.      Oh someone said there was a supermarket deal on Hay-off this week. Maybe we can grab a few with us when we do some shopping tomorrow?      That sounds like a plan. I’ve been trying to cut down on takeaways a bit, so having some decent home meals this week would be a nice idea. Speaking of which, are we still up for the park on Thursday? I fancied getting some fresh air before the weekend.      Yeah, that works for me. I need to get out of the office once in a while. I’ve been holed up all week dealing with reports and end-of-term finances. The fresh air would do me a world of good.      Me too! I was thinking of trying that new café on the corner as go-to-place on Friday. I’ve heard good things about their brunch.

Rather annoying that the TV’s still not working, isn’t it? I was just trying to catch up on that  Spartacus  show you told me about. I’ve only watched the first few episodes so far, but I’m quite into it.      Oh, you haven’t finished it yet? That’s a shame—it’s got some ridiculous drama and some really good Roman history thrown in for good measure. A lot of it’s fictional, obviously, but it gave me a new appreciation for, you know, the whole 'bread and circuses' thing.      Yeah, I was just reading about that in one of my books. I’m learning about the Roman Republic now, and it's wild how the empire was built on such shaky foundations. All the political infighting! I’m teaching my students about it next week and I think I'll show a clip or two from  Spartacus  for breakfast, no doubt. I've been making hummus for lunch ever since my trip to the Middle East a few years back. I bring home a mortar and pestle from that tour shop I visited.      Oh, really? I never thought about using one of those. I’ve just got my fancy electric blender. Still—it always messes up the texture, if you ask me. You can’t really get that right consistency with a machine. Anyway, speaking of texture, I’ve been trying out new ways to spruce up my herbal teas. I’ve got this mix of dried mint from Cyprus someone gave me and a few spices from a local market. It smells amazing.      Cyprus, is it? That must have been a cool trip. I’ve always wanted to go there because of the blend of cultures. Do you speak any Greek from your time there?      A bit—he fails at it. Not that I mind. I prefer the English-Cypriot slang. Makes for some good jokes. Speaking of which, did I tell you that I bought me a souvenir of a small bag of roasted chickpeas I tried there? It reminds me of the street food there. Those little yellow nuts are delicious, especially when sprinkled on homemade bread.      Chickpeas are brilliant for veggie dishes. I’ve been experimenting with some recipes from China lately too—they use them in stir-fries. Just don’t go into the tropics without some malaria pills. I’ve got some in my medicine box from when I taught in Kenya.

So did you get an A on the English test? I swear mine came out like cr p. The question about  Pride and Prejudice  nearly gave me a heart attack.      Nah, I got a B+… which I kind of expected. I didn’t revise much. But I saw the teacher  this morning  with the papers and I reckon overall the class did… not great. A few A grades, but mostly B’s and C’s.      Honestly, who needs to do English tests anyway? I’d rather be in art or French or the wind band. Did you hear we’ve got a new clarinet player for the school orchestra?      Yeah! Her name’s Liza, I think. She’s got this super cool bottle-green blazer and plays the most epic duets. I wish I played an instrument—my mom was  so  strict about piano when I was younger. I hated it. Honestly, I only ever sat through the lessons to avoid being grounded.      Ugh, why do parents always assume we need to do things they didn’t get to do? My brother plays the trumpet, and he’s still trying to get me on board. Imagine having to force yourself to blow into something rhythmically when all you want is to be – I don’t know – somewhere with paint, or just  chill ?      I know what you mean. I’d much rather be in the art room, even if it feels like the teacher just watches Strictly while we paint. Last time, she came in at the end and said, “Right, now you need to be ‘more imaginative’,” but she didn’t even make it sound about  us . It felt like she just watched the clock pass by.      True. Speaking of, shall we meet up after school to do the English homework together? I just found out that the text response is about speeches, and I have  zero  idea where to start. My brain is fried after pottery.      Yeah, I’ll be free. Meet at the bench near the bus stop at 4:15? I brought chocolate from my nan today, and let’s be real, that’s a bonus.      Deal. Oh, on another note, have you noticed how Charlie from French class is just… smiling at us  everything  he looks our way? It’s a bit weird, isn’t it?      Yeah, it is. And I think he even said, “You two laugh very nicely,” in French yesterday.

Rather a cold day for a café, innit? But I’d say it’s worth it for a nice cup of tea and some proper cake. Look at that view over yonder by the window, though! There’s a building site up near the hospital, I bet you anything they'll be moving more people out een a few days’ time. Heard one of the nurses saying the new wing's all digital now — aye, computers in every room! Got me thinking about education, mind you. The kids nowadays, pulling off fancy things with their devices, me bleedin’ thumbs aren't quite up to it.      Nan, you  promised  me a slice of Victoria sponge before you went on about hospitals and My turkey toast is getting cold! Besides, you’re a qualified teacher! I’m sure you can handle a phone, and I’ll teach you how. Or you can watch videos on YouTube — better than breakfast, innit? I just found out there’s videos on how to make cakes, play games, even code, even if you're not a proper student like me.      Aye luv, I’ve had better years for keeping up with your fancy words and gadgets. And for goodness’ sake, pass me that cup, will yer? I’m sure it’s “relevant” or some such. But while I’m at it, I heard tell there’s a trip planned somethin’ to do wi’ the north of Scotland. Dunno what the hills are called up there, but someone said castles and landscapes. If you’re interested, they might need someone to chaperone the kids.      Oh come on, Barbara, don’t make your granddaughter feel excluded because your Apple tablet is misbehaving! And you can bring your old self along on the trip — I’ve already said I’ll go. Not that I need convincing, mind. A bit of air, a bit of culture, and certainly no less than five different types of tea on the menu. I’ve done these sorts of things before, once I could afford it. Not that I need your help anymore, Anna, but I’ll admit, a young’un knows their way round a booking site better than the likes of us.      Right, Anna, you’ll be the one goin’ on ahead and plannin’ it all. While I sit here in the café, figuring out why the box of granola went up a quid since last week.

Rather annoying driving up from London today. The sat nav decided to glue the car in the middle of nowhere. I got turned around at least four times before I found this road!      You probably got thrown off course by one of the “Roundabouts of Doom" near Ely. They’re eeny weeny, and if you blink you miss the exit. I still get confused every time I go through that area.      I don’t get why you don’t just go the old fashioned way! Put a map on the table when you're in, get the jigsaw out too... like we did when we couldn’t afford a sat nav!      Ha, ha, well My turkey still cost me fifty quid though. I dropped it on the floor on the way in, and it landed in the hallway! Kicking myself for thinking I was being clever and carrying it upstairs.      That’s not a kitchen in there at all, you know. You have no floor space, no stove—and I mean none. I don’t know how you do any of your Christmas meals in that place!      I’ve done it for twenty-odd Christmases though. It takes longer, that’s all. Be grateful I bothered. Though I must say it looked better before I almost dropped it.      Well, it’s not that big a deal! You know what I blame for everything? Allergies and genes. I get sleepy in the car and dropped my sister off once a mile down the motorway.      I blame the lack of sugar being poured into my tea all week. My operation last month didn’t do wonders for my blood sugar control! I can barely keep my eyelids up.      Going under the knife is barely a week behind me too, so I entirely relate. But I’m cutting back on the sugar for good. I’ve seen what health looks like on the outside these days. I think it’s partly genes but mostly how people eat. I could see the bell curve as soon as I walked into a hospital.      Well, I’ve got enough fat going on that you could use me as a soppy! But hey, I go to the gym most days if you don’t count walking around the loos!      Darce, you might be a mechanic, your legs might be made of steel, but I’ve seen how you eat after work!

Rather annoyingly, I've got to update the Moodle course for my computer software class this week. The university is pushing for a more interactive format. I’m dreading it, honestly.      Why is it so bad? I thought the technical side of things was sorted. Is it more about writing and explaining the new content?      Exactly. It's not the platform that's the issue—it’s the content I have to put in. I’m teaching a new module on Excel Power Query, and it’s one of those things where the concepts are quite abstract when you don't see a direct application.      I can imagine. I remember learning about the different Python libraries when we were training for that MyUni course. You had to get to the point where you could visualise the problem the library would solve, or it just felt like fluff.      Yeah, very similar. I'm thinking of putting up step-by-step mini-videos in each week's topic. That way students can watch, follow along, and get a feel for the processes directly in the browser.      That’s a good idea. I used pre-recorded lectures to teach my human-computer interaction class last semester, and they worked surprisingly well. But it does take a lot longer to prepare than just doing it in-person.      True. I'm also considering a new set of tests that check for understanding at the end of each video—short quizzes that are automatically graded. Moodle can handle that, right?      Oh, absolutely. I did that when teaching the database systems module. Just make sure the questions don’t look obvious otherwise they’ll Google the answers and skip the whole thing about trying to learn independently.      Ha! Another thing to worry about. I might even add optional “recommended resources” below the topics—like short articles or videos that explain tricky parts in simpler terms. If they look at them, they’ll probably get the most out of the class.      That could help a lot. I remember one of your past students said your materials were the only thing they actually looked at besides the lunches we packed.      That's going back far! Okay, serious now. This course setup is going to set the tone for the entire term if we don’t get it right.      It really will. And it's not just about getting the content right—it’s about how you guide the students to build their own understanding from it.

Rather annoying jetlag, isn't it? I mean, I've only had an hour or two in bed... What time did you manage to go to sleep last night?      Around midnight, I think. Not quite enough to feel like I’ve caught up properly. But it was nice that the baby finally went to sleep around then. I was wondering if he might actually sleep all night this time.      Honestly, so was I. He was so settled, bless him, and you were snoring away before the night was out. Didn’t even want to wake you. You looked... peaceful.      Haha, thanks. What time are we thinking of leaving for that play at the arts centre? I’m still not sure how long this tiredness will last – I’m not normally one for restlessness in the evening, but tonight feels like it could’ve been 3 AM when I finally closed my eyes.      Oh don’t worry, the play doesn’t start until 7:30, and once we get going, I think the excitement will see us through. I’ve got the tickets in the kitchen drawer by the way. Did I tell you, it's one of those local production shows? You remember, the one from the university arts department?      Ah, yes, that one’s been huge in the community. The reviews were brilliant. And the venue’s not too far from the house either. What do you think, just walk there? It’s a summer evening and the weather's quite nice for once.      That sounds perfect. I can’t be driving in this state. I’m still feeling light-headed most of the time. I think I’ll manage a quick lie-down after we feed the baby. I just need to make sure he doesn’t try and take me with him when he wakes up to have his bottle.      Don’t worry, I’ll take care of him. You need your rest. And as for the play, I reckon you’ll be fine – just stick to water and fresh air. You always say you’re not affected by jetlag, but honestly, I’ve seen enough of you over the last few days to know you're feeling it.      You make it sound like I’m some sort of fragile thing! Still, I’m really looking forward to the play, particularly the choreography. It was one of the highlights in the preview they showed us in the newsletter.

Rather annoying to be honest. My wife’s sorting it, but everything’s tied up in red tape. We’d got the house checked out ages ago, but the mortgage people are dragging their feet. It’s a mad time in the housing market.      Yeah, I can imagine. My brother’s just beginning the visa process from Iraq. It took bloody   forever   just to get his papers sorted. The UK authorities love playing games with the best of us, don’t they? Especially when it comes to someone with a complex nationality or background like us.      Definitely. I mean, I can’t even imagine what it’s like for people from, say, the Middle East. Still, I managed to get Myra and me over years ago. Fun times. Well, back then, the red tape was manageable. But now, I think the world’s just got tighter rules for everyone.      I heard that Wahabi activists in some parts are inflaming tensions. People’s lives are getting caught in political crossfires, you know? I mean, I deal directly with this stuff as an interpreter, and it’s brutal. My cousin got stuck in Libya because of one of those conflicts and only made it out last year.      That’s awful. Have you got family still over there –?      No, none that stay in problematic areas. Most moved out years ago after that whole thing with the oil politics. I blame the greedy oil companies for a lot of it. Who starts a war for a bucket of oil? You're missing the point— tablet go bad . I remember it from my parents’ house.      I’ll remember that next time. Rather annoyingly, I haven't got anything to wear for tomorrow’s lesson.      Oh... What's the lesson?      Is it football again?      It is.      That's boring. That's right.      What time are they visiting?      They're flying in on the 3 o’clock plane to Heathrow and coming straight here over Zoom.      Wow that's so cool!      We could do karaoke next week.      That could be very good. I'd be up for that.      Yeah me too.      I think you're on the right wave of excitement. With that kind of energy, the whole school will be engaged.      I can show them how to make origami with your Japanese pen friends.      That will be great. Let's settle for that.      I can show my pigeon how to do karaoke too.      I'm particularly glad about that. I've had a word with the pigeon.

Rather annoying, though, isn't it? That whole  "she’s into you on Facebook"  nonsense... Like, how exactly does someone determine that from a few likes?      Hilarious, yes. Right, I just got in from work. That shift dragged. My feet are killing me, and I couldn’t be arsed to cook. You fancy some more ready meal, luv?      Can we not have some popcorn instead? I bet it’ll be like the cinema if we watch the movie and stuff. I don’t wanna eat dinner again just yet.      Popcorn? Cloudy with a Chance of Meatballs  or  whatev .      Oooh yeah! That one’s good. I’ve seen it before. The one where the boy inventions the food rain and the world goes mad and sad in the world? It’s not Disney and not about spaghetti. It’s about the environment and capitalism and how people are greedy. My teacher at school said that movies always tell us things about the world. The mayor suppresses knowledge so that people can’t invent better stuff. Just like in the real world where people’s voices are kept down.

Rather annoying to be honest. I mean, I understand the need for tax revenue, but it's not like it's making our lives any better. I’m more than a bit fed up with the whole lot of them, really. Not to start a political fight, mind you — wouldn't dream of it in a place like this. But I’ll say one thing:   New Labour   had more style than they did substance.      Fair comment, John. I’ve never been a big fan of Blair’s either. Too much flash and not enough follow through. Didn’t even want to watch the general election coverage last week, honestly. Still, I’ll give him this: he knew how to win a football match in terms of popularity — no matter what side you were on.      I see what you mean, Tony, but for me, it turned into a mess with Iraq, you know? Made a tactical breakfast, no doubt about that. Like some football manager playing in his head and not the real game. No team, no trust. All the political talk, and still we were left out in the cold, kicking stones, if you get the metaphor.      Metaphor and all, but let me tell you: I was behind the wheel during it all, from the “new beginnings” – Mate, I drove past enough people in Liverpool waving union jacks like they were trying to dance with the sky. Some bloke even asked me to turn the radio on to BBC News and said, “This is our Premier League final. Just not the one with red and blue.” Hard not to laugh, but the kid at the red and white corner still got his match – just not the one he wanted.      Ah, I love that story, Tony. It's always the most unexpected places you hear the best political commentary. Not that I’d ever have guessed a cab driver in Liverpool would be a better analyst than the lot of them in Westminster. Although, personally, I’d prefer to see it in a library than on the back of a taxi, you know what I mean?      Libraries and taxis being the only places left where people still speak a little English with some honesty left in it. I’d be lying if I said I’m not a man of simple tastes. Football? I’ll take Liverpool FC over any political game.

Rather annoying to be honest. I’d rather be hanging out with you all anyway. How’s work been? I got a rather cryptic message about the BNC recordings on Linked In this morning      Honestly? Not bad. I was shaking on the plane.      Oh my goodness, I never knew! I mean, I sort of expected you to have been born with a professional air about you.      So what are the plans today? Are we going for a walk after this? Pugs! I need to see pugs today. They're about the cutest excuse for pets in the world.      Definitely pugs, then. And what your research is about. Rather annoying to be honest. I'm not used to anyone being that curious.      Oh c'mon Claire, she's just excited because your new one's a cover design she saw last week and thought was amazing. You do know the rest of the office picked up on it straight away too?      Ugh. It was either that design or something with crows on it, and I figured I should keep it professional. If I live that long.      Now, now. Let's not get too dramatic. All my interns are thoroughly professional.      Only when the Wi-Fi's up and running and they haven't had their breakfast.      Noted. More importantly – have you seen our building's progress?      A little. They've got gothic details on the outside now and some kind of monochrome kitchen.      Hopefully it's not too boxy inside – Tom might have some issues with the ceiling heights.      You think we're going to get away with fewer belly flops to the floor?      Only if we're very lucky Claire. You know my philosophy – if it's got character, it's got issues.      Right. And we haven't even discussed the new windows yet.      Yeah. Windows are another story.

Rather than share a text-based conversation, I request a more interactive or audio-based format to engage with the typ...      Oh, I see. I suppose a written conversation would work best for this inquiry. Let me process that...      Just provide the conversation based on the guidelines provided and we can simulate the rest.      My apologies—simulations are a bit beyond transcription alone, but I'll generate a natural, multi-turn dialogue instead. Imagine us sitting in my kitchen as we chat.      Right, so I thought I’d pop over for dinner. I’ve baked these rosemary and olive oil focaccia slices, still warm. You won’t believe the turkey curry I found at the local corner store. It’s ridiculous! I’m half convinced the manager threw it in for free after he asked how I spend my evenings now that the kids are off at university.      Haha, I’m not at all surprised. That is you, shopping for indulgent takeaways when you could be marking essays or walking around Waterlooville, yes? Speaking of, I’ve been meaning to ask—how did the yoga classes go last week? I still haven’t got around to joining you, work’s been a nightmare.      Oh, don’t let me guilt-trip you. I’ve been there, buried in deadlines. The class was brilliant, though. The instructor is Italian, very knowledgeable. She’s travelled all over North Africa, which is also suspiciously similar to your line of work. Well, let’s start you off with something less dramatic—grilled courgettes and gochujang glaze if you’re brave. And that was simply the pace of our evening. We sipped box wine, shared stories, and tackled recipes like we were planting seeds in lives we’re yet to fully understand.  —The conversation ends as the two continue to laugh and eat, sound fading out into the evening silence of Birmingham.

Look, I'm not suggesting anything untoward, but I have made a line in the sand that I don't go further than that. I'm your husband, you don't have to get me to picture it.

Rather skip the new Marvel movie. I'm more into old-school Bond films, if you ask me. There's something elegant about James Bond from the 70s. ‘Mum said we’s goin’ to Jamaica Inn first. I thought it was ‘Minn like mince pies, not ‘Minn like mineshaft or summat.’      ‘Nah love, proper spelt like Jamaica Inn—get used to it. The Yellow Brick Road? Mummy said the road’s all red here. Somewhere like that. I seen pictures once of wind turbines lik’e great big white planes stuck in the sky. Proper magic.’      ‘Magic ain’t far off, luv. Trees, fields, the lot. Living in Manchester, you’ve never properly seen it. When I was your age I used to read  The Sherlock Holmes  books, you ever read em? Proper clever clogs those stories was—like solving riddles on the side of the road.’      ‘I liked  Alice in Wonderland , though. The Queen of Hearts an’ everything. Real cheeky, innit? You remember Mr West, from Bolton? He used to send messages by telegram before he died, and sometimes it was in code. Like the Binary sommat? All that Morse code and Silly Stones and Braille—proper old fashioned, innit?’      ‘Yeah, them telegraph man? It was all clicks and dashes an’ you had to be a mind reader to understand. When we get there I’ll take you for a walk, see the houses, the fields with all them wild flowers, and we’ll find the nearest beach where you can run up and down them waves like a mad thing.’      ‘I might write a letter in Morse code, like Mr West did.

Rather annoying the new rent here eh? You used t’pay less than twenty quid for a week’s stay in the big house back home. An’ yet here I am, stared up the bum by a little flat in Wincanton with a dicky boiler and wi’ a view o’ a field an een!      Aye, I know what yer mean lass. Back in the day I used t’stay in Lodges this big, an’ we’d have stew an’ fresh bread every night! Nuffin like nowadays. Funny how things’ve changed wi’ age. Used t’dream o’ gettin’ outta north west, now I’d kill fer a guid warm casserole and the turkey on Christmas Day back home.      Probably, but I reckon you're nostalgic, Dad. Crikey!

Rather annoying to be honest, eh?      Aye, it's always a bit much when you travel so far east. You'd think your body would get used to it after a while, but it doesn’t really, does it?
