Rather annoying this new A-Level system, innit? Seems like they’re trying to cramp ‘em all into one big exam, same as the old GCSEs. Not a good idea if ye gotta manage yer stress levels. Not to mention, the pass rate looks a bit shaky.      Yeah, I’ve been reading about it online. Seems like the government just wanted to cut costs, but in the end, it’s just the students who suffer. They’re bleedin’ right overworked, ain't they? And to be honest, once this new system’s out the door, we won’t get the skilled workforce we really need.      What I don’t get is why they made that choice, considering how bad the NHS already is. I mean, nurses and doctors ain’t being trained fast enough, and now they make school even harder? It feels like it’s a downward spiral. Wait, did you see that new advert about the NHS shortage? The ones at the hospital near us is desperate — they can’t even spare a doctor to check up on someone properly.      Yeah, I saw it. It’s sad, really. You’d think with the grief of the pandemic, they might’ve looked at increasing funding, not cutting it. Speaking of which, have you been to the petrol station recently? I almost had to queue for an hour the other day.      Oh aye, I saw the petrol queues on the news — it’s daft, someone said there was a lorry driver strike. Makes me wish I had a pushbike. Least you don’t gotta queue for a can of fuel with one.      You know, most people about now are asking themselves if it’s even worth it to own a car. Not just because of the crisis, but because of the plug-ins and everything. Although, as for me, I just found out that the hairdresser that used to do my hair cut his hours at the salon. I’m told it was all because he couldn’t meet his rent — waiting till I get a refund from the salon and then I’m off to see if I can find a new lass with a trimmer and a good eye for a bob.      Oh no! That goon really need to figure out something. If he can’t manage his finances, how’s he gonna manage a salon?

Rather annoying me a bit, eh? You know what me mam’s like—she’s always on about university... Like, I’ll get me results this week, and I can take a decision after that, innit?      No, I mean—get on with things sooner or later. Got eeny plans if I get into the one in Cambridge?      Proper jealous of you. You’ve got all them leafy turrets and all. Me mam says it’s daft to not get it. But me and Leeds? Bit more me vibe. Less posh.      Right, but it’s mostly bloody pricey. I meen, the grants are only lik e £10k what’s left? You’ve gotta get a job or take out more debts, innit?      Eww, I hated doing that—my uni was about 20 mins out. I worked 16 hours a week, which was in’t criminal. I didn’t want to finish, thinking to myself I’m so working the rest of me life.      Aww, don’t listen—there are way more things out there than just work. I dunno, like ... maybe starting me own thing. I proper hate financial stuff, but got no choice. My brother works in finance, he says, least way it’s stable.      He don’t know much then. Silly if you donn’t like what you do. Like, what's the point in having money if you're not happy? That's the feminist thought, innit?—job shouldn’t be about just surviving.      That’s all right for people who got the time and resources. Not all of us can be basking in the sun watching documentaries about vibes and stuff. Some of us need to be earning.      I mean, I understand. My grandma had to put up with stuff that no one should ever have to. I’m just saying, it's a start. At least trying to improve things, you know?      Ain't that what we're all doing, innit? Trying to figure a way to survive and do things we love. Me mam tells stories about the plague. Course, that's all she can go on about. But it was wild stuff—whole cities wiped out.      I had to do a project on that in history. Proper grim. But innit sad that people didn’t really understand what was going on? Just so much fear and not enough facts.      It's like, why not be more educated about the past so we can be smarter about the future?

Rather annoying isn't it, how grown-ups just expect you to glue sticks and all? I've been thinking... some friendships are like old pairs of trainers. They don't fit anymore, sure, but you feel awkward binning them.      Oh yes, exactly. And it's not that I'm ungrateful, but some people drift into your life and then suddenly expect all your evenings? I mean, I love my flatmate, but this isn't a B&B. Sometimes she turns up expecting dinner parties and moral support when she's got no cause for complaint. It's draining.      I get it! It's so tough, isn't it? When you start to feel like you're the turkey at Christmas dinner year after year. The cruel bit is knowing you need to phase them out, but without burning bridges.      It is, definitely. But how do you do it? I've tried this whole evasion plan... I'll say I'm busy, busy, busy, or make up some kind of nonsense weekend plans. It's working, but I feel like a bit of a fraud.      Oh, I did that for a few months. But then I tried something: I stopped responding to texts. I know, it sounds cruel. But if they weren't talking to me, I became less available to them, and eventually the pattern faded. It's not perfect, and yeah, I felt bad, but it worked.      Whoa, just ghosting them? That's bold. Did they ever twig it was on purpose?      Eventually. It comes through in subtle ways — like when they mention how you've gone about your business without them. But you just shrug and pass it off. Honestly, it's awkward and not fun, but better that than pretending everything's hunky-dory when it's not.      I wish I had the nerve for that. I'm a bit more diplomatic. But I think I might have to start being braver when it comes to who I let into my time.      Totally. It's a balance, really. Some friendships do need a bit of care and attention, but not all of them. That's the go. And I think life becomes more enjoyable once you stop overcommitting.      That's the box I'm aiming for. Maybe after this trip. It's been great, but I'm starting to think I'm ready to re-evaluate my little orbit.

Rather annoying to be honest. Loads of reading to do before lectures start again.      Oh, but dear, it's always something, isn’t it? I remember when you were applying, I was painting in my studio all day and you were rushing off to exams. Time flies.      Yeah, I mean I’m just grateful to have got in overall. I wanted to study art history so bad, and I actually got the best offer I could’ve hoped for.      That’s brilliant! You’ve always had a good eye for detail when it comes to art. You remember that little exhibition I had at Mary’s gallery? You helped me choose the frame for that Still Life.      Oh definitely! I still remember the rich red one you painted over, the one I nearly fell into when I was little.      Oh dear, yes, and you nearly knocked over my whole palette then.      I only repainted the wall, no harm done.      Well, I still use that palette now, by the way. My hands get a little shaky, but the colours are still sharp.      I love that, by the way. Watching you paint always reminded me of something out of a movie. All dramatic with the brushstrokes and the music, and sometimes that really strange scent of oils.      You know what? I still get that scent when I travel back to Italy, even though I was actually born in Vienna. Go figure.      Wait, I had no idea!      Neither did I for a long time. My mum was born in Italy, and my dad in Austria. I always thought I was Austrian-Italian! But my birth certificate says Vienna. Strange what you discover as you get older.      That does sound strange. I do love reading up on European art though, it’s all quite interconnected, really. I’m reading a book right now on the Renaissance, it’s talking about how Venice was a huge cultural bridge between Italy and the rest of Europe.      Then you’ll find my holiday plans very interesting! I’m thinking of going back there for a solo exhibition I’ve been invited to. They want some of my newer works for a show in Florence.      That's amazing, Nana! I’d go with you but I’ve already signed up for that ecology society trip to The Netherlands to look at post-industrial landscapes. It’s all regenerated sites and reclaimed land, like massive art installations, apparently.

Rather skip the gymfit and go for a swig of digestive. But you’d know, wouldn’t you? What with your job and all. I’m more of a, well, someone who’d rather lie on the floor and stare at the ceiling, I s’pose.      That’s alright if you  want  to look like a potato on legs. But c’mon, most people eat something before working out. Not that I do much, honestly. My legs are alright as they are, if you ask me.      Oh, right, the new vegan bar you fetch from the shop last evenin’—all processed and full of weird powders. Still, I managed to get the turkey and cheese bit done. The driver left it in the back by mistake, bless him. Drove off, and I sat there for ten minutes with my nose in the air and my heels muddy.      Well, you did drive in his place. I was busy getting lost in Kartuzy looking for the motorway. Good job I didn’t lose us over there, eh? We need to listen more next time. Anyway, your turn now to read the satnav.      Oh, brilliant. Because it’s always been such a struggle. I’m not – I’m not bad with roads, least, I wasn’t when I was working. But retirement don’t come with practice, Silly. Still, no one ever tells me what to do. Not like someone at full-time work would.      That’s oddly sour. You’re not still mad at him for the tea money and being late last week, are you? I spoke to him and told about how you don’t want the gold standard from strangers, you know? It’s just a motorway and not Buckingham Palace.      Well,  I  don’t mind, personally. I just like things done well. As for being English – and I daren’t say it where any bloody Pole can hear – I am bloody proud of it. I don’t know you, as being that sprite of equality and justice always trying to 'split a couple of whistles.'      Oh, for God's sake, like I started it by saying go back to my pond life if you don’t like change. But I meant the language, not that I’m any different from blokes. I’ve had all the same issues at work with men who think teaching English is a bit of a tea-time hobby.

Rather lovely day today, isn't it? That sun's doin' me garden the world o' good... got the roses bloomin' b'lier than Blenheim Palace!      Aw, it's sweet o' you to say, love—though I wouldn't say it was sunshine bright eenough to be  not  grey today. 'Course, if it carries on as it has, I reckon we'll have a decent spell before the next lot o' drizzle comes in. Still, worth 'aving a nice cuppa in the garden room, eh?      T'was a good idea o' yours, that—settin' it up the other night. Still warm from the electric fire. Though I must say, I’m gettin' a bit antsy 'bout the power situation. 'Ave heard the old lights up 'eads 'ave been 'aving blackouts again. I called 'em 'bout me cooker last month... I 'ad to boil me porridge by candlelight, can you believe it?      Oh, mercy—sounds like the good 'old days, doesn’t it? I remember in me youth, as a teacher, we only 'ad gas lamps in the classroom… plus, the roof leaked if it was a good rainfall. Not much for power then, but I 'ad me way with the kids…      Now don’t go making me feel old again, Dinah. You were a saint in them classrooms. 'Eard tell people still talk about you! 'Ow are those old Debra and Len? Still floring each other at the community centre?      Aye! Len's as cheeky as ever about his birthday... keeps saying it’s “not such a major birthday this time.” And Debra still goes on about her mums’ new project—hand-throwin’ mugs. My, they’re 'eady things, those mugs are. Demo 'er at me next lot o’ exercises. ‘Course, the last one ended up with a little beetle inside!      Oh ho! That’s a proper tale! 'Eve been potting with mugs myself last week. Got one shattered on me 'ead trying t’ fit the 'andle in goin’ the wrong way! 'Ow about you? Still made yer own milk? I see you're always goin’ on about it at your age.      I am! It keeps me moving in them stiff hours after breakfast. Though I 'ad to give up the goat, ‘cause Spot, the cow, wouldn’t let 'er near 'im... I'm makin' do with a nice soft cow, old thing.      Oh, I ‘ope she isn't too flighty when you're at it.

So do we get to take our bikes on the train, like, to Cornwall? Because I  really  want to go to Newquay and maybe do some surfing properly!      I'll need to check with the train company, but generally speaking you can take bikes on board — if they’re folded and packed properly. But if you're going to be out on the beach all day, don’t you think you should pack a towel  this  time, rather than relying on us?      Ugh, was that the  big  brown towel or the  small  one? I didn’t even know it was  mine . I just wanted to bring my supply of wet-wipes anditunes playlist.   Speaker_3 :   Right, well, the music for the journey is sorted, and I think I’ve managed to piece together enough for a playlist that’ll cover everyone. Pop, rock, surf rock — all with a bit of soul.      That sounds perfect, love. And the kids will appreciate the CD player more than their phone for the drive down. Speaking of, I’ve got the car booked out for Thursday to Sunday. Do you think we’ll still be able to get a rental bike once we get there, just in case?      Yeah, I saw online that there are loads of places you can pick them up. But if you want to save money, we could probably just hitch a lift with Ben and his family. He said they’re coming too.      Who’s Ben again?      Just my friend from school. He’s got a mum called  Sue , and a dad who works with Legos or something — you know the type. And he’s got two sisters — one who  collects  seashells and the other who is obsessed with superhero movies to the point where they hang up posters  everywhere .      Right, okay. Just one thing — any friends joining us on this trip need to be responsible when it comes to the shared space. No  superhero weapon imitations  in the tent.      They're not  real  weapons — they're foam ones. Plus, I told you, it's for  research . If I want to be a real spy in the navy one day, I need to know how the good guys fight properly.      Alright, alright. Just make sure you don’t wake us up pretending to be chased by invisible enemies at 3am. Last time, we ended up with a note from the Airbnb host.

Okay, I just can't get over that movie, "10 Things I Hate About You." Like, Patrick got the girl, she ditched poetry for music and  he  stared at himself in the mirror and suddenly everything was okay. Pfft, I mean, it's corny but it was kinda fun?      I know, right? But I reckon it's not all that different from a week in our lives, if you think about it. I mean, we're stuck with teachers who are like total control freaks and the guy who makes us recite poetry, but the second we do something a little rebellious, it's  us  who get promoted. It’s wild.      Honestly, our poetry mistress is like Heathcliff left in a GCSE class. We had to memorise a whole sonnet today and then she screamed at us because someone forgot to italicise the poem title. I nearly cried. I just want to say “Miss, chill!”      Same, I’m ordering her to chill so hard. And I reckon we should like, get into her room and paint “10 things I hate about you” all over her whiteboards. Do you think we’ll still be best friends if we get expelled for that?      Absolute no-brainer. We'd be expelled, but still, it's  so  worth the legacy. NowSpeaking of legacy, what do you think about the trip to London next month? Like, is this just going to be full of dress-uping boring tours of museums? I just want to cosplay a Mary-Anne from the Victoria and Albert or something.      I mean, it's not going to be nearly as epic as seeing Stratford's theatre, but it still beats watching “The Theory of Everything” again and again. Let’s explore the West End and stuff. I could wear my stockings with tights like that hipster Ausart guest speaker said we should.      Are you mental? Let's go all out. We could meet up with some Americans pretending they tour here. We'll sit in that cute little café behind the British Museum with lunches we packed and act all posh like we're studying art history for fun, not because it's a homework requirement.      I'm in if you risk getting fined for eating sandwiches made of cheese in the British Museum. Let's go, team!      Team Cheese Sandwich Rebellion, rise up! 10 things I hate about you start with teachers never letting us eat properly during breaks.

Rather annoying this new Facebook lot, innit? I tried to get onto it again last week ‘cos Susan showed me how to send messages ages ago now. But now I can’t find the messages where we used to chat about the grandkids’ birthdays, and Susan says it's been moved again. I swear it’s beginning to give me the hump with it all.      Oh come on, Cliff. A hump? That's more from all the tea than the internet, bless you. Besides, it’s just part of getting older—forgetting where things are, or what button you pressed to get everything to go wrong. I used to be good with technology when the grandkids still came to visit and made me MySpace, but now I’m still waiting for someone to show me how to upload photos again.      I think it’s funny how even with all the help we try to give, some of you old folks just get more confused with the new versions. But honestly, you’re not wrong, Cliff, the way they keep changing the layout drives everyone bonkers. I’ve been getting annoyed, too—especially when it starts asking me questions like, “Have you updated your preferences?” when I’ve done nothing but scroll for five minutes.      Speaking of frustration—I’ve been thinking a lot about OCD recently. I was marking some papers the other day, and the paper wasn’t quite aligned to my liking. Silly, I know, but you start focusing on the tiniest things. I found myself adjusting the margins thirteen times before realising it just wasn't going to make the paper any better. I suppose it’s part of being an adult now—I worry more over things that don’t matter.      That does sound a bit touchy, David. I've always said what you really need is a bit of religion. I mean, not too much, but to have something to believe in helps keep you calm. Mind you, I did once get chickenpox when I was older than any bloody kid I know. I was sixty-five for crying out loud!      Oh that’s right, wasn’t it around the time you volunteered to help with the church fete and Johnny’s grandchild must have caught it from another kid and passed it on to you? I remember your face was like a patchwork quilt. But you were still in the baking tent, bless you.

Rather annoying the new German lass finds our accents difficult, isn't it? She's been staying with us for the weekend and keeps asking me to clarify things more than I'd like, ha! She's a lovely person otherwise. Not quite used to the Kent lilt it seems.      Oh I'm sure she doesn't mean to be rude! I know if someone had an accent like that on a train I'd probably find it hard to catch every word. Still, easier said than done when you're someone like her—moving to the UK for work. Didn’t your wife get the place under some EU scheme like three years back?      That’s clever of her, choosing such a place in Kent. My visit a couple of years ago—you remember the weather, Speaker_1? London was sweltering, Kemsing had rain every hour like clockwork!      Oh yes, breakfast, no breakfast, always rain! But still a good trip. Me and Speaker_6 spent a lot of time in Germany many years back—restoring stained glass for that project. I do miss the way people talk there, so musical!      I’ve made several trips to Germany as well, visiting a silversmith friend of mine. Their way of speaking gives you so much personality—each town with its own vibe, and none of the parochialism we sometimes have around here.      You know what I found interesting? The way the German woman here is adapting. She says it’s also the phrasing differences—something to do with how British English tenses are used differently. I explained a bit to her being a copywriter—I speak more formally in my work, so I understand how confusing accents and usages can be.      It’s all a bit of a lark, really. Speaking of which, have we fixed up for the dinner celebration with Speaker_6 and the gang? I hope he passed on what he said about the new oven. I’d love something fresh, not the ready meals again!      My darling, you know as well as I do how hard it is trying to find ready-made dinners that survive the oven and retain the grace of fresh food. But I’ve got it covered! I met an American guy in Germany on a work trip and he taught me how to roast a chicken like kings, no fewer than three kinds of vegetables, and something with thyme and rosemary.

So, I heard you've been working at that new pub down in Exeter. How's it going? Still got the taste of garlic on your hands from your last experiment?      Haha, it's all over the place, honestly. We're trying to create this new menu — experimental stuff, fusions mostly. I'm loving it, but it's intense. My hands haven't been clean since last Friday. What about you? Got that internship sorted yet?      Yeah, I start next week! It's in London. A bit daunting, considering it's the first big step after my degree, but it feels right. I've been practicing my elevator pitch non-stop.      That's awesome, mate. I remember you being obsessed with journalism back at uni, always picking up the mic at the student radio. If there's anyone who can charm an editor, it's you.      You always knew how to give a bit of a confidence boost, thanks. I remember we used to go to those underground gigs in the uni basement, right? You’d drum with a jam jar for some of those DIY takes!      Oh, don’t remind me — I’ve still got a shiner from that one night. But seriously, it was something else. Back then we thought every new band was the next big thing. You ever support any of them?      A few! Remember that band, ‘The Flicker’? We did a live stream at the final-year showcase. They auditioned for a label just last year. Funny how some things come full circle.      That’s cool. I actually ended up cooking at one of their gigs about five years back. They opened up a local club here — had this weird vibes menu — edible confetti! I know that sounds like madness, but it worked somehow.      That  does  sound like madness, but I respect the concept. You and your culinary experiments. I'm still waiting for you to invite me to one of them.      Join my mailing list and I’ll send you a ticket. What with your communication skills and my whacky recipes, we could almost run our own night club.      Maybe one day. Actually, I've been thinking about getting back into playing music. Guitars line up after work, and maybe we could jam again?      Now you're speaking my language. I’ve been collecting odd percussion items in the kitchen just for times like this.

Rather do a half decent coffee than run in to the Drive Through again, mind you, it’s busy like a hive on a summer's day. I’m more than fed up with their loyalty promotions where you get a free teabag after 10 quid—  Lol  —Deirdre at the school says she  bought  one for the   teabag  .      Aye Aye, but I needed that stubby lolly off the loyalty card. It came in useful for the pizza drive-in the other day. Massive queue outside the supermarket but the bloke gave me a frozen toffee slice even! Not like that   drive through   at the petrol station, where you have to shout your order like you’re at   Wembley  .      I know what you mean, dear. Reminds me of when we lived in Newcastle and I took you shopping, ordering puff cakes and the like. Good times, those were—  Before the shop closed   for some daft rebrand I think. Maybe he had   better pickups   on his mobile phone than me. At least he'd have better sleepers for nap time. I tell you, I'd sleep in a converted van with a   camp bed   any day before sleeping on   those lumpy chairs   waiting for my order again.      You've clearly seen too much of the 'entrepreneurs' on the telly last night. That's where you get the idea of travel adventures and the notion of   business structures   on your own if you've not got a trade license.      I had a dream of a   van life   near your holiday town, like at   Durham  , with a kiosk and everything. As long as I don’t have to queue to buy a coffee like that ‘Drive Through’ we passed at the end of      the road.

Rather annoying isn't it, eh?      Aye, it's such a mither... What was the bloke's name now?      I've nearly remembered! It was Jim...      Jim Marsh? Wasn't he the one who was in hospital eenough times since he had the cancer?      Aye, that's the one. I should've known by his red hair! Poor old Jim, I remember his da ghiding in the rain once waiting to give him a lift to the hospital. Looks like he's still doing that. Probably better for breakfast, but then again...!      Aye, his missus was always in hides, you remember? She's still got the heart, though. For sure, and over time, when things settle down a bit, maybe the conversations go back to normal. But for now, people still talk about them, don’t they? Right backs you up mentally.

Rather annoying isn’t it? The queue for the toilets is longer than the one for the bar ‘ere. I swear, I’ll not hold m’pint much longer!      Aw, don’t be fair, love. Aye,  The Bird and the Gun . Sarah reckons they could sell out Wembley and still have enough of a vibe to fill the entire city of Doncaster with folk lullabies.      You’re not t’ think the world is still goin’ on without folk if you don’t get it. But I dig it. Rather annoyingly, Thea's birthday weekend is when the CBeebies pantomime comes through on panto weekend and I thought she'd love to see that. Rather annoying this wet weather, eh?      Aye, it's been damp ever since I got home. Never mind, at least it's keeping my plants well-watered. How about you, Kate? Rather annoyingly, I haven't had anything to eat since breakfast. I was supposed to write a proposal first thing this morning and well, forgot about the snacks. Blows it all, doesn't it?      Not to worry, there's a tin of shortbread on the coffee table if you want it. You  always  swoon when you're hungry, don't you? You'd probably lie down in a heap if someone made a grab for the shortbread before you.      It's a condition, I swear! So, what’s on the cards tonight, then? I've already read the book and I think it turned my stomach—too many childhood reflections, and very raw. Looked like they were –?      Duckfaces, because they were missing the stickers. Yeah, I don't know how he did that. Still in the same box – probably got wooden splinters in it from when I played.      That's sweet. Said it was a man’s book because goonie books were all about treasure hunting and not real stories.      I think it's fascinating how background and language—and where you were raised—form these early identities. I grew up down in Essex, after all, and heard all sorts of broad East Anglian tones on the telly and over the radio.

So did you really just take off to Majorca without anyone knowing? I had no idea you two were planning a trip like that!      Oh, we didn’t plan it  too long  in advance. A dream, if I do say so myself.      Last minute planning? That’s just you, Mum. I once tried that during a football season and ended up watching the match on the couch with baked beans  again . Classic.      That’s rich coming from you, son. You couldn’t even get to the post office on time! I’m glad I didn’t risk it with my holiday.      I was about to say something similar. I still can’t believe you just happened to leave when I was repainting the shed. I looked like a fella who’s never seen a tin of emulsion before by the time you got back!     老爷! You’d probably end up with a shed and a tea party!      And toilets! Don’t forget someone got stuck in the loo! That was unfortunately a bonding moment for  me  and  the cat .      Hey, Ernie’s a good listener when you need one! He might’ve been meditating in there the entire time.      Honestly, I don’t know why you worry so much about the cat. Next you’ll tell me Ernie walked behind you to the shed last week.      I’m not joking! The sod was trailing me every step on that DIY mission like some kind of disgruntled shadow!      Well, he did manage to jump through the paint can and make it all look like I lost 30% of my brain cells.      True to his name:  Ernie . Ernie the Mysterious, Ernie the Clumsy, Ernie the... well... Ernie.      You see? He’s got a personality.

Rather annoying this newfit in the kitchen ain't it? Che’s promising one thing, and ‘ere comes yet another "smart" gadget from the future. Rather annoying when the satnav takes us the long way round. I blame it for us being late to Reg’s last weekend. Never mind, it was a brilliant farewell dinner! How's he settling into Saudi Arabia? Rather annoying to be honest, eh? You know, ever since I moved to瑞典, I've been struggling with this dry skin. Maybe it’s the weather up here? Rather annoying when newfit’s got such a strong regional accent. My dad had her in for a week and she got the kids to teach them local Kent phrases. Blows my mind how specific those accents are! Mock each other's accents, and then talk proper through dinner. Now she’s gone, it’s just me and about five old TV programmes for company.      Oh, Grandpa… I’m sorry. That must be rough.      Aye, lass, it is, but that’s life. Got memories. Though I miss her more than anything. She used to say I was too loud, always shouting cos I tried to speak clearly when I was drunk. Not that I’m admitting that happened every night…      That’s not uncommon with your age group, love. My sister lost her dad after a long battle with alcoholism. It broke her up really bad. Gave up trying to get work at the care home and started looking after her own parents. She lives in the same house now.      That sounds familiar. Me mum had a heart attack two years ago after all the drinking she did.

Rather skip the new kid’s party. You know what happens with glue sticks and spider silk, don’t you?      Oh, come off it, mam. It’s a  Halloween party , not some physics lab experiment. If you want to meet someone, just say so. Is it love at first whisked egg white, now?      Look—I just have memories, okay? Being obsessed with roles where I’m pretending to fall in love is easier than trying to fall in love for real over a bowl of Cheetos and a        Arrr, alright. My boy’s grown soft. Just remember, romance, casting, and age of consent are all very different things. I swore to your dad you’d be wiser than that lad off telly who couldn’t tell the difference between a UNESCO site and a free toaster on a holiday special.

Rather lovely to have you here, my love. Thought we’d start the day right wi’ a proper Yorkshire breakfast, and a spot o’ tea, o’ course. Not like what they call breakfast in Swansea, is it? Still, I ain't complainin’ about the tea. You always insist on the right strength.      Right, because a weak cup o’ builder’s brew is no good to anyone, is it? Now he’s going to think I’m a menace.      That’s no go—least I hope he doesn’t. If he does, I expect I shall be forced to stand between you and the box, armed wi' a stamp and a threatening look.      You and your roles in society! So, what about you then, anything new on the social media madness front? Still pronouncin’ yourself a ‘Wigmore’ on all platforms?      Of course I am!

Rather annoying when people are late, isn't it? I mean, I was supposed to meet Emily at the coffee shop and she turned up twenty minutes after I’d ordered my second tea. It nearly drove me mad!      I hear you, man—some people treat punctuality like it’s optional. My friend Dan once turned up to a party with   seventeen minutes to spare  . The rest of us were all watching the clock like it was a quiz show. Oh, and by the way, someone once told me the word  “punctuality”  literally comes from the word  “puncta”  in Latin, which means "points," as in the idea of hitting marks or being on time. My English teacher definitely said that.      Honestly, I find the English language fascinating in general, but spelling is brutal. I screamed at my phone last night about the word   “weird”  —four letters, three vowels, and I still spelled it wrong. And the  “i before e except after c”  rule? Good for naught.      Haha, yes, spelling is absolute chaos! I did A-Level English literature and still grief over spelling. Honestly, I’ve been thinking—what if we used phonics for all words? Imagine if kids just learned to sound out everything. Though I guess that would eliminate half the fun of Scrabble.      Scrabble’s a killer. Last night, I played my uncle and he managed to get forty-three points for “quidnunc.” I had to look it up later. Some guy called it a Latin phrase meaning   “what now?”   That’s Scrabble cheating in my book. He nearly flunked his A-Levels but picked the game up like he was born with a dictionary in his hand.      I’d take it. Quidnunc? Jeez. I tried to play “oxymoron” once, but that only got me like seven letters’ worth. What about you, Emily? What are you studying now?      I’m halfway through a Media Studies degree—enough with people asking me if it's "just about gossip." No—it's about  critical theory ,  semiotics , the  historiography of film ... it's wild. If I go into editing or publishing, I’ll finally get to use all the spelling skills I’ve been honing all these years. It’s like I’ve been training for a roles in the BBC.      That’s cool. I’m doing a history degree—so much reading, so many essays. But the problem is all the words like   “declspecinate”   or   “antiparallel.”

Rather a gray day, isn't it love? Thoughtful weather for a bit of chinwag, if you ask me.      It's not doing much for the mood, is it? Got me stuck inside with no enthusiasm to read or even watch the telly. But I was just about to make a pot of tea. Would you like some?      Tea would be most welcome. I've had a cup or two already this morning, but what's a day without a proper dump of it, eh?      Funny you should mention it. I've been thinking about my tea shop down in Harrow. Oh, how I miss the clatter of cups and the chatter of mums and their little ones. Still, best to not dwell on what's gone, I suppose.      A sad business, the way things go, dear. Time’s a thief if ever I've known one. I've been thinking about the old Costessey days, planting the vegetable patch and mending the fence before the rain got the best of it.      My, those sound like sturdy times. I always admired people with land and gardens to tend. I only ever had my arms full with children and managing other people's homes. Ten little ones at one point, all red cheeked and eager to explore, and none happier than the day we painted the kitchen ceiling!      You always were a dab hand with the young 'uns. I remember the day Ethel brought in one of your girls to audition my knitting. It took me half a day to unstick the needles out of her red flannelette dress!      Yes, about that! Her mummy was none too pleased when the holes didn’t come out. I suppose you could say I was more manager of mishaps than childminder, most days.      And I've been less than a manager of anything. A bit of dillydallying here and there, pottery once, but that didn't last when I convinced myself I was making pots for the hoard of dragons under our garden.      Well, I do like your imagination, dear. Still, I wonder sometimes if we could have started something new even in our later years. Maybe if we'd had a go at it.      I suppose we could still box clever, love. Lift your legs and you might just find the future lives in your knickers drawer, where those sensible trousers never had the sense to look.

Rather skip the newfitnes apps, if you ask me. I've had my fill of buzzwords and... Well, rather stick to what I've always known. Proper food, real ingredients, no fancy gadgets getting in the way. Charming this bit of Devon, by the way. Quaint little home it is, and holidays like this don't come along every day.      Don’t get me wrong, I love tradition. But the new fitness app I’ve downloaded is actually quite clever. It’s supposed to track not just exercise, but also what you eat. Apparently, it suggests recipes based on what’s in your fridge. Still, I’ll give you a point—sometimes real, unprocessed food is the best medicine.      I’m curious to try it. Ten years I’ve been teaching and I can feel the years creeping in. A little push to take better care of myself doesn’t go amiss, no doubt. But this conversation’s not quite filling in my appetite. I for one looked forward to hearing what delights Mrs. Hoggard down the shop would throw in her stew.      Speaking of shop—there’s news about the train station. They said it’ll open in two weeks, finally. Long-awaited it was, and we’ve been put through the mill with delays. My Mate down at Royal Victoria Country Park was none too pleased having to take his old Landy nearly forty miles to catch the nearest train.      That’s brilliant news, isn’t it? Reviving the skyline for the village and everything. Children at the school have been doing a project on the project—there's a fair bit of excitement being stirred up at the expense of some ballet and flower arranging groups.      I’ll be quite the commuter again, then. Ten years teaching and I haven’t had to worry about rush hour! I’m thinking of car pooling with my new student, Holly. She lives just beyond the station entrance.      And have you tried the spinach recipe I mentioned before, dear? Using it in a pasta dish instead of the usual basil. It gives a wholesome twist to any meal. Next time we've lunches to prepare and meals to exchange.      Reminiscent of something my mother made back in the '70s. But I’ll tell you what—let’s go one better and simply line the plate with that green goodness. Who needs gadgets or gimmicks when your ingredients speak for themselves?

Rather annoying really, I haven't seen anything new at the cinema for ages. Everything's just a rehash... got to admit, I'd rather be playing FIFA than watching football at this rate      Same here, honestly. No disrespect to football, but half the teams are just gonna be awful anyway. I went out last weekend to this stag do and nearly got onto the bus as well they were a bit      That's a bit dodgy. Oh but I watched a comedy film last night. We've been invited to the seminar this week by the course mates and it's not too bad. It's about Shakespeare, apparently, so I'm hoping it's not too pretentious. On the telly the other day, I saw some documentary about the Bard and it was actually really interesting – who would have thought, right? I think he turned history upside down with his plays      Yeah, no doubt about that. Well, here's hoping the seminar isn't too stuffy. I'm not sure I could take any more political lectures. I mean, Europe's all over the news, and it's enough to give you a headache if you read the papers.      Honestly, I just read The Lie for fun last week and it was pretty good. Not as much as I read as before but I managed a bit.      Yeah, I've not got much time for books lately. I'm already doing enough at uni. It's all seminars this week      Yeah, my course's been alright. I had a bit of a lie-in this morning. So, have you being out recently? I need something to get away from it all      I went to a local place the other night, had wings and burgers. Not bad at all. Need to try somewhere new though. The problem is, I've not got a lot for cash just now.      Yeah, eating out can be a bit pricey. But I think it's worth it once in a while. I went out with the lads as well. We had a few pints and some lunches. I think it's good to have some time with the lads      For sure man. Yeah, go out with the boys, if you've got the chance. I made my choice in the end, between clubs. I went for the one with the better training facilities.

Rather skip the new barista café near the station and come back here—it's just like old times! So... got any news from Oxford? Or is it more of a “still staredown negativity” vibe with uni friends?      Honestly, half of them have moved abroad or started eeny weeny passive-aggressive texts with “I miss you” but never reply to your group chats. You’ve no idea how liberating it is to be back here. Oh, and congrats on pulling off that project! Heard it was a nightmare for months.      Not to downplay it, but when I saw you at the conference last term giving that killer presentation about marketing ethics… you nailed it. Still working on the same agency campaign? The one about the environmental charity?      I did—remember? But then my ex, Rohan, managed to ruin breakfast, bedtime and basically any therapy breakthrough I had... I still haven’t deleted his texts—vain, I know—personally I’m just waiting for him to legislate a “right to mourn grief of exes who still hide in contacts.”      No, I get it—he’s that one who got misty-eyed and tried to slap a quote from “The Little Prince” in every message? Honestly, I dated someone who refused to talk about anything that made sense and instead wrote ambient music at full volume to “express feelings.” He once tried to write a song about a toaster— a toaster , Joanna.      No way. You’re romanticising it about to make mine sound less bad. But seriously—my mum says I have to stop "crying over toasters and pickups" and get a proper handle on future planning. You’re the only person I've ever known who manages to balance work and actually seeing your parents.      Unhh. I see them once a term, and I miss waiting till 11pm to tell them  everything  as though they were always updated with my nuanced life crisis. But hey—you're welcome to join me next road trip, after I rewire my brain not to derail into gothic poetry on motorways if you start singing again.      Deal, but only if we stop off at that greasy spoon near your mum’s. The one that serves fluency in conservation and freshly-understood potholes with the toast. You know... to fuel up for life, metaphorically?      Is that a trap? I so miss that place. Always forget how good it is to talk, to catch up, even if we veer into madness or adventure and slightly-tongued lies about our ex-angers.

Rather annoying I know, innit. You’d think grans would get that herb garden sorted by now... got the lavender, chives, and oregano planted, but somehow the thyme’s still buckin’ about with the mint. Look like they’ve decided to throw a party in there. Got eeny mess on me hands from tryin’ to sort it out.      Oh aye? A lot o’ work t’done, but it’s easier said than done. I know someone once tried t’plant thyme an’ mint together... big mistake. Gave ’em to a fella down t’road who made some sort o’ herbal tea out of it. Supper tasted like a Mynt and Thyme disaster! Ha! Yeah... no one mentioned that, innit?      Eww, no chance I’d be making tea out o’ that gig! Wait, you said herbal tea? I mean, I’ve been in Cambridge a few weeks, and I’m tryin’ to get t’knotch up on my plant knowledge—especially for the kitchen, y’know? Any pointers?      Oh, definitely. Did you know oregano and thyme are good in soups or stews? Be careful with mint though. Great for iced tea, but stick it in savoury dishes and it’s like a party crasher. You din’t expect it, innit. Same with rosemary—it gives a strong piney smell. Takes chicken and potatoes t’another level. Used a bit of it last night on some carrots and potatoes—cooked it with a bit of butter and honey. Marg’lous.      Apple and butter with honey? That does sound b嘞! She’s watching this place like a hawk now, and I think it’s her idea o’ staying relevant. Garden as a way to have something goin’ on. I mean, her kids passed on, an’ the grandkids are all busy... told me she’s tryin’ to meet some new neighbours through passing on cuttings. She’s growin’ lemons in a pot now! London born, loves the heat innit.      That sounds like a gran I had growing up in the 'burg. goin’ on 80 and trying new things like building a cold frame just so she could see green veggies in the middle of winter. Family bonding can be weird like that. planting seeds, passin’ knowledge... one day I’m startin’ my garden like that with my kids, innit.      Mm, that’d be a proper legacy. The kind that stays alive. Speaking of, I’ve started trying to make my own jams too.

Rather skip the queue at the café, I've made us a decent coffee and brought it in. Hope that’s all right.      It's perfect, thank you, George. A bit of peace is always welcome with the weekend finally behind us. How was yours?      Rather enjoyable, if I do say so myself. My granddaughter came over to stay for the weekend. She's a fan of snooker — surprising, considering she’s only five. Oh, she watched a clip of Ronnie O’Shea grinding it out at the Crucible. Apparently, she wants to be a snooker player when she grows up. Rather imitate me, I suspect, seeing as I’ve been watching the sport since the 70s.      That’s a change from the usual football or dolls, I’d say. Fair enough though. Living in Tredegar, you’re better off with snooker if you want a decent local culture — football there’s more about Wales and oversized kit boots, you know?      Good point, Rhys. As for football, I’ve had some rather fruity conversations with one of the students about a certain striker and his early son. You’ll be glad to hear I managed not to say anything I’d regret. Difficult to mark essays when your head's half full of football and half full of gardening…      Now don’t go making me envious. I spent the weekend weeding the back yard, and I’m still nursing a back spasm from it. All my energy went into sorting out the rose beds. Some students had the grace to send me a plant from Marks & Spencer — a lily of the valley in a tiny pot. It's doing well, all things considered.      Plants and students — what an odd combo. Have you been swamped with marking this week?      My, yes. I took the weekend to start in on it, but that just shows me how unprepared I was. I think I might have to start using rubrics more stringently. We’re letting our standards slide. Though to be fair, some of the lunches we have on campus would leave the armed forces feeling guilty. The other day, I had this idea that if the kids here got govt testing on canteen food like entry into the police force, half the student body would fail.      Time we introduced boot camp training with a sandwich at the end. Speaking of which, have you checked out the hours the library stays open for revision this term?

Rather annoying to be honest, eh? You know what it's like working from home—the peace and quiet first thing in the morning, and then the kids come tearing down the stairs like something's on fire!      Chuff-chuff! Train! Train!      Oh, alright then!  Looks at the child  Which train is that then? The Express? Or is it the one that breaks down halfway to Leicester?      She’s into trains, Mum. This morning it was fire engines, yesterday it was fish. Just go with it. You won’t get far trying to reason with her.      I know, I know. It's like that every morning, isn’t it? So, have you got much work to do today, Anna? D’you think you’ll make it for little Isobel’s birthday tea at the weekend?      Yeah, I should be okay. I only got a few shifts at the café and one seminar, so I’ll be there. As long as she still wants me to come, that is—personally I think five is still young enough to forget your own birthday let alone remember who’s coming.      You’ll always be welcome, then. Mind you, we might actually have to book a babysitter, least for half an hour, just to get a slice of apple pie and not feel guilty about trying to enjoy it.      Ice cream! Ice cream at birthday!      That's the plan, yes. I said what you had to do about it, and she thought it through and came back with  ice cream . Prime minister stuff, about five minutes old.      She’s clever though, in her own little way. Last week she told me that when I’m older, I’ll be in charge of buying her presents for her Christening.      Well that’s all fixed. You’re on for the presents, I’m doing the cake, and your dad’s doing the actual cake topper as he promised. Let’s not forget, this is his idea of celebrating properly—you know how he took the concept of  celebration  as meaning  expense .      Yeah, he ended up getting a  gold  cake topper, like it’s Catherine the Great's christening. I said "Anna, your dad’s gone mad" but honestly, it's sweet in a weird kind of way.      True. I expect we’ll have to get a prayer book or at least a bag of sweets to match the scale of it.

Rather annoying the wet weather isn't it? I was looking forward to getting the garden in order over the weekend... What's the plan this weekend anyway? Going to visit my mam in Wolverhampton?      Yeah, we were going to pop in as well. Just need to drop off some old toys for Harry there, and we wanted to check on Gran. She always seems to be coming down with a cold when the sun disappears. Not that that's going to happen much round here this year! Anyway, you two sorted about New York yet? I've always wanted to go, but with Harry being so little... I don’t know if she'd like planes.      Still sorting out the dates and trying to pin Harry’s dad down on organising his share of the tickets. Harry’s dad works from home now, so maybe he and I could go the same time. It’d be far better than dragging Harry back and forth to Bucks then up to Birmingham. Reminds me—how did your stag weekend ever go again?      Oh God, that was over three years ago by now! Bit of a blur, to be honest—there I was in some land of clubs in Manchester, and only real memory is someone trying to give me a mini-piercing... Well, thank you very much. Ha – Mate’s been bugging me since!              Harry someone said ‘piercings!’ That made me think of your brother’s silly idea of getting a ‘cool’ nose ring in the sixth form. Still got it?      No, he actually gave it to me! Fit the shape of my ear quite well. Still there though, and not fading. Don’t know why I didn’t get lasered it out to be honest.      Well, no use crying over spilt milk. Come on, the more important thing is New York! Have you two looked at hotels?      Not really had time. I’m managing the store every Saturday this month. Official holiday isn't until next summer, but the schedule’s been set and I’m stuck with it. I told the boss I go every other one usually, but he's not hearing it. Gave me line about needing sales stats between April and May, bloke's mad. It really would have been nice to fly off one weekend and come back with a tan and belly full of bagels.

: Right, so I've got this load of paperwork from my thesis advisor this morning, and they’re like...  shuffles some sheets  half of it's comments I can take seriously, the other half I'm just like, “Er, yeah, I kind of already picked that up in the first chapter.”     : Oh no, that feels familiar. My supervisor basically read all the same things I said but just rephrased them in this  academic jargon  that makes it seem like a revelation. Like, “Your analysis of the structural underpinnings elevates the discourse” – what? That’s literally just page two.     : Exactly! I don’t know if it’s just the postgrad loop where we all speak to each other in this ridiculous overcomplicated way, or what. But anyway, I think the good news is— pulls out a highlighter —my core argument actually seems to land. He says “persuasive and well-structured,” so I'm taking that as a green light to maybe not rewrite the whole intro.     : Lucky! Mine was more like, “Passable, but your framework requires further refinement and engagement with interdisciplinary literature” – which in layman’s terms means, “Do more reading.” So I’m stuck – I read three new books this week and now I just don’t know if the paper is better or just twice as long and twice as confused.     : Mate, welcome to academia. You just have to dress the feedback in a way that sounds helpful, then go back and rewrite with hotter coffee and more caffeine. So, let’s be real—what’s the  real  issue here? Are we about to fall behind in the grading cycle again?     : Honestly? I’ve been distracted. Going back and forth with my nan worrying about whether she needs a new hip. My sister’s over here looking after her, so I’ve been running between that and thesis stuff. You know how it is being the  responsible one  in the family.     : Yeah, I get it. My sister’s always trying to rope me into helping her with her younger cousins’ homework. I swear I’m a postgrad with three course readers open, and yet I’m explaining how to do quadratic equations to a ten-year-old in Lancaster at six in the morning.     : Time to draft a ‘I’m a student, not a private tutor' emoji and send it to them both.     : True. Still, talk me through where you’re at with the paper again?

Rather annoying to wake up in the middle of a good dream. I had one last night about winning the National... got to pick the numbers off a cake like in the old football pool ads.      Oh, don’t start filling the kids' heads with lottery daydreams now, Dave. I saw the state of the kitchen last time they 'found a real princess' in their dreams.      I want to win so we can get a dog, Daddy. Imagine a golden retriever!      And then when the chase the ambulance or the fire engine up the road like three times a week!  laughs       Why not, Em? If you had the money, wouldn’t you want to get the kids a dog? Probably go to the rescue centre, get some old dog who’s been turned away from other homes – proper storytelling there.      I’m more curious about why you always dream in colour and smell, Dave. Last night you told me you were eating a ham and pineapple sandwich while standing on the cliff edge over the Thames, and it was like you were really there.      Could be grief of real life colour, love. Real life is always too muted. Dream sanwich ingredients just get so much more – sharper.      Mummy, do you dream too? I dreamt of a castle once and it smelled like lemon and cheese.      There are advantages to someone else dreaming in your house. I often dream about a time just before I left university – funny how something so awkward feels perfect in your head.      I dreamt of flying last night and about being at school. I don’t like school in the dream, but I’m really fast on the bike!      I tell you what – we should all go do something a bit over the top like bungee-jumping or a skydive at the weekend. Who knows – something bloody stupid might show up in someone’s dreams for a change.       laughs  Let’s not go there – with lunches we keep forgetting to pack, the last thing we need is you telling us we’ve got ‘victory in the skies’ written in our tea towels.      Just imagine it though – me in the jumper, green and orange stripes, diving off something high while your lot shout you to be careful. The kids' dreams might start manifesting some excitement for once, not just belly-flops and farm animals.      We can dream, darling.

Rather annoying I had to go to A&E last nigh', love.      Oh no, what happened?      Dropped me mug an' spilt scalding tea on me arm. Thought I'd better get checked out just in case.      That sounds rough. Did the nurse say 'ow bad it was?      Aye, said it was a second-degree burn. Gave me some cream and told me to keep it covered. Know you worked in the NHS for a while — what do you reckon?      It sounds about right. They can be a bit heavy-handed with A&E these days, though. Everyone 'as a bit o' sunburn and they treat it like a war wound.      I was thinking the same. Queue up for an hour, then a nurse is in and out in five mins. 'owever, at least I got me cream and some painkillers.      Yeah, I know 'ow that feels. I was over there myself, a couple months ago after a cracked rib. You don’t expect to end up in grief when you twist your back in the shower, do you?      Tell me about it. My nan's been in there three times in the last year for things that are just a bit of ache and nothing more. Seems like a place where the minor gets treated as major.      Aye, and the system's not made for a rush, love. I mean, what you had was serious enough. Keep an eye on it — if it starts blisterin' or smell funny, then we about to make another trip back.      I'll do that. Honestly, I was more embarrassed than anything. Got told I should handle me tea more carefully in future.      Aye, well — passed the test with that health and safety module the year before last. ‘E said he’d never meet a person more careful with hot liquids in 'is life.      That always comes with 'aving a couple of whiskeys, mind you.      Then again, if you're careful an' go in armed with your own plasters and painkillers, they'll at least chuck in a bandage.      Aye — well, you know me. I can't manage a day without a bit o' tea and a solid cup of worry.      ‘Ere, we’ll be lucky if you don’t go back in with a broken leg from tripping over your own feet.      Right backs you up, then. Let’s just hope I can survive the rest of the week without needing a medical opinion.

Rather annoying this new trade tax they're imposing, isn't it, James? I read it in the  Times  this morning, and honestly, I’m more than a bit worried for you after all this regulation.      Yes, it is a bit of a curveball, Arthur. I mean, running a small import-export business is one thing, but adding yet another tax on top… Well, let’s just say it’s starting to feel more and more like a battle with the government each month.      You and I both know what running a business is like when the rules keep changing. I often talk to my students about anticipating the unexpected. Though, I must say, I envy how you've made that business of yours thrive for years now. You got the knack for it.      Oliver, you flatter me. A good deal of luck and stubbornness, let’s be honest. I still remember those early days trying to source supplies from Portugal in '03, you ever met my first team of delivery lads? One was still in university, and the other was over 70—personally, I think he might have known your father.      Ha! That old Timothy? Good on you for taking a chance. I remember when he used to come over for Sunday lunch with his new cloak and boots and would act all important about something he had learned from the continent.      You know what I find interesting, though? What's happening in Europe at the moment. That new policy in Germany regarding renewable energy? It might actually give us a chance—piece of the puzzle for my next venture.      A venture, you say? Something new brewing in your mind?      Perhaps. I've been watching this boom in solar panel technologies. If I can get that compliant with new EU environmental regulations, I could be in to do something quite different for the next few years. Maybe set up a smaller venture branch.      Sounds a bit technical, but sounds very forward-thinking. I always knew you liked your challenges. As long as you're not going to outsource everything from the 'Chinese mafia' again—you know how I took the recent delivery of exercise books, the ones with the odd smell?      That one cost me about £2,000 in refunds, Arthur. I’m trying to be more careful with whom I partner.      So, have you made any contact yet, or is it all still tea and talk?

Rather skip the chips and meat pies tonight if I'm honest. I've had enough of takeaways this week... What d'you think about ordering the fish and chips? Not too heavy, and smells lovely from where we're sitting.      Fish and chips wouldn't be a bad idea at all—mind you, I was eyeing the steak and ale pie. But I don't fancy a carb coma just yet either. Maybe just the fish and a side of mushy peas? It's a dump of a place, mind you, but the décor's got a bit of charm.      Oh, I like it! The red walls and those old framed posters on the walls, like some kind of time capsule of 1980s football. The lighting’s just warm enough to make the whole place feel special, and I love the patchwork of green cloths on the tables. Brings back breakfast clubs and old English pubs!      Exactly! Feels like you're not in London, you know? With the transport outside and Woolwich full of that new development over there, you get places like this that just proudly stay put in the past.      It’s funny, I was just thinking… watching  Happy Valley  last night, and how that show loves its red buses and bleak moors, but still, it's comforting somehow. Like the grit and the warmth of these places tie you down.      True! Though we’d better not get too sentimental at the bar. Let’s talk about something else—like your brother’s new cat. That fluffball is going to get lost in the flat, I swear. Has he even taught it how to use a flapper?      Haha! No, he just fancies himself a purist and fails to accept that not all cats open doors like kings. Honestly, I'd have just found it a little bell like the ones at uni. Remember when ours would just tap into the bell and then ignore it?      Oh, you mean when we convinced our landlady we needed security measures after being out at 4 a.m.?. Classic.      Speaking of, I’d be careful with the music too. That’s the third time the guy behind us has sighed at the '80s hits. Genuinely, I don’t see the issue with Bowie, but maybe he’s more your Florence + The Machine?      I'm with you on Bowie. Even so, maybe we should have asked to queue up some jazz or something over this shuffle.

Rather annoying this wet weather, eh?      Aye, it's been damp as a cobbler's workshop this week. I’m more used to it being this wet in March than April, though.      That's true enough. I wouldn't say it was stopper een, mind ye, but it's kept me indoors more than I'd like.      Aye, I dinnae ken if this is a result of climate change or just a wretched spell o’ weather we're in. Either way, me plans fer gettin' out an' about have been thwarted again.      That’s a shame, I’d lik’e to have heard aboot them plans. I’ve been skint left tae right wi’ this weather – I've been takin' oots in the warehouse trainin’ an' all.      Well, no doubt if I’d been out, I’d be takin’ pictures. I’ve been tryin' to get moor int’rest in photography since I took up that project with the institute.      Photographer eh? So, what ye focusin’ on?      A mix of portrait an’ landscape. But I been doin’ more wee snapshots at the moment. I got a chap in february that wanted pictures fer a travel feature, somethin’ to do wi’ the highlands.      Aye, those are beaut’ful places. I’ve been up there a few times a’ead o’ work. Campo out o’ the train an’ skelp up the bealachs – decent way tae clear the head.      I hear ye. I picked the area ao’ because I had kin thar. My aunt Jackie ran her croft thar up til a few years back. I still have family, they’re mair tremped in Aberlour now.      You would hae mentioned ‘at times. So, hae you been out taking photographs thar while visiting?      Aye, always trying tae catch a moment whin the light is doin’ somethin’ magical. Then again, like now, the grey sky goon really works for shadows an’ patterns.      I like the way you see it. I go further thar on business, an' it’s more about the planning fluors an' conference rooms, mind ye. Never seen the hills properly like that.      Ah, you’ve missed out on a beaut’ful sight. Specially whin the light breaks through those cloud bands an’ it's just gold an' green.      Sounds a’ead, I’ll take your word for it. So, are ye plannin’ on travelin’ any further fer this photography stuff?      Somewhere in the Balkans. Still plannin’ it out, though.

Rather annoying the new barista at my local café, grumbling. I had her get my usual, and she got it so cold she had to start again. Blows! Any plans for the week, darling? Or am I gonna have to entertain the baby all week on my own?      I'm sorry to hear that, Mum. Yeah, I know he's still quite green, but most places train their staff now, don’t they? As for the week, well... I’ve got some planning to do. We’ve been invited to the school's open day on Thursday, and I’ve got to fetch the baby from nursery around 4 because I’ve promised to help the headteacher with another event on Friday.      Oh, you’re a star. It’s just that I’m not used to the nursery, is all. The baby has screamed practically every time she goes in there. Made me almost breakfast, honestly. You need to drop her off after I pick her up on Thursday, love?      Course I will, Mum. And I reckon she’ll calm down over time, you know? First placements are always tricky. I remember with my other students, once they got the hang of it, they were fine. You just need to work through it with the staff. They’ll know the best way to handle her.      Well, I’ve had a word with them already, mind you. Silly if they can’t foresee a situation where the baby’s upset. They just said to try to get her used to the place a bit more. I can do that, but still—there are times when I wonder if being an au pair would’ve been better in the long run...      That’s not you, Mum. She’s safe, she’s progressing, and you’re not alone. I’m right here beside you. And if it ever gets to be too much, we can look into other options. For now, just stick with them. The baby will learn to trust it, as I did with mine.      I hope you’re right. I just feel so torn. I’d always imagined myself as the stay-at-home one, but with your schedule, it's you bearing most of the day-to-day grind. That must be tough work being a teacher and a full-time parent.      It is, but that’s what we choose, isn’t it?

Rather annoying I had to cancel last minute innit, me n me lass got in late ‘n all... got heaps o’ stuff to sort for next week’s event! Y’all know where me head's at at the mo.      Yeah mate, cannae lie, it een't the ideal timing, but fair play for gettin’ things sorted. I’ve been stuck on a building site all week, flat on me back from all the weight I've had to shift. It’s like I’ve aged ten years in a matter of days!      Sounds exhausting. I like to think my job is  managed , but me goodness, the last supply deadline was a nightmare. I still can’t believe I’m in charge of a conference in Leeds next month, thanks to Elaine!      Y’know, why don’t ye lot help me get into one of those jobs, eh? Y’look way too relaxed out o’ all this. I tell ya, I fancy a gear change… maybe not conferences, but something less about diggin’ in the dirt – no respect in that trade!      Oh, I wouldn’t say no to a new line in the whole events scene either. Last night, I was out with some mates in Shoreditch, and dress-up dresses seem to be in a rush to trend again. Sounds better than me yesterday, I had to wear a hi-visibility jacket and a baseball cap for safety. No fashion statements there, but at least I was told to do it!      I’m saying this in a calm tone, but please go out of your way to wear something stylish tomorrow.      I’ll do that, but only if you lot can bear to stop your judgement with the latest fashion news! I might’ve been off the grid in Cambridge, but I know I’ll not be hearing about it on the building site!

Rather a cold day, ain't it? That’s me doin’ me herby sarnie first thing, and I’m still feelin’ it down me back! Mind, I think a proper cup of tea would sort me out.      Morning, dear. You haven’t skipped your vitamins, I hope? I made a pot of Earl Grey just now. My George used to say it was the only tea fit for a Queen—or that’s what he used to tell me, bless him.      Aha, George were always a romantic, weren't he? Still, I don’t like to waste good tea, so I’ve always kept to builders and a splash of milk. Never tasted like that Mylor brand, mind you! Goes to show how things change when you go to the shops.      I think modern tea is all wrong, if you ask me. When I were teaching, I’d always keep a kettle goin’ for the morning and the afternoon. Proper milk in first, then the tea—it's the only way to do it.      Come off it, Reg, you were up North! You lot probably put as much milk in as the leaves!           Well, then again, you’re from the East?      That’s Costessey, if you please. More tea-like than those clarty strong things you use up North. ‘Balderdash’, as me auntie used to say.      I think my brew is halfway between them two. I buy what you call the loose-leaf type and put a spoonful in a regular teabag. Best of both worlds, I daresay. My girls used to complain when the tea had “crumbs floating in it”, but I always said that was character!       laughs  That’s just like ‘em. They like things nice and neat. I used to tell them at me childminding job that any child who said the tea wasn't good was just waiting for a spoon in the eye! Those were the days!      And what about add-ins? Sugar? Slaters?      I’m a sugar-and-cream man—wait woman. Mm, that sounds funny. Always had it like that, since I was in the Sixth Form. Never could go with just one spoon.      You were lucky—you had it to look forward to during the long hours of childminding! I gave mine to two of the lads from over the road when I stopped work. One of them’s got my old corduroy apron now, full of tea stains and all!

Rather skip the new bar in Norwich. You know what a nightmare the queue was for the CRB check last time we went out, Mark. I was already feeling queasy by the time we got in!      Aw, don’t worry, Annie! The one near the station was doing rush-hour prices and holidays, yeah? I told you,   I reckon it's best to stick with the old pubs.   Nothing beats a decent pint in a place where the barman knows your name by now.      Honestly, the last time I had a drink before driving, I ended up getting stopped three times! One of the officers even joked I was training to be a drink-driver. It wasn’t funny at the time, I can tell you!      I’m with Professor Alan, on this one. I think the world should just make an app for checking if you’re sober enough. Or maybe universities teach safe drinking skills. Not that I’m promoting drinking more, obviously.      You lot are so serious. One time, I was taking a customer into a hotel and had to explain that circumcision doesn’t mean short attention span! Left the guy scratching his head for ages. Tell that story properly, John.      Mark, you’re relentless! – but it was actually fairly amusing, in a bizarre way. Alan, are the lectures still set in the new building next to the art gallery? I went there once with my sister, and the art was just... full on. Honestly, I thought my head might explode just from looking at it.      It's wild, and it’s split between realism and modernist ballet, or whatever it is about now. I walk past the same painting each week, and it still gives me the same headache. At least the coffee there is good!      Maybe we’re all just rebelling against the norm. My sister’s been going to a protest on the weekend for clean water. She told me she was singing songs with a group, shouting about pipelines and stuff. I told her good for her. Though I’m not sure how singing with people shouting can allow anyone to hear the lyrics!      That’s amazing. Pippa, you must’ve go it in the family blood if your sister does it so effortlessly! Speaking of relatives, are we still going to Sue’s place for the dinner?      I asked her earlier, and she was all for it.

:  [currently in the kitchen, making tea]  Hey, do you need a cuppa, or are you too far gone on that cereal?     :  [still lying in bed, slightly hungover]  A tea with two sugars would be brilliant, thanks! Anyway, you had the flat for yourself, and I thought it might be nicer if I  actually  got out of it for about forty-eight hours.     : She’s right, you know. I did enjoy having the place to myself. It’s the weirdest combination ever.     : I miss your mad binges. I’m such a creature of habit these days. Work always comes with lunches to keep and meetings that spin out till five.
