But, speaking of nightmares, how are things with your current job? You haven’t been hiding under your duvet since the nightshift?

Rather annoying that the new planning application for the old manor house was rejected, really. They'd been talking about selling it for years, and it would've sorted out that awkward path by the primary school.      Yeah, I know what you mean—some people wouldn't have been pleased if it'd turned into a block of flats anyway. Not that I'm complaining about the noise levels round here, but you’ve got to wonder if they'll ever do anything about the school car park. It was packed during drop-off again yesterday.      Ugh, it's always the same. You'd think the village council had even half a plan. I just wish someone would take responsibility and sort it out properly.      On another note—you spoke to Anna recently? I heard her latest scans came back not great, and she's in the hospital for chemo again.      Yeah, I called her yesterday. It's been tough for her and the kids. They were planning to move to that new development on the edge of the village, but now it all feels like it's been put on hold.      I can't imagine what it must be like for them. Her brother said they might have to sell the house before it goes into a decline from the utility bills. Poor thing?      I hope not. She’s trying hard to stay positive. We've been meaning to pop round with a casserole and some company, but we keep getting sidetracked by work. I feel so guilty.      Don’t beat yourself up. We’re still managing to meet her regularly and share the news through Paul. I think she just wants people to make their own time with their lives. Still, I do hope she can afford to keep the house for a little longer—that place is her family home.      Absolutely. Maybe we could do something, like start a small fundraiser for them. A garden tea or something. It’s not much, but it could give them a bit of breathing room.      That could work. As long as we can rope in the village committee to help with the logistics. I wonder what the caretaker at the school would say about it, after all.      Yeah, go talk to her. If anyone can help, it’s her.      I'll do. And in the long run, if the house goes up for sale, maybe it’s for the best—someone who can give it a bit of TLC and not worry about the planning stuff.

Rather annoying this newfit here eh?      Aye, it's mad. The first floor got the leak, and now it's like ducks and drakes with the cabbies. Had to bin a full box of washing last night, fookin legend.      Got eeny weeny passive aggro about it, didn’t I? Sorted it with the maintenance desk, but you’ve got to chase ‘em like they're dodging a debt. They promised it’d be fixed by Tuesday. We’re on Thursday now. Still dragging me chain through the mess.      Right, I’ve even taken to carrying a porta-mattress to the supply room now. On the bounce if the loo breaks down again. The new residents are getting properly antsy, ain't they? D’you pick up the tension in the halls? Like an unexploded bomb waitin’ for breakfast.      Fair dinkum. The other week a lad came bleatin’ that he saw a puff adder in the laundry. I nearly told him to bugger off, but I had to check it out. I mean, we’re not in the Sahara, are we?      Haha, reckon it was a rhythm of light from the window. Still, some of the ones new in aren’t cheery because they’re missing home. One lass nearly had a tic when the kettles broke down. ‘Balances on your ability to carry the heat’ someone said in one of them bloody self-help vlogs, but here's the sour truth – outta hot water is outta hope.      Can’t fault the dedication in the kitchens, eh? I mean, Steve from catering does his bobbins to keep the canteen running. But you try not to grumble when you’re served lukewarm lasagne for the third night in a row. 'Cos you’re guest speaker Friday and they want you active and all, innit?      Speaking of, I tried to do a little mood check with the dorms earlier and had one sprite of a woman rag me about the 'hopeless management.' I said "Ah, but let’s hope for management, luv." Picked a fight with the curtains goin’ on.      That’s one of the reasons me and the lads had a team huddle last week – we were due some new protocols. It’s like flu season up here, everyone’s touchy. Even the earnest ones with bellyfuls to accomplish, they start fallin over backwards if the food selector won’t work right.      Least we’re not falling over each other.

Rather annoying to be honest. I’d rather be hanging out on Brighton Seafront than crammed into a bus with 20 other English folk. I’m more than happy to take a walk      Aye, we had a bit o' that on our tour. We were in Antwerp een time and there was this group of English people all shouting over each other trying to get their photos taken. Made me feel right out of place      I remember that. It was quite a chaotic scene. We had to wait for the bus driver to chase them back into the queue. Honestly, I like to think of myself as fairly patient, but I was ready to tell them to calm down a little bit      I agree. I think it's because most of them had never been abroad before. But I was sad not to see any of the Christmas markets, they look really magical      You need to go in December, I reckon. Me and Ethel went to one in Germany, and it was magical. Real atmosphere. Christmas shopping directly from stalls, mince pies, and carols in the street      What did you buy Ethel? Something for the boys?      Aye, a little something for each. Though one of them is getting too old for toys and needs more      Yeah, I don't know how you do it. I've got two boys and every birthday feels like Christmas. Our budget just      Just because they're a bit older, it doesn't mean they don't need attention. It's the way of being their parents      You know, most people about our age are retired by now      Are you saying you're not doing things your age?      No, not at all. I just have more time for things like language learning. I've started to learn a bit of German since me trip. Thought it might come in handy next time      You must practice your conversational skills more than just that book of yours. Next time you take a trip I expect to hear your conversation with the locals, not just you trying to speak around them by pointing at the menus      Aye, you've got a point. I could do with more conversation practice, not just grammar rules from a book      It's all good though. I think meeting other English people in foreign countries can be really comforting. You know, to hear a familiar accent or get help with pronunciations and things

So do you know what the "equality vote" is, Mam? I was watching the news with Dad and it got me confused.      Huh? Not sure what you're talking about, love. What did it sound like they said?      They were talking about a vote on equality in Ireland, something to do with making sure people are treated the same in all parts of the country.      Oh, that! I think it was about marriage equality. It came up in the news a while ago. I remember people going out in the streets and stuff. Were you reading about the marriage vote in school?      Yeah, the teacher told us about how Ireland was the first country to legalise same-sex marriage by a public vote. But I don't get how the vote actually worked, like how people in school could be involved if most of us aren't old enough to vote.      I mean, you can't be part of the official vote unless you're 18 or older. But a lot of people your age still took part in their own way, maybe by talking about it, or supporting it in social media.      That sounds boring. I would’ve probably done something way funnier. Like, when we got married we had a friend dressed as a Royal Guard at the registry office because our mothers thought it was the height of fun. Spoiler: it was embarrassing.      Oh! That was  so  you, someone at the registry office looking suspiciously like a mannequin just for show. I told your mother it’d be a disaster, and she thought being overdressed was the same as being exciting. Still, it made about five people laugh.      Anyway, what did you think when they voted on marriage equality? Did you vote?      Yes, I did. I voted yes, of course. Everyone should be allowed to love who they want. It just seems unfair to treat people differently for something as simple as love.      You're getting all deep on me, Mam.      Sorry, love, but it's an important topic. People have been fighting for it for years, and it's nice to see it finally change. Of course, it doesn’t solve everything, but it’s a start.      I see your point. I guess I never really thought about it properly before. So, have you made plans for your birthday yet?      Ugh, not really. I might just sit in the garden with a glass of wine and hope nobody remembers I’m allowed one.

Rather annoying this new microwave of yours, isn't it, Doris? That Peggy's hamster kept scampering off again and ended up in the microwave today, eh? Not a very saf’ device, a microwave is, if you ask me. Look like it nearly frightened the life out of it!      Oh, I don’t think it was frightened, Sid. I read in one of my newspapers that hamsters have a natural tendency to burrow and crawl into small dark spaces. Imagine what it’s like to be a hamster and find a microwave! Didn’t Peggy get worried? I shouted at her for not securing the top lid! Not that I blame her, mind you, I’d have forgotten to block it up too if I hadn’t had my best years left behind me. Ten more, and I’d still be careful, I’d say.      It is a bit of an oversight if you’re looking after a small creature like a hamster, but in fairness, the microwave isn’t exactly an obvious danger, even to those of us who still work with tools directly. I mean, do tell, what are you working on now, Sid? You keep going on about these lathe tools. Something deadly precise, I assume?      Ah, lad, it’s not so much deadly – it’s more like a hobby, and I take quite a bit of pride in it. Used to work with tools like that at the mill when I was younger, but that was a good many years ago. Now, it’s more for peace of mind, a bit of fiddling about. Some folks paint, some knit – I wind up smoothing bits of brass and steel!      You know, I did knit once. My girls used to love it when I did cardigans. But I suppose you’re not likely to be interested in knitting over wind up lathes, Sid? Not that there’s anything wrong with it, mind. All passed its time with me.      It’s probably got its own kind of rhythm, like you said, Sid – just a slower one. Like your lathe tools. And if you ever want someone to keep an eye on your tools while you grab a bite, you can count on me.      Oh, go on then, Harry! I’d like that. Just don’t go slipping your head in the microwave like Peggy’s hamster, will yeh?      I won’t, promise!

Rather annoying this new bank thing eh? You know, having to glue sticks and plastic bags for no charge. I got to my local branch the other day and paid for my groceries with an actual plastic bag, and this young lad behind the counter wouldn’t stop grinning as if I’d just won a competition.      I understand the environmental point, but I reckon it’s not easy on people on a tight budget. I still use cash more than cards, but even cash machines are phasing out, or requiring apps. We’ve all got to keep up with the chase of technology or get left behind.      Technology! I remember when I used to write in the mirror, only to find out it made my My turkey look backward. I did enough spelling left-right backwards when I was young to be able to withstand a cryptic crossword today. Do you know what they said in the paper the other day about this cat, escaping from a flat in London and returning after three weeks like a postal worker, carrying letters in its mouth, to its owner. Madness!      It was rather amusing, yes, and it reminded me of this time I left my cat out one stormy night and it came back soaking wet, proud as punch holding on to a dead bird it had dragged from the garden. Not amusing – that one!      Let’s just hope this new cat gets a treat or two after that bizarre odyssey. Speaking of bizarre, American politics hit the headlines again, huh? Our newspaper just said the White House is filled with cats now, or is it ghosts?      Ghosts is a stretch, dear. It’s filled with ideology and crude promises. I’ve seen it all in about forty years of news. And you can bet your last bob that this administration will affect house prices again. My sister sold her place in Edinburgh two years ago, and now she can’t believe how much it has gone up. Enormous!      House prices are a minefield these days. I think it’s due to couples marrying for stability rather than love. We had to buy as soon as we got together, otherwise, we’d be left with the debt of the world.      Still, I think it’s best to think the good of it. At least it gives life a bit of shape.      I would say that, being a former headmistress, I’ve always told my pupils to shape their lives, and to shape their marriages, too.

Rather than playing with their electronic toys, I think they should do more reading.      I got the new Lego Ninjago set today, and I can build it all by myself!      Yeah! I have a Minecraft world where I built a castle with a dragon that breathes fire!      That’s great, love. Minecraft and Lego are creative too, but don’t you think you should read a bit more, especially with exams coming up soon?      Books are boring. They don’t move or make noise or let you play with dragons.      Yeah! In Minecraft, I can explore and build anything I want. It's like having your own world.      I know it’s fun, but reading is like exploring too. When you read a story, you imagine all sorts of things, just like you do in your gaming, but it doesn’t cost any money, and it helps you learn lots of new words and ideas.      But the stories aren’t like real ones. I mean, do any dragons get reading?      I like building towers.      And I like making fancy dragons in my Minecraft world. My castle is bigger than the Dragon Realm one.      Well, I’m not saying you can’t have fun, but balance is important. What if you read for 30 minutes after building or playing for a while? Then you can also share someone else's story for a bit.      Can we read about dragons? Some books about Minecraft?      Maybe. If I can find a really cool dragon book.      I’m sure I can find a few good ones. We can read part of a chapter together and maybe you’ll find that you enjoy it more than you thought.      Cool. Can we read about lava and volcanoes?      Yeah, and the book should have pictures too, like the video game worlds!      Of course. As long as we can balance it with building and game time, I’m all for it. How about we do the next building session after you finish the chapter?      Deal!      I’ll start building a volcano first.      Alright, let's get the box open then—and when the volcano is ready, we can have our reading session together. Deal?   Speaker_2 &    Deal!      Good lad, good lass. Now let's get started—remember, reading is like building, but with words and imagination. Let’s see which one you like best.      I still want a dragon in the story though.

Rather skip the queue at the café, I've made us a decent pot of coffee in, ‘ow’s that sound? I thought we could catch up properly, what with you both being back after such a long time.      That’s ever so thoughtful of you, Mum. Honestly, the café on the high street  is  a nightmare this time o’ day. I’m all for making a pot of that coffee in, if only to escape the chaos. So, tell me, what was it like in Barcelona? We’ve been dying to hear all about the holiday when we dropped you off at the station.      Oh, it was marvellous. The sun, the culture, the food... well, you know how I get with foreign food. I did feel a bit out of place at times, with all the younger couples twirling the little kids around the plazas, and me just lurking in the background with a camera!      That does sound amazing, thanks for taking us both, by the way. I was a bit hesitant at first, but I really did enjoy it, especially the visit to the Sagrada Família — quite a sight to see in real life.      Oh, I reckon you'd have liked it then. Now, let's see – what’s been new with you, Elsie?      Actually, I’m quite busy with uni assignments this week. I've got a final essay due by the end of the day, someone said full-time study would be boring. Pfft, they lied!      Well, don’t let it get too much to you, love. A break  would  do you good. I do hope you're taking time for you, the both of you, this job and study stuff is all well and good, but don't forget the treats of home.      That’s ‘cos we’ve both got our feet under the table, haven't we? Work-wise, it's a madhouse at the shop with the start of the season. I sort of stick to my head and not let it all get too overwhelming.      That’s sensible of you, Gemma. I’d be lost in the tills and displays if I had to manage goings on like that. I do miss those retail days at times.      Hopefully, I'll be done with the essay soon. Maybe after that, we could have a little afternoon out? We could take in some of those shops, maybe even find something fun to do on our way back.

Rather annoying the new testing system they've got at the school. My lass, she's real bright—what with the exams, she's been working like a good 'un. I've been baking a bit to help her along with the chocolates and the pizza. It's a treat for the two of 'em after all that studying, yeah?      I reckon it's not easy being in year 11. Rather annoying the new recording system we've got at the old people’s home, Richard. They play up like mince pies in a snowstorm half the time. But I suppose it's modern technology, eh?      Modern tech can be a fickle beast. Just like my university was full of it—smartboards, AI assistants, the lot. But I reckon it depends on how you use it. I’ve taught students how to use language tech too, but honestly, some bits are just as baffling as Chinese chess!      Oh, Chinese chess, that’s how we spent the morning, prior to breakfast. Mary has got the patience of a saint. I managed to beat the turkey twice, bless her! The rules are so intricate—what do you lot play for?      I make it forfeit a piece of fruit, usually a berry from the garden. I grow blackberries and raspberries. They're best in season, ripe, you know?      That’s a bit healthier than my university friends and I—coins and chocolates, mostly. We used to say it would be like gambling with your health. But still, it got competitive, let me tell you. One bloke even tried to confuse another with the rules of Scottish independence—he just wanted to get out of a loss!      Ha! You and your universities. All that theorizing and politics. Still, I suppose it’s good that universities teach those debates. They helped me when I had a suspicious tooth: my dentist said smiling more at people can do wonders—though I’d rather have a red bean stew and be done with it.      Red bean stew, I daresay is a type of comfort, right enough. We were talking over tea about what you said earlier about your work, Martin. English Literature, is it? That's far from just reading ‘Animal Farm.’ There’s deeper things in that.      Oh, absolutely. It's not just about comprehension. We look at linguistics, language structure, how people express themselves. Like how Mary explains to the old folk how to take their morning shots and pills—you hear the same words but with a far more careful delivering.      I try not to go overboard on the morning routine. I’d rather go straight for breakfast, even if I’m still half-asleep. That bloke at work, he goes on about his morning shower technique as if it's some sort of spiritual ritual.

Rather annoying the new testing regime they've introduced at the school. My students are just children, they don’t need to咄咄逼人的 standardized exam every week.      I know what you mean, Lucy. I feel the same about the kind of things I teach. It’s more about ticking boxes than real communication, isn't it?      Exactly! It’s not just a teaching issue, though. I’m working my fingers to the bone, and I’m still paying off what I owe.      It’s a mess, really. I read about a new place down the road the other day, something called „Młodszy Raj.” Any chance you’ve considered going there to teach as well? I had that done last week, but it’s coming up to a new one soon. They're such an ordeal, but you can't risk getting caught by the authorities without it.      Honestly, sometimes I think about how different things were when we started out. I had a serious row with a guy on Netflix the other day — you know how hot things get online.

So, I heard you got into Oxford for Human Sciences, that’s massive mate. How does it feel?      Honestly, it’s like a bit of a shock, you know? I wasn’t expecting it. I mean, Oxford… I grew up in Hillingdon, it’s not exactly on the usual list, haha. But I’ve got to start applying for accommodation now—there’s a waiting list that feels like it never ends.      No kidding. I’m going to Durham for Maths. We’ve got to hit the books pretty hard during the gap year. Still, I don’t like to think of it as  studying . I prefer to call it… prepping for adulthood in a posh way, you know?      Haha, well, I hear you. I’m trying to balance the whole preparation thing with actually enjoying my last proper summer before university. I’ve got plans to learn how to cook a decent meal though—no more takeaway for me. I want to show my mates I’m not dead when I’m not at rugby.      Oh, don’t worry, you won’t be dead if you land a few drinks and play a few games on the rugby pitch. I’m watching the RFU fixtures closely. If you’re going to Oxford, does that mean you’ll be trying out for Blues?      Yeah, I’m trying to get as strong as I can before term. Rugby’s what I’ve been doing most of my life. It’s one of the few things I know I’m good at. What about you? Still smashing it with your mates at the Slough Youth Development squad?      Yeah, we’re still in about five tournaments this summer. Although I’m starting to think about how I’m going to balance rugby and uni. Going into Durham is going to be a bit of a change for both of us.      For sure. But if anyone can balance rugby, academics, and a social life, it's us, right? We haven't gone a summer without at least one wild night out. Westfield has its limits though. Next time we've got to try the big one—maybe Notting Hill?      You saying this bar is too posh for us goons? I think it suits us. If nothing else, it makes us feel like we’re living the dream before the real thing—university, your elite rugby team, all that jazz.

Rather annoying isn't it, eh? You've got more money coming in now as a teacher, but it all seems to go straight out again. I’m more than happy to explain what’s going where, if you’re up for it.      Dad — well, you know I’ve always respected your mind when it comes to numbers. I’d really appreciate if you could clear something up for me. I’ve been checking my taxes and I’m a bit confused about where the money’s going. It’s like it vanishes!      Didn’t your mum always say I was a grudging teacher, but a good one at that? Well, let’s start with income tax first. On your salary, the government takes a percentage straight off. It depends how much you earn. I’m guessing you’re in the higher rate now?      Yeah, I think so. Around £35,000 a year roughly.      Right, you’ll pay 20% on the first £37,700 or so—after the personal allowance, of course. The remaining is taxed at 40%, unless you’ve got any deductions. For instance, as a teacher, you might have pension contributions or maybe a student loan repayment.      I do have a pension and I’ve just started repaying my master’s loan. It’s not much, maybe £70 a month, but it adds up.      Aye, and that’s all taken pre-tax, so it’s good for you. Then you’ve got national insurance. That’s money for the state pension, healthcare, and some welfare. Prime stuff, really, if you think about it. You can’t touch the NHS without it.      That part is clear to me. I’m puzzled, though, about how much the government actually spends on the things we need. It seems like they borrow more than they have.      Ah, now there’s the rub. The government runs on a budget every year, and as it stands, they’ve taken more in than they’ve spent a couple of years running. But if the economy slows, you can expect a budget deficit and borrowing will creep back in.      And that’s not great for people like me, is it? It increases the cost of everything, bloating the money supply and all that.      Exactly. Inflation’s the next beast you’ve got to keep your eyes on. If they print more money without more goods and services to back them up, prices rise.

Rather annoying isn't it? I've barely sat down since I got back from work this morning. The first thing I do is check my emails—_and oh_— I can already tell it's going to be chaos again today. Do we even know what day it is sometimes?      You always say that dear. Work will be work, I suppose. But if it gets too bad, you should let your colleague take some of the pressure off you this week. They gave you a week of annual leave, you should be using it.      Didn’t even get the chance. I came in early like three times last week, and when I mentioned taking a short holiday, they only nodded and said “maybe next month.” Just typical. I’m still waiting for that week off from three months ago.      You and I both know the government system— you give it a free pass and it'll breakfast, lunch and dinner you out of your plans.      It’s the deadline for that new policy project soon. All the paperwork and compiling the details for the committee is monumental.      I remember when I had to sort out all the student timetable clashes back in the day. I’m telling you, if I didn’t have a large mug of tea nearby at work, I wouldn’t even make it past the afternoon. Honestly, I miss my mum's home-made biscuits.      They’d better have been in the way of being tea-time otherwise I’m slipping your grandmother a note when she visits about how you’re clearly not eating properly.      Very supportive. But I suppose you’re not wrong. I do need to take better care of myself. Maybe I’ll treat myself to a takeaway this evening instead of another sandwich.      And maybe take a walk. Even a few steps outside can do wonders.      I’ll try. If my inbox allows.      Then it’s a battle plan. Grumpy project coordinator meets tea, biscuits, and fresh air. Now where's my bestie’s phone number so I go badger my son-in-law into posting something about work-life balance.      Please don’t. He lives for his opinions.      So do you sometimes, dear. So do you sometimes.

Rather annoying this new recycling schedule eh, love? Thought me and mine could just chuck it all in the bin... got to sort it out now. Otherwise they'll fine yer!      Aw, Grandpa, it's not that bad! We’ve got these bright red bins for paper and plastic and all the rest can go in the black one. Oh, I know. I just handed in a job application myself a few days ago. Was talking to someone from Sunderland about it too - nice chap. Said we should really get together again. Rather annoying to be honest. I’d love to go, but I can’t afford it on a TEFL teacher’s salary.      Oh come on, Steph, you know you’ll manage somehow. It’s £200, and it’s such a great chance to meet people in your field. I went last year and it was brilliant.      Yeah, well, I’ve just taken on a new class in the evenings and I’m barely making ends meet. Plus, who’s gonna watch the kids while I’m off for the weekend?      You could leave the kids with me. The last thing I want is for you to miss out on a good opportunity just because of childcare. And it’s not like you didn’t help out when I had to prepare for my own conference last year.      Oh, I remember that! You looked absolutely exhausted when you got back.      Tired, yes, but also inspired. It pushed me to change my whole approach to lesson planning, actually. Still, I’m a bit uncomfortable with applying for money when others go every year on full salary from their schools.      That’s just the system, Steph. You’re not the only one who can’t afford it. It’s about making it accessible.      Maybe you’re right. I’ll think about it.      That’s all I ask. It’s a shame you’ve been stuck in that teaching job since the kids were born.

Rather annoying this, having the GPS play up. I remember back in Cambridge, I’d always rely on pedometers and maps, maps with ink on paper, not this blinking digital nonsense.      Aye, we do love the convenience, don’t we, yet when it fails, it’s all chaos.  Points to the dashboard screen.  See if you can just toggle it off and on again. Happened to my brother’s car in Bury, funny enough; it flickered back on like someone said a prayer.      Didn’t work, but I appreciate the thought. I suppose we’ll just have to take a guess. That road round the back, seems likeliest. Though that MyFitnessPal reminder just pinging up—it left me feeling guilty about the fried pierogi I had in Zakopane. I think I turned into a piece of dough again by the end of it.      Che, everyone has a guilty food, and pierogi isn’t exactly frowned upon, you know. I say embrace it. Good for morale on the road. I do tell you—personally, I try to stay in short bursts of exercise as much as I humanely can, since I’m a teacher and spend all day pacing.      Hmm. Looking for that balance of burnout and, I don’t know, staying somewhat sprightly. Truth is, after Cambridge, I did have a period where I went back to education and ended up doing some part-time work at a language school—TEFL. You’d have been welcome to come to a lesson with me.      I’d be lying if I said I wasn’t in awe of you at times about how you always walk away from work seemingly unaffected. But then again, I’m progressing in what I’m doing now. I love that I can travel while teaching. Next month I’ll be in Berlin for a volunteering gig.      Oh, that’s smashing. I’ve done some small volunteering too, pottery and art workshops for kids. Not glamorous, but heartwarming to see their faces. Though being in a campervan with someone else sometimes feels like whittling away at the concept of privacy you once knew. Then again, like with the GPS, it becomes manageable with time.      True. But camping, even in a van, it's like being on a chartered adventure. Passes the time. I have that Tove Jansson book you recommended in my bag. I intend to read that over the next two days.

Rather than share a beer and watch the hurling, ye’d talk about gerontology, would ye?  laughs  That’s exactly what I love about ye, Niamh. I've been reading about telomeres recently. Apparently, they shorten as we age—some research suggests they might be key to anti-ageing if we can figure out how to prevent that loss. Ay, fascinated me as much as kayaking with that group from Clonakilty last summer.      Brian, ye know I ain't as obsessed with wine and me bleedin’ tablet as some, but the bloke at the creche, Eddie, his brother is doing some research into longevity in the US, and he mentioned telomeres too. It all reminds me of that documentary about the Vikings—ye know, how they figured out the Americas centuries before Columbus and lived in harsh conditions? But then you start thinking about the old age they’d get, no doubt nursing homes back in Anglo-Saxon times—terrible!      Ay, you'd think they had the pyramids to rely on for that—settle into a nice granite sarcophagus and be done with it! But no, as much as we grief over global warming and tectonic shifts changing the map tomorrow, we're still scrambling like humble ants. Though ye can’t blame us for thinking about arranging a weekend somewhere, even if it’s just a delayed speech of relaxation and not mortal peril.      Tell me about it. Last week I tried convincing someone at the library to book us a trip to Iceland. It's one thing to admire the volcanoes from the comfort of a documentary and another to be risking an actual flight where the pilot might end up being a Ger about to fall off the back of the plane from talking too much. I'm looking for a holiday where the worst that can happen is you get a bit of culture shock from the locals—being screamed at in Icelandic, no doubt.      Aye, and if we're talking culture, I was thinking about those icons used in autism awareness stuff. You ever see those stick figures with the puzzle pieces? Makes me think of how the Vikings used their runes—same idea of encoding meaning with symbols, just no toaster for translation. Mind ye, it's a wonder how we even go about explaining complex stuff like tectonics or immortality in symbols at all. Imagine trying to explain hydrogen atoms in a Norse cave drawing.

Rather annoying this new chair’s taken us weeks to get, innit?      Oh, I’m so sorry it’s taking so long, love. I’ll give the shop another nudge this afternoon. I’m sure they’ve just got a backlog after the holiday.      Right, well, I’ll not be faffin’ about with vouchers for next week’s shop. I’ve got bills to pay and the chickens aren’t budging unless we give ‘em a new feed.      Yeah, and when are we gonna get the sunnies? It’s like, literally, baked in already and I still haven’t got the right pair.      My dear, you said you’d get them last week. I’ve put the money aside for you, so maybe pick one today and get the receipt. Or you can choose at the weekend — better yet.      Love, with all this in, don’t forget planting the fruit tree we talked about. Blossoms and apples? That’d be nice for the garden. I do like the way it’ll look.      Right, as if I didn’t have enough on my plate already. First, there’s the referendum. I dunno what we’re voting on at the end of the day. I mean, who even really  knows  what’s what anymore?      You know what, Rhys? That’s the kind of thing you just have to cast an opinion on. Just because it’s a big choice, it doesn’t mean it’s something to fear. After all, you and I will be under the same roof whether it goes one way or t’other.      And talking of different areas, mind you — I’ve been thinking about the coffee maker again. I’d really like it fixed up so we’re not binning ‘em every time someone sneezes near it.      I’ve looked into a few options, love. We could get a decent machine or just sort out the existing one. Either way, funds are tight at the moment. Between lunches, a new baby chair, the chickens, the glasshouse, you name it — it’s tugging at the till.      Ugh, don’t get me wrong, I love the chickens, but I swear they’ve started a union or something. One day they’re good to go, the next it’s all kippa-kippa and “there’s not enough worms here to feed us properly!”      We can’t very well string up the lot of them over one complaint, Rhys.

Rather annoying the new neighbours, eh? You know, the ones who came from Germany last week?      Yeah, they're a bit mysterious. I haven't spoken to them yet, but their dog's lovely. Chases the rabbit I got as a birthday present.      That's true, I saw the dog the other day. Very clever. I wanted to welcome them round with a coffee but I haven't got around to it yet.      I know someone local. We can all meet up. You might like them when you get to know them. Germany’s not far from here really, just across the Channel.      That's true. Being that close, it's not surprising many others move here. It makes me curious, to be honest. D'you know much about German history?      A bit. From what I studied, Nazi era was obviously huge in creating modern Germany. The two Germanys split for decades as well, East and West.      That's right, I remember one of my A-level classmates going there on exchange. I think she did quite a few historical site tours and even visited a re-enactment of something—it wasn't exactly a traditional tourism thing.      Mate, I want to go there and actually take the tour myself some day. I reckon it's quite moving to see the real sites.      Absolutely. It’s all very different from here. But enough about that! How's your work going lately? I know it can get really stressful, what with meeting tight deadlines as a copywriter.      Oh, it's been about average. I finally pulled all-nighters to meet the client's vision for our latest project. Managed to make it sound fresh and professional. I'm quite proud of it, to be honest.      That's brilliant! As a nurse, I know all too well the pressure you folks cope with. Speaking of, I tried something new for your Christmas tree this year.      Oh yeah? What is it? Please don't tell me you painted the bulbs?      No, no. This is a nail polish called Matte goop. I usually use it professionally on clients, so I thought I'd try it on the tree toppers.      Proper!? It'll make the tree look clean and modern. You always manage to surprise me with those decorating ideas.      Just trying to keep up over the years. We've got a lot to plan—close friends are coming over for Christmas dinner, plus you still need to make plans with your boyfriend for New Year.

Right, thanks a million for helping me unpack today, Em. This flat is brilliant—the garden’s so much better than the flat in Bedford. Although I’m already regretting not getting a bigger fridge. Rather skip the starters and just go for the main, honestly. I've had such a mad week at work... got to meet some tight deadlines. Otherwise I’d have popped by your place like we’d planned!      Oh don’t worry, things at work have been hectic too — my grads on placement are running passive-aggressive campaigns against one another. But at least I’m actually in the office a bit now, not just working from home in my PJs.      Honestly, you should do a photoshoot in your pyjamas. Looks considerably more professional than I do right now... like, literally, I haven’t washed my hair in two days and I'm still wearing last Monday's socks. My turkey curry lunch is living with me now.      You're obsessed with your food, I swear. If I turned up at your flat with kale, you'd giggle and plant it in a pot. I mean, not that I’d ever turn up, you know, unless we’re going to do pizza and Netflix again. That was, what, like two months ago?      Yea I know! It feels like ages. Time's flying. Kind of makes me want to go on a holiday, just to confuse it. Have you booked any trips yet – anything fun?      I really should, but I’ve been avoiding it because every time I look for flights, I either panic about the cost or get inspired to join a cult-ish group tour in Iceland. Honestly, maybe not Iceland... a bit too dramatic for my mother.      Don’t even start with her, I still haven’t told her I’m moving abroad for a few months. She keeps asking about "the man in the office" like I’m meant to be preparing for marriage or something. Not that I’d say no, but we moved to entirely different continents, so that's not happening.      Parents. I have no idea how it happened but any memory I have of being a kid, I'm waiting for them to come crack my door down and hoist me off to orthodontics with lunches delivered in little containers with my name on. Was it like that for you?      Oh yeah, classic go-to-school-in-tongue-tie-tongue ties, and I once ate a whole pack of ants. Story for another time though – what your family up to these days?      Father’s in some high tea with the local gardeners, and my mum is obsessed with dolls now over some guy’s online dating profile.

Rather annoying when people think the whole of the North East is just Newcastle and Sunderland. We’ve got so much more going on beyond that!      Blimey, I know! It’s a bit like people thinking “Birmingham” is one thing—some people wouldn’t know it was once called “the Second City.” I mean, I was born there and still people reckon it all looks like a coney whetstone by 7 p.m.      Haha, yeah, pulling that off. We’ve got the North Tyne villages, Tyneside, the Middlesbrough... Not to mention the best united fanbase north of London, obviously.      Fair play, well said. Just wish I didn’t get so much stick for being from Birmingham anymore. I reckon the D2N2 and Birmingham City has turned round a lot of people’s opinions, even if it’s a bit late for Aston Villa!      Aye, the rivalry’s ever so! Speaking of, how’s the PhD going? I heard you were working on something to do with AI, yeah?      I am! Focusing on machine learning and how human biases translate into AI. A bit of a headache, but it’s fascinating nonetheless. You got anything new on at work?      Yeah, actually. We’re trying something a bit different—expanding our analytic model to predict trends for upcoming fashion trends toward the end of the season, which is a bit of a chicken and egg scenario. If you read about a trend, does it start or does it just finish?      That’s a solid problem to have. I bet it’s tricky when most people about fashion are more about flash in the pan, right? What with this whole mid-2000s comeback going on.      You're not wrong. I do miss the ‘90s though. There was something about the alternative rock vibe and the whole Britpop movement. Bands like Billy Bragg and Saint Etienne, you know?      Oh, I like them. They’ve had a bit of a cult following over the years. I’ve been trying to get back into more proper music after a while of just Spotify algorithms slapping away goon rock on repeat.      Haha, I get that. I’m trying to force myself to listen to some proper indie again. Seen some good live stuff happening in Newcastle too—Ministry of Sound’s putting on a few local artists down that way now.      That does sound good. We should go! It’d be the first time I’ve been to the North East since uni.

Rather than the new government’s policies, gran, I were readin’ ‘bout it online ‘n it all seems to be ‘bout taxes an’ stuff more than I can take in.      Aye, lad, they’ve got their mind on the tax yet again. I were born een time when there weren't more than a few 'nds on the income tax. It were not so long ago that folks like us worked hard t’ earn a livin’ an’ didn’t get taxed t’ near death!      So you're not liking the lot then?      No, I’m not. I’ve seen too much of this country go t’ the wealthy few an’ the rest of us suffer. I left school when I was fifteen, gone t’ factory work at sixteen, and I worked every single day of my life t’ make a bit of a go. But no matter ‘ow much I sweated or saved, there’s always some new bleedin’ law or policy to take it all from us.      I get it, gran—personally I think it’s all ruddy messed up. Why do they vote for the lot, then, if they’re like that?      Ah, now that’s the rub. People get scared. Scared of losin’, scared of change. They hear somethin’ that frightens ‘em, an’ they blame the wrong lot. And the ones in charge just milk ‘em for all they’re worth.      I dunno. Some o’ the speeches I see, though, sound like they’re all trying to make things better. Prime minister said in about helping poor folk an’ all.      Aye, they do say that—that’s part of the trickery! I remember when Thatcher were up, she said the same, ‘but she took the National Health service an’ gave it t’ them lot with deeper pockets. She told us ‘t was for our own good, but I’ve seen too many good folk lose good jobs and end up in the workhouse.      So wh’t do you think the answer is, then?      I think the answer is goin’ back t’ where we were once. T’ respect the country as it was built upon by folk like us, not by greedy men in suits. Rebuild the NHS, bring in better education, and stop the bleeding out o’ folk’s pockets. But that’s just me, I suppose. ‘Tis a hard time to see a better way.      Maybe if they were more people like you in charge, it’d be better gran.

Rather than share a moonlight dinner, we sat at the kitchen table surrounded by her crumpled up typewritten notes and half-finished mugs of tea. I leaned across the table, where my long fingers brushed mine. “So, Ma, I heard there's a  blood moon t night. Got eeny plans to  not  stare at it?”      Oh aye,   blood moons   are a beaut to witness, dear. But when you're in your seventies with a walking stick and frozen joints, it's mostly  planned sitting . Besides, the real night-time marvels are in the  company , no? You’ve all been so left out these past few months, dinner is the main event now, is it not?      Wait, what’s a  blood moon ? Is it like... when the moon’s  actually  red?      That’s right, love. It’s when the Earth passes between the moon and the sun, and the moon gets that beautiful red hue. It’s  very  rare, they say—it’s considered a special night in all sorts of cultures. Some even see it as a symbol of unity, others, as omens.      Now don’t go making them nervous, Siobhan. Last time you explained that, Fiona’s form teacher was someone who interpreted it as a suspicious omen from the  occult .      So, like aliens and politicians—scares the  crumby  out of people about cosmic stuff?      Not aliens, no—but  yeah , it does that to folks who don’t know their  moons  from their  moooooons . Speaking of which, passed Fitzgeralds Park on the way here. You know, where the kids all love to run around?      I hope they fixed that puddle over near the slide. It looked like a  mini-lake  during the last downpour.      Aye, I had Patsy the baby wading in that very spot once—fine child he was, but I think he might have started life as a  beluga .      Granny, seriously, why do you always say that? He’s just a year old, not a whale.      And yet, he oozes the  mystic . The way he looks up at the sky, I swear he once thought it was a  sea . Now—before someone tells me I’m being  weird again —did someone feed the fish last night?      Fiona,  yes , I did. With that pink food you like. Although I thought it looked like something out of a tutorial for “How to feed your child’s fish with dye.”      Deliberately pink.

Rather annoying this new eligibility criteria they've introduced at the college. I presented for an interview for a teaching post last week and they told me I’m now too old for it! Can you believe that?      Too old? For teaching? I mean, you've been helping out at the youth club on the seafront for years and the kids still clamour to sit at your table! Sounds like a bit of institutional nonsense from what I can tell.      Oh, don’t get me started. My colleague, Wendy, was taken off the interview shortlist when she hit the new arbitrary age limit too. It's like they've forgotten that maturity and experience count for something in education.      It’s a strange time for education policy. My niece’s school tried to do away with music lessons entirely, citing funding cuts and the need to focus on core subjects. I was at a parent meeting last weekend when it was announced. I said, “But education is only part heads and hands, the heart needs tending, too.”      Good for you! It’s important for the young to have well-rounded development. My daughter Emma agrees with me. She’s in her final year of teaching training and still remembers the music and art teachers who helped her through tough times. She said she’ll never forget those people who made school feel safe and inspiring.      Emma’s your pride and joy, right? I spoke to her the other day about the situation with the job applications. She was saying that the education system seems to be trying to attract a younger staff base now. Funny thing—job markets are full of young people with fresh degrees being told they’re too inexperienced, while people like us are told we’re too old!      It’s the craziest inversion. And it’s all coming at a time when the news barely stops worrying about the future of the country—what with that whole Scottish referendum fallout. My sister’s in Edinburgh and she said that the place is on the edge of a nervous breakdown with all the political tension.      I read a piece from one of the major papers suggesting the vote may not even take place on schedule. They’re running the same surveys every week—it's exhausting trying to keep up with it all! Still, I suppose goings-on on the coast are more our concern.

Rather annoying driving though Mate, eh?      Aye, it's such a mither when we don’t get out of the village before 12! These narrow roads are just a nightmare at peak hour. Not to mention those kerb-sitters at Tesco. Honestly, I don’t eenno if they  breathe  when they park!      Yeah, most people just whip through like it’s rush hour in Mumbai and don’t care if you’re stuck behind a dump truck or a floating cupcake stand from the mobile vendors.      Still, looks like we’re heading towards Aaron’s! Not bad, no? All this to grab a few bits for lunch and contemplate moving My turkey still hasn’t finished defroasting.      I’m not sure what the rush is, and I think the world record for longest defrost was about 87 hours. I still haven’t washed up this morning’s tea... I’m running at a personal best!      Ah, spare a thought for the pensioners, eh? I mean, do we truly need to have this constant anxiety every time we drive somewhere? What did it used to be? Philosophising with friends over a properly simmered stew? Now we’re in a petrol-powered suicide mission to fetch a Mate’s boiled eggs!      That’s true, but imagine us all sitting in the kitchen later, with the tea on and the board games out! It’d be better than staring at someone’s chicken Tikka Masala recipe on a computer screen. Besides, we can brag about surviving the Bedfordshire traffic.      Any tea in the house? I hadn’t even fully woken up about half an hour after I opened my eyes.      Nope. Only a bag of boiled lard and that lentil pottage you left out last week. You’re on your own for that. Maybe Aaron’s got some biscuits passed their best before date?      Unlikely. Aaron’s all about clean eating and accurate expiry dates. I think he’s the only man I know who keeps a  calendar  to track the lunches he’s made for the week.      Honestly, sometimes I think he’s more like a man with a masterclass in lunch prep than a man who just wants to eat.      Imagine him trying to teach English in a secondary school. “Class today we’re going to learn the technique for flattening a kipper into two neat slices with a single blow of your thumb to the pan.”

Rather annoying this new sat nav eh gran?      Aye, it’s mair confusing than the cow paths back home. I’m more used to askin’ folk where t’go.      No worries, we’ve got you sorted. Just follow the voice and eeny if it doesn't make sense, you shout and I'll explain.      Aye, and if it’s telly too much, we can always stop and ask a local.      Aye, and what abou’ them poor cows? I used t’live near a farm back in Timperley. I could tell the different breeds by their bleat and they didn’t even look the same as each other!      Gran, cows don’t bleat, they moo.      Oh dear, I’ve been saying it wrong all these years then. I thought they were like sheep!      Haha! No, you didn’t get it wrong, the term varies, but cows definitely moo and sheep bleat.      I mean, we even’ve cows with different size and shapes now, like the Highland ones in Scotland are always bigger, and then there’s the smaller ones down here near us.      Oh, that’s interesting! I remember the ones near me parents’ place were like the Silken Stones, or summat like that.      Silken Stones? Sounds more like a type of biscuit. Maybe you're thinking of the Southdown breed—small and fluffy.      That must be the one. They were precious little buggers. I used to feed them bairns the odd piece of leftover cake and they’d follow us round like little dogs.      That's so sweet! I bet they had a lot of character.      Aye, they dide. I used t’think one of them had a grudge with me when he started headbuttin’ me as soon as I walked past. Turned out the farmer told me the poor soul had been hit by the gate the day before and I was just passin’!      That's brutal life if you think about it. But at least you got the inside story, Gran.      Aye, and it’s funny how much things have changed since your day. Back in Sunderland where I grew up, even the new farms are more high tech now, with stuff like milking machines and them data systems that tell the farmer how much each cow's producing.      That's a lot t’take in, lass. I'd be lost looking at them screens.      You'd pick it up quicker than you think, Gran.

Rather skip the salmon and just go for the quiche, do you?      Oh, no, I’ll stick with the salmon today, actually. I need something light after walking the long stretch from Keswick with the choir last night. Did I tell you, we’re getting a new conductor?      New conductor, eh? I reckon it depends on how much they know about pho transcription and stuff. Not that that helps much with salmon.      For someone as old and slow as you, the walk doesn’t chase your spirit or anything, does it? Get the salmon, dear. Mary’s made a marigold soup to go with it, warm and gentle like a Sunday visit from an old friend.      Yes, I’m glad I remembered the walking, thanks for the reminder. I might need to take it again by the end of the week when we meet for choir rehearsals again.      Choir’s awfully good for the rhythm, even if it is a bunch of clucked verses and mercy songs. I do tell you—my old oil rig days would have put short attention spans to shame.      Oh, we’ve got something else for tomorrow, by the way. The grandchildren insist we take them for a countryside trek with the dog, and mind you, punctuality is expected. Children have no sense of time unless you give them a visual schedule.      That’s the spirit, someone has to teach them about natural beauty. I was a teacher once, oddly enough.      A teacher, and you thought being an oil industry planner was the best bet? Haha. I did technically transcribe drilling patterns for you, but I still found time to skip most of it.      Not that I mind the children, but we should probably consider the older sister. She’s just left for Manchester for college. Said she wants to get into publishing. You know, like something fresh, not the old print worlds we used to peddle.      Oh that’s nice of her! Perhaps she’ll find her way back to us with the same path I did—first a teacher, now a transcriber and editor. Don’t go wasting her on pond life if you see her again. Show her some libraries instead.      She’ll be publishing something soon, your lot. Now tell me, what’s the special dish this week? I’d go for the quiche even if it was just to avoid the sermon from the neighbor this morning.

Rather annoying this, but here we are. That’s six weeks of tax forms for the garage work. We’d be better off renting out the bungalow altogether, eh? No, no, Grandma, I like that one turkey shop.      The one you boys throw bits to the back room, Aiden? Easier to get the little ducks to take them for you, perhaps.      He doesn’t mind a bit of a joke in his early years, thanks to Elaine. That's where the lads picked it up. Then again, if we can get the curtains goin’ on time, if Liam's not chained to his phone.      Hopefully, but we’ll box all that in when the invites go out. Rather than chuck afit of the vapours, I were just mucking about wi' some real dialect roots... got me an idea for a bairnname game. See, words like "bairn” is owd-fashioned up north, like I ken what it means, but inna South y’ een say “child” more. Heard owt like that where yuun are?      Oh, definitely, but I think that's just a northern-southern thing. Let me dump my laptop. We can chuck sommat together for kicks. Here in Cambridge, the blokes up north get a bit of a reputation for their words—stories I've heard are outlandish!      My nan still says "bairn" left and right. Ten o'clock everyday she says, “go and pick owt the bairn from school.” Sounds proper to me. Got better than bairn—ken what this mean? "Scran." It’s northern, means "food." Used to say to me da, “I want me scran.”      Aye—personally I say “bit o' scran.” Got a mate once from Berwick who said “a wean,” which is roughly the same. I reckon it all got left out in the limelight down here with all them proper grammar rules.      Let’s make this into a proper game then. Silly as it sounds, we could make our own dialectical dictionary. You chuck in a northern word and I’ll counter with a southern equivalent, then we can do the etymology dance—sounds like a proper wind up and a half.      Yeah, let’s try it about daft northern words first. "Abbey" for example, but pronounced more like "ab-bee" than “ab-ee.” Then down south it’s just run of the mill. What ‘bout “bairn” or “liddle” for little?      Alright, I got one straight out of Hertfordshire for you. We say “mole” as in that creature, but up North it’s “lob.” I once asked what "lob" was and almost had a laugh trying to picture a mole growing like a man’s hands!      Ha! Aye, musta confused yun! Thought it was some kind o' rodent with big bongers. But naa, it’s just a mole! There’s others though—like "dreich," which means dreary, but to a southerner that sounds like some pronoun or owt! It's a proper bleak word up near Newcastle.      I can already see this turning into a bloody book. Dialectal madness for the budding linguists. Maybe we resurrect some words before they go the way of the dodo—so, what's the verdict?

Rather skip the queue an’ go through the back door, innit?      Oh, come on Claire, she’s makin’ more tea than we need anyway.      Nah, don’t start. Look, we’ve got half an hour before Hugo an’ Gaz een, an’ I wanna nap first. Not 'cos I’m tired—just wanted to say it.      Fair dos. Nap first, chat later. You used to nap in lectures as a fresher, remember? I nearly got us both run over, I was laughing so hard.      Yeah, and I still got a 2:1, so sue me! So what’re you listenin’ to these days? Still that weird techno stuff? I ain’t heard you talk about it in ages.      It’s not  weird ! It’s called experimental—art, innit. But alright, I’ll listen to some old classics for you. You ever go back to that folk album? The one with the bloke that sings like he’s gettin’ stabbed?      Aye,  Seamus and the Herring Bones , we used to sing it in the bath. Remember when we put our clothes on inside-out just to piss-off Gary cos he didn’t like it?      Aye, an’ he fell through the floorboards when he went to hit the tile. Lost a tooth in the bargain. Spent a week in plaster.      I still got the photo.      You  always  got the photos. That’s why you’re Prime Minister.      I’ll show it to your wife when she comes back. Bet she’ll laugh.      Aint funny no more. She moved out to do art, ‘cos I was playing techno constantly.      Aye, well, it ain't for everyone. Speaking of, I tried to play some when I went round to Casey’s flat—      Casey? She with that builder mate of yours?      That's the one. He's nice but like a mannequin— go in room, mannequin looks blank.      Sounds more like him, than you.      Anyway, Casey was like 'move the noise or I’m jumpin’.      Typical. Anyway, as long as you ain’t arguing with ‘er this time. We all know how that ended.      Don’t remind me. My fridge looked like a nuclear site.      And you said  you  want a nap.      Aye, but I want to feel proud as I do it. You got any ‘Mum-proof’ snacks in that bag?      Aye, if she brings us something, make sure you take it off her.      Aye, don’t worry—I’m the liability-free one, remember?

Rather annoying that the council planning meeting is tomorrow, I forgot they'd scheduled it for the middle of the week... What time are they expecting us to be there again?      I think it's 10 am. They said the meeting would last about an hour. We just need to lay out the plans clearly, mention the environmental impact study we handed over last week, and stress the need for a clean-up before listing any development provisions. We also agreed to highlight the financial forecast and how it would support local regeneration. We can't afford to present like this is another council development mess.      Right, right. Still, I'm not sure I've got the figures perfectly clear in my head. The breakdown of the projected cost for land demarcation versus the cleanup—what did the survey from the environmental group say again?      From memory, it was about 20% of the budget—around £180k for marking off the boundaries and preparing the site. The rest will go on building foundations and the initial structure. And the cleanup was actually less than I feared—ambient pollution levels were acceptable, just some occasional contamination in the corners.      Okay, that still sounds reasonable. The residents are going to be worried about their property values, so we should already have the report with the experts' comment on that ready to show. Also, I think we should include that line about the preservation of the old building toward the end—we might get a better response from the committee if they hear we also want to integrate the past into the future.      Exactly—especially with that grant from the Heritage Trust. It will help us make the plan more appealing because it shows we’re not just after quick money. We want sustainable development that respects this area.      What are we doing with the sale itself while all this is going on? I spoke to Lucy at the auction house, and she said they’re preparing the advertising and listing for next month. She told me to give them the final description soon, once we’ve got the council’s approval from the meeting.      Good. We’ll include a couple of the projected timelines from the planning committee in there too—gives the potential buyers a realistic expectation. Don’t go overboard on the details about the cost though. Just give a ballpark figure and mention the sustainable design features.
