I’m thinkin’ ’bout startin’ to sort me room out proper this weekend. That mess in the corner, only Rob would know wha’ it’s fer. I’ve bin meanin’ to take it to the car boot sale for weeks, but I ain’t got round to it.’      ‘You should do! I passed the one in Widnes this past Saturday, an’ there were a few people sellin’ desktop speakers, some games consoles an’ old costume bits. I reckon your lot o’ junk could fetch you a couple quid, maybe even more if there’s anything a bit quirky in there. It’s always funny, people buy odd things—like I saw a guy sellin’ a giant foam sword fer – guess what – duelin’ with in the park!’      ‘Ain’t that just like the whole charmin’ world ‘a advertisements? Makes you think they’re in this ‘big life’ game too. I swear my bloody phone is just one big advert magazine now—’fore I blink it’s a pop up for a ‘10k Ultra Marathon’ or a Prime membership.’      ‘You’re not the only one, my lot keep gettin’ stuff on online shopping sites about “boostin’ rho factor” and “detox diets.” I do bin thinkin’ though—on the Geo., if I had dyslexia and all them sorta learnin’ probs, I’d love how they teach it now through little games an’ all. It’s clever really. You think of NLP, or wha’ever the big whiskeys call it these days, but you can teach a whole bunch by just playin’ a game goin’ on ‘how you see patterns’ or somethin’!’      ‘Aye, bloke I went to uni with was into that lark, big believer in all that mind manifestin’ stuff. I mean, I’m not sayin’ it don’t have somethin’ in it, but I like the game angle more ‘cause I got somethin’ ta hold on to. Least, it always beats listenin’ to the news. I mean, the way they present it on TV you’d think it’s a Movit admercial—so cheery, but then you get the details.

Rather annoying isn't it, how some music apps only let you stream the songs if you hop through so many ads first. I've had it up to here with it. I mean, sure, they gotta make money, but there's a limit. Look at us—half our group is in media or writing. Hasn’t anyone invented something more user-friendly than this?      Look, I get it. I spend all day working on BBC content too and I’m right with you. It's just pulling teeth to get users to access the decent stuff. We tried introducing a "pay what you want" model for one of our series. People just made us nuts—some paid Â£30, others left Â£0.05. You learn quickly—you've got to find the right balance, or you’re sunk.      If it's any consolation, most of the customers we've managed have been breakfast-cereal-like: easy to understand but not exactly bursting in intellectual appetite. I'm the manager at a local distribution company, so yeah, I know people like them.      Come off it, Mark. Leeds is up here in the north land of Yorkshire, and we’ve got real brains ticking. You just need to listen. I've worked on a few radio docs and let me tell ya, it's often the simple, personal stories that really hit home. No fancy apps needed there. All you need is a phone and a tape recorder.      That’s exactly what I said at our last editorial meeting. We were brainstorming a new lifestyle supplement at the magazine. Some nut had the idea of a 12-part video series focusing on apps that make your daily routine better. I nearly about groaned. Why not interview real people from different cities: London, Birmingham, Leeds? We could talk about how their daily lives intersect with the media we produce. No algorithms, just humans.      That’s not a bad idea at all. A bit more honest, a bit less techy. Do you think we could meet up for a little focus group or something? As good as we all are as writers or editors, we've got to keep the conversation real—real food, real locations, real thoughts.      I’m on board. If we pull it off right, I could even pitch it as a mini-series at BBC. Imagine: a group of friends in a dining room in Birmingham, one from Yorkshire, another from London, chatting seriously about the state of the media and where it's all going.

Rather do I! The house was rather simple, but it had everything we needed. We had real string on the windows and rather cold winters, of course. But it was all a bit of a novelty, wasn’t it, Malcolm? Remember that kitchen you and I shared at our first flat in Haberfield?      Oh yes, that was the good old days! My goodness, the gas cooker nearly exploded that first week when I tried to light it. I had to borrow a match from a neighbor who was quite a grump. But I got the hang of it in the end.      Right, but enough of property. I remember when I met my wife, Eleanor, at a community event they had at our university. I was still a fairly serious postgrad student back then, wasn’t I, Daphne?      Oh indeed! You were far too earnest for your own good. But Eleanor was patient and clever—just like she is now. And what’s more, she agreed to marry you even though you told the whole college you had to travel to Athens for a postgrad course—only for it to start the very same day the dictatorship was declared!      That’s right, bloody awful timing. The university decided we should all stay put and “adjust,” which – no thanks – I fairly sneaked out with a couple of friends and caught the next ferry to Crete to “avoid the whole charade.” Bless my poor mother; she nearly died from the telegram I sent back in one of the Cretan seaside towns saying, “All is well. Gone out for lobster.”      Oh, that’s classic! I remember when we were all coming into the area about the same time—mostly for work. Malcolm had the dental practice, and I had a little EFL school. The housing was grim! I remember housing boards were sending people to places with just a ‘maybe’ response. Malcolm here nearly moved into a house with active rats at one point!      Do I look particularly thrilled about that? I had to sort out a dormer attic as a bedroom. Let’s just say it involved a great deal of new carpet and mothballs.      Still, I remember the day I first moved into my surgery in the high street. It wasn’t fancy by any means, but it made me feel like a real professional. And then the box of old instruments from the previous dentist arrived—there were two that I seriously question ever had a sterilization regiment.

Rather lovely day today, isn't it? That sun is just beginning to warm up the garden. Have you had a chance to get out much since you moved back?      Oh, only a little, really. Not quite used to the change in pace after living in Sydney all those years. Got a bit of a passive lifestyle down there with the heat and everything. Of course, as a speech therapist I often found myself rushing from clinic to clinic in air-conditioned rooms. Still, I'm quite enjoying pulling back the reins now.      Oh, I daresay the slow pace suits you wonderfully. It's a rather fetching change when you're used to the hurly-burly of city life like that. Now, I never had much luck with left-right, much less grammar, to be honest.      I think it's ironic that an artist of your calibre doesn't have an eye for details like that. I mean, with a gallery in Taunton, you must have an amazing sense of ordering the visual and the narrative. How did you start that—was it with antiques or art?      A bit of both, as it happens. I started off as an art student in Somerset, back in the sixties, and then gradually got drawn into the world of antiques when I married my late husband, who had a taste for the old and exquisite. It was a perfect blend for me—creativity through art and sentiment through antiquities. There’s something comforting about being surrounded by things that have a story to tell, don’t you think?      Most certainly. It reminds me of growing up in Australia with all those antique pieces in the family home. I was rather mischievous as a child—used to hide my coveted goldfish in thimbles and mismatched teacups to see if they'd handle it. My mother thought I was utterly ridiculous. But I was fascinated by objects. Though I suppose it's ironic that I chose to become a speech and language therapist instead of an art dealer.      I imagine working with people had as much charm for you as working with objects did with me. I think it takes a different kind of art, no less complex, to help someone with their voice or the way they express themselves. I daresay you had a gentle hand for it.      It was a calling. I loved seeing the blossoming in your clients' confidence.

Rather annoying to be honest. I mean, I understand why they do it, but it would be so much better if the government could just announce the schedule properly so people could plan their lives.      Yeah, it's like they're not even consistent from year to year. One year we get a two-week notice, the next it's four weeks. It drives me mad when I have plans and I'm just constantly checking my inbox for updates.      I think what gets me is that it's always at the busiest time of the year. If it was during the slow season, I could handle it more, but who wants to be stuck dealing with short notice disruptions when you're trying to make ends meet?      The worst part is when you rely on other people for your business or event, and then you have to constantly be playing catch-up with the changes. It creates a Domino effect, and before you know it, everyone has a problem.      I remember one time, the changes happened so late that we had to reschedule a major shipment and it cost the company a fortune in additional fees and impacts to the timeline. It was so stressful.      At least in your case, you probably have financial buffers to fall back on. For small business owners like myself, the same changes can mean making tough decisions about staff or even dipping into retirement funds just to keep things afloat.      That's the reality, isn't it? The businesses aren’t the only ones affected. Individuals are left guessing what their financial obligations will look like each year, and it complicates budgeting and financial planning for regular people as well.      It's like they don't consider the impact these last-minute changes have on our lives and incomes. We're left scrambling to adjust to new numbers and it just adds up to unnecessary stress.      If they were even slightly more transparent about the timelines and processes, it would go a long way toward helping us adjust. I think there is a lack of empathy or understanding about how such fluctuations can affect individuals and small businesses alike.      At the end of the day, it all comes down to delivering something sustainable. This back and forth with the tax rates every year doesn’t help anyone in the long run – it just makes it hard for everyone to plan and prepare.

Rather skip the new house in Oxford. You know I'd rather stay here.      Oh James, dear, I know you're comfortable at Cambridge. I just think it's time you broadened your horizons. Not to mention Oxford would make commuting back home easier.      That might be the case, Mum, but I'm actually considering London this time. I've got offers from a couple of publishing houses, and besides, doing this project isn't feasible anywhere else. It's easier pulling together interviews and sourcing material in the capital.      London? That's a big step from the university campus! Still, I suppose it works with your thesis and your ... actual career. Have you considered that the lectures and seminars are also top-notch there?      I have, I've spoken with Dr. Ellis about it. She supports the idea if I structure my thesis around something better linked to publishing—like contemporary narratives in print. Honestly, I think it'd make me more employable in the long run.      As long as you're happy—your father and I, we always wanted what's best for you. You're quite independent as it is. I only worry, with London's cost of living—it's going to be quite a task getting by on a graduate's wage?      I'm not blind to the costs, Mum. I found an affordable place to rent in Islington. It's not much, but it comes with a decent study space, someone said near an independent bookshop. That could be a bonus for meetings and research. Also, I had a word with my grant coordinators and they might be able to offer more support in London than Cambridge.      That's all well and good. But what about your future plans? Do you see yourself staying in London permanently?      Honestly, I think I'd do better sticking in publishing for the moment rather than jumping right into academia. Parents, I have no problem with it—this is just my chapter. I don't want you to worry I'm making a hasty decision.      No James, you've always been a planner. More importantly, you took the bull by the horns and are learning as you go. That's all any parent can ask really. But let me warn you—I'm coming for frequent check-ups in that Islington flat. And don't forget the family weekend at your Aunt Daisy’s in Bournemouth in September.

Rather exciting to be here at Cambridge Law Faculty for Alumni Day 2, isn’t it? I work on language research and documentation, so it’s fascinating to run into people from all sorts of disciplinary backgrounds.      Absolutely. I’m the language research administrator at our institute. We actually collaborate quite a bit—mapping dialects and linguistic change over time. I haven’t had the chance to travel as widely as you’ve probably done, but I love discussing how language reflects place and history.      Ah, journey! I'm the university lecturer and have spent much of my career talking about history and civilizations... often far from home. I've made a few excavations in the Middle East and have given quite a few lectures on the blending of ancient cultures with modern societies.      That sounds absolutely incredible! I’d love to hear about your excavations. We’re currently assembling a project on how languages evolve during times of cultural exchange. I've been particularly interested in early East Asian contact with Europe, and I recently conducted a field study looking at the linguistic aspects of ancient Chinese trade routes.      Oh yes, the Silk Road—there are so many layers of linguistic interaction to unpack. I’ve actually written an article on the Arab-Persian trade languages used along those routes. It’s remarkable how much history is hidden in words and dialects.      Indeed. One excavation I led was in a remote village in Jordan. We unearthed a number of artifacts that suggested a strong cultural link between that region and what is now Xinjiang in China. The inscriptions we found had a mix of Arabic and Turkic script. It was astonishing to see how these communities interacted centuries ago in ways we’re only beginning to understand today.      That’s absolutely riveting. It really shows how language can be a key to unlocking historical understanding. I’m currently working on a paper about linguistic assimilation among nomadic tribes—how words and phrases can act as bridges between people and societies.      You know, I once travelled to Turkey to conduct some regional language research. We visited a site where ancient Hittite inscriptions were found. The people there explained the rituals and cultural values still upheld today, even though the language is no longer spoken.      That kind of preservation is remarkable. I’ve often lectured on how oral traditions can keep the language of a bygone era alive, long after the written script has all but vanished.

Rather annoying to be honest. Loads of people think they're just skipping uni and watching videos all day when they're actually doing legit work. Just because I’m paid to make videos doesn’t mean I don’t work 80 hours a week some weeks.      That’s the biggest lie in the world! I work  so  hard every day, and I reckon people think I just bake muffins and clean the shop all day. But no, this morning I had to clean out the ovens, dump 10 trays of stale pastries, and also teach a new staff member how to fold croissants like three times. Still, it’s dead satisfying when customers come back just for the cinnamon rolls.      Yeah, I’ve had enough though. I run this café by myself everyday from five in the morning, and no one in the world wakes up with an alarm for 4.30AM unless it’s for something they truly love. Honestly though, in my opinion, people who work in creative industries, you know, like the film stuff, they actually get off lightly—there's no real structure.      Okay, I’m a film producer as well and I  promise  you that line of work is not easy. I've worked on set from 5AM to 11PM for weeks at a time, and sometimes it's just endless paperwork. One time I nearly had a heart attack because the phone call was meant to be at 8AM, but they said 'GMT' and I was in India. Just because my job's 'creative' doesn’t mean I’m floring the law.      But look at you lot all with your degrees and fancy jobs. I did an apprenticeship while I was still living at home, and it was brutal. I didn’t even finish school properly because I was working and I had to support my younger sister.      Oh yeah, I got dyslexic passed out by the way. I nearly didn’t finish school either. I was lucky my parents could afford a private tutor when I started uni. Not everyone had that.      That always comes with your background mate. Like me—my parents took the mortgage out to set up my café. I’m like a small business CEO now go me. I don’t know how working-class kids go at it.      I had to be the first in my family to finish uni

Rather annoying isn't it, how NHS funding always seems to get raided the minute there's a crisis elsewhere. I got to pick up my mother after her scan today and I can tell you, the waiting area looked like it hadn’t had a paint job since the 80s.      I mean, we're  not  even talking about efficiency. I reckon if they spent as much on preventive care as they do on flashy new policy gimmicks every year, half the queues would vanish. Plus, who needs to watch telly when the NHS is crumbling under the weight of underfunding?      Preventive care? Ha! Last time I talked to someone at the GP surgery, they were still using clipboards and a pen machine that probably dates back to the last century. And I’m not the only one noticing, Mark. I’ve been turned away from the mental health service three times since lockdown. Wait times, no funding, and this government’s still obsessed with balancing the books over people’s lives.      It’s the old political game, isn’t it? You try and do something, and the media or the Opposition takes one look and puts out a headline like, “Taxes Hiked for ... what? A doctor watching someone sleep?” But it’s about services, not just numbers. My brother’s been on a waiting list for physio for months because of his knee. He walks like an old man already and the government’s answer is ‘fix the budget first’? Unbelievable.      Honestly, I’d rather just close the pub down and start a petition out the back of this place than sit and listen to politicians talk about solvency when your grandmother can't see a GP about blocked fallopian tubes. At least the landlords here know how to mix a decent drink and don’t make you wait for it.      You're not wrong there. My sister texted me the other day about her mortgage. Said her friend was considering rent-to-own because they just can’t afford the payments with interest rates going bonkers. I mean, who knew finance could be so… emotionally draining. It’s like trying to budget for a new kidney while balancing the National Debt.      I’m just trying not to think about it when I go to teach my lecture tomorrow about educational policy. You go in full of optimism about how education can change lives, and the second thing the students say is, “Miss, what if I can’t afford to live in the city after I graduate?”

Rather lovely to have you all here for lunch, especially with such a promising bit of sunshine. I made potted shrimps with a shot of Worcestershire and a splash of lemon.      Oh, that sounds brilliant, Aunt Jane. You always were the queen of quick nibbles. I'm just so grateful I don't have to heat up a frozen pizza today.      I remember your famed shrimp provisions, old bean. I used to swear by them when we'd go horse riding as lads and fancy ourselves the very picture of adventure.      Yes, well, I had to make do when I was a schoolteacher and didn't always have time for proper cooking. My turkey casserole was my best though. The one you boys never wanted to hear the end of. Roast and bubble in the oven for hours—proper comfort for a chilly evening at home.      I happened to read a fascinating article on food traditions the other day. There’s been some interesting changes due to the internet and accessibility.      Nonsense, luv, it’s all the same in shortbread tins as it was back in the day, just more people buy in-country Thai duck now than trot through Westgate from humble Bedlin.      I agree with Horace there, Haylie. Some things, like family gathering for lunch, remain the very same. Still, one might say the younger generation dabbles in food tourism at every opportunity.      That is true, oddly. I buy so many international ingredients at the local specialist store these days. The publisher I used to work for did a special on global cuisines. I’m now a bit of a sauce connoisseur, I'm afraid.      Sauces are the key to everything, if you ask me. I do miss a good Burgundy baked potato though. Jane, passed it around here once and it could have converted the devil into something decent with it.      You must try making one. There are recipes and shopping lists online. Websites like BBC Good Food have amazing step-by-step guides. They're also quite good on wildlife too—there’s a nice series on birds of the E Midlands.      Birds or not, I rather think Horace and I would prefer a nice stroll down the river this weekend than read about one from behind a screen.      Oh, I understand, Aunt Jane. I think even I have a limit to how much I want to over-achieve online at the expense of real fun.

Rather than playing a new game on my phone, what are you doing these days, Fergus?      I'm playing Pokémon GO, more or less all the time.      A full £60 spent this week on things you picked up. Is it worth it? Has it ever been?      Pokémon is the best game on all platforms. It's not just a game, but an experience that helps you socialize. Oh, and you get to know someone if you catch 'em all.      It's the worst idea I've heard in ages.      I love it when the toddler, Cian, tries to play that My Little Pony game with me. He just runs around the house pretending he's a pony who needs rescuing, and I say "I'll save you with my magic spell!"      That sounds funny. I've never met someone who plays My Little Pony. I'm 20 years old, and I have no idea how that game works.      My, yes, we can say that the impacts of games don’t stay as bound as we might expect. They colour everything we do in unexpected ways.      For the way Cian plays – it's been a fairly long, warm way to stay stimulated and playful while the weather is not quite cooperating to go out and about for a proper walk.      There are also these walk apps now which track how much you walk. I use one called Stride. It tells me how much walking is going on in the real and virtual world.      You know, most people about our age don’t even play these anymore. You still play, but you're spending a fortune doing so.      I'm trying to connect with people my age. My friends like to hang out playing stuff like Pokémon GO. I feel cut off if I'm not there.      There's something to that. I remember when I was a girl my age, and I wanted to be part of the same group lunches and sports events. It's the same idea – you want to be part of something bigger.      M go MPP on pondy!      What's that line in the toddler speak, Darlin'? That might be "Mummy pony please," you know.      Oh gosh, I'm pretending to be a pony for him now. Do you want me to sound like this? "Neigh, neigh!"      Neigh, neigh!      That's the cutest thing I've ever heard.

Rather a lot of excitement in the air, isn’t there? Blimey, it’s only been a few weeks and I’m already starting to feel like a Christmas pudding! Any idea when we’re going to see the tree up at ANON’s?      Oh, dear, I believe it’s all planned for next weekend. The lassie [pointing at Speaker_4], she’s a bit ambitious with the decorations this year. Something about putting a riding school theme into it. I suppose pulling out the Christmas horses from the attic will take some time.      Right, because of course you'd choose horses. That’s the first thing that comes to her head in December? My turkey still hasn’t been defrosted and I’m not even over the festive music yet.      I think it’s going to be brilliant, actually. My art project at school incorporated British equestrian history this term. So... I’m just inspired! I even designed a desktop carousel, you know, for the sideboard. One of my horses is holding a lantern.      I’m going to make him hold a credit card. For  Stubborn Carol , of course. Because that’s how it will be. Dad said no pudding unless the table is set with mistletoe, but really, if we are going to have fun, we might as well go whole hog. And I might bring along my new boyfriend this year.      Another one! I do hope you don’t bring him over in the way you brought Ernie last year — remember when he sneaked in a bongo and tried to drum us all to sleep?      True story! Going to be easier to get the car serviced than unplug that lot after the mulled wine starts flowing. Speaking of, I’m going to have to book the garage for next week. Last time was such a scramble trying to get someone to change my oil on a Saturday after the market rush.      And don’t forget the lunches to keep the whole whirling mass of us fed. I’ve set aside a couple of extra tins of mince pies in the freezer. You never know if your antlered friend wants a refill at six in the evening, between carols.      Anyway, all jokes aside. I have been researching horse-related conservation and there’s an art exhibit opening in Norwich next year that might be perfect to take you lot to.

Rather annoying I had to take yesterday off for work, couldn't get the day off for my mum's birthday... What did you get her Anna?      I asked what she wanted, and she went all 'Oh don't bother love, I just want you to be happy' but I knew that wouldn't do. So I got her one of those vintage mug things with embroidered flowers all over it, a bit quirky, from that little shop in Canterbury.      She’ll love it, pulling out that old one you had was the one for when you served in the café.      That’s the one! I mean, I still love it, but I figured she could do with something that feels more special, you know? I also found her photo album from back in the 80s, hidden in the back of the cupboard. Some of those pictures are brilliant!      I still can’t believe I missed the birthday meal... I only just came back from the hospital and I'm knackered. I had to patch up three patients with stomach viruses—viral gastro, you know?—and one老爷爷 I think was trying to hide that he still had grief from his wife passing. I just kept holding his hand during rounds. It’s little things like that which matter at the end of the day.      That’s what makes you the best nurse around. All that emotional labour gets under your skin after a while though, eh? What's the plan for this evening then? I for one need to switch my brain off. Maybe a nice game night? Some Scrabble, some cheese and red?      That sounds good! We can continue the story about Dad about how he attempted to knit the entire living room in the 70s. I still have that mismatched cap of his.      Oh aye, he did do that, ‘cos he was hiding from guest speeches after the company lunch. The boss at the time said it was a ‘gestalt moment’ or something. Honestly, I haven’t seen anyone stick out such an uncomfortable time as much as him.      Hah, speaking of awkward times, do you remember when you took us to that fancy restaurant and the starter started with a glass golem of olive oil foam? It was  very  avant-garde, and it was all over your dress.      I still can't forget that. It was white linen too!

Rather annoying this, having the power off all day, ain't it? Me radio's been real mardy too, and I were mid-way through the cricket highlights this morning!      Aw, don’t fret, dear. No one can hear what you’re saying now anyway. I’ve been eeny-meeny-miny-mo-ing between cuppa and knitting. Almost finished that scarf for the grand granddaughter.      Honestly, I’ve barely noticed. The Wi-Fi might be out, but I’ve been perusing the latest developments in early years education in the garden. You'd think the birds would stop chirping if I so much as moved the hose, but no, they sing like they're auditioning for a concert!      Honestly, Ed, I was reading about how some schools handle curriculum reviews in areas with little infrastructure—like in Palestine or Kenya. Made me think breakfast, no laptops, no online tools. Reminds me of when we used to have the odd desktop computer, stored on removable disks.      Reminds me of when me and Bob—ah, gone now—used to take short trips out of Costessey. I tell ya, he still remembers the best fish and chips at that trotting in Beccles.      Speaking of mistresses, I swear that tabby of yours, Mr. Brown, tries to run the place when you're not looking. Last night, I found him sitting in the old armchair with full afternoon dress—properly trying to be a lord of the manor.      I think the secret to life being dull is owning a dog  or  a cat. Not both. My old setter was a saint until I adopted the tabby. Now it's like a house of cards!      I tell ya, if we moved in to the flat, like that series—y’know,  Big Brother —we'd have me thrown out in a week. I don’t cope with intenseness, I just grumble a lot and crack jokes about queens and shopping.      Oh, we'd survive it better than the church do these days. The services are positively  deserted . I told the vicar go for a more interactive crowd if you ask me.      I say let’s not dream about the telly or the church. Pass the biscuits and tell me what you made for tea? Oh and, we're going for a Saturday afternoon walk—do say yes, Ed. I’ve got a proper walking hat on and I’m not wearing a robe!

Rather than chuck a DVD in eh, innit?      Don’t be so pedy, Anne. I’m just makin’ more of a night of it, that’s all! Got me a fancy £10 lasagne from the shop round the corner. Proper posh for Cambridge een!      Aw, well done Lee. You reckon it actually tastes nice? I’ve been known to buy those just to pretend I’m a top chef.      Haha, well you might be the one who brings the red wine, then. Still vegan?      Still! Not because I like it, but the people I work wi' make such a big deal of it. You know how conferences are. I’m like the example, the poster child for sustainability at these events. I think the only thing I'm making sustainable is my headache.      Bucksy? I mean, I suppose I get it. People’s bosses ever get in a muddle ordering the catering and expecting a salad to pop out for everyone like magic?      Yea, absolute dabba! Felt a bit like a food human last week, trying to explain there was no possibility of vegan lasagne at a 200-person dinner at some arts estate in Brighton. I almost had to take off my shirt and write the recipe on it in Sharpie.      Bless you! You should’ve been a food critic, just someone who apologises for the amount of cheese everyone eats.      Now that’s something! But yeah, speaking of delicious and being posh—DVD ready yet?      I am! I finally pulled the plug and watched that Leonardo da Vinci biopic. Knows what you’re thinkin', that it's probably a bit dry, but it turned out to be daft ‘cos they made him look like he was passed out all the time. He couldnae afford sleep, he was too busy trying to grow wings!      We crack up about that over here. Auntie Margaret mentioned it at the lunches we have on the first Friday. She took the whole thing far too seriously, said it undermined the Renaissance!      Auntie Margaret—the queen of opinion! Any chance she’s made her line in the films? “Paint like you’re bloomin’ dying!”      That’s the one! You know what’s weird, though? I never think of her as old unless I see her in that ‘80s snap from the garden party. I’m always like, “Blimey, how come nobody stopped her from wearing that hippy skirt?”

Well, it is a classic! D’you reckon Homer will run for mayor again?      Don’t get started. Anyhow, before we all derail into midday nostalgia, can we do this Legofication properly? Rather chilly this morning, ain't it? I’ve just boiled the kettle and made us a pot o’ tea. You lot fancy one?      I'd murder for a cup, thanks! Got to keep me brain running for Chemistry this afternoon. It's a bit like staring at a coordinates grid and wondering if there  is  a formula for 'life'.      Ha! Sounds a bit ambitious, love. At me age, me brain follows a much easier equation: tea + scones = happiness! Put the kettle to the test again, Jean?      You don’t say, Horace. Though I’ll be having me tea without the scones, cheers. Too much sugar knocks me out. I’ve still got to knit that scarf for Harry over there.      Roight, I’ll be the scarf. Or an heirloom handwarmers gig if we’re fancy.      Stop mocking yer gran, lad. She’s got the eyes o’ a hawk and the hands o’ a clockwork monkey. That scarf will be ready for Christmas, guaranteed.      I remember when we used to walk to the flicks in York, Jean. Cold as this, but we didn’t bother with scarves. Just one cuppa at the barbie and we’d be right warm, eh?      Aye, don’t go making me nostalgic now, Horace. ‘Member when the old banger wouldn’t start and someone said, "We’ll just catch a bus past the pictures and pretend we’re late"? Some o’ the kids ran off in the dark and came back covered in soot after climbing in a dustbin!      That’s the best story ever! Did you get in trouble?      No trouble, just laughs. Times were different back then. No mobiles to record your nonsense. Just the wet socks and a lumpy coach seat.      Speaking o’ nonsense – any chance you can keep it down this evening, lad? I’ve got a GCSE paper to mark. You and the Xbox can wait till after dinner.      Sigh, exams, exams, exams. Can’t a man have a Saturday without a worksheet?      If you’d listened more in class instead of "practising for the future" on your games, you might not be sighing now.      Told me that when I was in yer shoes, Jean, and I’m still hearing it now. Same sermon, every year.      Is it true you didn’t go to school much, Gran?      Right you are, lad. I did me time in a class, but I dropped out early to help at mum and dad’s shop.

Rather than going to the theatre again, I've decided to do a bit of internet research and take the kids to see the Great Ormond Street hospital this week. I remember going there when I was a kid and it made a real impression on me. They do some children's ward decorations like the Peter Pan ward and I'm sure the kids will love it.      What's Peter Pan? I know the book, but I haven't seen the cartoon or the stage play.      What's a cartoon?      Didn’t your mum or dad read you the story? Or perhaps they read it to you when you were a baby? It’s a classic tale about a little boy who never grows up, called Peter Pan. He goes to a magical place called Neverland and has adventures with a fairy called Tinker Bell.      Oh, the Tinker Bell movie! I’ve seen that one. There’s loads of fairies dancing and lots of pretty lights.      I’ve seen a movie where they jump off a cliff and get pushed by big oceans waves, and a girl takes care of two boys who are pirates.      That sounds like the 2003 movie "Pan," which is actually a prequel to the Peter Pan story, but I can see how it mixed up in your head. The Peter Pan story is actually much older than that. It was written in the early 1900s by a man called J.M. Barrie. However, there are quite a few different film versions. Some are animated, some are live action and some even star real actors pretending to be fairies in sparkly costumes.      I like the story the best when it's on stage. It's like you're not just watching it, you’re in the room with the characters. The man who plays Peter does real tumbling and stuff.      Can I play Peter next time it's on? I want to fly with a harness and stuff.      That would be amazing. Though being Peter is a bit of a special role. It requires lots of jumping and acrobatics. You’d need a lot of training and practice! Maybe you can try go-karts on your own if you'd like to feel like you're flying?      I think the best part about Peter Pan is that he’s happy all the time, and he never feels like he has to grow up.

Rather annoying driving up from Southend to Devon to see you off. But I’d do it for the family any time, Claire. And with the kids at school and my own time on my hands, might as well make the most of it.      It's been great having you here, Geoff. We didn't expect you to come both times, really. I mean, it’s not like you're missing work or anything, but still, that's a long way to travel. The kids were thrilled to see you. Especially Tom, was he the one who used to play football with the granddad?      Oh yes! And he can still beat the 12-year-old team at five-a-side if the weather’s right. Still, enough talk of the children—what did I tell you about the Duet House, Elen? Do you like it? It must be far better than our first place when we moved from Taunton.      Oh absolutely! It’s modern, warm, and, to be honest, so much less of a walk from the school. I do miss the walk through the woods, but the mornings are short enough without a 20-minute trek. Plus, with the kids starting secondary this year, the bus option is a little too crowded.      I remember that place you first had, near the village hall. The bath tap used to run black water unless you boiled it first. Bit of a shock for a city girl, huh, Elen?      Let's not mention that. It took us weeks to get the stove hotter than lukewarm. But I suppose all that is in the past now. We’ve got better things to celebrate, like the house-warming in January. Have you still got that lovely fudge from your house in Somerset, Geoff?      Aye, aye, in my bag. That’s for the baked potato tin guest. Though I might save some for the airport shop. You know they never have decent fudge there. I tried once, and bless my wife, she sent me back with handmade biscuits after being 120 miles inland from the sea.      Well, let’s hope you remember to bring it with you. We’ll need the fudge for Christmas, right? I’ve already had three people at the school offer to bring the tree, so maybe we can box it up and send it your way with you. It’d be much better to ship it than leave it lying in the garden, like last year.

Rather a lot of dust in this ticket office, don't you think?      Oh aye, I’ll not lie—could do with a bit of a tidy-up. A proper Swedish massage for this building, if you know what I mean—get the knots out the place.       Laughs dryly.  Not sure I know what you mean about Swedish massage in a ticket office. A lot of people would know that from a booth, wouldn't they? It's quite a reasonable therapy. Know my wife was doing hers for her back during the chemo.      Right, I'm not talkin' about no therapy, love. I'm only likin' the sound of the term, you understand? Proper kneads the tension out. Ten years I spent lookin’ after a hotel, and I’ll tell you now, if you don't give the old place a bit of care—hospice this happened. Not a nice outlook.      Well, that's putting it rather dramatically. Still, I concur with your view—nursery education, yes, is vital. My granddaughter, she’s with the children as much as she can. Gave her the book on female equality—it wasn't exactly a bedtime story, but got her thinking. Important for young girls to know their worth, and not take no for an answer.      Aye, and I will say what I say—women bring more to the table than just what someone tells ‘em to. At my age, I've had time to see it. Gone out with a wife who ran a nursery and worked two mouths full. Not like I had to lift a finger, but I did lift me respect.      She must have been an inspiring woman. I can see why you are so fond of the term "female equality." At our age, the past hits you over the head like terminology that’s been passed down through generations. And now with the ME event next year? I hear it's talking about including more women in the conversation. About time too, if you ask me. They’ve seen more than their fair share of hardship and still held the world together, haven’t they? Still do, for that matter.      Exactly goin' on in my head. Not everyone wants to be in the spotlight, but if they’re given a chance—especially in an event like the one you’re talkin’ about—they can show the world how much heart they've got.

Rather annoying to be honest, I’d rather be going somewhere with decent beaches.      Oh, come on Claire, Barcelona is lovely this time of year. You’ll be having a great time.      I do hope so, Mummy! But wouldn't you rather lie in a pool all day than spend the weekend shopping with me and your sister?      Well, I’ve always wanted to see La Rambla in person and I’m sure your uncle Brian will keep me entertained as well. We can even pop to the beach when you're not looking.      Get in, then! Still, I’ll be shopping with you both the whole weekend.      It’ll be a proper girls’ trip. Fun for all of us. And I’m picking the hotel, so no arguments.      Fine then, but it’d better be something with character. Not one of those bland chain hotels everyone goes for.      Oh, I plan to, you’ll love it. I’ve stayed there before, and it’s got one of the most fantastic outdoor patios with loads of greenery and a view of the harbour. It’s only ten minutes from the city centre.      That does sound lovely. Was it far from the airport?      No, actually it's about an hour’s drive, but there’s a train as well which you can take if you fancy being a bit more adventurous, and the train route is beautiful.      That sounds like a good idea. I’d definitely prefer the train over the bus.      Then you’ll be safe and sound with the train there, and I’ve already booked our tickets for the 26th of June, just to be on the safe side.      Great! I’m so glad you sorted the transport; I just didn’t want us ending up waiting at the station like last time with that confusing timetable.      No problem, love. I’ll meet you at the station at 9 a.m., so you’ll be on the 9:45 with me to Torquay station, and then we grab our connecting train for Penzance around midday.      Actually Mummy, I’m going to take the early train at 8:15, I’m not comfortable with the idea of missing the connection. Better to be early than late, right?      Oh, okay, that’s fine by me. It gives us more time together in the morning over tea and pastries at the bakery near the station.

Rather annoying I had to take out 600 quid from the ATM just then, ‘cos I’d got to pay some university fees. Otherwise I’d still be scraping together what I’ve got left from last month.      That does sound a bit tight, but at least it’s sorted now? I always liked how we used to budget back home on the island. You know, making a plan before Friday night hoochies and stickin’ to it. Still, you gotta deal wif it here. Manageable, anyway?      Yeah, I’m alright. Just reminds me how thankful I am for you offering to lend a hand with the moving out plan last summer. That was like a relief, honestly. You’ve always been solid.      Nah, I’m just thankful for you pushin’ me to apply for this manager job in the first place. Made better sense when you pointed out that I was just playing cricket all week in rep team and not planting no roots in the real world.      Well, I reckon your bloke’s got talent both on and off the pitch. Y’know I still struggle to keep up with the scores and the off-the-field drama. Who was that bloke messin’ around with that T20 trophy winner last week?      Yeah, Haylie dropped me the dirt. Someone was leaking that Naomi Campbell and Silvia was spotting some big-time cricketer in Barbados. Our man someone said in one of them suspicious sidelong glances? It just sounds like tabloid talk, really.      Haha, still, I’d kill to hear your colleague’s take on it. I mean, y’all are all about the tea in the office, right?      Oh, you know that better than me. I handle the staff meetings, but my girl in HR’s got her ear to the ground. All I know is that she and Max have got all kinds of plans for the next family function when Arlo’s sister finishes her medical training.      That’s brilliant, honestly. I think it’s so cool how we’ve all managed to keep such a tight circle despite growing up in such different places. I still get homesick sometimes, you know?      I do. I remember that first time we were stuck in the Midlands rain and your mum was facetimeing me about the fried dumplings and cou cou we’d miss. It really hits diferrent, hearing your family talkin’ about ‘home’ while you’re miles away from it.

Rather annoying this newfit Skype eh? D’ya lot get used to it? Me ‘ere in Costessey and I’m often jigglin’ gadgets and I can’t say I much fancy me a computer screen as company over a nice cuppa and a biscuit.      Oh it’s all right when it works, love. Not like good ole phone calls, mind — no real feel to it. A shame too. I often miss chatting to you lot face to face. Imagine me, a retired childminder, now stuck behind a lens! Didn’t even get to visit Yorkshire last winter — my bad leg put a stop to that.      What’s wrong with Yorkshire? It’s brilliant that time of year. I’ve taken school kids up there on project trips more times than I count. D’you know there’s a youth hostel by the Humber Bridge now — brilliant for the lads when it comes to learning about geography and all that.      A’right, a’right, don’t bore the old man with education. I still say a nice garden and a bit of reading is better than all the fancy globes and land routes. Me and my grief when I was younger, I used to live on the edge of Norwich and dream about travel. Now I’m stuck – no train, no tube, no bus, barely no journey at all.      Bless you, Bill. Silly of you to blame yourself. We’ve been on those holidays, just someone older now. But I did catch a programme on the telly last night about a school with a project to build a miniature underground system in the classroom — very imaginative.      Oy, I did something like that years back — brought a model of the London Underground into the classroom. The kids absolutely loved it. They were learning to draw maps and handle measurements. Still, I bet the lot of ‘em would’ve rather been outside playing in the garden.      Aye. Me gardens was ‘me pride and joy’ back in them days when I ‘ad a crackin good leg and could shift me own weight. Used to take lunches to the allotment with me. Now I sit here in this chair and sip this tea.      Don’t go getting all maudlin on us. If your leg troubles get too much, we’ll do a group trip. Me, you and Tony — what say we plot ourselves a nice trip to somewhere? Somewhere with stairs, mind, to test your bad leg?

Rather annoying this, innit? I’ve been tryin’ to book these flights for tomorrow’s conference and it’s decidin’ to play up now o’ all times! I thought sure we’d sorted it last week.      Oh no, what’s the problem now? Overbooked again een? I remembah last time with the cabin crew saying if we book on a Saturday morning, they’re always A-bloody-OK! Why’s it gotta be so confusing?      Yeah, and now it’s like the options keep disappearin’ right before me eyes. I swear these sites are out to get united! I’ve been stuck between 9 a.m. and 11 a.m. flights, an’ neither of ‘em left. It’s ridiculous! I’m startin’ to think they pick on us twinks!      Well, let’s just leave it a couple of mins then and see if some more options turn up. Me dinner’s cold again by the way, you ordering the pizza or was that just me?      I ordered it, luv, I swear—checked I put two, even! Probably got lost in transit. Typical, innit? Bet they’re watching us right now. I saw a bloke putting pineapple on one – Mate, come on!      Ha ha, yeah, imagine that! Now don’t start again like you did with the curry toppings last week. Still shivered, huh? Remember what someone said in one of them ads—“it just wasn’t your week.” Hardly helped with the takeaway!      I know it wasn’t! I thought I was alright, but nooo, I had to try the chilli samosas. Anyway, what did we say about th’ conference again? Sat nav know the way?      Yeah, I mentioned to the uni, they said they’d have someone at the station ready to meet us. Bit worried about the weather though—saw frost advisories again this morning. Cambridge is lovely when it’s nice, but 7 degrees and 70% chance of rain? Rude.      Ugh, same. Me coat’s been in the dry cleaner and I haven’t had chance to go and collect it yet. I’ve been booking flights and eating microwave microwave ready meals in the interim, so…class act, innit?      Class act all the way, seriously! You know what’s gonna happen? We’ll get to Cambridge, stand there with no coats and start introductions over cold coffee. We are the very picture of professionalism. I can feel the team already groanin'.

Rather annoying this, isn't it, love? These supermarket prices. I was in the shop ‘yer first thing this mornin’ an’ the loaf o’ bread’s nearly £1.50! It ain’t right, honestly.      Grandad, I know it’s shocking. I saw the same thing last week. It’s ridiculous. I reckon it’s climate stuff, plus all the wars messin’ with supply routes. But this isn’t helping anyone, least of all retired folk who live on a fixed income.      Didn’t it get worse after the pound devalued like three years back? I mean, I still go to Tesco, but now I do it like twice a week, not once. Tryin’ to save a bit. Still, I ain’t the only one. I see it at the courthouse too – a lot o’ folks dressin’ down better than they could afford ‘fores this happened. Less meat on the menu at home, I reckon.      Grandpa, have you thought about switching to a budget provider? I know it’s a bit much for some老爷爷, but there are companies now that do decent deals if you sign on for a year or so.      I tried that once. Some provider from Spain – Mateo or Matisa, I think it was. Got some broken SIM and no customer service! Had to go through phone masts and all ‘fore I found someone who’d talk sense. Gave up in the end and just paid full price.      Oh no! That’s something I see a lot in my class. Young people complain about it all the time, but they’re at least about five times more likely to switch providers than the older generation. We’re used to standing in line for hours at banks or answering machines that barely understand English!      That’s just it. The system’s not fair. I hear about these mobile phone deals and all them extra services – video calls, ‘cloud storage’ – I dunno what people need half that for. But you try complain and they just tell you to read the small print. No wonder the whole lot of us have such a chip on our shoulder these days.      Still, I reckon goin’ on ‘line about it or talkin’ at the bank is just not for me. I don’t go ‘ere that much anyway. Passes me by. I have enough trouble fillin’ in these tax forms every year. I never did like accountin’ to be honest!

Rather annoying I know, innit? You know what me mam’s like—she’s always ‘Bring a present, don’t forget’ or something. It’s not like I’m going to a party or a bucko hen do, it’s just the in-laws at the house. But me mam’s always een it to sort out the place. She says 'We haven't celebrated properly in years!' Nonsense. She probably only misses the tea provisions and the cookies off the top shelf.      Aye, sounds familiar. Me auntie and uncles are the same—they act like we’re visiting Buckingham Palace. I had to make  two  trays o’ shortbread last year and still got docked like I’d forgotten a doorstep. Still, at least they’re predictable. Ten to one they’ll still moan if I pick up the tea towel the wrong way.      Oh lads, you're both missing the point! Anglo folk are into clocks and schedules. I’m from Ireland and we just, like, show up when the sun decides to stop directly above the Waterford crystal. If someone serves tea at ten, you might get shortbread. If it’s twelve, you get scones. If they’re late—it’s probably lemonade and a biscuit tin left in the hallway for dead people. No planning, no stress, it just  happens .      Aye, I dunno what it is about British in-laws, they all want this ‘big event’ for a two-day trip. At me grans, we’d just buy what we had—scones, tea, and a ‘fee-fi-fo-fum’ as we came in. I mean, I’m not the Queen, mam! She’s like “You should be cooking lasagne and not beans on toast”. Well, I’m a student nurse, notཀ—. My idea of complicated is mixing treacle with custard.      Honestly, the most chaotic was when I went to me uncle’s farm. Everyone turns up with a recipe card. Me cousin brought handmade preserves, Auntie brought shortbread wrapped with a ribbon, and someone tried to do chocolate soufflés. Still remember when the soufflé flopped the size of a go-kart on the plate. It was hilarious.      Soufflés are a soddin’ crime on a family day. If you ask me, bring cake or pasties and everyone’s happy.      Or, better yet, bring the animals for ‘duty’ while we eat them!      Fair play to that luv, but I still can’t get over the shortbread police.

Rather annoying to be honest. I’d rather be hanging out with you lads than crammed in the library... What's the point of uni if we're just stuck in there all week anyway      Look, I get it, the library is boring at times, but you've got to get on top of that art history essay if you wanna pass your modules      Yeah, I know. I just find it hard to get too worked up about art. Like, what's the point of it if no one's around to look at it anymore?      You don’t like art because you don’t  get  it. All those weird shapes and canvases with no real meaning? Either way, I can't be bothered to write six pages about Van Gogh's sunflowers      That’s just your starting point though – do a bit of reading, find out why he painted it in that style, what was going on in his life, what the critics say. It's not just about stating it was yellow      Oh Mate, I got a sneaking suspicion none of that’s gonna help me pass my history of art essay      If you actually start doing the work and stop playing those daft computer games      I don’t see why you moan at me. I have told you a thousand times – any bloody one can study      You study too much though. You should chill out sometimes. Let off a bit of steam with some computer games and not just write the same essay over and over      You're like a broken record. Anyway go write your essay before it's due or I am so not helping you anymore      Don’t go threatening me or something      I'm just saying I am not helping you with it after next week      It's not like you ever actually help me anyway

: Right, I've just got through scrubbing the grime off the oven. Do you think it was worth it?     : Honestly, I hadn't even stared cooking yet, but I'll make it worth your while. Rather annoying this new speaker’s consent form innit? Seems like we need to list our qualifications  twice  in the bloody thing. Just went through it yet agin, and I've a right proper headache.      No, I ken what you mean, Martha. It’s unnecessarily repetitive een my opinion. But I suppose the committee just want to make sure people know what they're getting into. I’ve only had to delete one paragraph so far though, to be fair.      Oh, and we’re supposed to present this at the seminar in, what, a week’s time? Right, I’ve sorted out the PowerPoint so far, but we need to double-check that we’re all on the same page wi’ the content. The talk is supposed to be about cultural sensitivity in international business interactions, innit?      Aye, and it’s a hot topic if ever there was one. We need to cover Anglo-Saxon attitudes in business meetings compared to Japanese nonverbal communication, or even the way Scandinavians approach negotiation. I’ve noticed quite a few students are keener on the cultural side of things these days instead of just the economic innit.      That’s probably due to the number of students we get from overseas these days. I think – no, I know – we should include some practical exercises in there as well. Role-plays maybe? You know, something that will get the delegates out o’ their seats and actually interacting. Our last seminar was full o’ theory and no activity.      I agree. Some case studies’d be a good idea too. Maybe a split-screen between a boardroom in London and one in Mumbai or Tokyo. I’m thinking about the verbal vs. non-verbal cues in different cultures. The subtlety o’ it all is what makes it fascinating.      Aye, ‘course. Maybe we can get some audio-visuals sorted. I’ve got a contact at the Business School media centre who might help wi’ some stuff from previous lectures. Just stick the key points up and let the delegates see what we’re trying to show.      Now, the next thing – how do we structure the seminar? I’m thinking 30 go at theory, 45 minutes of activities, then wrap it wi’ a Q&A. That’d give us a good hour an’ a half.      That’s sound to me. Rather annoying day today, isn't it? That meeting dragged on far longer than it needed to.      I know what you mean. I had my own set of headaches after lunch with a student inquiry that probably could have been resolved over email. By the time I got through it, my day just kind of... spilled into the evening.      I’m actually tempted not to go home today. Just find a quiet bar in this part of town and watch a couple of films.      That’s tempting. But what about the house, or the coursework you promised you’d mark by Friday? Still haven’t made that decision about the offer the other department made you?      Oh, I’ve decided. I left it on the back burner, to be honest. I can feel the rest of the school year pressing down with an agenda, and the idea of moving out doesn’t feel right right now.      And yet the offer is five minutes away from being retracted if you don’t respond. That university is still hot after you, and it's a chance for a bigger role. I mean, don’t let it go unremarked.      I know—it would be a promotion, a better title, more funding. But the commute would triple, and I wouldn’t actually live closer to campus. I imagine us both getting picked up and dropped off through phone calls at the front door while you cook your own tea and I microwave mine.      Fair point. At the very least, we should at least consider renting something closer to campus. Or at least consider being split in convenience: one house with one balcony, or two separate flats with two walk-in showers.      You’re trying to make house hunting sound like fun. I’m trying to convince myself it is. At the moment, the idea of ‘moving’ just feels like another inconvenience toward settling down.      You know, I was thinking about it last night, and I don’t mind living a little further out if it means we can have more of a real space. A proper living room and maybe even a small garden? We’ve been stuck in this studio for so long it’s starting to feel like a gothic room on a life-sized suffocation scale.      I’ll admit that green space does sound good, particularly in a country where all we see online are tutorials about fluency in conservation and stairs that never end.

Rather than share a meal, we seem to be going in opposite directions these days. Don’t you think we should be making an effort to have more family meals like we used to at our grandparents’ house?      I quite agree, the food was always so good there. But it was also always on time and there was no mess. It was like watching a TV series—predictable yet comforting.      I think that's one of the reasons it was easier to cook back then—everybody cooked. We didn't have the same pressure on ourselves to make everything perfect.      Right, but now even school is teaching us about food wastage and careers advice on how to make our own food more sustainable. I remember one of my interns left after a week of working in the kitchen because he couldn’t handle the mess.      It's sad, isn’t it? The same breakfast, the same lunch, but now everyone has a kitchen in their heads. I remember our teachers never thought of giving us work experience in the kitchen. Good for them.      Yeah, maybe we need more of that. I mean, with all the focus on industrialization and technology, we’ve forgotten that there are industries—what you might call ‘closed’ industries—like urban farming initiatives and furniture-making that are evolving along with our needs.      Let’s not forget about plastic bag charges and the whole move towards plastic-free environments. When I was your age, the supermarkets just gave bags full of plastic and expected you not to complain. It's amazing how much we've changed in just a decade.      And look at the decorating ideas! We’ve gone from cluttered Victorian about-ness to sleek minimalist designs. I watched a documentary where robots were used to rearrange furniture in a person's home. Not that I’d want it, but it’s interesting to think about.      Speaking of interesting topics, I was reading that in some cultures, arranged marriages are still common and involve dowries. I wonder if you ever thought about getting your career choice from such a system. Though as academically trained people with lunches to keep and careers to build, I suppose the concept no longer holds much water.      Maybe not, but go back 100 years and our social dynamics looked very different.      Hopefully, we'll go further in the future.      So, have you made dinner yet?

Rather annoying to be honest. The stress levels among the postgrads I’m working with are through the roof... It's starting to rub off on me more than I'd like to admit.      I hear you. Chasing those outcomes and results as a Health Psychologist can’t be easy. Has it affected your sleep again?      Yeah... sleep is not as blissful as I remember. A lot of reading and composing grants these days. Still, easier than rushing into bed while pulling posters for a primary school trip was, I imagine. Didn’t your class get the trip to the farm?       laughs  Oh no, that wasn’t me, that was my daughter’s class last month. I helped with permissions and risk assessments. The children loved it – I didn’t, honestly, with all the paperwork I had to sort out. Living with rules now far more than working with them when I was a teacher.      I suppose there’s a difference being the manager and having to follow the guidelines for the assessments now. How do you handle that—being the enforcing side, not the one receiving them?      It’s strange to be honest. It took me by surprise in the first few weeks. I miss the rhythm of classroom life. You’re in control – even though you often have to compromise – but it feels more human. This role is all policy and spreadsheets now.      I can imagine. Still, the pay’s better, I suppose?      Just a little unfortunately. It just covers the childcare costs now—what’s the point of a postgrad salary and being an Assessment Manager if I’m still in perpetual deficit because of school fees and birthday presents?       chuckles  You’re not alone there. My budget fails every time I go to the supermarket and have to decide whether to buy that expensive decaf coffee for the postdoc stress or survive on fruit.      Well, the biscuits are holding out longer, at least. I tried something new for your tea today—cinnamon and cardamom. You being academically-traumatized lunches requires a new kind of digestive strength.      Thank you, I appreciate the culinary adventures! Maybe it will even go down better than your last experiment with nutmeg.      That was a holiday special. Don’t go throwing stones—what’s your excuse for drowning your latest grant rejection in white wine at midnight?      Fair point, fair point. It’s just been a rough week, and this place is the only silence I get.

Rather lovely day today, isn't it? That sun gracin’ the window just like it’s makin’ itself at home, same as it was doin’ back when I used to take walks by the sea near Costessey. I’ve been thinkin’ about the days I used to lie in that patch of grass by the water’s edge with the sea gulls squawkin’ all round me.      Aye, I do too sometimes, Bill. Oh, how I’d love a spot by the sea again. My dear husband and I used to take trips to the coast every summer—we’d lie on the sand and talk about everything and anything. All those memories, gone now, but they still like to pop up when the sunset glows just so.      I’m glad I’m not alone, Edie. The loneliness has been a real beast in recent months. Cats ‘n’ breakfasts and old TV programmes just don’t seem to cut it these days. I’ve thought of callin’ some folk, but the truth is, I’m too proud and—well—pathetic, maybe.      I don’t think you’re pathetic at all, Bill. For what it’s worth, I’ve been walkin’ by that same patch of sand only last week near the park. Bringin’ my class in, I told ‘em, “You see those little baby blue tits? They’re fightin’ the world already.” It’s strange, isn’t it? They all come in one-year-olds with such a fire in ‘em, and we teachers do our best to make sure that fire stays lit.      That’s a beautiful way to put it, Tom. I remember when I was a child minder, those little ones had this way of lightin’ things up even when you were havin’ a bad day. These days, I just do a bit ‘o volunteering at the local library. Keeps me busy, gives me somethin’ to look forward to. It’s not the sea, but it’s a little bit ‘o purpose.      You bloke’s right, Tom. Family, keepin’ your brain active, doin’ somethin’ for the community—it all helps. I’ve been away goin’ on about money problems and all that again today. Gosh, even in my old age, it always seems to come back to money, one way or another. It’s like I lost me purpose when the roles reversed and my kids stopped needin’ me as much.

Nah I'm serious, they said the questions were weird. One of the lot who 'as done it said they asked ‘bout ‘discipline’ and ‘how do you ‘andle disappointment?’

Rather annoying isn't it, how grown-ups think they have to glue sticks and glitter in order to know anything about children?      I’m more than a bit tired of having to justify my lifestyle to people who probably don’t even know the rules of being a good parent yet.      Right? Like, I understand the concern, but   I think people forget that   being a parent is a day-to-day learning process. I mean, I see it every day in school.   These are human beings, not experiments.        Yeah, but don't even get me started on the people who assume I haven’t made a valuable contribution to society simply because I don’t have a job like everyone else thinks I should.   It's wild.        Honestly, I try not to bite, and I think I turned out alright. But I was lucky, you know. My parents, they trusted me and gave me space to make mistakes in a safe environment. And it worked out — not effortlessly, mind you — but I still came through it.      That's a nice way of putting it. I mean, we all make mistakes. But what I'm realising is that people aren’t always watching for the positive work we do when we’re not in the public limelight. Like, I deal with mess, sleepless nights, huge emotions, and no fanfare.      You know what I find interesting? We talk about step-parenting in this group — people always ask how   you   can be a good step-mom without a blood-tie connection, and it's a bit of a myth, in my opinion. I don't   think it matters nearly as much as people believe   it does. What   matters is consistency, kindness and a little bit of failsafe boundaries  .        I think you’re right.   But it’s hard when you’re constantly under the microscope — especially when people assume bad intent where there is none. You know, I once had someone question why I played with my daughter instead of being serious about "parenting."      Ugh. That’s the kind of thing that just drives people like me mad. Like, where do these ideas come from? That's actual go-to parenting. But it's not always everyone else's cup of tea, even in close relationships.      I can see where people get confused. It's all so new to me, but I'm trying to focus on growth and staying solid in what I believe to be right for my child.

Rather annoying when the TV’s on and no one’s watching it. I was just flickin through the channels... got to the re-runs of _Coronation Street_ and thought, blimey, I haven’t watched that since uni. She used to send me screenshots of it on Pinterest... “Michael has the most tragic eyes,” she’d say.      Right, I get it! I still can’t get enough of the drama, though. How much does that cost you, then? I mean, it's not like she’s into expensive somethin’. You know what she’s like—prefers a fiver at the chemist’s for coffee.      Honestly, maybe not a lot? It just has to look the part—Pinterest’s got plenty of DIY type guides. Maybe a weekend craft project for us both? If you’re up for it, I reckon we could knock it up in the afternoon.      Sure, what the hell! I know that place off Eddington Street, the one with all that crafty nonsense. Burgundy and treacle ones. I passed it last week on the way into work. Thought they sold something bloody pricey pottery.      Perfect. I’ll pop in while you’re at your end of Cambridge doing what you always do with lunches and data and whatnot. They have birthday stations, no doubt—balloons, cake tins, the lot. Then go for a pint afterwards?      Just don’t expect me to drink the entire session without food. Rather annoying that the chandelier we liked on eBay is now sold. I was hoping it would work in the dining room and give it a bit of elegance.      Yeah, I remember that one. It was £200, wasn’t it? Cheaper than the ones I’ve seen on other sites. But I guess it’s one of those things that people just jump on straight away — a bit too popular for its own good.      Oh, don’t get me started. I’ve just been flicking through the search again. Looks like chandeliers with a glass effect fetch the most attention. Still, I’ll keep browsing. There must be something suitable out there.      Just don’t spend too long though. I’ve been looking at some houses on Rightmove, and I thought one of them might interest you. But it would cost an arm and a leg.      Not necessarily, if we did it ourselves. Or at the very least, hired the right people at the right time of year. Another thought — it might be better if we fixed up the kitchen  before  we start browsing for ‘new’ homes.      Absolutely. Bigger isn’t always the right answer. But I do miss the idea of a kitchen you can walk through without feeling like you're in a tight squeeze. Let me check which one you were looking at.      I can send over the link once I’m off this machine. I’ll get the details goin’ on your phone if that works for you. But for now, shall we go back to the lights?      Go on then. But only for 10 more minutes. After that, we tackle the tea and maybe think about what new life we might want for the kitchen.

Rather annoying the new cleaner at the nursing home isn’t she? I mean, her organisational skills are  not quite up to scratch , shall we say.      Oh yes, I’ve noticed it too. Rather annoying I thought, isn't it? That whole  "just sleep eight solid hours and you're golden"  thing. My students are better when I'm not bone-achingly tired. And then we lost the way back in the morning. I swear we saw a stream from the car earlier, and suddenly it's been replaced by a hill and some swampland. Yeah, go figure. I suppose life is full of those kinds of wrong turns—both literal and metaphorical. You just adjust the course and move on.
